# Dedication.

---

->To the abode of all virtues, the storehouse of knowledge, one who has labored immensely in the medical sciences <note>original: "vaidyakashastreshu kritabhuriparishrama"</note>, the restorer of diverse<-
->texts, the benefactor of the nation, the most honorable and eminent physician, the illustrious<-
->Lala Shaligram Ji!<-

Sir!

You are forever showering the rain of your grace upon me. Your affection always brings joy to us three brothers. Whenever I am distressed and agitated by worldly troubles, whenever my body is exhausted by fatal diseases, whenever my heart feels as if it is being uprooted by excruciating pain, it is you who, at every such moment, comforts me, takes me into your lap, soothes me with love, and restores me to health through every form of medical treatment. Last year, it was only through your favor that my life was spared; you love me even more than a son. By distributing medicine without charge to thousands of patients and restoring them to health, you are truly performing a great service to the world. Therefore, overcome by the aforementioned gratitude, this great work titled "Varahi Samhita" <note>The Varahi Samhita, also known as the Brihat Samhita by Varahamihira, is a foundational 6th-century Sanskrit encyclopedia of astrology, planetary movements, and worldly wisdom.</note>, along with its vernacular translation, is dedicated into your lotus-like hands. Please accept it kindly and make my labor successful.

<br>

10th day of the bright half of Bhadrapada <note>August-September</note> } &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; Your humble servant,
Year 1945 of the Vikrama Era <note>Approximately 1888 CE</note> &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; } &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; Baldev Prasad Mishra.
&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; Moradabad.

# Introduction

-> ❧ <-

The *Varahi Samhita* <note>also known as the Brihat Samhita</note> is a primary text of Jyotish <term>Jyotish: traditional Indian astrology and astronomy</term>. Its creator, the teacher Varahamihira, was the son of Adityadasa and a resident of Avanti <note>modern-day Ujjain</note>. After studying all the sciences from his father, Varahamihira went to the city of Kapittha, where he performed penance to the Sun God and received a boon. Whatever the case may be, in the introduction to this book, we must determine the era of Varahamihira and the creator of the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>a seminal Sanskrit treatise on astronomy</note>. By establishing the dates for these figures, the timing of many other astronomers will also be clarified. Varahamihira wrote in his book titled *Pancha-Siddhantika*:

-> "The sun’s southward journey once began from the midpoint of the constellation Ashlesha, and its northward journey from the start of Dhanishtha." <-
-> "This was certainly the case at some time, as stated in the ancient scriptures." || 1 || <-
-> "Currently, the sun’s southward journey begins from the start of Cancer, and the other (northward) from the start of Capricorn." <-
-> "The shift from what was previously stated is a visible change, evident through direct observation." || 2 || <-
-> "One may know this by observing the sun at sunrise or sunset against distant markers (stars)," <-
-> "Or by the marks of the entry and exit of a shadow within a large circle." || 3 || <-
-> "If the sun turns back without reaching Capricorn, it destroys the south and west directions." <-
-> "If it turns back without reaching Cancer, it destroys the north and east directions." || 4 || <-
-> "Having passed the point of the northward journey, the sun’s return brings an increase in well-being." <-
-> "When the sun remains in its natural course, it is auspicious; any unnatural movement brings fear." || 5 || <-

<note>The verses above are translated from the original Sanskrit slokas provided in the text.</note>

The southward journey <term>Dakshinayana: the sun's movement toward the south</term> used to begin in the latter half of Ashlesha, and the northward journey <term>Uttarayana: the sun's movement toward the north</term> certainly began at the start of Dhanishtha in some era, because such records exist in the ancient scriptures || 1 || Currently, the sun's southward journey begins at the start of Cancer and the northward journey begins at the start of Capricorn; therefore, in the absence of the ancient solstice points, the change is clearly perceived || 2 || (Method for knowing the shift of the solstice): One should know this by distant markers (constellations, etc.) at the time of the sun's rise and set, or by observing the entry and exit of the shadow of a central gnomon <note>a pillar used to track the sun's shadow</note> against fixed marks in a large circle || 3 || If the sun returns in its northward journey without reaching Capricorn, the south-west direction is ruined; if it returns in its southward journey without reaching Cancer, the north-east direction is destroyed || 4 || By returning after reaching the start of Capricorn, the sun is a bringer of welfare, and this is its natural motion; if there is any distorted motion other than this, the sun becomes a bringer of misfortune || 5 ||

# Introduction

The first two verses of the teacher Varahamihira help us in accepting the time periods of two specific astronomers: first, the ancient authors of the scriptures, and second, Varahamihira himself. Bhattotpala, the commentator on Varaha’s work, has identified the "ancient scripture" as the *Parashara Samhita* <note>An ancient Sanskrit text attributed to the sage Parashara dealing with astrology and omens</note>. In his commentary, he has also quoted statements from said scripture regarding the positions of the seasons.

For example:—
> “From the beginning of Dhanishtha to the end of the first half of Revati is the Winter season (*Shishira*). From the second half of Revati to the end of Rohini is Spring (*Vasanta*). From Mrigashira to the end of the first half of Ashlesha is Summer (*Grishma*). From the second half of Ashlesha to the end of Hasta is the Rainy season (*Pravrit*). From the beginning of Chitra to the end of the first half of Jyeshtha is Autumn (*Sharad*). From the second half of Jyeshtha to the end of Shravana is the Pre-winter season (*Hemanta*).”

From the beginning of Dhanishtha to the first half of Revati is the Winter season. From the latter half of Revati to the end of Rohini is the Spring season. From the beginning of Mrigashira to the first half of Ashlesha is the Summer season. From the latter half of Ashlesha to the end of Hasta is the Rainy season. From the beginning of Chitra to the first half of Jyeshtha is the Autumn season. From the latter half of Jyeshtha to the end of Shravana is the Pre-winter season.

The zodiac is divided into twenty-seven parts. In each part, one <term>Nakshtra</term> <note>Constellation</note> resides; therefore, the span of each constellation covers 13 degrees and 20 minutes of the zodiac. In the Spring season, the point in the zodiac where the Sun is located when day and night are equal is considered the beginning of the sign of Aries. At that location resides the junction star of our astronomy, Revati, known in Western astronomy as <term>Piscum</term> <note>Zeta Piscium</note>. According to the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>A major treatise on Indian astronomy</note>, the junction star Revati is located at 359 degrees and 50 minutes of the zodiac. However, according to Brahmagupta and others, Revati is at 360 degrees—that is, at the very beginning of the zodiac. The polar longitudes and latitudes of the constellations as determined by the astronomers will be published in their proper places.

By looking at the list written below, it will become clear which positions of the zodiac were occupied by all the seasons as determined by Parashara.

| Beginning | End | Season |
|----------|----------|----------|
| From 283° 20' | to 353° 20' | Winter (*Shishira*) |
| 353° 20' | 53° 20' | Spring (*Vasanta*) } Northern Solstice |
| 53° 20' | 113° 20' | Summer (*Grishma*) |
| 113° 20' | 173° 20' | Rainy (*Varsha*) |
| 173° 20' | 233° 20' | Autumn (*Sharad*) } Southern Solstice |
| 233° 20' | 293° 20' | Pre-winter (*Hemanta*) |

By the time of Varahamihira, all seasons began at the start of the zodiac signs; therefore, in his time, the Winter season began when the zodiac reached 270 degrees. This means that from the time of the author of the *Parashara Samhita* to the time of Varaha—

# Introduction.

The precession <note>original: "ayana"</note> (293. 20-270) = has advanced by 23 degrees and 20 minutes. This means that compared to the time of the author of the *Samhitas* <note>referring to ancient Vedic astronomical texts</note>, the seasons in Varaha's time were changing 23 degrees and 20 minutes earlier. In English mathematics, this movement is called the Precession of the Equinoxes <note>original: "samratridivabindu" or "krantipata"</note>. According to Western mathematical calculations, the annual rate of precession is 50.1 seconds; therefore, an advancement of 23-20 degrees indicates a passage of 1676 years. For this reason, according to Western calculations, there appears to be a difference of this many years between the two astronomers. Once the time of Varahamihira <note>a 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath</note> is firmly established, it will be possible to determine exactly when Parashara <note>an ancient sage and astronomer</note> lived.

Now we must observe how many degrees the precession has moved forward from the time of Varahamihira to the present day. By examining the almanacs <note>term: "panjika" - traditional Hindu astronomical calendars</note> of Bengal, it is known that at the start of the Shaka year 1815 <note>approximately 1893 CE</note>, the precession had advanced 20-54-36 seconds. This means that in the present time, all seasons begin that many degrees earlier than in Varaha's time. Since the current zodiac signs have been determined, a relationship has been established between the signs and the months. Therefore, by adding the degrees of precession <note>term: "ayanansha" - the longitudinal difference between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs</note> to the zodiac signs, the true position of the sun for the present time is proven.

->The seasons as calculated by the Bengali almanacs can be presented in this manner:<-

| Approx. Date | Start | Season | Remarks |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 10 Pausha | Capricorn | } Shishir (Winter) | } Winter Solstice. |
| 10 Magha | Aquarius | } | |
| 10 Phalguna | Pisces | } Vasanta (Spring) | } Northern Progress <note>original: "Uttarayana"</note>. |
| 10 Chaitra | Aries | } | } Vernal Equinox |
| 10 Vaishakha | Taurus | } Grishma (Summer) | } Summer Solstice. |
| 10 Jyeshtha | Gemini | } | |
| 10 Ashadha | Cancer | } Varsha (Monsoon) | } Southern Progress <note>original: "Dakshinayana"</note>. |
| 10 Shravana | Leo | } | |
| 10 Bhadrapada | Virgo | } Sharad (Autumn) | } Autumnal |
| 10 Ashvina | Libra | } | Equinox. |
| 10 Kartika | Scorpio | } Hemanta (Pre-winter) | |
| 10 Margashirsha | Sagittarius | } | |

Therefore, by setting the annual rate of motion at 54 seconds, 1394 years have passed since the precession reached the degrees recorded in the Bengali papers. Thus, according to said papers, the time of Varaha and the author of the *Surya Siddhanta* is known to be the Shaka year 421 <note>approx. 499 CE</note>. Different almanacs in our country provide different degrees of precession. According to some, the precession for the current year is 22-53. According to others, it is 22-31. Some opinions differ from the Bengali papers...

# Introduction

...is found. The almanac of Bapudev Shastri <note>Bapudev Shastri (1821–1900) was a renowned mathematician and astronomer from Varanasi</note> is more accurate than all other almanacs. From examining it, it is known that in the current year, the precession of the equinoxes <term>Ayanamsha: the longitudinal difference between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs</term> is progressing at 22 degrees, 9 minutes, and 24 seconds. Now, by fixing the annual motion of the equinox <term>Kranti-pata: the intersection of the ecliptic and the celestial equator</term> at 50.1 seconds and performing the calculation, it is known that Varahamihiracharya lived approximately 1592 years before the present time. To support this conclusion, I am publishing the celestial observation results of the famous astronomers Hipparchus of Egypt and England.

Hipparchus wrote that in his time, the star Chitra <note>Spica</note> was 6 degrees west of the vernal equinox point, and Mr. Herschel <note>William Herschel, the British astronomer</note> has written that at the beginning of 1750 AD, the said star had advanced 20 degrees and 24 minutes east of the equinox. Therefore, from the time of Hipparchus to the time of Herschel, the equinox point has advanced 26 degrees and 24 minutes eastward. Thus, according to precise mathematics, it is known that Hipparchus observed the sky 1897 years before Herschel, which is before 147 BC. In Hipparchus's time, the star Chitra was located at 174 degrees of the zodiac. However, in the time of Varaha and the author of the *Surya Siddhanta*, it had advanced 6 degrees eastward; that is, the equinox and the star Chitra were at the same position in the zodiac, or at 180 degrees. Therefore, by fixing the annual motion of the precession at 50.1 seconds and calculating, it is known that the author of the *Surya Siddhanta* and Varaha were born 431 years after Hipparchus, which is in 284 AD. It has already been stated that the author of the *Parashari* published the positions of the seasons 1676 years before Varaha; therefore, he lived 1392 years before the Christian Era.

Now it is revealed that Aditya-das did not commission the writing of the *Surya Siddhanta*. Varahamihiracharya has written his father's name as Aditya-das in the *Varahi Samhita* and the *Brihat Jataka*. At the end of the *Brihat Jataka*, there is this verse:

> ->The son of Aditya-das, having obtained knowledge from him,<-
> ->In the village of Kapittha, having received the grace of the Sun God,<-
> ->Varahamihira of Avanti, having thoroughly studied the teachings of the Sages,<-
> ->Composed this beautiful work on Horoscopy. (9)<-
> ->With a mind graced by bowing at the feet of the Sun, the Sages, and the Guru,<-
> ->This scripture was compiled; salutations to the ancient authors!<-
<note>original: "Adityadasatanayastadavaptabodhah... namo'stu purvapranitribhyah"</note>

# Introduction

Varahamihira, the son of Adityadasa—who attained profound knowledge of the Vedas while residing in Avanti <note>Modern-day Ujjain, a historic center for Indian astronomy</note>—having received the grace of the Sun God in the city of Kapittha, carefully deliberated upon the opinions of the learned and composed this sweet *Horashastra* <term>Horashastra: A treatise on predictive astrology or horoscopy</term>. The grace arising from prostrating at the feet of the Sun, the Sages, and the Guru is the primary cause for the compilation of this scripture; therefore, I bow to them again and again.

From observing the positions of the lunar mansions <note>original: "Nakshatravasthan"</note> given in the *Surya Siddhanta*, it is known that it was composed during the same period as Varaha. Now we encounter these theories—1. Perhaps Varahamihira himself composed the *Siddhanta* and named it after his father or the Sun, or 2. His father composed it and named it the *Surya Siddhanta* himself. In his work *Panchasiddhantika* <term>Panchasiddhantika: "The Five Astronomical Treatises," a core text by Varahamihira</term>, Varaha mentions the name of the *Saura Siddhanta* among the five systems; for this reason, it is clearly demonstrated that the *Surya Siddhanta* was not authored by him. Thus, it appears that the said text was composed by his father, Adityadasa. For the observation of the readers, the positions of the lunar mansions as written in the *Surya Siddhanta* and by Brahmagupta are published below.

| $\times$ Lunar Mansion (Nakshatra) | Imagined Shape | Longitude (Dhruva) mentioned in Surya Siddhanta | Longitude (Dhruva) written by Brahmagupta | Latitude (Akshansha) North or South | Distance of the Junction Star from the start of each Mansion | Number of Stars in each Mansion | Sequential Number |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Ashwini | Horse Head | 8° | 8° | 10 N. | 48 N. | 3 | 1 |
| Bharani | Yoni (Vulva) | 20° | 20° | 12 N. | 40 S. | 3 | 2 |
| Krittika | Razor | 37° -- 1' -- 10' | 37° 28' | 40--30 N. | 65 S. | 6 | 3 |
| Rohini | Cart | 49° -- 30' | 49° 28' | 40--30 S. | 57 E. | 5 | 4 |
| Mrigashira | Deer Head | 63° | 63° | 10 S. | 58 N. | 3 | 5 |
| Ardra | Gem | 67° -- 20' | 67° | 11 S. | Middle 4 | 1 | 6 |
| Punarvasu | House | 93° | 93° | 6 N. | 78 S. | 4 | 7 |

During the time of Brahmagupta <note>A prominent 7th-century mathematician and astronomer</note>, the star Chitra <note>Spica</note> was situated at 183 degrees; that is, from the time of the author of the *Surya Siddhanta* and Varaha, the star Chitra advanced three degrees eastward. Therefore, Brahmagupta was born 215 years after Varahamihiracharya, specifically in the Shaka year 421 <note>approx. 499 CE, though the author's calculation here suggests a later period for Brahmagupta's activity</note>.

It is said that in the court of Shah Naushirvan <note>Khosrow I</note> of Persia, there was a minister named "Buzurjmihir." Because this name bears some resemblance to the name Varahamihira, some might speculate that he was a member of Shah Naushirvan's court (who reigned from 534 CE to 590 CE). If such people were to learn the facts, their misconception would be cleared—specifically the idea that it was by this minister's order that Vishnusharma’s *Panchatantra* was translated into the Persian language. Furthermore, another reason is that Vishnusharma mentioned Varahamihiracharya’s name in the *Panchatantra*; how then could Varahamihiracharya have lived during the time of Naushirvan? <note>The author argues against the identification of the Indian astronomer with the Persian minister based on internal literary evidence.</note>

Varahamihiracharya, in his work *Brihat Jataka*, mentioned the names of many astrologers who preceded him, such as: Maya, Yavana, Manittha, Shakti, Satya, Bali, Vishnugupta, Devasvami, Siddhasena, Jivasharma, Prithuyasha, etc. Varaha also acknowledged that the Yavans <term>Ionians, Greeks</term> possessed special proficiency in the science of astronomy/astrology. He says:

> "The Yavans are indeed foreigners, yet this science is well-established among them. Even they are honored like sages; how much more so then a twice-born Brahmin who is a knower of the celestial science?" <note>original: "म्लेच्छा हि यवनास्तेषु सम्यक् शास्त्रमिदं स्थितम् । ऋषिवत्तेऽपि पूज्यन्ते किं पुनर्दैवविद्विजः ॥"</note>

Among the "Mlechha" (those of foreign conduct) Yavans, there is a specialized critique and study of this science <term>Predictive Astrology</term>; for this reason, they are worthy of worship like Rishis (sages). If the knower of the scripture is a Brahmin, then what more need be said? Seeing this statement, it is inferred that Varaha was also acquainted with the astronomers residing in Egypt.

# Introduction

The primary ancient astronomers of the earliest times also considered the state of the <term>Ayanamsha</term><note>The longitudinal difference between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs, often referred to as the precession of the equinoxes.</note> to be oscillating (moving back and forth). However, it was <term>Vishnuchandra</term>, the author of the <term>Vashistha Siddhanta</term>, who first revealed the revolution of the equinoctial points as a full circle.

According to the view of <term>Aryabhata</term>, in one <term>Kalpa</term><note>A vast cosmic period or "aeon" in Hindu cosmology.</note>—that is, in 4,320,000,000 years—there are 1,582,237,500,000 sidereal risings (rotations of the stars); therefore, in these many years, there are 1,577,917,500,000 days. Many later astronomers have used the measurements of years determined by Aryabhata in their own respective books. The author of the <term>Brahma Siddhanta</term> wrote that in one Kalpa there are "fifteen trillion, eight hundred twenty-two billion, three hundred sixty-four million, five hundred thousand" sidereal risings. <term>Brahmagupta</term>, the author of the <term>Brahma-sphuta-siddhanta</term>, also wrote the same. As follows:—

> The planetary calculations spoken by Brahma, which had become corrupted over a great length of time, are now being clearly stated by Brahmagupta, the son of Jishnu. Those whose vision is blocked by the veil of ignorance and who speak differently from the Brahma Siddhanta—I shall explain the errors they make regarding the differences in the start of the Yugas and other matters. In one Kalpa, there are 1,582,236,450,000 sidereal risings.
<note>Original Sanskrit: "ब्रह्मोक्तं ग्रहगणितं... प्रति नक्षत्रोदया ॥"</note>

Because the aforementioned planetary calculations made by Brahma had become obsolete due to being ancient, Brahmagupta, the son of Jishnu, writes a "corrected" version (<term>Sphuta</term>). He describes the faults regarding the differences in the start of the ages (<term>Yugas</term>) found in the words of those ignorant people who deviate from the Brahma Siddhanta. In one Kalpa, there are 1,582,236,450,000 sidereal risings.

<term>Bhaskaracharya</term>, who held Brahmagupta in the highest regard, also published the year measurements and sidereal positions determined by Brahmagupta in his work, the <term>Shiromani</term>.

The author of the <term>Surya Siddhanta</term> and other primary astronomers have conceptualized the <term>Ayana</term><note>The movement of the solstice/equinox.</note> as being in an unstable or oscillating state. However, to refute this view, Bhaskara wrote in the <term>Vasana Bhashya</term>: "If this was the case, even if not directly observed, why did the authors of the Surya Siddhanta not describe it as a full circular revolution, similar to the circumference of the planetary orbits, based on the authority of the scriptures?" <note>Original Sanskrit: "यद्येवमनुपलब्धोऽपि... कथं तैर्नोक्तः ।"</note> That is to say, if the era of the Surya Siddhanta and others was entirely consistent regarding the Ayanamsha, why did they not reveal the view of the stellar sphere revolving like a circumference, following the opinion of the man (Vishnuchandra) in the Vashistha Siddhanta? However, Bhaskaracharya expressed this opinion without truly knowing the reason, which shall be written later. It is written in the Surya Siddhanta:

# Introduction.

> In a Great Age, the circle of stars moves forward to the east six hundred times. 
> Multiply the desired days by this number and divide by the total terrestrial days in an Age. 
> Take the sine of the result, multiply by three, and divide by ten; this is known as the <term>Ayanamsha</term> <note>The value representing the displacement of the equinoxes from a fixed starting point in the zodiac</note>.

In one Great Age <note>Mahayuga</note>, the stellar cycle advances eastward 600 (30 $\times$ 20) times. By multiplying the desired days (<term>Ahargana</term> <note>The total count of elapsed days from a fixed epoch</note>) or years by 600 and dividing by the terrestrial days or years of the Age, take the "arm" <note>the sine-equivalent in Indian trigonometry</note> of the result, multiply by three, and divide by ten to obtain the <term>Ayanamsha</term>. Both the writing and the meaning of this verse are extremely complex. The fundamental point is: why should so much effort be spent in explaining a simple matter? This method is not desirable in mathematics. We shall write later regarding the different meaning that <term>Bhaskaracharya</term> <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> understood from this.

In another text of astronomy, the meaning of the final line of the verse describing the <term>Ayanamsha</term> has also become complicated. For example:—

> In an Age, the stellar cycle moves forward six hundred times. 
> Multiply the days by that and divide by the terrestrial days; the result is the motion of the equinox.

Here, if the word "Dyugana" is not interpreted as <term>Ahargana</term>, it cannot be reconciled with the previous verse in any way. Mr. Davis <note>likely referring to Samuel Davis, an 18th-century British orientalist and mathematician</note> also did not interpret this verse correctly. He wrote:—

> —Multiply Ahargan (Number of mean solar days for which calculation is made) by 600 and divide the product by savan days in a yug, of quotient take sine and multiply 3 & divide by 10 to get ayanansha. <note>original: "Multiply Ahargan ( Number Of mean solar qays for whieh calculaton is made ) by 600 and divide the product by savan days in a yug, of quotient take sine and multiPfy 3 & divide by 10 to get ayanansha."</note>

Whatever the case may be, it is understood from the first verse that according to the opinion of the <term>Surya Siddhanta</term> <note>The "Sun Treatise," a foundational text of Indian astronomy</note>, the annual motion of the equinox is 54 seconds <note>Vikala</note>.

The opinion of Parashara is that in one Kalpa <note>an immense cosmic cycle</note>, the stellar cycle moves 581,709 times; according to <term>Aryabhata</term>, it moves 578,159 times. Therefore, according to these two opinions respectively, the equinox advances eastward by 52'—3'' and 52'—1'' seconds every year. The <term>Parashari Samhita</term> is the very foundation of <term>Aryabhata's</term> system; this is inferred from the excerpts of his book. The author of the <term>Parashari</term> is the first proponent of the shifting state of the equinoxes. According to him, the equinoctial cycle oscillates between two points 27 degrees east and west of the sign of Aries <term>Mesha Rashi</term>. <term>Aryabhata</term> compared his own celestial observations with those written in the Parashari and applied his intellect to other matters as well. In the book <term>Aryashtashatika</term>, he [describes] the equinox...

It highlights discrepancies in historical interpretations, including those by Western scholars like Mr. Davis.</summary>

<header>Introduction</header>

A different opinion regarding the *Ayana* <note>The precession of the equinoxes, or the shifting of the celestial equator</note> has been recorded—according to that view, "the cycle should move forward by twenty-four degrees," meaning the *Ayana* cycle moves 24 degrees in both directions. In his later work, the *Dashagitika*, he refuted this opinion and upheld the strength of the ancient view. From the two opinions he published, it is inferred that by writing 24 degrees, he was indicating the estimated limit of the *Ayana* during his own time. Therefore, it is known that he was born when the *Ayana* cycle had advanced 24 degrees from the western point. During the time of Varaha <note>Varahamihira, the 6th-century astronomer</note> and the author of the *Surya Siddhanta*, the *Ayana* cycle had advanced 27 degrees from the western point; thus, in Aryabhata's time, the *Ayana* cycle was 3 degrees west of Aries. For this reason, he was born 215 years before Varaha, or 9 years before the Shaka era <note>The Shaka era began in 78 CE; this places Aryabhata around 69 CE by this specific calculation</note>. Mr. Apurva Chandra says that Aryabhata lived sixteen centuries after Yudhishthira. Mr. Colebrooke is of the opinion that Aryabhata was a contemporary of Diophantus, the inventor of Greek algebra. Diophantus was born sometime around 319 CE. The honorable Bal Gangadhar Tilak of Poona, having published the book titled *Orion* (referring to the constellations *Mrigashira* and *Ardra*), used Vedic evidence to show that the theory of a shifting *Ayana* cycle is mathematically incorrect.

The *Garga Samhita* is also an ancient text of astronomy. Varaha frequently mentions the name of this text in his *Brihat Samhita*. Professor Kern, the English translator of the *Brihat Samhita*, quoted passages from the *Garga Samhita* and wrote that it was composed 44 years before the Christian era. That passage is as follows:—

> ->Then, having attacked Saketa, as well as the Panchalas and Mathura,<-
> ->The Greeks <note>original: "Yavana"</note> of wicked prowess will reach the City of the Flower-Standard <note>Pataliputra/Patna</note>.<-
> ->Then, having reached the Flower-City <note>Pushpapura</note>, while the famous mud <note>likely referring to a period of chaos or "muddied" social order</note> is beneficial,<-
> ->All the provinces will undoubtedly be in turmoil.<-

The wicked Greeks <note>term: Yavana - originally referring to Ionians/Greeks, later used for various foreign invaders</note> will attack Saketa, Panchala, and Mathura and go to Pataliputra (Patna). Upon reaching Kusumapura <note>Another name for Pataliputra</note>, they will loot it and lay it to waste. Mr. Kern says that the invasion of Saketa took place 144 years before the Christian era, during the time of the Bactrian King Menander. Therefore, the author of the *Garga Samhita* lived only after this invasion. Whatever Garga wrote regarding the *Ayana*, it is known that he took the subject from Parashara, because both expressed the same opinion when describing the auspicious and inauspicious effects of the *Ayana*.

# Introduction!

As stated by **Parashara**— <note>Parashara is one of the foundational sages of Indian astrology/astronomy.</note>
->When the Sun reaches the end of the Vaishnava constellation <note>original: "Vaishnavantam"; referring to the Shravana nakshatra</note> and moves toward the northern path,<-
->Or reaches Ashlesha in the south, it indicates great fear.<-

**Gargaji** writes—
->When the Sun turns back upon reaching Shravishtha <note>Another name for the Dhanishta constellation.</note> during the northern solstice,<-
->And begins the southern path before reaching Ashlesha, the wise should fear a great calamity.<-

Both verses carry the same meaning: the Sun's <term>Uttarayana</term> <note>The northward journey of the sun, beginning at the winter solstice.</note> occurs after traveling to the end of <term>Dhanishta</term>, and the <term>Dakshinayana</term> <note>The southward journey of the sun, beginning at the summer solstice.</note> begins after traveling to <term>Ashlesha</term>; if these shifts occur otherwise, one should suspect great danger. The antiquity of **Parasharaji's** writing is evident from the meter of his verse itself.

The circular revolution of the <term>Krantipata</term> <note>The Precession of the Equinoxes; the slow change in the orientation of Earth's rotational axis.</note> was first revealed among Hindu astronomers by **Vishnuchandra**, the author of the <term>Vasishtha Siddhanta</term>. His view is that the <term>Krantipata</term> revolves 189,411 times in one <term>Kalpa</term> <note>A vast cosmic time cycle in Hindu cosmology, equal to 4.32 billion years.</note>. Therefore, it is known that according to his view, the solstice advances eastward by 60.06 <term>Vikala</term> <note>Seconds of arc.</note> every year. Whether this view was taken from the books of the two Greek astronomers **Hipparchus** and **Ptolemy**, or was discovered by the Aryan <note>In this context, "Aryan" refers to the ancient Indian scholars themselves.</note> astronomers themselves, we cannot fully determine. However, looking at the annual motion of the solstice determined by both [Greek] astronomers, it appears that **Vishnuchandra** expressed this independently. According to **Hipparchus**, the <term>Krantipata</term> advances one degree in approximately 85 years, and according to **Ptolemy**, one degree in 100 years.

**Bhaskara** has written;—Chapter 6 of the <term>Shiromani</term> <note>Referring to the Siddhanta Shiromani, a major 12th-century astronomical work.</note>:
> The intersection of the celestial equator and the ecliptic is called the Krantipata.
> Its revolutions, as stated in the Surya [Siddhanta], are thirty thousand in a Kalpa in a reverse direction. || 17 ||
> The movement of the solstice was described by Munjala and others; it is the same thing.
> In his school, the number of revolutions in a Kalpa is 199,669. || 18 ||

The meeting point of the <term>Vishuva</term> <note>The celestial equator.</note> and the <term>Krantimandala</term> <note>The ecliptic; the sun's apparent path.</note> is called the <term>Krantipata</term>. According to the <term>Surya Siddhanta</term>, its <term>Bhagana</term> <note>Total number of revolutions.</note> in one <term>Kalpa</term> is thirty thousand. <term>Ayanachalana</term> <note>The shifting of the solstices/precession.</note> and <term>Kranti-pata</term> are the same thing. According to **Munjala** and others, there are 199,669 <term>Bhagana</term> of the solstice in one <term>Kalpa</term>. **Munishvara**, the commentator on the <term>Shiromani</term>, has interpreted the word "Vyasta" <note>meaning "reverse" or "multiplied" in different contexts</note> as Vi = twenty × Asta = multiplied, i.e., (20 × 30,000) = 600,000 (six hundred thousand) to reconcile it with the <term>Surya Siddhanta</term>. According to **Munjala** and others, the annual motion of the solstice is 59.9 <term>Vikala</term>.

It provides specific calculations for the annual movement of the solstices according to various Indian astronomical traditions.</summary>

# Page 12
## Introduction |

According to the opinion of some astronomers, the <term>Ayanamsha</term> <note>The longitudinal difference between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs, caused by the precession of the equinoxes</note> began in the year 444 of the Shaka era. These astronomers believe that the equinox moves forward by one degree every 60 years. Their formula is as follows:

> <note>original: "शको वेदाब्धिवेदोनः षष्टिभक्तोऽयनांशकः । देयास्ते तु रवौ स्पष्टे चललग्नादिसिद्धये ॥"</note>
> Subtract 444 from the Shaka year and divide by 60 to obtain the precession (Ayanamsha). By adding this to the sidereal Sun, the tropical Sun's ascensional difference and the ascendant (Lagna) can be determined.

It is estimated that later astronomers derived this erroneous opinion from Bhaskaracharya’s *Karanakutuhala*. The *Karanakutuhala* was written in 1105 Shaka, and in it, eleven (11) degrees of precession are recorded. Therefore, according to the ratio of one degree every 60 years, 11 degrees would equal 660 years. Later astronomers subtracted 660 from the Shaka year 1105 to find the "start" of the precession. However, we do not consider Bhaskaracharya’s opinion to be accurate. Bhaskara wrote:

> <note>original: "ब्रह्मगुप्तादिभिः स्वल्पान्तरत्वान्न कृतः स्फुटः । स्थित्यर्द्धपरिलेखादौ गणितागत एव हि ॥ नक्षत्राणां स्फुटा एव स्थिरत्वात् पठिताः शराः । दृक्कर्मणायनेनैषां संस्कृताश्च तथा ध्रुवाः ।"</note>
> Because the precession was very slight, astronomers like Brahmagupta did not calculate the <term>Sphuta-shara</term> <note>True celestial latitude</note>! In the <term>Sthityardha</term> <note>Half-duration of an eclipse</note> and <term>Parilekha</term> <note>Graphical representation or projection of an eclipse</note>, the true values are found through calculation. Since the stars remain fixed (they do not move), only the true latitudes of the stars are recited; similarly, the true polar longitudes of the stars, corrected by <term>Drik-karma</term> <note>Reduction to observation/visibility calculation</note> and <term>Ayana</term> (<term>Declination</term>), are also recited.

Therefore, it appears that in Bhaskara’s <term>Drik-karma</term> (<term>Observation</term>) <note>Original text spells it 'Obsaervtion'</note> results, there may have been an error of 1 or 2 degrees. Many astronomers existed before Bhaskara. The dates of several astronomers, as told to Mr. Hunter by the scholars of Ujjain, are written below.

| Name of Scholar | Year | Era |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Varahamihiracharya .... .... .... .... .... | 122 | Shaka Era |
| * Second [Varahamihira] .... .... .... .... .... .... | 421 | ” |
| Brahmagupta .... .... .... .... .... .... | 550 | ” |

---

* This person was born in this Shaka year. Evidence of this is found by looking at the commentary on the *Brihat Samhita*. See the end of the commentary book. For example: "On the second day of the dark fortnight of Phalguna, on a Thursday, in the Shaka year measured by eight, eight, and eight (888), this explanation was completed by me." <note>The quote refers to the completion of a commentary, likely by Utpala, though the text links it to the timeline of Varahamihira.</note>

# Introduction

| Person / Text | Year (CE) | Shaka Era |
| :--- | :---: | :--- |
| Bhattotpala .... | 890 | Shaka -- |
| Shvetotpala .... | 939 | " |
| Varunabhatta .... | 962 | " |
| Bhojaraja .... | 964 | " |
| Bhaskara .... | 1072 | " |
| Kalyanachandra | 1101 | " |

In one inscription of Bhojaraja, the dates 919 Samvat <note>The Vikrama Samvat era, starting 57 BCE</note> and 784 Shaka <note>The Shaka era, starting 78 CE</note> are written. From this, it is known that there have been several individuals named Bhojaraja in India. For this reason, one must proceed with a steady gaze and careful scrutiny in every task.

Shatananda composed the book named *Bhasvati* in 1021 Shaka. This is a small *Karana* text <note>A concise astronomical manual used for practical calculations</note>. In this, the mathematics determined by the *Surya Siddhanta* and Varaha <note>Varahamihira</note> is written in a condensed, magnetic style.

As follows:—
> "Having bowed to the lotus feet of the Lord of Murari, the illustrious one known as Shatananda speaks this *Bhasvati* for the benefit of his disciples, in the Shaka year diminished by the moon (1), the wings (2), the void (0), and the one (1) <note>original: "shashi-paksha-kha-eke" - a numerical code for 1021</note>.
> The Shaka year joined with the nines (9), the mountains (7), the moon (1), and the hands (2) becomes the elapsed years of the Kali Yuga. Diminished by the sky (0), the eyes (2), and the Vedas (4), that is called the collective years of the Shastra.
> The elapsed Kali years, abandoned by the four ages (4), the sky (0), and the fires (3), indeed become the Vikrama year. The Shaka year on this earth is that which is separated by the arrows (5), the fire (3), and the moon (1).
> Now I shall speak briefly, following the instruction of Mihira <note>Varahamihira</note>, in accordance with the *Surya Siddhanta*..."

At the end of the book it is written:
> "When 4220 years of the Yuga had passed, by the divine word of the illustrious Purushottama, the illustrious Shatananda, son of Saraswati and Shankara, composed this."

Seeing the phrase "following the instruction of Mihira" written by Shatananda, Mr. Bentley <note>original: "Ventale" - likely referring to the British orientalist John Bentley</note> concluded that Varahamihira was the teacher of Shatananda. For this reason, he placed him in the year 1060 AD; but readers! You should well remember that Bentley did not understand the meaning of this. <note>The author implies Shatananda was following Varahamihira's ancient teachings, not that he was a contemporary student</note>

Ganesha Daivajna, the son of Keshava Samvatsara, composed the *Grahalaghava* or *Siddhanta-Rahasya* in 1442 Shaka. The writing of this gentleman is extremely complex.

<header>Introduction.</header>

## Introduction.

Up to this point, the chronology of the astronomers has been determined. Although our primary objective was to establish the time of the great teacher Varahamihira <note>Varahamihira (c. 505–587 CE) was one of the most influential Indian astronomers and mathematicians</note>, several other matters were critiqued as they arose in context. The text titled *Brihat Samhita* <note>literally "The Great Compilation," an encyclopedic work covering astrology, planetary movements, eclipses, rainfall, agriculture, and architecture</note> is so excellent that by studying it, a person becomes skilled in all endeavors. It was a matter of great surprise that such a magnificent work lacked a vernacular commentary and had not been printed in Bombay. However, considering the needs of the present time and place, this simple language translation of the text was prepared with great labor. It was immediately printed and published by our great benefactor and devotee of Lord Vishnu, Seth Gangavishnu Shrikrishnadas ji, at his Lakshmi Venkateshwar Press. The full copyright of this translation has been surrendered to the aforementioned Seth ji; therefore, no gentleman should attempt to edit or alter this translation. My highly venerable elder brother, the renowned and eminent scholar Pandit Jwalaprasad Mishra, has purified <note>corrected and edited</note> this text from beginning to end, for which he is thanked repeatedly.

In the work of this translation, assistance was received from several books, which are mentioned below. Namely: the Sanskrit commentary by Bhattotpala <note>a 10th-century commentator essential for understanding Varahamihira</note>, the commentary by Panchanan Tarkaratna published by the Bangavasi Office, and the Arunodaya commentary published in the Dravidian <note>Southern Indian</note> region. The publishers and translators of these works are also thanked repeatedly. If the light of knowledge is transmitted into the heart of even a single person upon reading this translation, I shall consider my labor successful. I request the kind-hearted readers to look upon this translation with a favorable eye. Aside from them, the fault-finders will surely see defects in every part. Goswami Tulsidas ji has truly written:

> Those who witness the faults of others with a thousand eyes; but in the matter of others' welfare, their minds are like a fly in ghee <note>meaning they spoil the good or find it distasteful</note>.
> They abandon their own bodies to cause harm to others; just as hailstones destroy the crops and then melt away themselves.
> They are like the demon Rahu to the full-moon glory of Vishnu and Shiva; and like the thousand-armed Kartavirya Arjuna in hindering the work of others.

Wherever any errors may remain, the readers should correct them as they read.

-> Humble Petitioner— <-
-> Baldev Prasad Mishra, <-
-> Neighborhood of Deendarpura, <-
-> Moradabad. <-

->Salutation to the Auspicious One!<-

# Written by the Great Scholar Varahamihira

## The Varahi Samhita
<note>Also known as the Brihat Samhita, a 6th-century encyclopedic work on astrology, planetary movements, and natural sciences.</note>

### With Vernacular Commentary

---

# Chapter One

Victorious is the Sun, the source of the entire universe, the soul of all that exists, the natural ornament of the sky, and he who is adorned with a garland of a thousand rays resembling molten gold. || 1 ||

Having observed the truthful scriptures extensively described by the first sages <note>referring to Brahma and other ancient seers</note>, I, Varahamihira, am now prepared to clearly explain the essence of those works through a composition that is neither too brief nor too expansive. || 2 ||

If one argues that only ancient works composed by sages are excellent and that works composed by men are not, I ask: when the meaning is identical and the only difference lies in the phrasing, what special merit exists in the sage’s words over the man’s, provided they are not sacred mantras? || 3 ||

If Brahma <note>the Creator</note> stated, "The day of the Son of the Earth <note>original: 'Kshititanaya'; refers to Mars/Tuesday</note> is not auspicious," and a man writes, "The day of Mars <note>original: 'Kujadina'</note> is unfavorable," what is the difference between the divine and the human composition other than the choice of words? || 4 ||

Having studied the vast extent of the scriptures as they have descended in succession from Brahma onwards, this work is being composed with [conciseness...]

---

He who is the place of origin for the entire world, who is the soul of the entire world, who is the natural jewel of the sky; may that Lord Sun, who shines with a garland of rays like molten gold, be supremely victorious. || 1 ||

Having observed the truthful scriptures described in detail by the first sage (Brahma), I, Varahamihira, have set out to describe that same knowledge clearly through a composition that avoids both extreme brevity and extreme length. || 2 ||

If you say that only those scriptures composed by sages (Brahma and others) and which are ancient are superior, and that scriptures composed by humans cannot be superior—to that I say: in matters other than sacred mantras, if the meaning of a human-authored scripture is equal to the words of a sage, and the only difference is in the syllables, then what specialty can there be in the ancient sage's words over the human's? For example, in the book composed by Brahma it is written: "The day of the Son of the Earth is not a doer of good"—meaning Tuesday is not auspicious. And in a human-authored book it is written: "The day of Mars is unfavorable"—meaning Tuesday is harmful. Here, besides the variation in text, what specialty is there in the sage's work over the human's?

<summary>This opening page of the Varahi Samhita features an invocation to the Sun God and Varahamihira's justification for writing a new, accessible compendium of astrology that simplifies the vast, ancient teachings of the sages.</summary>
<keywords>Varahamihira, Brihat Samhita, Sun God (Savita), astrology, Brahma, Tuesday, Mars, Sanskrit literature</keywords>

--- Page 26 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory remarks of Varahamihira, transitioning from the invocation of the divine to the philosophical origins of the universe and the structural definition of the Varahi Samhita (Brihat Samhita).</meta>

<page-num>2</page-num>
->The Varahi Samhita<-

Therefore, I have the enthusiasm to undertake this work. || 5 || In the beginning, it is said, this universe was shrouded in darkness. Within that darkness, a golden egg appeared in the waters. From the two halves of that egg, Brahma—the creator of the universe, whose eyes are the sun and the moon—was born. || 6 || Regarding the cause of this universe, Kapila <note>The founder of the Samkhya school of philosophy</note> speaks of *Pradhana* <note>original: "Pradhana" - primordial matter or nature</note>; Kanada <note>The founder of the Vaisheshika school</note> speaks of substances and atoms; some claim Time is the cause, others say it is Nature, and still others say it is Karma <note>The result of past actions</note>. || 7 || But enough of this excessive detail; determining the truth of such matters is a vast undertaking. Here, I must instead explain the definitive components of the science of Jyotisha <note>term: Jyotisha - the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</note>. || 8 || The science of Jyotisha, which covers many different subjects, is established upon three branches <note>term: Skandha - literally "tree trunk," referring to the major divisions of the science</note>. The sages declare that the work which brings together the entirety of these subjects is called a *Samhita*. In this system, the branch dealing with the motion of the planets through mathematical calculation is called *Tantra*. The second branch is called *Hora*, which deals with the determination of the effects on limbs <note>referring to horoscopy and individual destiny</note>, and the third branch is the one currently being discussed <note>the Samhita itself</note>. || 9 || I have already described the retrograde and direct motions, as well as the settings and risings of the star-planets <note>the five planets visible to the naked eye: Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn</note> in my work on astronomical calculation <note>note: referring to the *Panchasiddhantika*</note>.

---

Is there anything else? That is to say, nothing; seeing the vast expansion of all the scriptures created by Brahma and others, my enthusiasm is directed toward illuminating this science in a systematic and concise manner. || 3 || 4 || 5 || At the time when there was no creation, this entire world was filled with darkness. Within that very darkness, a brilliant golden egg was produced in the waters. It split into two pieces representing heaven and earth. From those pieces, Lord Brahma was born, whose eyes are the Sun and the Moon. || 6 || Regarding the origin of the world, many different opinions of the sages are observed. Kapila says that *Pradhana*—that is, primordial nature—is the cause of the universe. The sage Kanada says that substances and other material categories are the cause of the world's origin. Some call Time the cause, others call Nature <note>original: "Svabhava"</note> the cause, and the Mimamsakas <note>followers of the Mimamsa school of ritual and ethics</note> say that Karma is the cause of the world. || 7 || There is no need for further elaboration regarding the description of the world's origin. To decide this matter, many subjects would have to be described, and that topic is by no means small. For this reason, leaving that consideration aside, we must here only determine the branches of the Jyotisha scriptures. || 8 || The Jyotisha scripture, which has many types of divisions, is divided into three parts: *Samhita*, *Tantra*, and *Hora*. That which contains a description of all the subjects of Jyotisha is called the *Samhita* branch. That in which the movement of the planets is described through mathematics is called the *Tantra* branch. And that which describes the determination of "limbs"—meaning the description of journeys, marriages, and so on—is called the *Hora* branch. || 9 || In my composed astronomical treatise named *Panchasiddhantika*, I have described the retrograde motion, direct path, setting, and rising of the five star-planets (Mars, etc.). And in the books *Brihat Jataka* and *Brihat Vivaha-patala*, I have described births, journeys, and marriages...

<summary>Varahamihira explains the mythological and philosophical origins of the universe before defining the three branches of Jyotisha: Tantra (astronomy), Hora (horoscopy), and Samhita (omens and general astrology).</summary>
<keywords>Cosmology, Brahma, Golden Egg, Kapila, Kanada, Jyotisha, Samhita, Tantra, Hora, Panchasiddhantika, Varahamihira</keywords>

The details regarding the hour of birth <note>horoscopy</note>, as well as matters of travel and marriage, have been fully explained by me previously. || 10 || Having set aside the lengthy dialogues of questions and answers found in other treatises, the various narrative contexts of little practical use, and the myths regarding the origins of the planets—all of which are of small value—I shall now declare the essential and true substance of these matters in its entirety. || 11 ||

->Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Introduction to the Treatise," in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the illustrious Varahamihira. || 1 ||<-

# Chapter Two

->Now, therefore, we shall explain the "Rule for the Astrologer."<-

In this regard, the Astrologer <term>Samvatsara: a master of the cycles of time</term> should be of noble birth, pleasant to look upon, modest in dress, a speaker of truth, free from envy, and of even temperament. He should have well-knit and well-developed joints and limbs, being free from any physical deformity. His hands, feet, nails, eyes, chin, teeth, ears, forehead, eyebrows, and head should all be shapely and well-formed. He should possess a handsome body and a deep, sonorous voice. For, generally, virtues and defects follow the physical form and appearance of the body. || 1 || Regarding his inner qualities: he must be pure, dexterous, bold, and an eloquent speaker. He should be ready-witted...

---

...and others have already been described in detail at the very beginning. || 10 || Now, the questions posed by disciples at the start of various treatises composed by sages such as Garga, the answers given by those sages, various types of narrative contexts, and the useless stories regarding the birth of the Sun and other planets—as well as ancient accounts in the old compilations <note>Samhitas</note> that contradict the reality of the celestial sphere—are of very little practical use. For this reason, having abandoned all those worthless discussions, I describe in this book the essential and factual matters. || 11 ||

->Thus ends the first chapter, "Introduction to the Treatise," in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the teacher Varahamihira, with the commentary in the common tongue written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region. || 1 ||<-

First, the characteristics of the Astrologer <term>Jyotishi</term> are stated here: He should be born into a beautiful <note>noble</note> family, be pleasing to the sight, dress modestly, be a truth-teller, and not find faults in the virtues of others. He should be beautiful in all his limbs, not lacking any part of his body. His hands, feet, nails, eyes, chin, teeth, ears, forehead, eyebrows, and head—all these parts should be endowed with excellent marks. His body should be robust and lovely, and he should speak with a deep voice. Such a person is fully qualified to be called an Astrologer, because usually, all virtues and defects correspond to the body and its shape. || 1 || He should be holy, clever, bold (meaning one who speaks well in an assembly), skillful in conversation, quick-witted, a knower of time and place, and in his heart...

<summary>Varahamihira concludes his introduction by dismissing mythological fluff in favor of scientific essentials and begins Chapter 2 by defining the ideal physical and moral qualities of a professional astrologer.</summary>
<keywords>Varahamihira, Brihat Samhita, Astrologer qualifications, Samvatsara, Jyotishi, physiognomy, Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra</keywords>

# The Varahi Samhita

<page-num>4</page-num>

->**The Qualities of an Astrologer**<-

An astrologer should be a person of noble character, knowledgeable in geography and time, and possessed of a calm temperament. He must not be timid in public assemblies nor easily intimidated by his fellow students. He must be skillful, free from vices, and well-versed in the sciences of <term>Shantika</term> <note>rituals for averting evil or calming disturbances</note>, <term>Paushtika</term> <note>rituals for increasing prosperity and health</note>, and <term>Abhichara</term> <note>rituals involving magic or spells</note>, as well as the sacred baths. He should be devoted to the worship of the gods, observant of vows and fasts, and possess a reputation for knowledge gained through his own independent and extraordinary mastery of the science. 

He should be capable of answering questions accurately, and except in cases of divine calamities <note>original: "daivatyaya," referring to unavoidable natural disasters</note>, he should be a master of the meanings of the texts on planetary mathematics (<term>Graha Ganita</term>), the Compendium (<term>Samhita</term>), and Horoscopy (<term>Hora</term>). || 2 ||

Regarding planetary mathematics, he must be a knower of time and space as defined in the five <term>Siddhantas</term> <note>The five foundational astronomical treatises: Paulisha, Romaka, Vasishtha, Saura, and Paitamaha</note>. This includes the divisions of time: the Great Age (<term>Yuga</term>), the year, the half-year (<term>Ayana</term>), the season, the month, the fortnight, the full day and night, the three-hour watch (<term>Yama</term>), the <term>Muhurta</term> <note>a unit of 48 minutes</note>, the <term>Nadi</term> <note>24 minutes</note>, the <term>Vinadi</term> <note>24 seconds</note>, the breath (<term>Prana</term>), the <term>Truti</term> <note>a tiny fraction of a second</note>, and even smaller subdivisions. || 3 ||

He must also understand the causes behind the four types of months—Solar, Civil (<term>Savana</term>), Sidereal (<term>Nakshatra</term>), and Lunar—as well as the occurrence of intercalary months (<term>Adhimasa</term>) and omitted days (<term>Avama</term>). || 4 ||

He must know the beginning and end of the lords of the sixty-year cycle, the five-year <term>Yuga</term>, the year, the month, the day, and the hour (<term>Hora</term>). He should be expert in demonstrating the similarities, differences, suitability, and unsuitability of the various measurements like the Solar and Lunar systems. Even when there are differences between the various <term>Siddhanta</term> texts, he should be able to reconcile them through direct observation at the turning of the solstices, using the intersection of the prime vertical <note>original: "samamandala-rekha"</note> and the shadow and water-clock instruments to align observation with calculation.

## Chapter 2: With Language Commentary

He must be skilled in demonstrating mathematical proofs with consistency. He should understand the causes behind the fast, slow, southern, northern, low (perigee), and high (apogee) motions of the Sun and other planets. Regarding eclipses of the Sun and Moon, he must be an instructor capable of predicting the time of contact, the time of liberation <note>the end of the eclipse</note>, the direction of contact and liberation, the magnitude, the duration, the total obscuration <term>Vimarda: the period of total darkness during an eclipse</term>, the color, and the location. He must also predict future planetary conjunctions and planetary "wars" <note>Graha-yuddha: when two planets appear very close in the sky</note>.

He should be skilled in determining the measurements of the orbital paths <term>Kaksha</term> of each planet in terms of leagues <term>Yojanas: an ancient Indian measure of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</term>. He must be knowledgeable in the fields of space, time, and calculation, including the rotation and positioning of the Earth and the circle of asterisms, latitude, colatitude, the radius of the diurnal circle, the "ascensional difference" <term>Charadala: used to calculate the length of day and night</term>, the rising times of the zodiac signs, shadows, the water-clock <term>Nadi</term>, and the various astronomical divisions of time.

His speech should possess substance born from the ability to resolve various types of challenging questions. He should be a speaker of the science <term>Shastra</term> that has been purified—much like gold that is made even cleaner after being tested on a touchstone, heated in fire, and polished.

It has been said:
"How can one be known as a knower of the Shastra if he cannot convey a definite meaning, cannot answer a single question when asked, and cannot teach his students?" ☸ "The ignorant man who interprets a text one way when it means another, and miscalculates the astronomical treatises, is like a lecherous man who approaches the Creator <note>Brahma/Pitamaha</note> and praises a vulgar woman." ☸ "When the astronomical system <term>Tantra</term> is well understood, and the ascendant <term>Lagna</term> is accurately determined through shadows and water-instruments, and the science of horoscopy <term>Hora</term> is firmly grasped, the speech of the seer never goes in vain." ☸

It was also said by the venerable Vishnugupta <note>An ancient authority, often identified with Chanakya or a later astronomer</note>:
"A man crossing the great ocean might, by the force of the wind, eventually reach the other shore; but without [proper knowledge], one cannot reach the end of this great ocean called the 'Time-Person' <note>Kalapurusha: Time personified as a cosmic being</note>..."

# The Varahi Samhita

### Page 6

Even a sage might only rarely reach the far shore of this science, even in his mind. ☸ In the study of **Horoscopy** <note>original: "Horashastra," the branch of astrology dealing with individual birth charts and timing</note>, one must master the strengths and weaknesses of the zodiac signs, the half-signs, decans, ninth-parts, twelfth-parts, and thirty-degree divisions. One must determine the various types of planetary strengths through their direction, position, time, and movement. This includes understanding the nature, elemental humors, substances, castes, and behaviors associated with the planets.

Furthermore, it encompasses the moment of conception, the wonders of the birth time, the methods of providing reliable predictions, cases of immediate death, the calculation of longevity, major and minor planetary periods, the "eight-fold division" system <note>original: "Ashtakavarga," a specific method for calculating planetary strength</note>, royal combinations, lunar combinations, and combinations of two or more planets. It covers the results of celestial configurations like the "Sky-based" yogas, the influence of the houses, planetary aspects, the manner of death, future transitions, and the signs indicating good or bad fortune for questions asked at a specific moment. It also governs the performance of rituals such as marriages.

Regarding **Journeys and Expeditions** <note>original: "Yatra," specifically referring to military marches or royal travels</note>, the science details the lunar days, solar days, half-days, constellations, auspicious moments, rising signs, and planetary combinations. It includes the interpretation of bodily twitches, dreams, victory-baths, sacrifices to the planets, group rituals, the omens of fire-shapes, and the movements and gestures of elephants and horses. It covers the "six-fold policy" <term>Shadgunya: the six strategies of statecraft—peace, war, marching, sitting encamped, seeking alliance, and double-dealing</term>, auspicious and inauspicious omens, the selection of ground for military encampments, the colors of ritual fires, and the timely employment of ministers, spies, messengers, and forest-dwellers. It also provides methods for capturing enemy fortresses.

As the ancient teachers have said: This science, which includes the movement of the celestial spheres, is spread across the world as if it were displayed openly, written upon the intellect, and cast into the very heart of the scholar who understands it well.

---

<margin>A person who knows the mathematical systems, who can determine the rising sign through shadows, water-clocks, or instruments, and who is an expert in Horoscopy—the words of such a man can never be false.</margin>

The Great Sage **Vishnugupta** <note>Also known as Chanakya or Kautilya</note> has also said: If a man wished to cross the great ocean, he might eventually reach the other side by the force of the wind. However, no man—other than a divine sage—can reach the far shore of this "Ocean of Time" known as Astrology, even in his thoughts.

In this study of Horoscopy, there is the determination of planetary strength through many means: the signs, the half-signs, decans, ninth-parts, twelfth-parts, and thirtieth-parts; their positions, timing, and motions. It includes the study of physical nature, the bodily humors <note>The three Doshas: Vata, Pitta, and Kapha</note>, materials, castes, and behaviors. It covers conception, the time of birth, the creation of confidence through accurate predictions, sudden death, the span of life, and the various cycles of planetary periods. It explains the results of all planetary combinations, the influence of the twelve houses, the gaze <note>aspects</note> of the planets, the journey of the soul after death, and the auspicious or inauspicious reasons behind questions asked at any given time.

It is the basis for all groups of rituals like marriage and the description of expeditions. It details the lunar dates, days, constellations, and the throbbing of limbs. It covers dreams, victory, baths, planetary sacrifices, the signs shown by fire, the signals of elephants and horses, and the movements of the army. It explains the six-fold diplomatic measures, the omens of good and bad luck, the lands where an army should dwell, the color of fires, and the strategic use of ministers, secret agents, and scouts according to the time. All these matters are the essence of the science of Horoscopy. The ancient masters have said: this science, when mastered, is like something widely publicized in the world, written in the mind, and molded into the heart.

# Chapter 2 with Language Commentary

One who has the scriptures, along with all their constituent parts, firmly established in his heart—as if poured into it—his predictions shall never fail. || 5 || Only a man who has mastered the *Samhitas* <note>The 'Samhita' is the encyclopedic branch of Jyotisha (astrology) dealing with collective omens and natural phenomena.</note> can truly be called a *Daivajna* <note>A diviner or knower of fate.</note>. This is because the following subjects are determined within the *Samhitas*:

The movements of the Sun and other planets; their natural states, variations, size, color, rays, brilliance, and shapes; their settings, risings, and paths; their transitions between paths, retrograde motions, and prograde motions; the results of planetary conjunctions and their movements through the lunar mansions (*Nakshatras*).

The distribution of effects across various countries according to the *Nakshatra-Kurma* division <note>A method of mapping the geography of India onto the body of a symbolic tortoise to predict regional events.</note>; the movements of the star Canopus (*Agastya*) and the Great Bear (*Saptarishi*); the planetary influences and the arrangement of the stars; the "triangular" planetary configurations (*Shringataka*); planetary wars and conjunctions; the fruits of the yearly rainfall and the "conception" of clouds <note>Garbha-lakshana: the observation of atmospheric conditions months before the monsoon to predict rainfall.</note>; the conjunctions of the Moon with the stars Rohini, Swati, and Ashadha.

Signs of immediate rain; the blooming of flowers and creepers; atmospheric halos (*Paridhi* and *Parivesha*); mock suns (*Parigha*); winds, meteors, and the "burning of the quarters" <note>An atmospheric phenomenon where the horizon appears to be on fire.</note>; earthquakes and the colors of the twilight; "cities of the Gandharvas" <note>Fata Morgana or complex mirages in the sky.</note>; dust storms and thunderclaps; the fluctuation of prices and the growth of crops; the festival of Indra’s Banner and the rainbow.

Architecture (*Vastu-vidya*); the science of bodily omens (*Anga-vidya*); the omens of crows (*Vayasa-vidya*); the various "circles" of omens related to the inner regions, deer, horses, and the wind; the characteristics of palaces and temples; the characteristics of idols and their consecration; the "Ayurveda of trees" <note>Vrikshayurveda: the ancient science of plant health and botany.</note>; the science of finding underground water (*Udargala*); the lustration of arms (*Nirajana*); the wagtail omen; the pacification of calamities; the "variegated peacock" omen; the characteristics of ghee, blankets, swords, and royal fillets.

The characteristics of roosters, tortoises, cows, goats, horses, elephants, men, and women; reflections on the inner harem; the characteristics of baskets, umbrellas, torn clothes, chowries, staffs, beds, and seats; the examination of gems and the signs of lamps—

The characteristics of lamps, the auspicious and inauspicious omens associated with tooth-sticks <note>original: "dantakastha"; twigs used for oral hygiene, whose fraying or breaking was used for divination</note>, and other general signs concerning the world, every individual, and the Earth itself must be constantly contemplated by an astrologer <term>Daivajna: one who knows the divine will through stars</term> who is devoted to no other task. It is not possible for a single person to observe these omens day and night. Therefore, a well-supported astrologer should be assisted by four others learned in the same science. Among them, one should observe the East and the South-East directions. Another should watch the South and the South-West; a third, the West and the North-West; and a fourth, the North and the North-East. This is because omens such as the falling of meteors <note>original: "ulkapata"</note> occur swiftly. Their results are determined by their shape, color, glossiness, size, and their impact upon the planets and constellations. || 6 ||

It has been said by the great seer Garga:
The King who does not honor an astrologer who is skilled in all the limbs and sub-limbs of the science <note>referring to the six Vedangas or branches of astrology</note> and who is perfect in horoscopy <term>Hora: predictive astrology</term> and mathematics, meets with utter destruction. || 7 ||

Even those who have retired to the forest, who are free from worldly attachments and possess nothing, still inquire of the scholar who is an expert in the movements of the heavenly bodies. || 8 ||

Just as the night is without a lamp, and the sky is without the sun, so does a King without an astrologer wander like a blind man on a path. || 9 ||

The auspicious moment <term>Muhurta: a unit of time approx. 48 minutes</term>, the lunar day, the lunar mansion <term>Nakshatra: the 27 star clusters of the zodiac</term>, the seasons, and the solar half-years—all of these would fall into confusion if the Royal Astrologer <term>Samvatsara: literally 'the one of the year'</term> did not exist. || 10 ||

---

All auspicious and inauspicious omens, including those based on the characteristics of lamps and tooth-sticks, are revealed through this Compendium <note>The Samhita</note>. It is proper for astrologers, without applying their minds to other tasks, to always consider all ordinary and extraordinary auspicious and inauspicious signs for the world and for every man regarding all earthly matters. However, deciding the good or bad of these matters day and night is not the work of a single man; therefore, along with a well-provided astrologer, the King should appoint four other men who know this scripture. Among them, one man should watch for matters in the East and the South-East corner. The second should watch the South and the South-West, the third the West and the North-West corner, and the fourth should watch the North and the North-East corner, so that omens like falling meteors may be known quickly. Because the fruit of these falling meteors is linked with their shape, color, glossiness, size, and their striking of planets and constellations. Sage Garga has said—the King who does not worship an astrologer skilled in the limbs and sub-limbs, and clever in the subjects of horoscopy and mathematics, soon reaches destruction. || 6 || 7 || Even forest-dwellers, those without attachments and those who accept nothing, ask everything of the pundits who know the movement of planets and constellations. || 8 || Like a night without a lamp and a sky without the sun, a King without an astrologer does not shine; rather, like a blind man, he wanders on an evil path. || 9 || Without an astrologer, the auspicious moment, the lunar day...

# Chapter 3

There was certainly a time when the southward journey of the sun began from the middle of the <term>Ashlesha</term><note>The 9th lunar mansion (nakshatra)</note> constellation, and the northward journey began from the start of <term>Dhanishtha</term><note>The 23rd lunar mansion</note>; this is why it was stated so in the ancient scriptures. || 1 || Currently, the sun's southward journey begins from the start of Cancer, and the other (northward journey) begins from the start of Capricorn. As stated—

<column-break/>

<gloss>Like a desire</gloss>, the command of an ignorant man may occasionally come true by chance. || 19 || A king should discard a fortune-teller who is "endowed with wealth"—meaning one who tells many types of meanings just for gain—or one who loves useless talk and is arrogant due to a tiny bit of knowledge. || 20 || Kings seeking victory should worship and welcome a fortune-teller who possesses excellent knowledge in <term>Hora</term>, <term>Ganita</term>, and <term>Samhita</term>. || 21 || A single thinker of the divine who knows the context of time and place can perform a task that a thousand elephants or four thousand horses cannot do. || 22 || By listening to the lunar-constellation discourse from the mouth of a fortune-teller, bad dreams, bad visions, and bad deeds are destroyed instantly. || 23 || Astrologers seek the welfare of a powerful king to increase their own fame in a way that even the king's father, mother, relatives, or brothers cannot. || 24 ||

->Thus ends the second chapter of the vernacular commentary composed by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western Province, on the Brihat Samhita written by the great teacher Sri Varahamihira. || 2 ||<-

Certainly, at some time, the southward solstice from the middle of the Ashlesha constellation and the northward solstice from the beginning of Dhanishtha were prevalent; otherwise, why would it be described so in the earlier scriptures?

# Chapter 3: Commentary on the Sun's Course

### Section 2-3: Observation of the Solstices

The state of change <note>original: "vikriti"</note> is revealed through direct observation and testing. || 2 ||

The examination of the solstice <term>Ayana: the northward or southward journey of the sun</term> is conducted either by piercing the marks of distance at the time of the Sun's rising or setting, or by observing the marks of the entry and exit of shadows within a large graduated circle. || 3 ||

### Section 4-5: Omens of Irregular Movement

If the Sun turns back without reaching the sign of Capricorn <note>the Winter Solstice</note>, it destroys the South and West directions. If it turns back without reaching the sign of Cancer <note>the Summer Solstice</note>, it destroys the North and East directions. || 4 ||

If the Sun turns back only after crossing the northern solstice <note>Uttarayana</note>, it brings well-being and increases the growth of grain; this is called the Sun remaining in its natural state <note>Prakritistha</note>. However, if the Sun’s movement is distorted <note>Vikrit</note>, it creates fear. || 5 ||

### Section 6-9: Solar Omens and Dark Spots

If a phenomenon named Tvashta <note>a specific type of solar eclipse or dark spot</note> veils the solar disc without it being the time of a regular eclipse <note>Parva: the new or full moon periods</note>, it will cause the death of seven kings and the destruction of people through weapons, fire, or famine. || 6 ||

There are thirty-three types of "Comets" <note>Ketus</note> known as the sons of Rahu, such as the Dark Spikes <note>Tamas-Kilaka</note>. One should determine their effects by observing their color, position, and shape upon the solar disc. || 7 ||

If these appear on the solar disc, they bring evil results; however, if they appear on the lunar disc, they are generally auspicious. But if they appear on the Moon in the form of a crow, a headless torso <note>Kabandha</note>, or a weapon, they are inauspicious even there. || 8 ||

Upon the rising of these omens, the world is thrown into turmoil: the water becomes muddy, the sky is filled with dust, and a fierce wind blows, crushing the peaks of mountains and trees and carrying pebbles. || 9 ||

<margin>Trees bloom out of season; wild animals and birds appear agitated; the directions seem to burn; and portents such as thunderbolts and earthquakes occur.</margin>

# The Varahi Samhita
## Chapter on Solar Portents

> ...portents. || 10 || If these forms—the Crested, the Wedge-shaped, or the Rahu-forms—are seen, their effects are not distinct from one another. One should declare the results of these cometary bodies <note>original: "Ketus"</note> based on the specific cause of their appearance. || 11 || In whichever lands these spots appear within the solar disc <note>original: "Surya-bimba"</note>, the ruin of the rulers of those specific lands is to be understood. || 12 || Even sages, their bodies exhausted by hunger and having abandoned their righteous conduct and traditional duties, will carry their fleshless children in their arms and travel to foreign lands with great difficulty. || 13 || With their wealth plundered by thieves, their eyelids heavy and sighing deeply, the virtuous will live with withered bodies, their vision clouded by the tears of sorrow. || 14 || Emaciated and filled with self-loathing, oppressed by their own kings or by the armies of foreign invaders <note>original: "para-chakra"</note>, men will speak ill of the conduct and the past deeds of their own sovereign. || 15 || Though the clouds appear pregnant with rain, they shall not release their waters; the rivers will dwindle to a trickle, and crops will grow only in a few scattered places. || 16 || If a staff-like shape <note>original: "Danda"</note> appears in the sun, the King dies; if a headless trunk <note>original: "Kabandha"</note> appears, there is fear of disease; if the shape of a crow <note>original: "Dhvanksha"</note> appears, there is fear of thieves; and if a pillar-like spot <note>original: "Kilaka"</note> appears on the sun, a famine occurs. || 17 || If the sun is pierced by shapes resembling royal regalia—such as the parasol, the banner, or the fly-whisk—it brings about a change in the monarchy. If it appears like a spark...

---

The trees act contrary to the seasons; deer and birds run toward or cry out from the "blazing" quarters <note>The cardinal directions associated with ill omens</note>; there is a burning of the horizon, thunderclaps, and earthquakes—these are the great portents. || 9 || 10 || Among these sons of Rahu, if Rahu is seen in the form of an arrow or a club, the results should be stated as before. In this manner, one should judge the cause of their rising and the good or evil fruits of the Ketus. || 11 || In whichever countries the Ketus within the solar disc are seen, the kings of those very countries will meet with misfortune. || 12 || Upon their rising, even the forest-dwelling sages, their bodies weary with hunger and fallen from their own Dharma and noble character, will take their skin-and-bone children in their hands and go to other lands with extreme suffering. || 13 || Thieves will steal the wealth of the holy men; for this reason, they will remain with distressed bodies, letting out long sighs and shedding tears from their eyes, their throats choked with grief. || 14 || At that time, men will become extremely thin and reproachful due to oppression from their own king or a foreign military circle <term>Rajachakra: a coalition of neighboring kings or an invading force</term>. Some will even criticize the character or the previous actions of their local king. || 15 || The clouds will remain "pregnant" <note>holding moisture but not releasing it</note> and will not give much water; the rivers will become low in water, and grain will be produced only here and there. || 16 || If a staff-shaped Ketu is seen in the solar circle, the death of the king occurs; if a headless torso is seen, fear of disease arises; if a crow-shape is seen, there is fear of thieves; and if the shape of a pillar is seen, there is a famine. || 17 || If the sun is pierced by shapes of royal equipment like the parasol...
