->By smoke and other signs, the destruction of people. <-

If the sun is obscured by sparks or smoke, it brings death to all mankind. || 18 || A single sign <note>referring to the umbrellas or banners mentioned in previous verses</note> causes famine; two or more such signs lead to the destruction of the king. If the sun is pierced by these signs in colors of white, red, yellow, or black, it destroys the various castes respectively. || 19 || Wherever these great portents <term>utpata: unnatural or miraculous phenomena signaling disaster</term> appear arising from the solar disc, fear will come to the people of that specific region. || 20 || When the sun’s upward rays are copper-colored, it destroys the commander-in-chief; if yellow, the prince; and if white, it kills the royal priest. || 21 || If the sun’s rays are multicolored or smoky, the earth will be troubled by thieves and the clash of weapons, unless it rains quickly. || 22 || The sun is auspicious if it appears copper or tawny in the cool season <note>Shishira: approx. Jan-Feb</note>, the color of green saffron in the spring, pale gold in the summer, and white in the rainy season. || 23 || It is also favorable if it resembles the heart of a lotus in autumn and blood-red in the winter. During the monsoon, a glossy appearance is beneficial, as is a natural appearance in all seasons. || 24 || A rough, white sun destroys the <term>Brahmins: the priestly class</term>; a reddish one destroys the <term>Kshatriyas: the warrior/ruling class</term>; yellow destroys the <term>Vaishyas: the merchant class</term>; and black destroys the <term>Shudras: the laboring class</term>. A glossy or bright appearance, however, brings good fortune. || 25 ||

---

If signs such as banners or fly-whisks <note>traditional symbols of royalty</note> appear to pierce the solar disc, there will be a change in the government. If the sun is covered by sparks or smoke, it signifies the death of all people. || 18 || If the sun is pierced by one of the aforementioned signs like an umbrella, famine occurs; if by two or more, the king is destroyed. If pierced by these signs in white, red, yellow, or black colors, then the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras are destroyed in that order. || 19 || Wherever these great portents are seen in the solar disc, the people living in those lands will experience fear. || 20 || If the rays on the upper part of the sun are copper-colored, the commander-in-chief is destroyed; if yellow, the prince; and if white, the royal priest. || 21 || If the sun's circle of rays is multicolored or smoke-colored, and if it does not rain soon, the entire earth will be distressed by thieves or the falling of weapons. || 22 || The solar disc is auspicious when it is copper or tawny in the cool season, like green saffron in the spring, somewhat pale (a mix of white and yellow) and like gold in the summer, white in the rainy season, like the beauty of a lotus interior in the autumn, and blood-colored in the winter. However, in the rainy season, if it is too oily/glossy, it is inauspicious. <note>The commentary here notes a slight variation from the verse regarding the 'glossy' quality in the rainy season.</note> || 23 || 24 || A dry or white appearance leads to the destruction of Brahmins; a blood-like glow destroys the Kshatriyas; a yellow color destroys the Vaishyas; and a black color destroys the Shudras. If there is a luster or brilliance in all these colors of the sun, it is considered auspicious. || 25 ||

# The Varahi Samhita

->Page 14<-

In the summer, if the sun appears red, it causes fear for all living beings. In the rainy season, if it appears black, it causes a drought. In the winter, if the sun is yellow, it quickly brings the fear of disease. || 26 ||

If the body of the sun <note>literally: "the one with a thousand rays"</note> appears split or broken by a rainbow, it foretells conflict between kings. During the rainy season, if the sun shines with pure, clear light, it brings immediate rain. || 27 ||

If the solar disc resembles the color of a *Shirish* flower <note>Albizia lebbeck; a pale greenish-yellow flower</note> during the rainy season, it brings rain immediately. However, if it resembles the feathers of a peacock, there will be no rain for twelve years. || 28 ||

When the sun is dark, there is a danger of pests <note>or "insect plagues"</note>. If it is the color of ash, fear of foreign armies is expected. If the sun appears with a hole or dark spot while positioned in a king's birth star <term>Nakshatra: the lunar mansion or star sign associated with an individual's birth</term>, that ruler will meet his destruction. || 29 ||

If the sun in the sky resembles the color of rabbit's blood, battles will occur. If it appears pale like the moon, the king will soon be killed and another king will take his place. || 30 ||

If the solar disc is shaped like a pot, people will perish from the flames of hunger. If it appears fragmented, it kills the king. If it is devoid of rays, it brings fear. If it takes the form of an archway <note>toraṇa</note>, it destroys the city. If it resembles an umbrella, it leads to the destruction of the country. || 31 ||

If the sun appears trembling, rough, or shaped like a flag or a bow, wars will break out. If a black line is seen across the sun, the king will be destroyed by his own minister. || 32 ||

If a meteor, a thunderbolt, or lightning strikes the sun as it is rising, the current king will be destroyed and—

# Chapter 3 with Vernacular Commentary

<page-num>( 15 )</page-num>
->**Header: With Vernacular Commentary, Chapter 3**<-

When falling stars, thunderbolts, and lightning strike, one should know it signifies the death of the king and the establishment of another ruler. || 33 ||

If the sun <note>original: "ahimakiraṇaḥ" - the one with hot rays</note> is surrounded by a halo every day at both twilights, or if it rises and sets while colored deep red, it creates another king <note>i.e., a change in government or a coup</note>. || 34 ||

If the sun is obscured at both twilights by clouds shaped like weapons <term>praharaṇa: weapons such as swords or spears</term>, it brings war. If the clouds resemble deer, buffalo, birds, donkeys, or young camels, it brings great fear. || 35 ||

Just as gold attains purity after suffering the intense heat of fire, so too do the constellations <term>nakshatras: lunar mansions/stars</term> suffer great distress from the heat of the sun's rays before becoming pure afterward. || 36 ||

A mock sun <note>original: "pratisūryo" - a parhelion or "sun dog"</note> situated to the north of the sun brings rain; to the south, it brings wind. If situated on both sides, there is danger from water. If it appears above the sun, it destroys the king; if below, it destroys the people. || 37 ||

If the sun appears blood-red in the sky, it brings the end of the king's reign before long. The same occurs if its body is reddened by harsh dust. || 38 ||

A sun that appears black, variegated, blue, or harsh-looking brings the slaughter of the people, especially if accompanied by the terrifying cries of birds and beasts at the start of the night. || 39 ||

One whose body is stainless, whose circle is not distorted, and whose rays are clear, vast, and pure...

---

...the establishment of another king occurs. || 33 || In whatever country the Sun God possesses a halo <note>original: "paridhivāle"</note> daily at morning and evening, or rises and sets assuming a red color, in that country there will certainly be another king. || 34 || If at morning and evening the solar disc is surrounded by clouds shaped like weapons, there will be war; and if covered by clouds resembling deer, buffalo, birds, donkeys, and elephants, there will be extreme fear. || 35 || Just as gold, having undergone great suffering from the heat of fire, becomes pure afterward, so all the constellations suffer distress from the heat of the sun's rays and then become pure. || 36 || If a mock sun is seen in the northern direction of the Sun God, there will be rain; if seen in the southern direction, there will be a storm or cyclone. If seen on both sides of the sun, there is danger from water; if seen below, the destruction of the people; and if seen above, the destruction of the king. || 37 || If the sun appears red in the upper part of the sky, or appears red due to a terrifying mass of dust, the death of the king occurs quickly. || 38 || If the solar disc becomes black, variegated, or blue and assumes a terrifying form, and if at twilight the sounds of birds and deer are as terrifying as the braying of a donkey, then all the people are destroyed. || 39 || The sun which has a stainless body, a round circle, and very clear, long rays, and whose body is without defect and color is also without defect...

# Chapter Four

Just as one half of a water-pot <note>original: "Kumbha"</note> placed in the sunlight is made white by the sun's rays while the other half remains dark due to its own shadow, so too is the half of the Moon—which always resides below the Sun—rendered white by the solar rays. || 1 ||

The rays of the Sun, falling upon the watery body of the Moon, destroy the darkness of the night, much like the rays of the Sun striking the surface of a mirror destroy the darkness within a house by reflection. || 2 ||

As the Moon leaves the vicinity of the Sun, a whiteness <note>the waxing phase</note> clings to its western side; in this manner, due to the influence of the Sun, the Moon's brightness increases from its lower part upward. || 3 ||

Thus, day by day, due to its specific position relative to the Sun, the increase of the Moon's whiteness occurs on its western side, just as it does on a water-pot in the afternoon. || 4 ||

If the Moon <note>original: "Shitakirana," the cool-rayed one</note> passes to the south of the constellations Jyeshtha, Mula, or the two Ashadhas <note>Purva-ashadha and Uttara-ashadha</note>, it destroys seeds, aquatic animals, and forests, and brings the danger of fire. || 5 ||

---

->When the Sun is free from distortions and no marks appear in the solar disc, the Lord Sun becomes the benefactor of the world. || 40 ||<-

->Thus ends the third chapter in the vernacular commentary <note>original: "Bhashatika"</note> of the *Brihat Samhita* composed by Acharya Varahamihira, as translated by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province. || 3 ||<-

By placing a pot in the sunlight, that half which faces the sun becomes white from the sun's rays, and the other half remains black from its own shadow; in the same way, the half of the Moon situated in the lower region of the Sun is illuminated daily by the sun's rays, and the other half remains dark-colored due to its own shadow. || 1 || Just as the essence of the sun's rays falling upon a mirror enters a dark house and destroys the darkness inside through its reflection, so the sun's rays falling upon the watery Moon destroy the mass of the night's darkness. || 2 || As it leaves the lower part of the sun, the western part of the moon assumes whiteness according to the power of the sun's rays; it becomes increasingly illuminated starting from the bottom. || 3 || In this way, every day, due to its specific location, the whiteness of the moon increases via the sun on its back part, like a water-pot during the third watch of the day <note>afternoon</note>. || 4 || Jyeshtha, Mula, Purva-ashadha, and Utta- <note>text breaks off mid-word</note>

# Chapter 4 | With Commentary

->**The Transit of the Moon**<-

When the Moon passes to the right side of the *Ashadha* <note>original: "राषाढा"; likely referring to the Purva or Uttara Ashadha constellations</note> nakshatras, there is a loss of seeds, water, and forests, and a danger of fire arises. || 5 || When the Moon moves to the right side of the *Vishakha* and *Anuradha* constellations, it is called a "Sinful Moon" <note>original: "पापचंद्रमा" (Papachandrama); an inauspicious lunar position</note>. However, if the Moon stays in the middle portion of *Vishakha*, *Anuradha*, and *Magha* <note>original: "पित्र्यस्य" (Pitryasya); Magha is ruled by the Pitris or Ancestors</note>, the results are auspicious. || 6 ||

From *Revati* to *Mrigashira*, six constellations meet the Moon in the "un-arrived" <note>term: "अनागत" (Anagata); referring to a specific astronomical conjunction before the Moon fully enters the station</note> state. From *Ardra* to *Anuradha*, twelve constellations meet the Moon in the middle. And from *Jyeshtha* to *Uttara Bhadrapada*, nine stars meet the Moon in the "passed" <note>term: "अतिक्रान्त" (Atikranta); conjunction after the Moon has passed the station's center</note> state. || 7 ||

### The Shapes of the Lunar Horns

If the horn of the Moon is slightly raised and attains a vastness like that of a boat, it is called the **Boat Configuration**. In this state, sailors suffer distress, but for all other people, it brings well-being. || 8 ||

When the horn of the Moon is half-raised, it is called the **Plough Configuration** <note>original: "लाङ्गल" (Langala)</note>. This causes suffering to those who live by the plough <note>farmers</note>, but kings remain joyful without specific cause, and there is an abundance of food. || 9 ||

If the right horn of the Moon is half-raised, it is called the **Evil Plough**. The result of this Moon is that the army of the King of the *Pandya* country <note>an ancient kingdom in South India</note> will attempt to kill their own sovereign. || 10 ||

If the Moon rises with both horns equal, there is abundance, welfare, and rain, just as on the first day. If the Moon rises straight like a **Staff** <note>original: "दण्ड" (Danda)</note>, there is suffering for cows and oxen, and kings become harsh in their punishments. || 11 ||

If the Moon rises in the shape of a **Bow** <note>original: "धनुष" (Dhanush)</note>, wars occur; however, victory belongs to the country toward which the bowstring <note>original: "मौर्वी" (Maurvi)</note> is directed. If this horn is spread out toward the South and North, it is called the **Station** or the **Yoke** <note>original: "युग" (Yuga)</note>; this causes earthquakes.

->...the harvest is excellent.<- ॥ 20 ॥

If the horn of the Moon, the lord of the stars, is struck by **Mars**, then the wicked kings of the barbarian lands <note>original: "Mlechha-desha"; referring to non-Vedic or foreign territories</note> are destroyed. If the Moon's horn is struck by **Saturn**, there is fear of weapons and fear of hunger. If the Moon's horn is pierced by **Mercury**, there is a lack of rain and famine. If it is by **Jupiter**, the greatest kings are destroyed, and if by **Venus**, then minor kings perish. However, if the Moon's horn is pierced by a planet during the bright fortnight <note>the waxing phase of the moon</note>, these results are only slight; the results for the dark fortnight <note>the waning phase</note> are described below. ॥ 21 ॥

If in the dark fortnight the Moon's horn is afflicted by **Venus**, then for seven months, pestilence or destruction falls upon the lands of Magadha, the Greeks <note>original: "Yavana"</note>, Pulinda, Nepal, Bhrungi, Maru, Kutch, Surat, Madras, Punjab, Kashmir, Kuluta, Purushada, and Usinara. ॥ 22 ॥

If the Moon's horn is pierced by **Jupiter**, then for ten months, the people of Gandhara (Kandahar), Sauviraka, Sindh, Kira, the Dravidian lands, the Brahmins of the mountain regions, and all the grains of those lands will suffer great distress. ॥ 23 ॥

If the body of the Moon is pierced by **Mars**, then for a period of six months, it destroys the industrious kings along with their vehicles <note>chariots or mounts</note> in the lands of Trigarta, Malwa, Kaulinda, Ganapati, Shibi, and Ayodhya, as well as the noble warriors <note>Kshatriyas</note> of the Kuru, Matsya, and Shukti regions. ॥ 24 ॥

If the orb of the Moon is pierced by **Saturn**, then for ten months, it brings suffering to the kings of the Arjunayana and Kuru dynasties living in the eastern regions, along with their ministers and warriors... ॥ 25 ॥

->**The Course of the Moon**<-

If the son of the Moon <note>The planet Mercury</note> should appear to cross through the Moon, he brings suffering to the regions of Magadha, Mathura, and the banks of the Vena river. In other regions to the West, he shall usher in a Golden Age <note>original: "Krita Yuga"; the first and most perfect age of the world</note>. || 26 ||

If the Moon is pierced by a comet <note>original: "Shikhi" or "Ketu"</note>, it destroys peace, health, and abundance. It brings ruin to those who live by the profession of arms and causes great distress through an increase in thieves. || 27 ||

When the Moon is already eclipsed by Rahu or Ketu <note>the nodes of the moon responsible for eclipses</note> and is then struck by a meteor, the King in whose birth-star the Moon is then situated will meet his death. || 28 ||

A Moon that appears like ashes, or is reddish in body, or devoid of rays, or dark-hued, or appears cracked or trembling, portends fear from hunger, war, disease, and bandits. || 29 ||

When the Moon appears as white as frost, the jasmine flower, the white water-lily, or a crystal—as if it had been carefully polished by Parvati, the daughter of the Mountain King <note>Himalaya</note>, to bring blessings to the night—such a sight brings prosperity to the entire world. || 30 ||

If the "Cool-Rayed One" <note>The Moon</note> is as white as a lily, a lotus stalk, or a pearl necklace, and waxes and wanes according to the proper laws of the lunar days, maintaining a natural orbit and radiance, it brings victory to all men. || 31 ||

In the bright fortnight <note>the waxing phase</note>, if the lunar days increase, the power of the Priests <note>Brahmins</note>, the Warriors <note>Kshatriyas</note>, and the common subjects also increases. If they decrease, there is loss; if they remain equal, there is stability. In the dark fortnight <note>the waning phase</note>, all these results are reversed. || 32 ||

## Chapter Five

> Because he tasted the special sweetness of the nectar <note>Amrita: the elixir of immortality</note>, it is said that even though the head of this demon was severed, it was not abandoned by its life-breaths. Some say it attained the status of a planet <note>Graha: a celestial seizer or planet</note>. || 1 || Because it is black in color and shaped like the discs of the Sun and Moon, it is truly not seen in the sky except at the time of the nodes <note>Parva: the time of an eclipse</note>, owing to a boon granted by the Lotus-Born <note>Kamalayoni: a title for Brahma, the Creator</note>. || 2 || Others teach that he has the form of a serpent with a body divided into a head and a tail. Still others say that the one called the Son of Sinhika <note>Sainhikeya: a name for Rahu</note> is formless and composed of darkness. || 3 || If Rahu were a physical body, or a head, or a circular disc, and moved with a fixed motion, how could he cause an eclipse when separated by half a zodiac <note>Bhaganardha: 180 degrees or six signs of the zodiac</note>? || 4 || If his motion were truly irregular, how could his presence be determined by calculation? And if he is defined as having a head and a tail, why does he not cause an eclipse in the interval between them? || 5 || Or if he has the form of a lordly serpent and seizes with his tail or his mouth, then why does he not seize that which stays between the head and tail?

---

If the Moon increases excessively, then the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and the subjects prosper greatly. If the Moon is diminished in the same way, there is loss for all; if it is middling, all attain equality. However, if this occurs during the dark fortnight, the result is the opposite. || 32 ||

However, because Rahu—which has a shape similar to the solar and lunar discs—is black in color, it is not visible in the sky at any time other than the moment of an eclipse due to a boon from Lord Brahma. || 1 || 2 || Some scholars say that this Rahu is serpent-like with a mouth and a tail, while other scholars say that this Rahu has no form at all, but rather is made of darkness. || 3 || If this Rahu wandering in the sky were a physical body, or just a head, or a disc, then how could this Rahu of fixed motion cause an eclipse even when separated by half a zodiac—that is, a distance of six signs? || 4 || If there were no stability in Rahu's motion, how could it be known through mathematics? And if it were of a shape possessing a mouth and a tail, why would an eclipse not occur at times other than the New Moon <note>Amavasya</note> or Full Moon <note>Purnima</note>? || 5 || If...

# The Varahi Samhita

->Page 22<-

**Why does it not cover half of the zodiac? (6)** <note>original: "bhaganarddham" - half of the circle of the stars. The author is arguing against the idea of a giant celestial serpent causing eclipses, as such a body would be visible elsewhere.</note> **If there were two Rahus, then when the Moon is eclipsed at sunset or sunrise, the Sun would also be seen eclipsed by the other Rahu moving at the same speed. (7)**

**In its own eclipse, the Moon enters the shadow of the Earth; in a solar eclipse, the Moon enters the Sun's disk. Therefore, an eclipse of the Moon does not begin from the west, nor does an eclipse of the Sun begin from the eastern half. (8)** <note>Because the Moon moves eastward, it enters the Earth's shadow from the west, but its own body covers the Sun from the west during a solar eclipse.</note>

**Just as the shadow of a tree falls long on one side, so too, night after night, the Earth's shadow is cast due to the obstruction of the Sun. (9)**

**When the Moon is in the seventh sign from the Sun and has not deviated too far to the north or south, it moves eastward and enters the Earth's shadow. (10)**

**The Moon, situated below, covers the Sun like a cloud coming from the west. Because of this, the Sun's eclipse appears different in various countries due to the observer's line of sight. (11)** <note>This explains parallax—why a solar eclipse is not visible everywhere at once, unlike a lunar eclipse.</note>

**The obstruction of the Moon is large, therefore its "horns" appear blunt when half-eclipsed. The obstruction of the Sun is small <insert>relative to the Moon's path</insert>, which is why the Sun's "horns" appear sharp. (12)** <term>Horns (Vishana): The pointed tips of the crescent shape formed during a partial eclipse.</term>

**Thus, the cause of eclipses has been explained by the ancient teachers who possessed divine vision. The statement that "Rahu is the cause" is merely a traditional scriptural convention. (13)** <note>Varahamihira is distinguishing between scientific reality and religious metaphor.</note>

**That demon who is called Rahu was granted a boon by Brahma: that he should be nourished during eclipses by the offerings made to the gods...**

***

If its shape were like a serpent, then the eclipse would sometimes happen at the mouth, sometimes at the tail, and sometimes even at the middle of the body. (6)

If someone says there are two Rahus, then while the Moon is eclipsed, rising, or setting, it would be seen that the Sun is also eclipsed by a second Rahu moving at the same speed. (7)

Whatever the case may be, at the time of a lunar eclipse, the Moon enters the shadow of the Earth, and at the time of a solar eclipse, <insert>the Moon</insert> enters the solar orb. This is the reason why a lunar eclipse does not begin from the west and a solar eclipse does not begin from the east. (8)

Just as the shadow of a tree spreads to one side by blocking the Sun, similarly, because of the blocking of the Sun, the Earth's shadow also grows long every day. (9)

At the time when the Moon stays in the seventh sign from the Sun and does not travel too far to the north or south, then the Moon, moving toward the east, enters the Earth's shadow. (10)

(At the time of a solar eclipse) the Moon, situated below the Sun, comes from the west and covers the Sun's disk like a cloud. This is why the eclipse of the Sun occurs in various ways in different countries depending on the line of sight. (11)

In this way, because the Moon's covering is large, the "horn" of the half-eclipsed Moon is very blunt, and the Sun's covering is very small, which is why the Sun's "horn" is extremely sharp. (12)

The teachers with divine vision have described the cause of eclipses in this way; however, saying that Rahu is the cause regarding the occurrence of eclipses is merely the traditional sentiment of the scriptures. (13)

The demon named Rahu...

# Chapter 5 | With Commentary

Lord Brahma granted Rahu <note>The shadow planet or demon responsible for eclipses in Indian mythology</note> a boon: "You shall be satisfied by the portions of offerings made by people during the time of an eclipse." || 14 || For this reason, Rahu's presence is recognized at the time of an eclipse. Because of this, the moon's motion is also calculated as being to the north or south <note>referring to the lunar nodes</note>; an eclipse cannot occur at any other time. If signs of an eclipse appear at any other time, they are considered merely as portents of calamity <note>original: "utpata," referring to unnatural or ill-omened events</note>. || 15 || 16 ||

An eclipse cannot be caused simply by the conjunction of five planets. Furthermore, wise scholars should not place their faith in the scriptural instruction of pouring oil into water on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight to predict an eclipse. || 17 || The extent of the solar eclipse is known through "avanati" <note>parallax in latitude</note>, and the direction is known through "valana" <note>deflection or celestial latitude</note> and "avanati." I have already explained how to determine the exact time based on the end of the "tithi" <note>lunar day</note> in my treatise on astronomical calculation <note>term: Karana - a concise astronomical text used for practical calculations</note>. || 18 ||

Brahma, the Moon, Indra, Kubera, Varuna, Agni, and Yama—these seven deities are the lords of the eclipses according to the six-month cycle of increase. || 19 || During an eclipse where Brahma is the presiding lord, there is an increase in the population of the twice-born <note>the priestly or scholarly class</note> and livestock; there is prosperity, health, and an abundance of grain. The same occurs during the Moon's period, though scholars may suffer and there may be a lack of rain. || 20 || When Indra is the lord of the eclipse, there is conflict among kings. The autumn crops are destroyed, and there is misfortune. During Kubera's [period]...

As Garga says: "On the eighth day, having cast oil into the water, one should point out the location," etc.</margin>

# Chapter 5 | With Commentary

If the eclipse begins in the first, third, fifth, or seventh odd <term>Akashamsha</term><note>A division of the sky; specifically one-seventh of the total duration of the day or night</note> of the sky, it destroys those who live by fire—such as goldsmiths and smiths—as well as virtuous Brahmins and those living in hermitages. || 28 ||

If the eclipse begins in the **second part** of the sky, it brings destruction to farmers, heretics <note>original: "Pakhandi"; referring to those following non-Vedic or unorthodox paths</note>, merchants, warriors <term>Kshatriyas</term>, and army commanders. If the eclipse begins in the **third part** of the sky, it destroys artisans <term>Karuka</term><note>Those who earn a living through manual crafts or skills</note>, laborers <term>Shudras</term>, barbarians <term>Mlechhas</term><note>A term used for foreigners or those outside the traditional Vedic social structure</note>, and government ministers. || 29 ||

If the eclipse begins in the **middle part** of the sky—that is, at midday—the King’s central territories are destroyed, though the price of grain remains favorable. If the eclipse begins in the **fifth part** of the sky, there is destruction for grass-eating animals, ministers, the royal harem, and the merchant class <term>Vaishyas</term>. || 30 ||

An eclipse in the **sixth part** of the sky harms women and laborers. If it begins in the **seventh part**—that is, at the time of sunset—it destroys thieves and those living in the borderlands or caves. However, in whichever part of the sky the <term>Moksha</term><note>The "release" or end of the eclipse</note> occurs, there will be prosperity and auspiciousness for the people and regions associated with that specific part. || 31 ||

An eclipse occurring during the **Northern Transit** <term>Uttarayana</term><note>The six-month period when the sun moves north</note> harms the priestly and warrior classes. During the **Southern Transit** <term>Dakshinayana</term>, it harms the merchant and laborer classes. Furthermore, if the shadow-demon <term>Rahu</term> is seen appearing from the North, East, South, or West, it harms the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras respectively in that clockwise order. || 32 ||

If seen in the **Northeast**, it harms the barbarian tribes; in the **Southeast**, it harms travelers; in the **South**, it harms aquatic creatures and elephants; and in the **North**, it is inauspicious for cattle. || 33 || When the Demon <note>Rahu</note> arrives from the **East**, he fills the earth with water <note>indicating heavy rains or floods</note>. From the **West**, he leads to the destruction of farmers, servants, and seeds—

---

<note>1. By dividing the total duration of the day or night on the day of the eclipse into seven parts, one determines the "seventh part of the sky."</note>

It concludes that while the start of an eclipse brings destruction to specific groups, the point of its "release" brings blessings to those same groups.</summary>

<header>Chapter 5, with Vernacular Commentary</header>

If an eclipse occurs in **Sagittarius** <note>Sanskrit: Dhanu</note>, it destroys ministers, noble horses, the people of Videha, wrestlers, and the Panchala region; it also brings ruin to physicians, merchants, and those skilled in unconventional weaponry. If the eclipse occurs in **Capricorn** <note>Sanskrit: Makara</note>, it destroys fish, families of ministers, the low-born, those skilled in counsel or the preparation of medicines, and elderly warriors.

## 41

If the eclipse occurs in **Aquarius** <note>Sanskrit: Kumbha</note>, it destroys hill-dwellers, westerners, carriers of heavy loads, thieves, the Abhira people, the Daradas, the Aryas, the people of Singhapura, and the Barbarians. If it occurs in **Pisces** <note>Sanskrit: Meena</note>, it destroys those living on the seacoast, products derived from the ocean, honorable men, scholars, and those who earn their living from water, such as fishermen and boatmen. Thus, the results of the eclipse are declared according to the "Instruction of the Tortoise" <note>Sanskrit: Kurmopadesha; a traditional geographical arrangement of India mapped onto the body of a divine tortoise</note>.

## 42

In the eclipses of the Moon and Sun, there are ten types of "grasps" <note>Sanskrit: Grasa; referring to the way the shadow enters or covers the celestial body</note>:
1. *Savya* (Right-sided)
2. *Apasavya* (Left-sided)
3. *Leha* (Licking)
4. *Grasana* (Swallowing)
5. *Nirodha* (Obstruction)
6. *Avamarda* (Crushing)
7. *Aroha* (Ascending)
8. *Aghrata* <note>The Sanskrit text uses 'Aghrata' (Smelling), while the commentary uses 'Aghata' (Striking)</note>
9. *Madhya* (Central)
10. *Tamontya* (Edge-darkening)

## 43

If the shadow moves to the right (*Savya*), the world becomes flooded with water, and the people are joyful and free from fear. In a left-sided eclipse (*Apasavya*), the subjects are destroyed due to the oppression of kings or thieves.

## 44

If the shadow licks the lunar orb like a tongue, that eclipse is called *Leha* (Licking). When this occurs, all creatures on earth are delighted, and the earth receives abundant rain.

## 45

When one-quarter, one-half, or three-quarters of the planetary orb is seized, it is called *Grasana* (Swallowing). This leads to the loss of wealth for arrogant kings and causes distress—

# Varahi Samhita
### On the Regions || 46 ||

If the darkness <note>Rahu, the shadow planet</note> seizes the edges and then remains concentrated like a lump in the center, this is known as **Obstruction** (*Nirodha*). It brings joy to all living beings. || 47 ||

If the shadow completely covers the orb and remains for a long time, it is called **Crushing** (*Avamardana*). This darkness-filled state destroys the principal regions and the most prominent kings. || 48 ||

If, after the eclipse of the orb, the darkness is seen to cover it again immediately, it is called **Ascending** (*Arohana*). This causes fear to kings through mutual conflicts and wars. || 49 ||

If the orb appears obscured on one side, like a mirror clouded by the breath of a person, it is called **Scented** (*Aghrata*). This brings the blessing of good rains and prosperity to the world. || 50 ||

If the darkness enters the center while the surrounding circle remains clear of shadow, it is called **Central Darkness** (*Madhyatama*). This causes the destruction of the middle countries and brings fear of diseases of the belly <note>internal or abdominal ailments</note>. || 51 ||

If the darkness is very thick at the edges and very slight in the center, it is called **Edge-Darkness** (*Tamontya*). This brings the fear of "iti" <note>the six calamities of agriculture: drought, floods, locusts, rats, birds, and foreign invasion</note> to the crops and fear of thieves. || 52 ||

If the shadow of Rahu is white, one should predict safety and abundance, but also suffering for the Brahmins <note>the priestly class</note>. If it is the color of fire, there is fear of fire and suffering for those who live by fire <note>such as blacksmiths or priests performing sacrifices</note>. || 53 ||

# Chapter 5 with Language Commentary
## Page 29

The destruction of crops occurs through various calamities <note>original: "iti" - refers to the six traditional agricultural calamities: drought, flood, locusts, birds, rats, and foreign invasion</note>. If Rahu appears reddish-brown <note>original: "kapila"</note>, there will be the destruction of swift-moving creatures and barbarians <note>original: "mleccha" - historically referring to non-Vedic or foreign peoples</note>, followed by famine. || 54 ||

If the color resembles the dawn sun, there will be famine, drought, and suffering for birds. If it appears somewhat smoky, one should predict welfare and abundance, though the rains will be slow. || 55 ||

If Rahu appears the color of a pigeon, dawn-red, reddish-brown, or dark brown, a fear of hunger is indicated. A pigeon-colored or black-colored Rahu brings disease to the laborer class <note>original: "shudra"</note>. || 56 ||

If it is yellow like a clear gem, it signifies the destruction of the merchant class <note>original: "vaishya"</note> but also a time of abundance. If it resembles a flame, there is a danger of fire, and if it appears like red ochre, there will be wars. || 57 ||

If Rahu appears dark like a blade of Durva grass or yellow like turmeric, a plague <note>original: "marak"</note> should be predicted. If it resembles the pale-red Trumpet flower <note>original: "patali"</note>, it brings the fear of lightning strikes. || 58 ||

A dusty or reddish appearance leads to the destruction of the warrior class <note>original: "kshatriya"</note> and brings rain. If it bears the likeness of the morning sun, a lotus, or a rainbow, there will be "wrath of the sword" <note>outbreak of armed conflict</note>. || 59 ||

Now the effects of planetary aspects are described:
If Mercury <note>original: "Saumya" or "Budh"</note> gazes upon the eclipsed orb, there will be a scarcity of ghee, honey, and oil, and fear among kings. If Mars <note>original: "Bhaum"</note> gazes upon it, there will be crushing defeat in battle, the wrath of fire, and fear of thieves. || 60 ||

Venus <note>original: "Shukra"</note> causes the destruction of crops and creates various afflictions upon the earth. Saturn <note>original: "Ravija" - literally 'son of the Sun'</note> causes drought, famine, and fear of thieves. || 61 ||

Whatever inauspicious effects have been stated through these observations of the planets at the beginning of an eclipse or at the moment of liberation <note>original: "pramokshana" - the ending of the eclipse</note>...

It also swiftly destroys the King of Kalinga along with his ministers and servants. > If an eclipse occurs in the month of *Margashirsha* <note>November-December</note>, it destroys the people of Kosala, Pundra, and the Mruga people, as well as those living on the western frontiers. It also strikes those who drink the *Soma* <note>referring to Vedic ritualists</note>. However, under this lunar influence, there will be good rain, safety, and an abundance of food. ॥ 70 ॥

> In the month of *Pausha* <note>December-January</note>, there is an obstruction or oppression of the Brahmins <note>priestly class</note> and Kshatriyas <note>warrior/ruling class</note>. Those known as the Saindhavas, the Kukuras, and the inhabitants of Videha perish. In this period, there is also scanty rain and fear, though mixed with some availability of food. ॥ 71 ॥

> In the month of *Magha* <note>January-February</note>, Rahu <note>the shadow planet responsible for eclipses</note> brings suffering to those devoted to their mothers and fathers, those of the Vashistha lineage, and those dedicated to sacred study and their religious duties. It also affects elephants and horses, and the people of Vanga, Anga, and Kashi. However, it brings rain exactly as the farmers desire. ॥ 72 ॥

> An eclipse in the month of *Phalguna* <note>February-March</note> brings pain to the regions of Vanga, Ashmaka, Avanti, and Mekala. It also causes distress to skilled dancers, the finest crops, beautiful women, archers, the warrior class, and ascetics. ॥ 73 ॥

> In the month of *Chaitra* <note>March-April</note>, distress touches painters, scribes, those addicted to singing, those who live by their beauty <note>such as actors or courtesans</note>, those knowledgeable in the *Nigamas* <note>sacred scriptures/Vedas</note>, and those who trade in gold. The people of Pundra, Odra, Kaikaya, and Ashmaka also suffer, while the rains are varied and unusual. ॥ 74 ॥

> If an eclipse occurs in the month of *Vaishakha* <note>April-May</note>, cotton, sesame, and green gram <note>mung beans</note> meet with destruction. The Ikshvakus, Yaudheyas, Shakas, and the people of Kalinga face disturbances, yet there will be a general abundance of food. ॥ 75 ॥

# The Varahi Samhita
<note>original: "वाराहीसंहिता" - also known as the Bṛhat Saṃhitā, a 6th-century encyclopedic work by Varahamihira covering astrology, planetary movements, and eclipses.</note>

...rain and great multitudes are destroyed, as well as noble men, the inhabitants of the Salva country, and the tribes of the Nishadas. <note>The Nishadas were ancient indigenous forest-dwellers or hunters mentioned in Vedic literature.</note> ॥ 76 ॥

If an eclipse occurs in the month of **Ashadha** <note>June–July</note>, then wells, embankments, river currents, and those who live on fruits and roots—such as gardeners and foresters—as well as the regions of Gandhara, Kashmir, Pulinda, and China are destroyed; however, the King of Gods <note>Indra</note> will cause rain to fall upon the earth. ॥ 77 ॥

If an eclipse is seen in the month of **Shravana** <note>July–August</note>, it destroys Kashmir, Pulinda, China, the Yavanas <note>Greeks or foreigners from the West</note>, Kurukshetra, and the Central Country <note>Madhyadesha</note>. Aside from the Kambojas, the "single-hoofed" animals <note>horses and mules</note>, the autumn crops, and the aforementioned regions, the people of other lands will rejoice with abundant grain and cover the entire earth. ॥ 78 ॥

If the Demon <note>Rahu, the celestial body responsible for eclipses</note> approaches in the month of **Bhadrapada** <note>August–September</note>, it destroys Kalinga, Bengal, Magadha, Saurashtra, the Mlecchas <note>foreigners/non-Aryans</note>, Suvira, Darada, and the Shakas. It causes the destruction of pregnancies in women, yet it brings about a time of good harvest and plenty. ॥ 79 ॥

If the Demon is seen in the month of **Ashvina** <note>September–October</note>, it destroys the Kambojas, Chinese, Yavanas, grain-thieves, the people of Bahlika and those living on the banks of the Indus River, as well as the physicians of Anarta and Paundra, and the Kirata people; however, it also brings about great abundance and food security. ॥ 80 ॥

There are ten ways in which the Sun and Moon are released from an eclipse <note>Moksha: the ending or "liberation" of the eclipse</note>; namely:
(1-2) Two types of **Jaw-cleaving** <note>Hanubheda</note>,
(3-4) Two types of **Belly-cleaving** <note>Kukshibheda</note>,
(5-6) Two types of **Wind-cleaving** <note>Vayubheda</note>,
(7) **Vomiting** <note>Samchardana</note>,
(8) **Digestion** <note>Jarana</note>,
(9) **Middle-splitting** <note>Madhyavidarana</note>, and
(10) **End-splitting** <note>Antavidarana</note>. ॥ 81 ॥

If the liberation occurs from the South-West or North-West corners, these are the two **Anus Cleaving** <note>payu-bheda: a technical term for the lower quadrants of the lunar disk</note> liberations, Right and Left respectively. Both cause minor diseases of the private parts and light rain; however, the Left one specifically causes the demise of the Queen. || 86 ||

If the eclipse begins at the Eastern part of the orb and the shadow retreats back toward the East, it is called the **Vomiting** <note>Sancharddana</note> liberation; this brings welfare to the world and happiness through abundant grain. || 87 ||

When the eclipse begins in the East but the liberation occurs toward the West, it is called the **Decay** <note>Jarana</note> liberation; when this occurs, where can people go for refuge? They are distressed by hunger and the fear of weapons. || 88 ||

If the center of the moon becomes bright first, it is called the **Middle Splitting** liberation; this causes internal rebellion or mental anger among living beings, and though it provides food, it does not bring excellent rain. There is turmoil in the kingdom. || 89 ||

If there is clarity all around the edges of the moon's disk but a thick darkness remains in the center, it is called the **Internal Tearing** <note>Antar-darana</note> liberation. # Varahi Samhita

...and there is a destruction of crops in this period. || 90 || All these modes of "release" <note>original: "moksha"; refers to the ending phase of an eclipse</note> described for the Moon should also be applied to the Sun; however, there is one distinction: where the East was specified for the Moon, the West should be assumed for the Sun. || 91 ||

If, within seven days after the release of the eclipse, there is a fall of dust, it causes a scarcity of food. A mist or fog brings the fear of disease. An earthquake signifies the death of a prominent king. || 92 ||

A falling star <note>original: "ulka"; meteor</note> destroys the ministers. Clouds of various colors appearing <insert>outside of twilight</insert> bring incomparable fear. Thunder causes the destruction of embryos <note>miscarriage or crop failure</note>, while lightning causes suffering to kings and tusked creatures <note>original: "danstri"; refers to animals like boars, tigers, or snakes</note>. || 93 ||

A halo around the sun or moon <note>original: "parivesha"</note> brings the pain of sickness. A "burning of the quarters" <note>original: "digdaha"; a preternatural redness of the horizon</note> brings fear of kings and fire. A harsh, strong wind brings fear arising from thieves. || 94 ||

A thunderclap without clouds <note>original: "nirghata"</note>, a rainbow, or a "staff" in the sky <note>original: "danda"; a vertical atmospheric phenomenon</note> brings the fear of hunger and invasion by an enemy army. A "war of the planets" <note>original: "graha-yuddha"; a close conjunction</note> leads to war between kings, and the appearance of a comet <note>original: "ketu"</note> brings the same. || 95 ||

If there is a fall of pure, natural rain within seven days of the eclipse's end, then a period of abundance <note>original: "subhiksha"</note> should be predicted. In that case, all the evil effects generated by the eclipse come to an end. || 96 ||

If a solar eclipse occurs at the end of the same fortnight <note>original: "paksha"; a 15-day lunar cycle</note> after a lunar eclipse has ended, it leads to injustice among the subjects and mutual enmity between husbands and wives. || 97 ||

But if a lunar eclipse is seen after a solar eclipse, then the Brahmins <note>the priestly/scholarly class</note> obtain the fruits of many sacrifices, and the subjects live in joy. || 98 ||

# Chapter Six
## The Movement of Mars

If Mars begins its retrograde motion <note>vakra: the apparent backward movement of a planet</note> in the seventh, eighth, or ninth mansion from the constellation of its rising, that retrograde is called **"Ushna"** (The Scorching). During this rising, those who earn their living through fire <note>such as smiths or cooks</note> suffer distress. || 1 ||

If Mars turns retrograde from the tenth, eleventh, or twelfth constellation from its rising, that retrograde is called **"Ashrumukha"** (The Tearful Face). At the time of its rising, all juices <note>rasas: essential fluids, sap, or flavors</note> become corrupted, and it causes diseases and a lack of rain. || 2 ||

Similarly, if the ripening <note>vipaka: the manifestation of effects</note> or retrograde of Mars occurs in the thirteenth or fourteenth constellation from the one in which it sets, this retrograde is named **"Vyala"** (The Serpent/Beast). This causes distress from tusked animals, serpents, and wild beasts, yet results in a good harvest. || 3 ||

If the retrograde of Mars occurs from the fifteenth or sixteenth constellation from its setting, it is the retrograde named **"Rudhirana"** (The Bloody-Faced). At that time, people suffer from diseases of the mouth and fear, though a good harvest prevails. || 4 ||

If the sub-retrograde <note>anuvakra: a secondary backward movement</note> of Mars occurs from the seventeenth or eighteenth constellation from its setting, it is named **"Asimushala"** (The Sword and Club). This causes fear of thieves, fear of weapons, and a lack of rain. || 5 || If the planet Mars, having risen in the constellations of Purva Phalguni or Uttara Phalguni, then turns back...

---

If a lunar eclipse occurs one fortnight after a solar eclipse, the community of Brahmins shall obtain the fruits of many sacrifices and perform many rituals; the subjects will be joyful. || 98 ||

If Mars is retrograde in the seventh, eighth, or ninth constellation from the constellation in which it rises, that retrograde is called **"Ushna"**; during this "Scorching" retrograde rising, people who live by fire suffer pain. || 1 ||
If Mars is retrograde from the tenth, eleventh, or twelfth constellation from the rising constellation, that retrograde is called **"Ashrumukha"**; at the time of its rising, all juices are spoiled, and there is disease and drought. || 2 ||
Likewise, in whichever constellation Mars sets, if the ripening or retrograde of Mars occurs in the thirteenth or fourteenth constellation from that setting constellation, the name of this retrograde is **"Vyala"**; in this, there is pain from tusked creatures, snakes, and deer, but there is a good harvest. || 3 ||
If the retrograde of Mars is from the fifteenth or sixteenth constellation from the setting constellation, the **"Rudhiranan"** retrograde occurs; at that time, people have mouth diseases and fear, and a good harvest occurs. || 4 ||
If the sub-retrograde of Mars is from the seventeenth or eighteenth constellation from the setting constellation, the **"Asimushala"** retrograde occurs; from this, there is fear of thieves, fear of weapons, and drought. || 5 ||
If the planet Mars, having risen in the Purva Phalguni or Uttara Phalguni constellations, returns...

# The Varahi Samhita

If Mars <note>original: "Bhauma"</note> begins its retrograde motion in the constellation of *Uttara Ashadha* and sets in the constellation of *Rohini*, it causes suffering across all three worlds <note>Heaven, Earth, and the Underworld</note>. || 6 ||

If Mars rises in *Shravana* and enters a retrograde cycle in *Pushya*, it brings suffering to consecrated kings <note>original: "murdhabhishikta," literally 'those whose heads are sprinkled with holy water,' referring to the warrior caste or royalty</note>. In whichever constellation Mars rises, it destroys the people living in the direction associated with that constellation. || 7 ||

If the Red Planet <note>original: "Lohita," a name for Mars</note> moves back and forth through the middle of the *Magha* constellation, then the Pandya King <note>a dynasty in Southern India</note> will perish, and there will be danger from weapons and a lack of rain. || 8 ||

If Mars pierces through *Magha* and then pierces *Vishakha*, it causes famine. If it pierces through *Rohini* as it moves, it causes a terrible plague <note>original: "maraka"</note>. || 9 ||

Moving to the south of *Rohini*, the Son of the Earth <note>original: "Mahija," a name for Mars</note> causes high prices and suppresses the rains. If he appears smoky or possesses a crest <note>likely referring to a cometary appearance or atmospheric distortion</note>, he will destroy those living in the Pariyatra mountains <note>the western Vindhya range</note>. || 10 ||

When the Son of the Earth <note>original: "Kshmatanaya"</note> wanders through *Rohini*, *Shravana*, *Mula*, the three *Uttaras* <note>Uttara Phalguni, Uttara Ashadha, and Uttara Bhadrapada</note>, and *Jyeshtha* <note>original: "Shakra"</note>, he causes the destruction of the clouds <note>drought</note>. || 11 ||

The rising and movement of Mars <note>original: "Kuja"</note> are considered auspicious when they occur in the constellations of *Shravana*, *Magha*, *Punarvasu* <note>original: "Aditya"</note>, *Mula*, *Hasta*, *Purva Bhadrapada* <note>original: "Ekapada"</note>, *Ashvini*, *Vishakha*, and *Rohini*. || 12 ||

If the Son of the Earth <note>original: "Medinija"</note> appears large and clear in form, with the color of the *Kimshuka* or *Ashoka* flower <note>vibrant red/orange</note>, with bright and beautiful rays and a glow like heated copper, and if he travels the northern path, he brings prosperity to forest-dwellers and joy to the people. || 13 ||

# Now Begins the Seventh Chapter

-> The Transit of Mercury <-
<note>original: "Budha-chara". In Vedic astrology, Mercury is known as Budha, the son of the Moon.</note>

The son of the Moon <note>Mercury</note> never rises without some portentous event occurring. His appearance usually brings the fear of floods, fire, or high winds, and causes either a decrease or an increase in the price of grain. || 1 ||

When the son of the Moon wanders through or "crushes" <note>an astrological term for an unfavorable transit or occultation</note> the constellations of Shravana, Dhanishta, Rohini, Mrigashira, or Uttarashadha, he causes a lack of rain and the fear of disease. || 2 ||

If the son of the Moon stays in any of the constellations starting from Ardra up to Magha, there will be suffering for the people due to the clash of weapons <note>war</note>, hunger, fear, disease, drought, and great distress. || 3 ||

If the son of the Moon wanders through the six constellations starting from Hasta <note>Hasta, Chitra, Swati, Vishakha, Anuradha, and Jyeshtha</note>, it is inauspicious for cattle, causes the price of oils to rise, but fills the earth with many kinds of food grains. || 4 ||

If the constellations of Uttara Phalguni, Krittika, Uttarabhadrapada, and Bharani are struck by Mercury, it causes the wasting away of the bodily humors <note>dhatus</note> in living beings. || 5 ||

If the son of the Moon pierces the constellations of Ashwini, Shatabhisha, Mula, and Revati, it brings disaster to trade goods, physicians, sailors, aquatic products, and horses. || 6 ||

If the son of the Moon should crush even one of the three "Purva" constellations <note>Purva Phalguni, Purva Ashadha, and Purva Bhadrapada</note>, then hunger, weapons, thieves, and sickness—

---

<note>The following paragraph is the conclusion of the previous chapter regarding Mars, followed by the formal closing of that chapter.</note>

A Mars that is the color of an Ashoka flower, with clear and beautiful rays, and possessing the luster of molten copper, brings good fortune to kings and happiness to the people when it wanders in the northern path. || 13 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter of the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the Great Teacher Varahamihira, with the commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province. || 6 ||

# Chapter 7: The Transit of Mercury (with Commentary)

According to the opinion of the sage Devala, the motions of Mercury are classified as follows: **Straight**, **Rapid Retrograde**, **Retrograde**, and **Irregular**. The duration for each of these stages, starting from the Straight motion, is calculated by multiplying the numbers five, four, two, and one by six respectively <note>This results in 30, 24, 12, and 6 days for each phase</note>. || 15 ||

The **Straight** motion is beneficial for all living beings. **Rapid Retrograde** motion destroys wealth. **Retrograde** motion brings the fear of weapons <note>likely referring to war or conflict</note>, and **Irregular** motion generates fear and disease. || 16 ||

If the son of the Moon <note>Mercury, known as *Budha* in Sanskrit</note> is visible during the months of *Pausha*, *Ashadha*, *Shravana*, *Vaishakha*, or *Magha* <note>roughly spanning mid-winter to mid-summer</note>, it brings fear to the world. However, if it sets <note>becomes invisible</note> during these months, it produces auspicious results. || 17 ||

If the son of the Cold-Rayed One <note>Mercury</note> is seen in the months of *Kartika* or *Ashwayuja* <note>autumn</note>, then there is danger from weapons, thieves, fire, disease, floods, and hunger. || 18 ||

Those scholars who are well-versed in the movements of Mercury say that cities which are besieged or blockaded when Mercury sets are liberated when the planet rises again. Others, however, state that if Mercury rises in the West, those cities will experience gain and prosperity. || 19 ||

When the son of the Moon possesses the brilliance of gold, or the green hue of a parrot, or resembles the color of an emerald <note>original: *Sasyaka* gem</note>, and when his form is clear, bright, and large, it is for the welfare of all. If the appearance is the opposite of this, it does not bring good fortune. || 20 ||

### Thus ends the Seventh Chapter, titled "The Transit of Mercury," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 7 ||

---

<column-break/>

The motions are of four types: namely, **Straight**, **Rapid Retrograde**, **Retrograde**, and **Irregular**. The duration for which these motions exist is, in order: 30 days, 24 days, 12 days, and exactly 6 days. || 15 ||

**Straight** motion is beneficial to the subjects; **Rapid Retrograde** motion causes the destruction of wealth; in **Retrograde** motion there is fear of weapons; and in **Irregular** motion, there is fear and sickness. || 16 ||

If the planet Mercury is visible in the months of *Pausha*, *Ashadha*, *Shravana*, *Vaishakha*, or *Magha*, the world faces fear. If it sets during this time, it is auspicious. || 17 ||

If Mercury, the son of the Moon, is seen in the months of *Kartika* or *Ashwin*, then there is fear of weapons, thieves, fire, disease, water, and hunger. || 18 ||

Pandits who are thoroughly knowledgeable in the transit of Mercury say that cities which are restricted <note>besieged</note> during the period Mercury is set are released at the time of Mercury's rising. Some say that if Mercury rises in the western direction, then all the cities in that direction receive benefits. || 19 ||

When the color of Mercury, the son of the Moon, is like gold, or like a parrot, or like an emerald, and when Mercury's image is stainless and large, then everyone's well-being is assured. If it is not so, then only inauspiciousness occurs. || 20 ||

# Chapter Eight

## The Transit of Jupiter

The year is to be named after the lunar mansion <term>Nakshatra; one of the 27 sectors of the sky along the moon's path</term> in which the Minister of the Lord of the Gods <note>original: "devapatimantrī" referring to the planet Jupiter</note> rises. The years follow the sequence of the months. || 1 ||

The years, beginning with Kārttika, are assigned to two lunar mansions each, starting from the constellation Āgneya <note>the star Krittikā or the Pleiades</note>. However, the fifth, eleventh, and twelfth years in the sequence are assigned to three lunar mansions each. || 2 ||

In the year of Kārttika, there is suffering for those who live by the cart <note>traders and nomads</note> and those who live by fire <note>blacksmiths or priests</note>, as well as distress for cattle. There is an outbreak of diseases and violence from weapons. However, there is an abundance of red and yellow flowers. || 3 ||

In the year of Saumya <note>the year associated with the month of Mārgaśīrṣa</note>, there is a lack of rain. Crops are destroyed by deer, mice, locusts, and birds <note>original: "andajaiḥ" or 'the egg-born'</note>. There is fear of disease, and even among friends, kings find enmity. || 4 ||

The year of Pauṣa brings welfare to the world. Kings abandon their mutual hostilities. The price of grain increases two or three-fold, and there is success in all nourishing and protective rites <term>Pauṣṭika; rituals performed for growth and prosperity</term>. || 5 ||

In the year of Māgha, the worship of the ancestors <note>Pitṛs</note> increases, and there is a sense of goodwill among all living beings. There is health, good rainfall, fair prices for grain, wealth, and the gaining of friends. || 6 || In the year of Phālguna, in some places...

---

When Jupiter, the minister of Indra, rises in the lunar mansion of a particular month, that year is named after that month. || 1 ||

Since there are twelve months, there are twelve such years. Starting from the Krittikā mansion, each year generally covers two mansions. However, among these twelve years, the fifth, eleventh, and twelfth years will cover three mansions each. For example, if Jupiter rises in Krittikā or Rohiṇī, it is called the year of Kārttika. || 2 ||

(1) If it is the year named Kārttika, those who earn their living by carts (such as traveling traders), those who live by fire, and the cattle suffer distress. People are afflicted by diseases and the fury of weapons. Red and yellow colored flowers flourish. || 3 ||

(2) If it is the year named Saumya, there is a drought. Grain is damaged by deer, rats, locusts, and birds. Men fear disease, and kings become enemies even with their friends. || 4 ||

(3) In the year named Pauṣa, the world fares well. Kings set aside their mutual animosity. The price of grain becomes double or triple, and there is an increase in acts of prosperity. || 5 ||

(4) In the year named Māgha, the worship of the ancestors increases. All creatures experience well-being. There is health, excellent rain, good prices for grain, great wealth, and the acquisition of friends. || 6 ||

(5) In the year named Phālguna, there is prosperity and an increase in grain in some places; however, there is misfortune for women, a prevalence of thieves, and harshness among kings.

Kings are mild-mannered. There is an increase in the treasury and grain, but those who are beautiful suffer distress. || 8 ||

In the year of **Vaishakha** <note>Approx. April-May</note>, the subjects are devoted to righteousness, free from fear, and joyful. The kings are virtuous. There is a tendency toward performing sacrifices <note>Yajna</note>, and all crops reach fulfillment. || 9 ||

In the year of **Jyeshtha** <note>Approx. May-June</note>, kings are considered superior in caste, lineage, wealth, and status, and they are knowers of the law. All grains suffer, except for foxtail millet and the legume varieties. || 10 ||

In the year of **Ashadha** <note>Approx. June-July</note>, crops grow, but there is a lack of rain in some places. <term>Yogakshema</term> <note>A compound term meaning the acquisition of what one does not have (Yoga) and the preservation of what one already possesses (Kshema)</note> is mediocre, and the rulers of the earth become very anxious. || 11 ||

In the year of **Bhadrapada** <note>Approx. August-September</note>, creeping plants and early crops reach fulfillment. Other crops do not grow; in some places there is abundance, and in others, there is fear. || 13 ||

In the year of **Ashwayuja** <note>Also known as Ashwin, approx. September-October</note>, water falls incessantly. The subjects are joyful and secure. There is a restoration of vitality for all living beings and an abundance of food. || 14 ||

When **Jupiter** <note>Sanskrit: Brihaspati</note> moves to the North of the constellations, he brings health, abundance, and security to men. When in the South, the opposite occurs; in the middle, the results are moderate. || 15 ||

If Jupiter wanders through two constellations <note>nakshatras</note> in a single year, it is considered auspicious. If he traverses two and a half constellations in that time, the results are mediocre. However, should he ever wander through more than that in a year, it results in the total destruction of crops. || 16 ||

If Jupiter appears the color of fire, there is a danger of fire; if he is yellow, disease follows; if dark or blackish, a war is coming. If he appears green, there will be suffering caused by thieves; if red, there is fear of weapons <note>war or violence</note>; and if he is the color of smoke, there will be a drought. If the Guru of the Gods <note>Jupiter</note> is seen during the day, it foretells the death of a king. If he is seen at night, large, clear, and with bright rays, the subjects will be healthy and at peace. || 17-18 ||

The constellations Rohini and Krittika <note>original: "analabham," the fire-star</note> are the body of the Year-Spirit <note>Vatsara-tanu</note>; the two Ashadhas <note>Purva and Uttara</note> are the navel; Ashlesha <note>the serpent star</note> is the heart; and Magha <note>the ancestral star</note> is the flower. If these are clear and unaffected, the results are auspicious. If the body of the Year-Spirit is afflicted by cruel planets <note>malefics like Mars or Saturn</note>, there is danger from fire and wind. If the navel is afflicted, there is fear of hunger. If Pushya is afflicted, there is a loss of roots and fruits; and if the heart is afflicted, the destruction of crops is certain. || 19 ||

Take the years elapsed since the era of the Saka King <note>the Shalivahana era, starting 78 CE</note>, multiply them by eleven, and then multiply that product by four. To this, add 8589. Divide the total by 3750. || 20 ||

Add the resulting quotient to the original Saka era years. Divide this sum by sixty, and then divide the remainder by five. This identifies the Yugas <note>five-year cycles</note> beginning with the one dedicated to Lord Narayana; the remaining years follow in their respective order...

> ...shall be. || 21 || Add one to each of the years multiplied by nine, then separately add twelve in sequence; having multiplied... <note>original: "स्युः ॥ २१ ॥ एकैकमब्देषु नवाहतेषु दत्त्वा पृथग्द्वादशकं क्रमेण । हत्वा"</note>

---

Add 8589 to the product. Divide this sum by 3750. Then, add this quotient to the digits of the Shaka year <term>Shaka year: an era in the Indian calendar starting in 78 CE</term> in the second position; divide this total by 60 (the remainder will indicate the year in the cycle starting from Prabhava). It is then proper to divide that remainder by 5; whatever is obtained from this division, that quotient represents the Era of Narayana (Vishnu) etc., and the remaining digits indicate how many years of that specific era have passed. || 20 || 21 || Divide the number of said years by 12. Add the quotient to this nine-fold digit and divide by 4; the resulting number indicates the constellation <term>Nakshatra: lunar mansion or star cluster</term> in which Jupiter is present—

---

<margin>+ By dividing by this, the quotient gives the years. Multiply the remainder by 12 and divide by 3750 to get the months. Then multiply the remainder by 30 and divide by the same divisor of 3750 to get the days. Multiply the remaining by 60 and divide by 3750 to get the <term>Danda: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term>. Multiply the final remainder again by 60 and divide by 3750 to get the <term>Pala: a unit of time equal to 24 seconds</term> and so on. Continue this process of multiplying by 60 and dividing by 3750 until no remainder remains. After establishing all these values according to the rules, add them to the digits in the second position.</margin>

-> $\frac{( Shaka \times 11 \times 4 ) + 8589}{3750} + Shaka \div 60$ = Result of the Jovian Year etc. <-

The calculation is as follows—for the Shaka solar year 1813—

-> $\frac{( 1813 \times 11 \times 4 ) + 8589}{3750} + Shaka \div 60$ = Result of the Jovian Year etc. <-

1813 $\times$ 11 $\times$ 4 = 79772. 79772 + 8589 = 88361. 88361 $\div$ 3750 = 23 Years, 6 Months, 22 Days, 29 Dandas, 21 Palas, 36 Vipalas. 1813 + 23 | 6 | 22 | 29 | 21 | 36 = 1836 | 6 | 22 | 29 | 21 | 36. 1836 | 6 | 22 | 29 | 21 | 36 $\div$ 60 = 30 (Remainder - Jovian Year). The remainder is 36 | 6 | 22 | 29 | 21 | 36. Dividing this by five gives 7 (Quotient - Era/Yuga). From this, it is known that of the 60 years starting from Prabhava, the 36th year has passed, and 6 months, 22 days, 29 Dandas, 21 Palas, and 36 Vipalas of the 37th year have elapsed. The quotient for the Era is 7; this means 7 Eras of the Vishnu cycle have passed and the 8th Era is current, and 1 year, 6 months, 22 days, 29 Dandas, 21 Palas, and 36 Vipalas of this Era have passed. This is the calculation for the beginning of the month of Vaishakha <note>April-May</note> in the Shaka year 1813.

# Varahi Samhita (The Compendium of Varahamihira)

## The constellations beginning with Vasu <note>Dhanishta</note> are divided by four; the remainder indicates the portion of the year. || 22 || Vishnu, the Teacher of the Gods <note>Jupiter/Brihaspati</note>, the Destroyer of Cities <note>Indra</note>, the Fire-God <note>Agni</note>, Tvashtar, and the Lord of the Uttara-Prosthapada <note>Ahirbudhnya</note> are the lords of the Yugas in order, followed by the Ancestors <note>Pitris</note>, the Universal Gods <note>Vishvedevas</note>, the Moon <note>Soma</note>, Indra-Agni, the Twin Physicians <note>Ashvins</note>, and Bhaga. || 23 || The first year is Samvatsara (ruled by Fire), the second is Parivatsara (ruled by the Sun), the third is Idavatsara (ruled by the Moon), the fourth is Anuvatsara (ruled by Prajapati), and the fifth is Idvatsara (ruled by the Lord of the Mountain’s Daughter <note>Shiva</note>). || 24 || Rain falls at the beginning of the first year, is abundant in the second, and is released later in the third...

Understand this: during calculation, one should count from the 24th constellation. * That is, if the result is 1, it refers to the 25th constellation, Purva-Bhadrapada; if 2, then the 26th, Uttara-Bhadrapada, and so on. || 22 || In the sixty-year cycle of Jupiter, there are 12 Yugas in total; each Yuga consists of five years. The presiding deities of these twelve Yugas are, in order: 1. Vishnu, 2. Brihaspati, 3. Indra, 4. Agni, 5. Tvashtar, 6. Ahirbudhnya, 7. The Pitris, 8. The Vishvedevas, 9. Soma, 10. Indra-Agni, 11. The Ashvins, and 12. Bhaga. The Yugas are named after these presiding deities, such as the Narayana-Yuga, the Brihaspati-Yuga, the Indra-Yuga, the Agni-Yuga, etc. || 23 || Within these Yugas, the five individual years have specific names and deities + (these are distinct from the sixty-year names). Their names and lords are: 1. Samvatsara (Lord: Agni), 2. Parivatsara (Lord: the Sun), 3. Idavatsara (Lord: the Moon), 4. Anuvatsara (Lord: Prajapati), 5. Idvatsara (Lord: Mahadeva/Shiva). || 24 || Regarding the description of these five years...

->* (60-year cycle × 9) + (60-year cycle ÷ 12)<-
->--------------------------------- = The constellation occupied by Jupiter.<-
->4<-

Calculation example: 36. 6. 22. 21. 21. 36. Jovian sixty-year cycle etc.
->(36 × 9) + (36 ÷ 12)<-
->--------------------- = 36 × 9 = 324. 36 ÷ 12 = 3. 324 + 3 = 327. 327 ÷ 4 = 81 and 3/4.<-
->4<-

---

Since the <term>Bhachakra</term> <note>the zodiacal wheel</note> consists of 27 constellations: 81 divided by 27 leaves a remainder of 3. Thus, it is known that Jupiter is currently in the 24th constellation. Since the remainder was 3/4, it has passed the third quarter of the 24th constellation and is currently in the fourth quarter. This is a general calculation; occasionally, minor differences may be observed. For precise accuracy, one should consult the <term>Panchasiddhantika</term> <note>Varahamihira's treatise on the five astronomical schools</note>. It is not detailed here for fear of making the text too long.

+ According to Varahamihira, these years begin at the start of the Yuga. According to the famous scholar of law Raghunandana Bhattacharya, these years begin from the start of the month of Vaishakha. In his view, one should donate sesame seeds and other items during these years. "The donation of sesame in the Samvatsara year yields great fruit," etc. This is also the opinion found in the <term>Dana-Sagara</term> <note>Sea of Charity</note> composed by Ballala Sena, as mentioned in the *Malamasa-Tattva*.

# Chapter 8 | With Language Commentary
## Page 46

The fourth year is said to have little water, and the fifth year is described as having moderate rain. || 25 || There are four primary eras (Yugas) among these, whose presiding deities are **Vishnu**, **Indra**, **Jupiter**, and **Agni** <note>The Fire God</note>. These four eras are the best. The four middle eras are of middling quality, and the final four should be known as the lowest or least auspicious. || 26 || When **Jupiter** <note>Sanskrit: *Surejya*, the teacher of the gods</note>, having entered the first part of the **Dhanishta** constellation, rises in the month of **Magha** <note>January/February</note>, then the first year of the sixty-year cycle, named **Prabhava**, begins. That year is beneficial for all living beings. || 27 || Although during the current year of **Prabhava** there may be drought in some places, disturbances from wind or fire in others, and outbreaks of <term>Iti-bhaya</term> <note>The six agricultural calamities: drought, floods, locusts, rats, birds, and foreign invasion</note> or diseases caused by phlegm <note>Sanskrit: *Shleshma*</note>, nevertheless, people do not experience great suffering in this year. || 28 || After that, the second year is declared to be **Vibhava**, the third is **Shukra**, the fourth is **Pramoda**, and the fifth is **Prajapati**. These years are progressively more auspicious in their results. || 29 || During these years, the kings rule the earth <note>Sanskrit: *Bhutadhatri*, the supporter of beings</note> in such a way that, by the virtue of their governance, the earth abounds in crops like rice, sugarcane, and barley. It becomes free from fear, hostilities are pacified, and the people are joyful and liberated from the vices of the **Kali Yuga** <note>The current dark age in Hindu cosmology</note>. || 30 || In the second era (the era of **Jupiter**), there are five years named: **Angira**, **Shrimukha**, **Bhava**, **Yuva**, and **Dhata**. Among these, three are auspicious and the other two are mediocre. || 31 || During the three years starting with **Angira**, there is abundant rain—

It has been said: in the first year of this cycle, there is rain; at the beginning of the second year, there is rain; in the third year, there is excessive rain; in the remainder of the fourth, there is rain; and in the fifth year, there is ordinary rain. || 25 || Regarding the twelve eras previously described, the first four among them—whose lords are <term>Vishnu</term>, <term>Indra</term>, <term>Jupiter</term> <note>Brihaspati</note>, and <term>Agni</term>—are the best. This year is a benefactor to all creatures. || 27 || While the year named Prabhava is active, even if there is a lack of rain in some places, or the wrath of wind and fire in others, or <term>Iti-bhaya</term> <note>Agricultural pests or disasters</note> and suffering from phlegm-related illnesses in some places, even so, living beings do not face extraordinary sorrow in this year. || 28 || The name of the second year is Vibhava, the third is Shukra, the fourth is Pramoda, and the fifth year is named <term>Prajapati</term>. In the Era of Indra <note>Shakra Yuga</note>, the first year is called **Ishvara** <term>Lordly</term>, the second is **Bahudhanya** <term>Abundant Grain</term>, followed by **Pramathin** <term>Tormentor</term>, **Vikrama** <term>Valor</term>, and **Vrisha** <term>Bull/Virtue</term>, according to the movement of Jupiter. (33)

The first and second years are auspicious, making the subjects feel as if the Golden Age <note>Krita Yuga</note> has returned. However, the year **Pramathin** is sinful. The years **Vikrama** and **Vrisha** provide good harvests but also bring the fear of disease. (34)

The first year of the fourth era (the Era of Fire) is called **Chitrabhanu** <term>Bright Sun</term>, which is said to be excellent. The second, named **Subhanu** <term>Beautiful Sun</term>, is mediocre; it brings disease but is not fatal. (35)

Following that is **Tarana** <term>Crossing/Rescue</term>, which brings abundant rain, and **Parthiva** <term>Earthly</term>, which is celebrated for the growth of crops. The fifth is **Vyaya** <term>Expenditure/Passing</term>, which is considered beautiful and filled with festivals, where the power of desire <note>Manmatha</note> prevails. (36)

In the Era of Tvashtar <note>the Divine Architect</note>, the first year is called **Sarvajit** <term>All-Conquering</term>, and the next is **Sarvadhari** <term>All-Supporting</term>. After these come **Virodhi** <term>Opposing</term>, **Vikrita** <term>Deformed</term>, and **Khara** <term>Harsh</term>. In this group, the second year is favorable, while the rest lead to fear. In this era, the first three are beautiful, **Manmatha** yields moderate results, and the last one is the worst. (38)

In the seventh era <note>The Pitri Yuga</note>, the first year is Hemalamba, followed by Vilambi, then Vikari, Sharvari, and the fifth year according to the movement of Jupiter is known as Plava. **[39]** In the first of these years, there is a prevalence of calamities <term>iti: six traditional agricultural disasters including droughts, floods, and pests</term> and heavy winds with rain. In the second year, crops are sparse and there is little water. In the third, there is great anxiety but abundant water. The fourth year leads to famine, but the year Plava is auspicious with plenty of water. **[40]**

In the era of the Universal Gods <note>The Vishvadeva Yuga</note>, the first year is Shobhakrit, the second is Shubhakrit, the third is Krodhi, followed in order by Vishvavasu and Parabhava. **[41]** The first and second of these bring joy to the people. The third year brings many faults and hardships. The final two are mediocre, but in the year Parabhava, there is danger from fire, weapons, and disease, as well as distress for priests <note>Brahmins</note> and cows. **[42]**

The first year in the ninth era <note>The Saumya Yuga</note> is Plavanga, the next is Kilaka, followed by Saumya, Sadharana, and the fifth is Rodhakrit. The years named Kilaka and Saumya are givers of great fortune. **[43]** The year Plavanga brings much suffering to the people. In Sadharana, there is little rain and fear of calamities. In the fifth year, named Rodhakrit, there is wonderful rain and a wealth of crops. **[44]**

# The Varāhī Saṃhitā
<note>Also known as the Bṛhat Saṃhitā, an encyclopedic 6th-century Sanskrit text on astrology and natural omens by Varāhamihira.</note>

->Page 48<-

...and the one named [Ananda]. In the year **Paridhavi**, there is destruction in the Middle Country <note>Madhyadeśa, the central region of ancient India</note>, loss of kings, little rain, and danger from fire. In the year **Pramadi**, people become extremely lazy; there is rebellion <note>original: "damara," meaning riot or civil unrest</note> and the destruction of red-colored flowers and seeds. The following year, **Ananda**, brings joy to all people. The year **Rakshasa** causes decay, as does **Anala**. Specifically, in the Rakshasa year, summer crops are produced, while the Anala year brings the wrath of fire and provides hellish suffering. ||45-47||

In the eleventh cycle <note>The Ashvini Yuga</note>, there are five years: 1. **Pingala**, 2. **Kalayukta**, 3. **Siddhartha**, 4. **Raudra**, and 5. **Durmati**. In the first of these, there is heavy rain, fear of thieves, and diseases such as asthma and coughing that causes the chin to tremble. The year **Kalayukta** brings many faults and evils. The year **Siddhartha** possesses many virtues. The year **Raudra** is described as extremely fierce and destructive, while **Durmati** brings moderate rainfall. ||48-49||

In the twelfth cycle, presided over by Bhaga <note>The deity of fortune</note>, the first year is named **Dundubhi**; it causes a great increase in crops. After that, the second year, named **Udgari** <note>In other traditions called Rudhirodgari</note>, leads to the destruction of kings and uneven rainfall. The third year is called **Raktaksha**; in this year, there is fear of biting creatures <note>original: "danstra," referring to fangs or tusks</note> and diseases. The fourth year is named **Krodha**; it causes much anger and leaves the districts empty due to conflicts. ||50-51||

The final year of this final cycle is named **Kshaya**. It causes much destruction and brings fear to the Brahmins <note>The priestly/scholarly class</note>, but it grants growth to the farmers. It brings prosperity to the Vaishyas and Shudras <note>The merchant and laboring classes</note> and to those who live by others' wealth. Thus is described the entirety of the sixty-year cycle...

## The Transit of Venus.

The Go path consists of Ashwini, Revati, Purva Bhadrapada, and Uttara Bhadrapada. || 2 || In the Jaradgavi path are the three mansions starting from Shravana...

In this manner, the entire results of the sixty-year cycle have been told in brief. || 50 || 51 || 52 || If Jupiter, the teacher of the gods, who possesses pure rays, a stout body, and a luster like the white lily, the Kunda flower, or crystal, is not pierced by any planet and moves in the best path, he is beneficial to men. || 53 ||
