# The Varāhī Saṃhitā
<page-num>50</page-num>

The first path begins with the constellation Anuradha <note>original: "Maitrādyam"</note>. The constellations Hasta, Vishakha, Chitra <note>original: "Tvāṣṭra"</note>, Ashwini <note>original: "Aja"</note>, the two Ashadhas, and Krittika <note>original: "Dahana"</note> follow in sequence. ॥ 3 ॥

There are three paths each located in the Northern, Middle, and Southern routes. Within those, each individual path is further situated in a northern, middle, or southern position. ॥ 4 ॥

Other authorities describe the paths of the stars as they are actually situated in the sky. The stars of the constellations are likewise positioned in the south, north, or middle. ॥ 5 ॥

Some state that the Northern Route begins with the constellation Bharani <note>original: "Yāmya"</note>, the Middle Route begins with Purva Phalguni <note>original: "Bhāgya"</note>, and the Southern Route begins with Purva Ashadha. These are the routes as defined by some. ॥ 6 ॥

Astrology <term>Jyotish: the science of light and heavenly bodies</term> is a traditional scripture <term>Agama-shastra: sacred tradition handed down</term>; it is not appropriate for us to simply speculate when there are contradictions. Rather, I shall state the opinions of many authorities. ॥ 7 ॥

When Venus <note>original: "Shukra"</note> rises or sets while situated in the Northern Paths, it brings abundance of food and well-being. In the Middle Paths, it gives moderate results, and in the Southern Paths, the results are painful. ॥ 8 ॥

One should declare the results as: most excellent, excellent, slightly less, even, middling, low, poor, painful, and most painful, respectively, according to the paths starting from the northernmost one. ॥ 9 ॥

The first circle <term>Mandala: a group or cycle</term> consisting of the four constellations beginning with Bharani brings abundance. It influences the regions of Vanga <note>Bengal</note>, Anga, Mahisha, Bahlika, and Kalinga...

---

In the constellation Krittika <note>Dahana</note>, the path is known as the "Burning Path." ॥ 3 ॥ In this way, with twenty-seven constellations divided into nine paths, each path occurs three times. Therefore, among all these paths, three paths each reside in the Sun's Northern, Middle, and Southern routes. Furthermore, each one is situated sequentially in a northern, middle, or southern track. For example, there are three "Serpent Paths" <note>Naga-vithi</note>; the first is in the Northern Route, the second in the Middle, and the third in the Southern Route. ॥ 4 ॥

Some great souls say that just as the junction stars <term>Yoga-tara: the principal star of a lunar mansion used for astronomical calculations</term> of all constellations are situated in the northern, middle, and southern parts of the asterismal path, all the planetary paths are situated exactly the same way. ॥ 5 ॥

According to the opinion of some scholars, the Northern Route begins from Bharani, the Middle Route from Purva Phalguni, and the Southern Route from Purva Ashadha. ॥ 6 ॥

Astrology is a traditional science; resolving a matter through mere doubt is beyond my (a person like me) capability. Therefore, (without blaming the opinion of any sage or supporting only one), I shall reveal the opinions of many. ॥ 7 ॥

At the time when the preceptor of the demons, Venus <note>Shukracharya</note>, is situated in the Northern Path during its rise <margin>•</margin> or setting, then there will be abundance of food or auspiciousness. Being in the Middle Path results in middling fruits, and being in the Southern Path results in troublesome consequences. ॥ 8 ॥

Starting from the constellation Ardra and ending with Mrigashira, there are nine paths; if the rising or setting of Venus occurs in these, the results produced are, in order: most excellent, excellent, diminished, even, middling, low, base, painful, and most painful. ॥ 9 ॥

The circle or path that consists of the four constellations starting from Bharani—

# Chapter 9: With Language Commentary

-> Fear Arising in the Nations <-

When Venus rises or sets in the first path <note>the first 'vithi' or celestial lane</note>, there is abundance; however, there is fear in the lands of Anga, Vanga, Mahisha, Bahlika, and Kalinga. || 10 ||

In this first circle <term>Mandal: a division of the zodiac</term>, if another planet ascends over the risen Venus <note>original Sanskrit: Shukracharya, the preceptor of the titans</note>, then the kings of Bhadrashva, Shurasenaka, Yaudheyaka, and Kotivarsha will meet their destruction. || 11 ||

The four lunar mansions <term>Nakshatras: star clusters used in Indian astronomy</term> starting from Ardra constitute the second circle. If Venus rises or sets in these, it results in abundant rainfall and a wealth of grain. However, it is inauspicious for the priestly class <note>Brahmins</note>, especially those who engage in cruel or harsh deeds. || 12 ||

If Venus in this second circle is attacked or eclipsed by another planet, then injustice touches the barbarians <note>Mlechhas: foreigners or those outside the Vedic fold</note>, forest-dwellers, those who live by horses (such as traders), the Gomanta (those who live by dogs or possess vast herds of cows), the low-born, the Shudras, and the inhabitants of the Videha country. || 13 ||

If Venus rises while wandering through the five constellations starting from Magha and ending with Chitra, it causes the destruction of all crops. There arises the fear of hunger and thieves. The lowly rise to power, and there is a mixing of social classes <note>Varnasankara: the blurring of traditional social boundaries</note>. || 14 ||

If the teacher of the titans <note>Venus</note> in this third circle (starting from Magha) is obstructed by another planet, then sailors, the Shabara people, Shudras, the Pundra people, the grain of the western borders, the Shulikas, forest-dwellers, Dravidians, and those living by the sea are destroyed. || 15 ||

The three constellations of Swati, Vishakha, and Anuradha constitute the fourth circle. The transit of Venus through these brings freedom from fear and creates abundance for the priestly and warrior classes, though it causes dissension among friends. || 16 ||

If this fourth circle is attacked by another planet, the King of the Kiratas <note>mountain tribes</note> dies. Furthermore, those of the Ikshvaku dynasty, the inhabitants of the borderlands or Avanti, the Pulindas, the Tanganas, and the residents of Shurasena...

It is filled with abundant wealth, herds of cattle, and plenty of grain, though there is fear in some places. || 20 || If Venus ascends here, the people of Shulika, Gandhara, and Avanti are oppressed. The King of Videha is destroyed, but there is an increase in the population of border-dwelling Yavanas, Shakas, and slaves. || 21 || Of the circles described, the two circles beginning with Swati and Jyeshtha are auspicious when they appear in the West. The circle beginning with Magha <note>original: "Pitryadyam"</note> is auspicious in the East. The remaining circles give results as previously stated. || 22 || If Venus is seen before sunset, it creates fear; if seen throughout the entire day, it causes hunger and disease. If seen at midday or together with the Moon, it causes the destruction of kings, armies, and cities. || 23 || If Venus <note>referred to as the son of Bhrigu or Shukracharya</note> travels while piercing the constellation of Krittika <note>original: "Analaksham" - the fire-star</note>, the earth becomes leveled as the high and low places are hidden by rivers overflowing their banks; that is, a great flood occurs. || 24 ||

---

...are nourished. || 17 || The fifth circle comprises the five constellations from Jyeshtha to Shravana. In this, there are obstacles of hunger, thieves, and disease. If the son of Bhrigu <note>Venus</note> should ascend in this, then the people living in Kashmir, Ashmaka, Matsya, Charudevi, and Avanti, as well as the Abhira caste, the Dravidas, Ambashtas, Trigartas, Saurashtras, the men of Sindhu and Sauvira, and the King of Kashmir are destroyed. || 18 || 19 ||

The six constellations from Dhanishtha to Ashwini are called the sixth circle; these are auspicious. In this, all people become extremely happy, possessed of much wealth, grain, and cattle, but some places remain fearful. Upon the ascent of Venus in this, the people living in Shulika, Gandhara, and Avanti suffer; the King of Videha is destroyed, and there is an increase in the Yavanas <note>Greeks or foreigners</note>, Shakas <note>Scythians</note>, and slaves of the borderlands. || 20 || 21 ||

Among the six circles described, the two circles starting with Swati and Jyeshtha are auspicious because they occur in the western direction. The single circle starting with Magha is extremely auspicious when it occurs in the eastern direction. The remaining circles give fruits as previously mentioned. || 22 ||

Fear arises from Venus being visible before the sun sets. If it is visible all day, hunger and disease occur. If it is visible at midday or visible with the Moon, there is division or destruction among kings, armies, and cities. || 23 || If the teacher Shukracharya <note>Venus</note> travels by piercing the Krittika constellation, the high and low places of the earth become indistinguishable due to rivers carrying vast amounts of water beyond their banks; meaning, a very great flood occurs. || 24 ||

When the "Cart of Rohini" <note>original: *Prajapatya Shakata*; a specific V-shaped star formation in Taurus</note> is pierced by Venus, the earth takes on a horrific appearance, strewn with hair and fragments of bone, as if she were performing the *Kapalika* penance <note>A radical ascetic vow involving carrying a human skull as a bowl, here symbolizing a land devastated by famine or war</note> for a great sin committed. || 25 ||

If Venus <note>original: *Ushanas*</note> enters the constellation of *Mrigashira*, there is a destruction of liquids and grains. If it moves into *Ardra*, the regions of Kosala and Kalinga are destroyed, yet there is an abundance of water <note>heavy rainfall</note>. || 26 ||

When the preceptor of the demons <note>Venus/Shukracharya</note> moves into *Punarvasu*, great lawlessness or misfortune befalls the people of Ashmaka and Vidarbha. When it enters *Pushya*, there is plentiful rain, but conflict arises among the *Vidyadharas* <note>A class of celestial beings or perhaps a specific group of scholars/artists</note>. || 27 ||

The passage of the Sun <note>The commentary here notes the Sun, though the context remains Venusian influence</note> through *Ashlesha* brings fear of serpents and intense suffering. If it pierces *Magha*, it brings trouble to the *Hastipakas* <note>elephant-drivers or mahouts</note> but results in heavy rainfall. || 28 ||

If *Purva-Phalguni* is pierced by Venus, the Shavara and Pulinda tribes are destroyed, though rain is plentiful. If *Uttara-Phalguni* is pierced, rain falls but the lands of Kuru-Jangala and Panchala are ruined. || 29 ||

If the constellation *Hasta* is pierced by Venus, the Kauravas and painters <note>or artisans</note> suffer, and the rains are withheld. If *Chitra* is pierced, those who dig wells and the "egg-born" <note>birds and reptiles</note> suffer, though the rain that does fall is beautiful. || 30 ||

When Venus enters *Swati*, there is much rain, but misfortune touches messengers, merchants, and sailors. Even in *Vishakha* <note>original: *Aindragni*</note>, one should know there will be good rain but fear among the merchant classes. || 31 ||

# The Varahi Samhita
<note>Also known as the Brihat Samhita, a foundational 6th-century Sanskrit encyclopedic text by Varahamihira covering astrology, weather, and omens.</note>

When Venus enters the mansion of **Anuradha**, there is conflict among the warrior class <term>Kshatriyas: the ruling and military caste</term>. In **Jyeshtha**, there is great distress for the leaders of the warriors. In **Mula**, the chief physicians suffer. Furthermore, while Venus remains in these three specific mansions, there is a total lack of rain. || 32 ||

In **Purva Ashadha**, those who live by the water suffer. In **Uttara Ashadha**, diseases break out violently. In **Shravana**, there are ear-related ailments, and in **Dhanishtha**, those belonging to heretical sects <term>Pashandis: those following non-Vedic or unorthodox paths</term> live in fear. || 33 ||

In **Shatabhisha**, the distillers and vintners suffer. In **Purva Bhadrapada**, those who live by gambling are afflicted. During this transit, Venus also brings rain to the lands of the Kuru-Panchalas <note>Ancient kingdoms in northern India, near modern-day Delhi and Uttar Pradesh</note>. || 34 ||

In **Uttara Bhadrapada**, fruits and roots are destroyed. In **Revati**, travelers and infantrymen suffer. In **Ashwini**, the keepers of horses are afflicted, and in **Bharani**, the Kiratas <note>Mountain-dwelling tribes</note> and Yavanas <note>Greeks or foreigners from the West</note> suffer from fever and distress. || 35 ||

If the son of Bhrigu <note>Venus</note> rises or sets on the fourteenth, fifteenth, or eighth day of the dark fortnight <term>Krishna Paksha: the waning phase of the moon</term>, then the earth appears as if it is made entirely of water due to heavy rains. || 36 ||

When Jupiter and Venus are positioned in the east and west respectively, or are in the seventh sign from each other, the people are afflicted by disease, fear, and grief, and they see no water released by Indra <note>The god of rain and storms</note>. || 37 ||

When Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, and Saturn all follow the path of Venus <insert>moving ahead of it</insert>, then wars break out between humans, Nagas <note>Serpent deities</note>, and Vidyadharas <note>Celestial beings/sorcerers</note>, and destructive winds prevail. || 38 ||

Friends no longer abide by the spirit of friendship; the twice-born <term>Dvija: the upper castes, specifically Brahmins</term> do not perform their rituals correctly. Indra does not grant even a drop of water, but instead strikes the heads of kings with his thunderbolt. || 39 ||

# Chapter 9 | With Vernacular Commentary

When **Saturn** <note>Sanskrit: *Shanaishchara*</note> moves ahead of **Venus** <note>Sanskrit: *Shukra*</note>, the foreigners <note>original: *Mlechchha*; historically referring to non-Vedic or outside tribes</note>, cats, elephants, donkeys, buffaloes, black grains, and pigs suffer. Likewise, the *Pulinda* people <note>a forest-dwelling tribe</note>, the *Shudra* class, and the inhabitants of the Southern regions <note>Sanskrit: *Dakshinapatha*</note> meet their end through diseases of the eyes and disorders of the wind <note>Sanskrit: *Marut*; likely referring to Ayurvedic Vata imbalances</note>. || 40 ||

If **Mars** <note>Sanskrit: *Kshitija*</note> travels in front of **Venus**, the subjects are destroyed by fire, weapons, hunger, drought, and thieves. All things, moving and stationary, particularly in the Northern regions <note>Sanskrit: *Uttarapatha*</note>, are ruined, and the directions are afflicted by lightning and dust storms. || 41 ||

When **Jupiter** <note>Sanskrit: *Brihaspati*</note> is situated in the path ahead of **Venus**, all white/pure substances, the twice-born <note>Sanskrit: *Dvija*; the priestly and scholarly classes</note>, cattle, and the temples of the gods are destroyed. The Eastern direction suffers, clouds rain down hail, and there is a great prevalence of throat diseases, though the autumnal crops will be abundant. || 42 ||

When **Mercury** <note>Sanskrit: *Saumya*</note> stands before **Venus** at the time of its rising or setting, it brings rain but also causes diseases, specifically those born of bile <note>Sanskrit: *Pitta*</note> and jaundice <note>Sanskrit: *Kamala*</note>. It nourishes the summer crops, yet it destroys ascetics, those who maintain the sacred fire <note>Sanskrit: *Agnihotrika*</note>, physicians, those who live by performing sacrifices, horses, the merchant class <note>Sanskrit: *Vaishya*</note>, cows, kings along with their vehicles, yellow-colored objects, and the Western direction. || 43 ||

If the color of **Venus** appears like fire, there is danger from fire; if it appears blood-red, there is provocation of weapons (war). If it appears pale-yellow like gold tested on a touchstone, diseases occur. If it appears green or tawny, there is an outbreak of asthma and coughs. In such a state, water does not fall from the sky—

# Now begins the Tenth Chapter.
## The Transit of Saturn.

If the Son of the Sun <note>original: "Arkasuta" (Saturn)</note>, appearing glossy and lovely, stays in the asterisms of Shravana, Swati, Hasta, Ardra, Bharani, or Purva Phalguni, he covers the earth with abundant water. ॥ 1 ॥ While moving through the asterisms presided over by the Serpent, Varuna, or Indra <note>Ashlesha, Shatabhisha, and Jyeshtha</note>, he brings great well-being but not excessive rain. If he moves through Mula, he causes hunger, danger from weapons, and drought. This is the general effect; now I shall describe the specific effects for each asterism. ॥ 2 ॥ When Saturn is in Ashwini, horses, horse-keepers, poets, physicians, and ministers are harmed. In Bharani, dancers, instrumentalists, singers, and those who earn their living by small boats suffer loss. ॥ 3 ॥ If Saturn is in Krittika, those who work with fire and kings are afflicted. In Rohini, the people of Kosala, Madra, Kashi, Panchala, and cart-drivers are troubled. ॥ 4 ॥

If the color is dry like ashes or black, there is no rain from the sky. ॥ 44 ॥ When the Preceptor of the Demons, Venus, has a luster like curd, the lily, or the moon, and the brilliance is clearly reflected with spreading rays, moving with excellent gait, without deformity and endowed with victory, it is as if the Golden Age has arrived for all creatures. ॥ 45 ॥

->in the North-Western provinces, on the Brihat Samhita<-
->composed by the teacher Sri Varahamihira. ॥ 9 ॥<-

If Saturn, the son of the Sun, sits in the Shravana, Swati, Hasta, Ardra, Bharani, or Purva Phalguni asterisms and possesses a charming color, then much water falls upon the earth. ॥ 1 ॥ If Saturn wanders in the Ashlesha, Shatabhisha, or Jyeshtha asterisms, there is great auspiciousness, but not extreme rain. If he wanders in the Mula asterism, there is hunger, fear of weapons, and a lack of rain. This was the general result; now the specific result of Saturn's transit through each individual asterism is stated. ॥ 2 ॥ If Saturn wanders in the Ashwini asterism, there is loss for horses, horse-riders, poets, doctors, and ministers. If he wanders in the Bharani asterism, there is loss for dancers, musicians, singers, and men who sustain their livelihood by small boats. ॥ 3 ॥ If Saturn is in the Krittika asterism, those who live by fire and kings suffer pain.

# Chapter 10: With Language Commentary

(57)

### The Effects of Saturn’s Transit

If Saturn is situated in the **Rohini** <note>The 4th lunar mansion, associated with the star Aldebaran</note> constellation, then the regions of Kosala, Madra, Kashi, and Panchala, as well as those men who earn their livelihood by carts <note>original: "shakatas" - likely carters or transport merchants</note>, suffer distress. || 4 ||

When Saturn resides in the **Mrigashira** <note>The 5th lunar mansion, "The Deer's Head"</note> constellation, the people of the Vatsa region, sacrificers, patrons of sacrifice, noblemen <note>original: "Aryas"</note>, and the inhabitants of the Middle Country <note>Central India</note> are afflicted. If Saturn is in the **Ardra** <note>The 6th lunar mansion, associated with Betelgeuse</note> constellation, the people of the Ramatha country, oil-millers, washermen, dyers, and thieves suffer greatly. || 5 ||

If Saturn dwells in the **Punarvasu** <note>The 7th lunar mansion</note> constellation, the Punjab, the borderlands, Surashtra <note>modern Gujarat</note>, Sindh, and the Sauvira regions face great distress. If there is a conjunction of Saturn in the **Pushya** <note>The 8th lunar mansion</note> constellation, then bell-ringers, heralds <note>those who make public proclamations</note>, Ionians <note>original: "Yavanas" - referring to Greeks or foreigners from the West</note>, merchants, villains, and all flowers are harmed. || 6 ||

When Saturn is in the **Ashlesha** <note>The 9th lunar mansion, "The Serpent"</note> constellation, it brings harm to lotuses and serpents. If it is in the **Magha** <note>The 10th lunar mansion</note> constellation, obstacles arise for the people of Bahlika <note>Bactria</note>, China, Gandhara, Shulika, and Parata, as well as for the merchant class <note>Vaishyas</note>, treasuries, and traders. || 7 ||

While Saturn stays in the **Purva Phalguni** <note>The 11th lunar mansion</note> constellation, those who sell liquids <note>juices, oils, or essences</note>, prostitutes, maidens, and the Maharashtra region face obstacles. If Saturn is in **Uttara Phalguni** <note>The 12th lunar mansion</note>, then kings, jaggery <note>unrefined sugar</note>, salt, monks, water, and the city of Taxila <note>an ancient center of learning in modern Pakistan</note> encounter difficulties. || 8 ||

If Saturn is in the **Hasta** <note>The 13th lunar mansion, "The Hand"</note> constellation, then barbers, potters <note>or those working with wheels</note>, thieves, physicians, tailors, elephant-catchers, unchaste women, the people of Kosala, and garland-makers suffer pain. || 9 ||

If Saturn is in the **Chitra** <note>The 14th lunar mansion, "The Bright One"</note> constellation, then women, writers, those skilled in the art of painting <note>gloss: "musauvir" - artists</note>, and various types of commodities are afflicted. If Saturn is in the **Swati** <note>The 15th lunar mansion</note> constellation, then the people of Magadha, messengers, spies, charioteers, sailors, and actors/dancers suffer. || 10 ||

When Saturn wanders through the constellation known as **Vishakha** <note>The 16th lunar mansion</note>, then the Trigarta, China, and Kuluta regions, as well as saffron, lac <note>a resin used for dye</note>, grain, madder <note>a red dye plant</note>, and safflower face destruction...

# Now begins the Eleventh Chapter.
## The Course of Ketus (Comets).

Having examined the works of Garga, Parashara, Asita, and Devala regarding the movements of "crested" stars <note>comets or meteors</note>, as well as many other authors, this clear and uncomplicated account of their course is being composed. || 1 || Their appearance or disappearance cannot be calculated or predicted through mathematical methods alone...

---

Having seen what the teacher Garga, Parashara, Asita, the sage Devala, and other scholars have said regarding the movements of Ketus <note>comets/meteors</note>, all of that is synthesized here into a definitive account. || 1 || The rising or setting of these Ketus cannot be known in any way through mathematics...

<summary>This page concludes the astrological omens associated with Saturn's color and position, transitioning into a new chapter on the unpredictable nature of comets (Ketus) based on ancient sage traditions.</summary>
<keywords>Saturn, Varahamihira, Brihat Samhita, Comets, Ketu, Astrology, Omens, Social Classes, Garga, Parashara</keywords>

--- Page 84 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial omens from the Varahi Samhita (Brihat Samhita), specifically focusing on the classification and characteristics of comets.</meta>

# The Varahi Samhita
->Page 60<-

Comets are of three types: celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial. <note>original: "divya-antariksha-bhauma." This classification distinguishes between phenomena in deep space, the upper atmosphere, and those appearing near the earth's surface.</note> || 2 || Aside from fireflies, phosphorescent spirits <note>original: "pishachalaya," likely referring to 'will-o'-the-wisps' or marsh gas</note>, ink, and jewels, whenever a non-luminous object takes on the fiery appearance of a flame, it is called a **Ketu** <note>term: Ketu — while often meaning the lunar node in later astrology, here it refers to comets and meteoric portents</note>. || 3 || Those appearances seen on banners, weapons, houses, trees, horses, and elephants are "atmospheric" comets. Those appearing among the stars are "celestial," and all others are considered "terrestrial" crested portents. || 4 ||

Some scholars say there are one hundred and one comets; others say there are a thousand. However, the sage **Narada** declares that there is only one Ketu, which manifests in many different forms. || 5 || Whether there is one or many is of little consequence; what matters is that their effects must be predicted based on their rising, setting, position, contact with stars, and their colors, such as smoky-grey and the like. || 6 ||

For as many days as a comet remains visible, its effects will last for that many months. The ripening of these fruits <note>the manifestation of the omen's results</note> begins after the first three fortnights <note>45 days</note> have passed from its first appearance. || 7 || A comet that is small, clear, glossy, straight, pleasing in appearance, and white when it rises is a favorable omen, bringing abundance and happiness. || 8 || A **Dhumaketu** <note>literally "smoke-bannered," a common term for a comet</note> that possesses the opposite characteristics is not auspicious; this is especially true for those that mimic the colors of a rainbow or possess two or three "crests" <note>tails</note>. || 9 ||

# Chapter 11: The Description of Comets (61)

Those comets that possess the appearance of a necklace of pearls, gems, or gold, and are endowed with crests <note>original: "shikha" or tails</note>, are known as the **Kiranas** (The Radiant Ones). They appear in the East or the West and are born from the Sun. They are twenty-five in number. Their appearance causes conflict among kings. ## 10

Those comets that resemble a parrot, fire, the Bandhujīvaka flower <note>a bright red mid-day flower</note>, lac, or blood, and appear in the South-East, are the sons of Fire. They are also twenty-five in number. Their appearance brings the danger of fire. ## 11

The twenty-five comets that have curved crests, appear rough and black, and are seen in the Southern direction, are the sons of Death <note>Yama</note>. Their appearance announces the coming of a plague or pestilence. ## 12

Those that are circular like a mirror, lack a crest but are endowed with rays, and have the luster of water or oil, are the twenty-two sons of the Earth. They appear in the North-East. Their appearance brings famine and fear. ## 13

Those that resemble the rays of the moon, silver, snow, the white water-lily, or the Kunda flower, are the three sons of the Moon. They appear in the North and bring about a time of plenty and good harvests. ## 14

There is one comet born of Brahma, known as **Brahmadanda** (The Staff of Brahma). It has three crests and three colors, and it portends the end of an era <note>Yugānta</note>. There is no fixed rule for the direction in which it may appear. ## 15

In this manner, one hundred and one comets have been described. Now, I shall describe the remaining eight hundred and ninety-nine comets with their clear characteristics. ## 16

The eighty-four comets known as the sons of Venus appear in the North and North-East...

<column-break/>

<margin>These are inauspicious factors. ## 9</margin>

The comets resembling pearl necklaces or gold, appearing in the East or West, are the **Ravija** (Sun-born). They are named **Kirana**; they are twenty-five in number. Their rising causes opposition between kings. ## 10

Comets resembling a parrot, fire, the mid-day flower, lac, or blood seen in the South-East are born of Fire, and they are also twenty-five in number. (25 + 25 = 50). Their rising causes fear of fire. ## 11

The twenty-five (50 + 25 = 75) that have crooked crests, are dry and black-colored, and appear in the South, are born of Yama; their rising causes death and pestilence. ## 12

The twenty-two comets (75 + 22 = 97) that are round like a mirror, without a crest, possessing rays, and having a luster like watery oil, appearing in the North-East, are born of the Earth. Their rising causes famine and fear. ## 13

The three (97 + 3 = 100) comets resembling moonbeams, silver, snow, or the Kunda flower are the sons of the Moon and appear in the North. Their rising brings good harvests. ## 14

And there is one comet born of Brahma called **Brahmadanda**, which brings the end of an age. (100 + 1 = 101). It has three crests and three colors; it can appear in any direction without rule. ## 15

Thus, the description of one hundred and one comets is written. Now, the description of 899 comets is given with clear characteristics. ## 16

# Chapter 11: With Commentary in the Common Tongue
->( 63 )<-

The seventy-seven comets known as **Aruna** <note>meaning "the reddish ones"</note> are born of the Wind; they are sinful in influence and harsh in appearance. **[24]**

The comets known as **Ganaka** are the sons of Prajapati <note>the Creator deity</note>; they are eight in number and resemble a cluster of stars. The comets known as **Brahmasantana** <note>offspring of Brahma</note> are two hundred and four in number and are square in shape. **[25]**

The thirty-two comets named **Kanka** are born of Varuna <note>the deity of the waters</note>; they appear like a cluster of shrubs or thickets. They possess a brilliance like that of the Moon and are said to bring intense, fierce results. **[26]**

The ninety-six comets known as **Kabandha** <note>meaning "headless trunks"</note> are the sons of Time (Kala); they are shaped like headless bodies. These are fierce, fear-inducing, and are considered "crested" stars with deformed appearances. **[27]**

The nine comets born from the intermediate directions appear as large, single white stars. Thus, the one thousand comets have been described <note>The text calculates the total by adding previous groups to reach 1,000</note>. Now, I shall speak of their specific individual characteristics. **[28]**

The comet that rises in the West and stretches toward the North, possessing a large and oily <note>glossy or smooth</note> form, is called **Vasaketu**. Its appearance immediately causes pestilence, yet it also brings about an excellent abundance of food. **[29]**

The comet with similar characteristics but which appears parched <note>rough or lusterless</note> is called **Asthiketu**; it is said to bring the fear of hunger. If a similar comet appears in the East and is oily, it is named **Shastraketu**; it leads to civil strife and pestilence. **[30]**

The comet visible on the New Moon day with smoky rays and a crest is called **Kapalaketu**. It generally wanders through half the sky and causes hunger, pestilence, drought, and disease. **[31]**

In the eastern path of Agni <note>the Fire-god</note>, a comet appears with a point like a trident and rays that are dark, parched, and copper-colored. It travels through a third of the sky and is called **Raudra**...

# Chapter 11: The Course of Ketus (Comets)
## With Hindi Commentary

( 67 )

If the comet affects the lunar mansion *Magha*, the King of the Asikas dies; in *Purva Phalguni*, the King of the Pandyas; in *Uttara Phalguni*, the Lord of Ujjain; in *Hasta*, the Lord of Dandaka; and in *Chitra*, the expert should predict the death of the King of Kurukshetra. In *Svati*, the Kings of Kashmir and Kamboja will not survive. || 56-57 ||

The Lords of the Ikshvaku and Ratnaka dynasties are slain if the comet appears in *Vishakha*. In *Anuradha*, the King of Pundra dies, and in *Jyeshtha*, the death of the Universal Emperor <note>Sanskrit: *Sarvabhauma*, a ruler of the entire known world</note> occurs. || 58 ||

In *Mula*, the Kings of Andhra and Madra perish. In *Purvashadha*, the King of Kashi meets his death. In *Uttarashadha*, the Yaudheyas, Arjunayanas, Shivi, and the <term>Chaidya King</term> <note>The ruler of the Chedi Kingdom</note> are destroyed. || 59 ||

Furthermore, if the six stars starting from *Shravana* are afflicted, the Kings of Kekaya, Punjab, Ceylon (Simhala), Vanga (Bengal), Naimisharanya, and the Kiratas are destroyed respectively. || 60 ||

If the crest of the comet is struck by a meteor, it is auspicious. If it is accompanied by rain in every way, it is extremely beneficial. However, this same phenomenon brings misfortune to the Chola, Afghan (Avgana), White Huns (Sita-Huna), and the Chinese. || 61 ||

In whichever direction the crests of the comet bend or move away from, or whichever constellation they touch, those countries are destroyed as if by divine power. Just as Garuda <note>The divine eagle and mount of Vishnu</note> enjoys devouring the hoods of serpents, a conquering King will joyfully seize and enjoy those lands. || 62 ||

---

->Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Course of Ketus," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 11 ||<-

The King of Pandya dies in *Purva Phalguni*; the Lord of Ujjain in *Uttara Phalguni*; the Lord of Dandaka in *Hasta*; the King of Kurukshetra in *Chitra*; the Kings of Kashmir and Kamboja in the constellation *Svati*; the Lords of Ikshvaku and Ratnaka in *Vishakha*; the King of the Pundra country in the constellation *Anuradha*; and the Universal Emperor dies in the constellation *Jyeshtha*. || 54-58 || If the constellation *Mula* is smoked or touched by a Ketu, the Kings of Andhra and Madra meet their death. In *Purvashadha*, the Lord of Kashi; in the constellation *Uttarashadha*, the Yaudha King, the Arjunayana King, the Shivi monarch, and the <term>Chaidya King</term> are destroyed. And if the six constellations starting from *Shravana* are afflicted, the Kings of Kekaya, Punjab, Ceylon, Vanga, Naimisharanya, and the Kirata country are destroyed in sequence. || 59-60 || If the crest of the Ketu is pierced by a meteor, it is auspicious. If it is fully accompanied by rain, it is a great blessing. But by this very occurrence, misfortune comes to the Chola, Afghan, White Hun, and Chinese lands. || 61 || Those countries from which the crests of the Ketu turn away or bend, or those countries whose constellations are touched by it—all those countries are destroyed as if by divine power. Just as Lord Garuda is happy after consuming the serpent's hood, Kings become happy in the same way by attacking and occupying those countries. || 62 ||

# Chapter Twelve
## The Course of Agastya

-> By whom the Vindhya mountains, whose peaks had grown high to obstruct the path of the sun, were halted; by whom the demon Vātāpi—the enemy of the gods who used to rip open the bellies of sages—was digested; by whom the ocean was drunk; and who, being an ocean of penance himself, adorned the southern quarter: I now describe the course of that Sage Agastya, who possesses the brilliance of water. [1] <-

-> The ocean was made even more beautiful by him when he suddenly depleted its waters; the underwater mountains, their peaks torn by the claws of crocodiles, were revealed along with heaps of excellent gems and jewels mixed with falling pearls. It was as if the ocean, in former times, was displaying these to mock the gods despite their own white crowns and jewels. [2] <-

-> Even when the water was removed by him, the ocean shone even more brightly, adorned by the coral-bearing mountains, gems, jewels, and the serpents that emerged from within. [3] <-

-> The great ocean, where whales and sea-elephants moved crookedly and heaps of jewels were cast about, was brought to a state of celestial splendor by him who drank its waters, even though the sea had fallen into a state of calamity <note>The "calamity" refers to the ocean being emptied of its water</note>. [4] <-

The Lord of Rivers <note>The Ocean</note>, though its waters were taken away, remained filled with moving whales, shells, and conchs. It bore the beauty of a lake in autumn, adorned with waves, white lotuses, and swans. In that space where the clouds were like dark whales, the stars like jewels, the moon like crystal, and the gems on the hoods of serpents were like rays—

<header>Chapter 12, with Commentary in the Vernacular Language</header>

->...bearing a splendor like that of a lake in autumn. <-

He who created the sky in the form of a waterless autumnal sea—where the dark clouds are like moss, the stars like jewels, the moon like a crystal, and the three-fold light of the gems on the hoods of serpents <note>original: "phani-phana-upala"</note> serves as the foam; where the curly hair of the clouds adorns the firmament.

The Vindhya mountain once rose up with the intent of blocking the path of the Sun’s chariot. As its peaks moved and grew, the *Vidyadharas* <note>Celestial musicians or semi-divine beings</note> living upon them became terrified. Fearing they would fall, their beloved consorts clung to their shoulders, their bodies dangling in the air. At that moment, their garments fluttered like hoisted banners, beautifying the mountain with these living flags. 

The inner regions and waterfalls of the mountain were made home by the <term>Mrigendra</term> <note>Lion; literally "King of Beasts"</note>. Upon the heads of these lions, swarms of bees hovered, drawn by the fragrance of the ichor <note>rut-fluid from elephants</note> mixed with blood; these bees appeared like garlands of *Bana* flowers worn as crests. 

With its towering peaks, the mountain seemed to be scratching the very surface of the sky. These peaks echoed with the deep, melodic humming of intoxicated bees, who were startled when great elephants uprooted flowering trees. The mountain heights were inhabited by hyenas, bears, tigers, and <term>Shakhamrigas</term> <note>Monkeys; literally "branch-deer"</note>. 

The mountain was embraced in solitude by the river <term>Reva</term> <note>The Narmada River</note> as if by a passionate mistress. Its forests were inhabited by gods and populated by many Brahmins—some subsisting only on water, some renouncing grain, some eating only roots, and others living on nothing but air. 

He <note>The Sage Agastya</note> who halted the growth of this mighty Vindhya mountain—listen now to the description of his rising...

# The Varahi Samhita

### Chapter on the Rising of Agastya

Listen further: || 7 || Just as the hearts of the virtuous, though once tainted by the impurity of associating with the wicked, become pure again by their very nature, so too do the waters—muddied by the wash of the rains—become crystal clear upon the rising of the sage named Agastya. || 8 ||

The river shines like a smiling young woman; her teeth are represented by the rows of calling swans, and her lips, reddened by betel nut <note>original: *tambula*; a traditional breath freshener that stains the lips red</note>, are mirrored by the ruddy sheldrakes <term>Chakravaka: orange-brown waterfowl often used in poetry to symbolize lovers</term> stationed upon both her banks. || 9 ||

With blue lilies situated near white lotuses, and adorned by hovering lines of bees, the river appears like a clever woman in the throes of passion, casting side-long glances with the playful movement of her vine-like eyebrows. || 10 ||

To behold the moon’s glory, now unveiled by the departure of the clouds, the pond—wearing a bracelet of rippling waves—opens her "eyes" at night. These eyes are the white water-lilies <note>original: *kumuda*</note>, whose petals contain resting bees that look like dark pupils behind beautiful lashes. || 11 ||

The Earth, as if extending her hands in the form of lakes filled with various wondrous lotuses, swans, ruddy sheldrakes, and water-fowl, offers a respectful tribute <term>Arghya: a traditional offering of honor to a guest</term> of abundant gems, flowers, and fruits to the sage Agastya. || 12 ||

The water that was released by the command of Indra <note>The king of gods and bringer of rain</note>, which had been tainted by the fiery poison emitted from the fangs of serpents hidden within the clouds, becomes auspicious and healing once more at the mere sight of Agastya. || 13 ||

If the mere memory of him drives away sin, what then might be said of the hymns sung to him, the lotus-born son of Varuna? <note>Agastya is mythologically the son of the sea-god Varuna</note>

<summary>This page uses vivid poetic imagery to describe the purification of nature during the autumn rising of the star Agastya (Canopus), comparing the clearing landscapes to beautiful women and virtuous hearts.</summary>

# Chapter 12: With Commentary

(71)

I shall now describe the ritual of the <term>Arghya</term> <note>a respectful offering of water or gifts to a deity or guest</note> for the benefit of kings, exactly as it was proclaimed by the ancient Sages. || 14 ||

A wise scholar, having calculated the specific timing for each country according to the rules of mathematics, should announce the star's appearance. In the city of Ujjayini <note>modern Ujjain, the prime meridian of ancient Indian astronomy</note>, this occurs when the true Sun has reached seven degrees less than the sign of Virgo <note>original: "Kanya-rashi"; this corresponds to roughly 23 degrees of Leo or early September</note>. || 15 ||

When the darkness of night is slightly pierced by the nether-rays of the dawn, in the southern direction—the quarter having been pointed out by the <term>Samvatsara</term> <note>the royal astrologer or astronomer</note>—the King, with a composed mind, should offer the Arghya upon the earth. || 16 ||

The offering should consist of fragrant seasonal flowers, fruits, gems born of the ocean, gold, fine garments, a cow, a bull, edible sweets mixed with <term>Paramanna</term> <note>rice boiled in milk, a sacred food</note>, curd, unbroken grains of rice, fragrant incense, and ointments. || 17 ||

A King who presents this Arghya with faith becomes free from disease and conquers the ranks of his enemies. If he performs this ritual correctly for seven years, he becomes the lord of the earth, which is girded by the oceans.

---

<margin>How can we fully describe the fruit of praising the Sage Agastya? The procedure for the Arghya of Agastya, as told by the Sages for the welfare of kings, is now stated. || 14 || Scholars shall command the observation in all countries after calculating the rising of Agastya according to mathematical rules. When the Sun is at 4 signs and 23 degrees (this usually occurs around the 22nd to 24th day of the month of Bhadrapada), then the rising of Sage Agastya occurs in the city of Ujjayini. || 15 || When the night's darkness is somewhat destroyed by the rays of the Sun (the hour of dawn), and having received the command of the <term>Daivajña</term> <note>astrologer/diviner</note> regarding the directions ("This is the South; offer the Arghya to Lord Agastya in this direction"), the King should offer the Arghya upon the earth. This Arghya is composed of autumn flowers, fruits, sea-gems, gold, cloth, a cow, a bull, food with rice-milk, curd, rice, fragrance, incense, and sandalwood. || 16 || 17 || If the King holds this Arghya with faith, he remains healthy and defeats all enemies. If he gives the Arghya in this manner for seven years, he becomes the master of the ocean-waisted earth.</margin>

---

<note>1. "Agastya is at the end of Gemini at eighty degrees." The star visible at the end of the sign of Gemini and at 80 degrees southern latitude is Agastya. "Swati, Agastya, Mrigavyadha, Chitra, Jyeshtha, Punarvasu, Abhijit, and Brahmahridaya—all these thirteen stars rise or set at thirteen degrees of time." — From the <term>Surya Siddhanta</term> <note>The "Sun Treatise," a foundational text of Indian astronomy</note>.</note>

It specifies Ujjain as the geographical reference point for the star's rising in the southern sky during autumn.</summary>

# The Compendium of Varahamihira

...he attains the sovereignty of the earth. || 18 || A <term>Brahmin</term><note>The priestly or scholarly class</note> who offers an <term>Arghya</term><note>A traditional water offering to a deity or star</note> with whatever materials are available to him, attains mastery of the <term>Vedas</term><note>The most ancient Hindu scriptures</note>, beautiful wives, and sons. A <term>Vaishya</term><note>The merchant or agricultural class</note> obtains cattle and abundant wealth, while a <term>Shudra</term><note>The laboring class</note> gains the cessation of disease and the fruits of righteousness. || 19 ||

If the star named Agastya appears harsh or rough, it causes disease; if it is tawny, it brings a lack of rain; if it is smoke-colored, it brings misfortune to cattle; if it is quivering, it portends fear. If it resembles the color of madder <note>a reddish dye</note>, it causes hunger and war; and if it appears minute or small, it leads to the siege of cities. || 20 ||

If it appears like gold <margin>1</margin> <note>The commentator Utpala notes that while the word 'Shatakumbha' can mean gold or silver, here it refers to silver.</note> or like crystal, satisfying the earth as if with a flood of rays, then the earth becomes rich with abundant grain and is filled with people free from fear and disease. || 21 || If the star is struck by a meteor or by a <term>Shikhi</term><note>A comet or "crested" celestial body</note>, it brings the fear of hunger and pestilence. It is said that he <insert>Agastya</insert> becomes visible when the Sun enters the constellation of <term>Hasta</term> and sets when the Sun reaches <term>Rohini</term>. || 22 ||

...he becomes a universal emperor. || 18 || If Brahmins offer an offering to Agastya with whatever items they can obtain, they become entitled to the four Vedas and obtain beautiful wives and sons. When the Sun travels into the constellation of Hasta, the star Agastya becomes visible in all lands, and when the Sun travels into Rohini, it sets in all lands. || 22 ||

# Chapter Thirteen

## The Movement of the Seven Sages

> Like a woman wearing a single-string pearl necklace, adorned with a garland of white lotuses, smiling and protected by her lord, the northern direction shines with the Seven Sages. <note>The "Seven Sages" (Saptarshi) refer to the stars of the Big Dipper.</note> ॥ 1 ॥
> Guided by the instructions of the Pole Star <note>original: "Dhruva"</note>, their leader, the northern sky seems to dance as they revolve. I shall now describe their movement according to the teachings of the Elder Garga. ॥ 2 ॥
> The Sages were stationed in the lunar mansion of Magha <note>Regulus</note> when King Yudhishthira ruled the earth. The era of that king is determined by adding 2526 to the Shaka era. <note>This is a famous chronological verse used to date the Mahabharata era.</note> ॥ 3 ॥
> They remain in each lunar mansion for a period of one hundred years. They always rise in the north-east, accompanied by the virtuous Arundhati. ॥ 4 ॥
> In the eastern part stands the Lord Marichi; to his west is Vashistha; behind him is Angiras; then Atri; and close to him are Pulastya, Pulaha, and the Lord Kratu, situated in order from the east. Among them, the virtuous Arundhati remains close to the great sage Vashistha. ॥ 5 ॥ 6 ॥
> If these stars are struck by meteors, thunderbolts, or smoke, or if they become discolored, dim, or small, they destroy their respective classes of people. If they appear large and bright, they bring prosperity to those classes. ॥ 7 ॥

---

The northern direction, wearing a garland of white lotuses like a beautiful woman, appears radiant by wearing a single-string necklace of the Seven Sages; she seems to possess a gentle smile and a protector. Furthermore, the northern direction seems to dance repeatedly with the Seven Sages who wander here and there under the instruction of the Pole Star, their leader. According to the views of the Elder Garga, the subject of their movement will be explained. ॥ 1 ॥ 2 ॥

When King Yudhishthira ruled the earth, the Seven Sages were in the Magha constellation. One should know the time of Yudhishthira by adding 2526 to the Shaka era numeral. ॥ 3 ॥

They wander in each constellation for a hundred years. They always rise in the north-east direction along with the virtuous Arundhati. ॥ 4 ॥

In the eastern part is Lord Marichi; in the western direction of Marichi is Vashistha; behind him is Angiras; thereafter Atri; near him Pulastya, Pulaha, and Lord Kratu are seated in order starting from the east. Among them, the virtuous Arundhati has taken refuge with the best of sages, Vashistha. ॥ 5 ॥ 6 ॥

If they are struck by meteors, lightning, or smoke, etc., or become discolored, lightless, and diminished, they destroy their respective groups; and when they are large or bright, they increase their respective groups. ॥ 7 ॥ If Marichi is afflicted in any way...

<note>1. There is a difference in the arrangement of this Seven Sages circle compared to the opinion of Shridhara Swami in the commentary of the Shrimad Bhagavatam.</note>

If the star Marīci <note>one of the stars in Ursa Major</note> is afflicted, it is known to cause suffering to the Vidyadharas <note>a class of celestial beings or spirits possessing magical knowledge</note>. || 8 || If Vasiṣṭha is struck, he destroys the Shakas, Yavanas <note>Greeks or foreigners from the West</note>, Daradas, Paratas, and Kambojas, as well as ascetics living in the forests; however, when he is endowed with bright rays, he brings prosperity. || 9 || Angiras is said to represent those endowed with knowledge, the wise, and the Brahmins. If Atri is afflicted, those born in the wilderness, aquatic products, the ocean, and the rivers are destroyed. || 10 || The Rakshasas, Pisachas, Danavas, Daityas <note>various classes of demons and spirits</note>, and serpents are remembered as belonging to Pulastya. To Pulaha belong roots and fruits, and to Kratu belong the sacrifices along with those who perform them. || 11 ||

# Chapter Fourteen
## The Division of the Tortoise <note>Kurma Vibhaga: a traditional Hindu method of mapping geography by imagining the earth as a tortoise facing East</note>

By grouping the constellations into sets of three, starting from Krittika <note>the Pleiades</note>, the countries of Bharatavarsha <note>India</note> are divided into nine parts, starting from the center and moving toward the East and other directions. || 1 || The central region includes Bhadra, Arimeda, Māṇḍavya, Sālva, Nīpa, Ujjihāna, Saṅkhyāta, Maru, Vatsaghoṣa, Yāmuna, Sārasvata, Matsya, and Mādhyamika. || 2 || Also Mathura, Upajyotiṣa, Dharmāraṇya, and Śūrasena.

When Marīci is troubled, he causes pain to the Gandharvas, gods, demons, those dealing in mantras and medicines, Siddhas, Yakshas, Nagas, and Vidyadharas. || 8 || If Vasiṣṭha is afflicted, he destroys the Shakas, Yavanas, Daradas, Paratas, Kambojas, and forest-dwelling ascetics, but when full of rays, he causes growth. || 9 || Angiras, when struck, destroys the learned, the wise, and the Brahmins. If there is an obstruction to Atri, then forest-products, water-products, the ocean, and rivers are destroyed. || 10 || Through obstacles to Pulastya, the Rakshasas, Pisachas, Danavas, Daityas, and serpent-groups suffer; from the piercing of Pulaha, roots and fruits suffer; and from obstacles to the sage Kratu, those performing sacrifices face hindrances. || 11 ||

->Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Hindi commentary composed by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra,<-
->resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the Brhat Samhita composed by the great teacher Sri Varāhamihira. || 13 ||<-

---

There is one group for every three constellations <term>Nakshatra: lunar mansions used in Vedic astrology</term>. In this manner, there are nine groups. All these groups begin from the constellation Krittika. All the countries within Bharatavarsha have been divided by these groups according to the sequence of circumambulation <note>clockwise direction</note>. || 1 || The Central Country <note>Madhya-desha</note>: <gloss>10</gloss>Bhadra, <gloss>11</gloss>Arimeda, <gloss>12</gloss>Māṇḍavya, <gloss>13</gloss>Sālva, <gloss>14</gloss>Nīpa, <gloss>15</gloss>Ujjihāna, <gloss>16</gloss>Saṅkhyāta, <gloss>17</gloss>Maru, <gloss>18</gloss>Vatsaghoṣa, <gloss>19</gloss>Yāmuna, <gloss>20</gloss>Sārasvata, Matsya, Mādhayamika, Māthura, Upajyotiṣa, Dharmāraṇya, Śūrasena, Sauragrīva, Udehika.

In the **North-West** direction are the Mandavyas, Tusharas <note>Tocharians</note>, Talas, Halas, and Madras; the Ashmakas, Kulutas, Lahadas, the Kingdom of Women, and the Narasimhavana...

# Chapter Fifteen
## The Array of the Asterisms <note>Sanskrit: Nakshatra-vyuha. This chapter categorizes all earthly things under the influence of the 27 lunar mansions.</note>

Under the domain of **Krittika** <note>The Pleiades; associated with the god of fire, Agni</note> are those who deal in white flowers, performers of fire-sacrifices, experts in sacred chants, those knowledgeable in the commentaries on the aphorisms, miners, barbers, the twice-born <term>Dvija: members of the three upper castes—Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas</term>, potters, royal priests, and astrologers who know the secrets of the year. || 1 ||

Under **Rohini** <note>Aldebaran</note> are those of noble vows, merchants, kings, the wealthy, practitioners of Yoga, carters, cattle, bulls, aquatic animals, farmers, mountains, and those endowed with great prosperity. || 2 ||

Under **Mrigashira** <note>Orion's head</note> are fragrant clothes, lotuses, flowers, fruits, gems, forest-dwellers, birds, deer, those who drink the Soma juice in sacrifices, celestial musicians <note>Gandharvas</note>, the lustful, and messengers. || 3 ||

Under **Ardra** <note>Betelgeuse</note> are those who engage in killing, imprisonment, falsehood, adultery, theft, villainy, and creating discord; also those dealing in husked grains, and those skilled in fierce incantations, black magic <note>Abhichara</note>, and the summoning of spirits <note>Vetala-karma</note>. || 4 ||

Under **Punarvasu** <note>Castor and Pollux</note> are the finest grains, truth, generosity, purity, high birth, beauty, intelligence, fame, and wealth; also merchants accompanied by craftsmen in service...

---

If the entire group is afflicted by malefic planets and the like, then in due order, the kings of the Panchala, Magadha, Kalinga, Avanti, Anarta, Sindhu-Sauvira, Harahoura, Bhadra, and Kuninda countries are destroyed. || 32 || 33 ||

# Chapter 15: The Systematic Description of the Asterisms

( 81 )

Thieves, shepherds, hunters, <term>kinashas</term><note>original: "कीनाश" (kinasha); refers to cruel agricultural laborers or those who kill animals</note>, the low-born, those of wicked conduct, men devoid of religious vows, and those skilled in wrestling or hand-to-hand combat [belong to the constellation of Purva Bhadrapada]. ॥ 23 ॥

In **Ahirbudhnya** <note>The presiding deity of Uttara Bhadrapada</note>, reside Brahmins, those engaged in sacrifice, charity, and penance, the very wealthy, those living in hermitages, heretics, kings, and the finest grains. ॥ 24 ॥

Under **Revati** are the products of the water: fruits, flowers, salt, gems, conch-shells, pearls, and lotuses; also fragrant flowers, perfumes, merchants, and boatmen or sailors. ॥ 25 ॥

In **Ashwini** are horse-stealers, generals, physicians, servants, horses, horse-riders, wealthy merchants, and handsome men. ॥ 26 ॥

Under **Yamyas** <note>The constellation Bharani, ruled by Yama, the god of death</note> are those who eat blood and flesh, the cruel, those addicted to killing, binding, and beating, husked grains, the low-born, and those lacking in courage or virtue. ॥ 27 ॥

The three "Purvas" <note>Purva Phalguni, Purva Ashadha, and Purva Bhadrapada</note> along with **Krittika** belong to the Brahmins. The three "Uttaras" <note>Uttara Phalguni, Uttara Ashadha, and Uttara Bhadrapada</note> along with **Pushya** belong to the Kings <note>The Kshatriya or warrior class</note>. **Revati**, **Anuradha**, **Magha**, and **Rohini** <note>The text mentions Prajapati's star, which is Rohini</note> belong to the farmers. ॥ 28 ॥

**Hasta**, **Abhijit**, and **Ashwini** are said to be the stars of the merchant class. **Mula**, **Ardra**, **Swati**, and **Shatabhisha** belong to the fierce or powerful classes. ॥ 29 ॥

**Mrigashira**, **Jyeshtha**, **Chitra**, and **Dhanishtha** are the masters of the servant class. **Ashlesha**, **Vishakha**, **Shravana**, and **Bharani** are designated for the <term>Chandala</term><note>A historical term for marginalized groups outside the traditional four-fold caste system</note> classes. ॥ 30 ॥

When a star is occupied by the Sun or Saturn, or is pierced or crossed by the retrograde motion of Mars, or is eclipsed, or struck by a meteor, or otherwise afflicted by the Moon... ॥ 31 ॥

# Chapter 16: The Language Commentary

### The Moon's Domain
...lamps. **The Moon** is the lord of the following: sweet juices, flowers, fruits, water, salt, gems, conch shells, pearls, and water-lilies; **rice**, barley, medicinal herbs, wheat, and <term>Somapa</term><note>Those who drink the Soma juice during Vedic sacrifices</note> Brahmins; white and beautiful horses, amorous young women, army commanders, food, and fine garments; horned animals, night-wanderers <note>original: "nishachara" - often referring to nocturnal spirits or those active at night</note>, farmers, and those skilled in the performance of sacrifices. **|| 6-8 ||**

### The Geography of the South and West
The Moon also rules the following regions and rivers: the Shona, the Narmada, and the western half of the Bhimaratha; the Nirvindhya, Vetravati, Shipra, Godavari, and Vena rivers; the Mandakini, Payoshni, Mahanadi, Sindhu, Malati, and Para rivers; the northern Pandyas, and those living near the Mahendra, Vindhya, and Malaya mountains; the Cholas, Dravidians, Videhas, Andhras, Ashmakas, Bhasapuras, and Konkanas, along with the Mantrishikas; the people of Kuntala, Kerala, Dandaka, Kantipura, and those of mixed or foreign <term>Mleccha</term><note>A term used for non-Vedic or foreign tribes</note> descent. **|| 9-11 ||**

### The Domain of Mars
**Mars** <note>original: "Vasudhasuta" - Son of the Earth</note> is the lord of the following: the people of Nasikya, Bhogavardhana, Virata, and those dwelling on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains; those who drink the sweet waters of the Tapti and Gomati rivers; city-dwellers, farmers, and the <term>Paratas</term><note>An ancient tribe, possibly the Parthians or a border tribe</note>; those who live by fire or weapons; forest-dwellers, inhabitants of fortresses and small towns, executioners, the cruel, and the prideful. **|| 12-13 ||**

Mars also governs: princes, elephants, the deceitful, children, victims of assault, and livestock; red fruits and flowers, coral, commanders, molasses <note>original: "guda"</note>, intoxicants, and sharp objects; treasuries, fire-temples <note>original: "agnihotri"</note>, metal mines, Buddhist monks <note>original: "shakya-bhikshu"</note>, and thieves; the treacherous, those who harbor long-standing enmities, and gluttons. **|| 14-15 ||**

## 39

## 40
By the opposite characteristics mentioned above, the things under a planet's jurisdiction suffer decay. In such times, people become fearful of riots and afflicted by disease, and kings fall into great distress.
## 41

# Chapter Seventeen

### Planetary Warfare

The learned scholars who know the three divisions of time <note>past, present, and future</note> have predicted when and how the warfare of planets occurs. I have already established the scientific understanding of this in my treatise on astronomical calculation <note>original: "Karana-grantha," referring here to the Panchasiddhantika</note> according to the teachings of the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>The "Sun Canon," a foundational Sanskrit text on astronomy</note>. || 1 ||

Though the planets move in the sky one above the other, each established in its own distinct path, they appear to the observer from a great distance as if they have come together on the same plane. This appearance is what scholars call <term>Planetary Warfare</term> <note>original: "Graha Yuddha"; an astronomical conjunction where planets appear to collide or overlap</note>. || 2 ||

The ancient sages, such as Parashara and others, have stated that there are four types of planetary warfare based on their proximity and alignment: *Bheda* (Cleaving), *Ullekha* (Grazing), *Anshumardana* (Clashing of Rays), and *Apasavya* (Passing from the South). || 3 ||

In a *Bheda* (Cleaving) conflict, there is a destruction of rain, and discord arises among friends and noble families. In an *Ullekha* (Grazing) conflict, there is fear of weapons, disagreements among ministers, and a scarcity of food. || 4 ||

In an *Anshumardana* (Clashing of Rays) conflict, there are wars among kings, injuries from weapons, disease, and suffering from hunger. In an *Apasavya* (Passing from the South) conflict, the kings engage in battle. || 5 ||

The Sun is designated as the <term>Akrand</term> <note>The "Crier" or "Appealer"; a classification of planets based on their position and effect on certain social classes</note> at midday. In the forenoon, the planets are termed <term>Paura</term> <note>The "City-dwellers" or "Civic" planets</note>, and in the afternoon, they are termed <term>Yayi</term> <note>The "Marching" or "Invading" planets</note>. Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn are always considered *Paura*. The Moon is always *Akrand*. || 6 ||

Ketu, Mars, Rahu, and Venus are *Yayi*. If these planets are "defeated" <note>dimmed or overtaken in conjunction</note>, they bring destruction to the *Akrand*, *Yayi*, and *Paura* classes respectively. If they are "victorious" <note>brighter or superior in position</note>, they bring victory to their own respective groups. || 7 ||

When a *Paura* planet is defeated by another *Paura* planet, the city-dwellers and the civic kings are destroyed. In the same manner, when *Yayi* and *Akrand* planets, or *Paura* and *Yayi* planets, are struck by one another—

# The Varahi Samhita
<page-num>( 88 )</page-num>

...those who travel for war, those who cry out in distress, and the planetary lords of city-dwellers are destroyed. || 8 ||

A planet is considered **defeated** if it is situated in the southern direction, appears rough, trembling, retreats before reaching its destination, is minute, obscured by another planet, distorted, lusterless, or discolored. || 9 ||

A planet possessing the opposite characteristics is declared **victorious**. However, even if a planet is in the southern direction, it is considered victorious if it is large, glossy, and radiant. <note>This exception primarily applies to Venus; see the footnote below.</note> || 10 ||

If both planets in a conjunction are large, glossy, and joined by rays, it is called "mutual affection." In such a case, there is peace; however, if they appear the opposite, they destroy their own sides. || 11 ||

Whether it be a "war" or a "conjunction," whatever characteristics are manifested by the planets, the same results will unfailingly apply to the kings on Earth. || 12 ||

If **Jupiter** defeats **Mars**, the people of Bahlika <note>Modern-day Balkh region</note>, those traveling for war, and those who live by fire <term>Agnivatta: likely blacksmiths or priests performing fire rituals</term> suffer. If **Mercury** defeats **Mars**, the Shurasenas, Kalingas, and Salwas are oppressed. || 13 ||

If **Saturn** defeats **Mars**, the city-dwellers are victorious, but the common subjects suffer and perish. If **Venus** defeats **Mars**, there is distress for storehouses, foreigners <term>Mlechha: a term used for non-Vedic or foreign peoples</term>, and the warrior class <term>Kshatriyas</term>. || 14 ||

If **Mars** defeats **Mercury**, then trees, rivers, ascetics, and the lords of the Ashmaka people suffer...

---

### Notes
1. This specific rule <note>regarding victory in the south</note> applies only to Venus. In the chapters on planetary war, it is written that no planet except Venus remains victorious when situated in the southern direction. It is important to know that whether Venus is in the north or the south, it is usually the victor: "Whether in the north or the south, the son of Bhrigu <note>Venus</note> is generally victorious."
2. The meeting of planets is categorized as "War" <term>Yuddha</term>, "Conjunction" <term>Samagama</term>, and "Setting" <term>Astamana</term>. According to the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>A foundational Sanskrit text on astronomy</note> in the chapter on planetary conjunctions: the meeting of the five planets (Mars, etc.) with one another is called "War"; their meeting with the Moon is called "Conjunction"; and their meeting with the Sun is called "Setting" <note>Heliacal setting/combustion</note>.

# Chapter 18: The Conjunction of the Moon with the Planets
## With Commentary in the Vernacular

If the Moon passes to the north <note>original: "udak"</note>, there is victory for the powerful mountain tribes; the warrior class <term>Kshatriyas: the ruling and military caste</term> along with those on the march <note>travelers or marching armies</note> rejoice, and the earth becomes gladdened, being filled with abundant grain. || 2 ||

If the Moon passes to the north of Mercury <note>original: "Budha"</note>, it leads to victory for city-dwellers, creates abundance, increases the harvest, brings joy to the people, and fills the treasuries of kings. || 3 ||

If the Moon passes to the north of Jupiter <note>original: "Brihaspati"</note>, there is an increase in the righteousness <term>Dharma: moral and religious duty</term> of the citizens, warriors, Brahmins <note>the priestly class</note>, scholars, and the Middle Country <note>Madhyadesha, the central region of ancient India</note>; there is plenty of food, and the subjects are satisfied. || 4 ||

If the Moon moves to the north of Venus <note>original: "Bhargava/Shukra"</note>, there will be an increase in wealth, elephants, and horses; victory will come to those on the march and to the archers, and the grain harvest will be excellent. || 5 ||

If the Moon should pass to the south <note>original: "pradakshinam/dakshin"</note> of Saturn <note>original: "Ravija/Shani"</note>, there is victory for the city kings, and the Shakas, Bahlikas, Sindhus, Pahlavas, and Yavanas <note>various historical groups and Greco-Bactrian peoples of the northwest frontiers</note> are filled with joy. || 6 ||

When the cool-rayed Moon passes to the north of the asterisms <term>Nakshatras: lunar mansions or star clusters</term> without being afflicted, it nourishes the resources, the citizens, and the devoted regions; however, by passing to the south, it destroys them. The fruits of the Moon being to the north of the planets have been described; if it is to the south, the results are entirely opposite. Thus the conjunctions of the Moon with the planets and stars are declared. Indeed, a "war" <note>astrological conflict or occultation</note> never occurs between the Moon and the planets or stars. || 7 || 8 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Conjunction of the Moon with the Planets," in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by Sri Varahamihira, with the vernacular commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the northwest region. || 18 ||

It concludes the 18th chapter of the Brihat Samhita, noting that unlike other planets, the Moon does not engage in "planetary warfare."</summary>

# Chapter Nineteen
## The Results of the Planetary Years

->The Earth everywhere is covered with sparse crops; the forests are infested with wild beasts, biting insects, and are prone to forest fires. The rivers do not flow with abundant water, and medicinal herbs do not possess their full potency. <- 1

->The Sun <note>original: "Aditija," son of Aditi</note> shines with intense heat even during the winter season. The clouds, though appearing as large as mountains, do not release much rain. The sky is filled with stars and a moon that have lost their luster, and communities of ascetics and herds of cattle suffer. <- 2

->Kings, equipped with the unbearable strength of elephants, horses, and infantry, and carrying an abundance of bows, swords, and clubs, roam about. They destroy various regions in battle along with their followers during the year, month, or day presided over by the Sun. <- 3

->The sky is pervaded by clouds resembling moving mountains, possessing the dark hue of snakes, collyrium <note>eye-black</note>, bees, or buffalo horns. These clouds fill the entire earth with pure water, and the quarters of the sky echo with their deep, longing-filled thunder. <- 4

->The waters are filled with lotuses, lilies, and blue water-lilies; the groves are filled with blossoming trees and the humming of bees. The cows yield abundant milk and are pleasing to the eye, and beautiful women constantly delight their lovers with amorous play. <- 5

---

If the Sun is the lord of the year, the lord of the month, or the lord of the day, then everywhere on Earth there will be little grain. In the forests, insects will infest the trees in various places. There will not be much water in the rivers, and due to the prevalence of disease, medicinal herbs will lack their great strength. Even in the winter season, the Sun will produce sharp heat. Mountain-like clouds will not rain much water. In the sky, the brilliance of the moon and the stars will fade. There will be sorrow for the cattle and the families of ascetics. Kings, possessed of the formidable strength of elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers, taking up many arrows, bows, swords, and clubs, will wander about destroying all countries by fighting alongside their followers. 1, 2, 3.

If the Moon is the master of the year, then clouds resembling moving mountains—dark like black snakes, eye-salve, bees, and buffaloes—pervade the sky. Filling all directions with a heavy, anxious sound, they saturate the earth with pure water. In the lakes, lotuses, water-lilies, and blue lilies bloom. The gardens are filled with blossoming trees and resonate with the sound of bees. Cows give plenty of milk. Women, who are pleasing to the eyes, continuously delight men with their passion. Wheat, rice, barley, and excellent grains are prosperous. The land is marked by <term>Chaityas</term> <note>small shrines or sacred monuments</note> and is purified by the holy sounds of <term>Yajnas</term> <note>Vedic fire sacrifices</note> and <term>Homas</term> <note>oblation rituals</note>...

<summary>This page describes the astrological omens and worldly effects when the Sun or the Moon acts as the ruler of a specific time period. The Sun's rule brings drought, war, and diminished vitality, while the Moon's rule brings abundant rain, agricultural prosperity, and social harmony.</summary>

# Chapter 19: With Language Commentary (93)

The earth, filled with excellent sugarcane fields, cities, and mines, is protected by kings. It is marked by sacrificial altars and the resonant sounds of seasonal rites and sacrifices <note>original: "ritu-ishti"</note> when the Moon <note>original: "shishirago," literally 'the cold-rayed one'</note> is the ruler of the year. || 6 ||

When Mars <note>original: "avanisuta," literally 'son of the earth'</note> is the ruler of the year, a most fierce fire, driven by the wind, wanders about with the desire to burn down villages, forests, and cities. Multitudes of mortals on earth, struck down by the falling of gangs of bandits <note>original: "dasyu"</note>, cry out "Alas! Alas!" as they are rendered destitute and deprived of their cattle. || 7 ||

Even though the clouds are gathered in dense forms high in the sky, they do not release much water anywhere. The crops on the borders of the land wither away, and even those that reach maturity are carried off by others due to a lack of discipline or lawlessness. || 8 ||

Kings do not have their minds intent on properly protecting their subjects. There is an abundance of diseases arising from bile <note>original: "pitta," one of the three humors in Ayurvedic medicine</note> and a great provocation of serpents. In this way, when the year belongs to the Son of the Earth (Mars), the subjects are afflicted and the crops are ruined. || 9 ||

When Mercury <note>original: "Budha"</note> is the ruler of the year, there is an increase in those skilled in illusion, magic <note>original: "indrajal," literally 'the net of Indra'</note>, trickery, and mines, as well as city-dwellers, musicians, scribes, mathematicians, and those learned in weaponry. Out of a desire for mutual affection, kings wish to give one another wonderful sights and gifts that produce satisfaction. || 10 ||

In the world, the professions <note>original: "varta," referring to agriculture and commerce</note> remain true, and the Threefold Knowledge <note>original: "trayi," the three original Vedas</note> functions without defect. The science of government <note>original: "dandanishi," literally 'the policy of the rod'</note> proceeds properly, just as it did under Manu <note>the legendary first lawgiver</note>. Some people apply their intellects deeply to every syllable of the scriptures, seeking the supreme state through the science of logic and inquiry <note>original: "anvikshiki"</note>. || 11 ||

In his year or month, the planet Mercury thus brings to the earth those who know how to laugh, messengers, poets, children, eunuchs, and those skilled in logic and bridge-building...

# The Varahi Samhita

### The Effects of the Moon’s Son (Mercury)
In the year or month ruled by the Moon-born <note>original: "mṛgalāñchanajaḥ" - Mercury, the son of the Moon</note>, he brings joy to messengers, poets, children, eunuchs, and those skilled in logic or strategy. He satisfies those who live by bridges, waters, and mountains. During this time, medicinal herbs grow in great abundance upon the earth.

### The Year of Jupiter (The Guru of the Gods)
When Jupiter is the lord of the year, the sound of the Vedas chanted during sacrifices <note>term: "adhvare" - a Vedic sacrificial ritual</note> rises to the heavens. This great sound pierces the hearts of those who would destroy the sacrifice, while bringing constant joy to the hearts of the best of the twice-born <note>term: "dvija" - the priestly class</note> and the gods who partake in the sacrificial offerings.

The earth becomes rich with the finest crops and is filled with many elephants, horses, and vast herds of cattle. Protected by the rulers of the earth, the land prospers so greatly that the people seem to rival the inhabitants of heaven. In this auspicious year of the Preceptor of the Gods, the earth is covered by various towering clouds that satisfy the ground with water, leading to supreme prosperity and bountiful harvests.

### The Year of Venus
When Venus is the lord of the year, the earth is laden with rice and sugarcane. The fields are filled with water released from clouds that resemble mountain peaks. The land, scattered with ponds where the water is hidden by beautiful lotuses, shines like a young woman adorned with fresh jewelry.

The warrior class <note>term: "kshatra" - the ruling and military caste</note> destroys the strength of their many enemies, and the sound of victory echoes in every direction. Protecting the earth with its cities and mines, the rulers bring joy to the disciplined and virtuous while destroying the wicked.

In the season of Spring, men drink honey-wine repeatedly in the company of their beloveds. They sing songs that are pleasing to the ear, accompanied by the flute and the lute <note>note: "veṇuvīṇā" - traditional bamboo flute and stringed instrument</note>. They feast continually with guests, friends, and kinsmen...

<summary>This page describes the astrological prosperity associated with the regency of Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus, emphasizing agricultural abundance, religious harmony, and social joy. It highlights the transition from Vedic ritual success under Jupiter to the sensual and courtly pleasures under Venus.</summary>

...they enjoy meals together with guests, friends, and kinsmen; in the year of Venus <note>original: "Sita"</note>, the victory of the God of Love <note>original: "Madana"</note> is proclaimed everywhere. || 18 ||

When Saturn <note>original: "Shani"</note> is the lord of the year, the nations are troubled by gangs of thieves who have abandoned their vows and by numerous battles. When Saturn is the lord of the year, all kingdoms are distressed by thieves of wicked vows and the occurrence of many wars; the livestock and wealth of many are lost; people weep greatly due to the separation from their relatives; they are very troubled by the strikes of hunger and diseases. If an inauspicious planet is the lord of the year or the lord of the month, then the fruits produced by its weight are obtained; otherwise, auspicious fruits are also obtained. || 22 ||

### Chapter Twenty

#### On the Conjunctions of Planets

In whichever direction the star-planets <note>The "star-planets" (Taragraha) refer to Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn, distinguishing them from the Sun and Moon.</note> are seen entering the Sun, the inhabitants of that direction will suffer fear from the clashing of weapons, hunger, and intense anxiety. || 1 ||

When the planetary configurations appear in the shapes of a wheel, a bow, a triangle <note>original: "shringataka," literally a place where four roads meet or a triangular nut; here referring to a specific geometric alignment</note>, a staff, a city, a spear, or a thunderbolt, there will be famine and drought in the world, and kings will engage in war. || 2 ||

In whichever lunar mansion <note>term: "Nakshatra" (lunar mansion) - the 27 divisions of the sky through which the moon passes</note> a garland of planets is visible at sunset, a new king will take power there and there will be great trouble from foreign armies. || 3 ||

The planets destroy the people associated with the specific lunar mansion in which they congregate. However, if the planets do not collide with one another and their rays remain bright and clear, it brings prosperity to those people. || 4 ||

I shall now describe the characteristics and results of the planetary combinations known as *Samvarta* (The Overturner), *Samagama* (The Meeting), *Sammoha* (The Delusion), *Samaja* (The Assembly), *Sannipata* (The Coalescence), and *Kosha* (The Treasury). || 5 ||

When four or five "Traveling" planets <note>term: "Yayi" (Traveling) - planets currently in motion through the zodiac, often used in political astrology to represent invading forces</note> meet with "City" planets <note>term: "Paura" (City/Stationary) - planets representing the established government or home territory</note> in a single lunar mansion, it is called *Samvarta*. If Rahu or Ketu <note>The north and south nodes of the moon, responsible for eclipses.</note> are involved in this meeting, it is called *Sammoha*. || 6 ||

When a "City" planet joins another "City" planet, or a "Traveling" planet joins another "Traveling" planet, it is called *Samaja*. If another planet enters the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter, it is called *Kosha*. || 7 ||

If one planet rises in the West and another rises in the East simultaneously, it is called *Sannipata*.
