### Chapter Twenty-One
#### On the Symptoms of Cloud-Pregnancy <note>The "pregnancy" of clouds refers to the early atmospheric signs that indicate rain will fall several months later.</note>

Food is the very life of the world, and food is dependent upon the rainy season. Therefore, the rainy season must be examined with great effort. || 1 || Having observed the symptoms recorded by the ancient sages, I have composed this work based on the writings of Garga, Parashara, Kashyapa, Vatsya, and others. || 2 || The astrologer who remains focused day and night on the symptoms of cloud-pregnancy possesses speech like that of a sage; his predictions regarding water will never be false. || 3 || What other science is superior to this? By knowing this science alone, even in this destructive age <note>referring to the Kali Yuga, the current age of spiritual decline</note>, a person becomes a seer of the three periods of time <note>past, present, and future</note>...

---

*Sannipata* is the name given to a gathering of planets; in a meeting—that is, in a conjunction with the Moon—the planets are without distortion, glossy, large, and blessed. || 8 || The fruit of *Samvarta* and *Samagama* is equality; in *Sammoha* and *Kosha*, there is fear for the subjects; in the *Samaja* designation, there is excellent balance, and in *Sannipata*, there is enmity and anger. || 9 ||

->Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the great teacher Sri Varahamihira, with the Hindi commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province. <-

Food is indeed the life of the world, and food is under the control of the rainy season; for this reason, one should examine the rainy season with diligence. || 1 || I have created these symptoms of cloud-pregnancy after seeing all the signs of rain composed and bound by the sages Garga, Parashara, Kashyapa, Vatsya, and others. || 2 || Those men who know the divine and remain cautious, fixing their minds day and night on the symptoms of cloud-pregnancy, their words—like those of the sages—never prove false in the calculation of clouds. || 3 || What other science is greater than this? By knowing which great science, even in the destructive Kali age, people become seers of the three times...

# Chapter 21: Signs of Cloud Pregnancy
## With Commentary

The same reversal occurs in all other directions regarding the wind. <note>original: "viparīto bhavati vāyośca" - referring to winds blowing from directions opposite to their seasonal norms</note> || 13 ||

When the wind blows from the North-East <term>Ishana: the direction governed by Shiva</term> or the East, and is pleasant and gentle, the sky becomes clear. At such times, the moon and the sun are surrounded by glossy, thick, and white halos. || 14 ||

The sky is filled with thick, abundant, and glossy clouds, or clouds shaped like needles or razors, or tinted red. When the sky appears dark like a crow's egg <note>a deep, matte blue-black</note>, and the moon and stars shine with pure brilliance... || 15 ||

...and when rainbows, deep rumbling thunder, lightning, and parhelia <term>mock suns</term> appear; when the twilight is beautiful and groups of birds and wild animals cry out peacefully from the North, North-East, or East; || 16 ||

When the planets are large, moving in a clockwise direction <term>pradakshina: auspicious movement from left to right</term>, possessing glossy rays and free from portents of evil; when trees sprout without disease and both humans and four-legged animals appear joyful; || 17 ||

All these conditions nourish the "embryos" of the clouds. I shall now describe the specific characteristics produced by the nature of each season regarding the growth of these cloud-pregnancies. || 18 ||

In the months of Margashirsha <note>November-December</note> and Pausha <note>December-January</note>, if the twilight is red and clouds are accompanied by halos; if it is not excessively cold in Margashirsha but there is heavy snowfall in Pausha... || 19 ||

In the month of Magha <note>January-February</note>, if there are strong winds and the sun and moon are dimmed by frost; if it is extremely cold and the sun rises and sets behind clouds, it is considered a blessing. || 20 ||

In the month of Phalguna <note>February-March</note>, if the wind is harsh and violent, and there is an accumulation of clouds; if they are thick, and the sun appears reddish-brown like fire...

-># Chapter 21: With Language Commentary<-

If the embryo stays in a single lunar mansion for twenty days or three days <note>depending on specific astrological combinations mentioned in previous verses</note>, it yields rain from five sources. || 30 || If the embryos are joined by malefic planets, they produce hail, thunderbolts, and "fish-rain" <note>likely a reference to rare meteorological phenomena or symbolic of heavy, destructive downpours</note>. However, if the Moon or Sun is joined or aspected by benefic planets, they bring abundant rain. || 31 || If there is excessive rain during the "conception" period of the embryo without a natural cause, the embryo is destroyed. If the rainfall exceeds one-eighth of a <term>Drona</term> <note>a traditional unit of liquid measurement, roughly 512 handfuls</note>, the embryo is considered to have miscarried. || 32 || If a well-developed embryo does not rain at the time of delivery due to planetary afflictions, it will instead release water mixed with hail during its next natural cycle. || 33 || Just as the milk held for a long time within a cow becomes hard, so too does the water of an embryo become hard <note>turning into hail</note> when its time for delivery has passed. || 34 || An embryo formed by five natural signs <note>wind, rain, lightning, thunder, and clouds</note> rains over an area of one hundred <term>Yojanas</term> <note>a distance roughly equal to 8-9 miles</note>. For every sign that is missing, the area of rainfall is reduced by half. || 35 || An embryo with five signs yields one <term>Drona</term> of rain; one formed by wind yields three <term>Adhakas</term> <note>1/4 of a Drona</note>; by lightning, six <term>Adhakas</term>; by clouds, nine; and by thunder, twelve <term>Adhakas</term> at the time of delivery. || 36 || That embryo which is accompanied by wind, water, lightning, thunder, and clouds is very rich in water. If it releases too much water during the conception period, it will only produce a fine drizzle when the actual time for delivery arrives. || 37 ||

### Thus ends the Twenty-First Chapter, titled "Signs of Rain Embryos," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 21 ||

...rain occurs. || 30 || When joined with malefic planets, all embryos rain hail, thunderbolts, and fish; when the Moon or Sun is joined with or seen by benefic planets, they rain very heavily. || 31 || If there is much rain without cause during the conception time, there is a lack of embryo; if it rains more than one-eighth of a <term>Drona</term>, the embryo is destroyed. || 32 || If a healthy embryo does not rain due to planetary strikes, it rains water mixed with hail during its own cycle. || 33 || Just as milk kept for a long time in cows reaches a state of hardness, similarly, the water of the embryo reaches hardness after many days have passed. || 34 || An embryo nourished by five types of causes spreads and rains up to a hundred <term>Yojanas</term>; in the absence of each single cause, the rainfall decreases by half of the hundred <term>Yojanas</term>. || 35 || That is, a four-cause embryo rains 50 <term>Yojanas</term> (200 <term>Kosh</term> <note>a unit of distance, approx 2 miles</note>), a three-cause embryo 25 <term>Yojanas</term> (100 <term>Kosh</term>), a two-cause embryo 12.5 <term>Yojanas</term> (50 <term>Kosh</term>), and a one-cause embryo rains up to 5 <term>Yojanas</term> (20 <term>Kosh</term>). An embryo with five causes rains one <term>Drona</term> of water; that caused by wind rains three (3) <term>Adhakas</term>, and that caused by lightning rains 6 <term>Adhakas</term>. || 36 || An embryo that has wind, water, lightning, thunder, and clouds—

# Chapter Twenty-Two
## The Conception of Clouds

<note>The text uses the metaphor of "pregnancy" (garbha) to describe the period when clouds form and hold moisture before the monsoon rains.</note>

In the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha <note>mid-May to mid-June</note>, starting from the eighth day, there are four days designated for observing the "holding of the winds." These days are considered auspicious if the winds are soft and favorable, and if the sky is covered with smooth, glossy clouds. ॥ 1 ॥

If it rains during those same four days when the moon is in the asterisms <term>Nakṣatras</term> starting with Svātī, then the corresponding months starting with Śrāvaṇa <note>July-August</note> will be characterized by "overflowing" conceptions <note>meaning the rain will be excessive or displaced</note>. ॥ 2 ॥

If these four days remain uniform in character, it is a good omen; however, if they are inconsistent, it does not lead to well-being and is said to bring fear of thieves. On this subject, there are also verses by the sage Vasiṣṭha: ॥ 3 ॥

Conceptions accompanied by lightning, water droplets, and winds carrying dust, where the sun and moon are veiled by clouds, are considered excellent conceptions. ॥ 4 ॥

When superior lightning flashes from favorable directions, the wise man should then predict an increase in all types of crops. ॥ 5 ॥

It is also auspicious if there are light showers of dust and water, or if children are seen playing <insert>in the dirt</insert>. The sweet songs of birds and their frolicking in dust or water are also positive signs. ॥ 6 ॥

If the halos around the sun and moon are glossy and not excessively distorted, then rainfall should be expected for all crops... <note>The Sanskrit text breaks off here, followed by the Hindi commentary/translation of the previous chapter's conclusion and the start of this one.</note>

...is endowed with five omens, it yields much water; if it rains heavily during the period of "conception," then during the time of "delivery" <note>the actual monsoon</note>, it will only rain in droplets. ॥ 37 ॥

In the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, the four days starting from the eighth are the days for gaining knowledge of the "conception" through the wind. It is best if there is a soft, auspicious wind or if the sky is covered with glossy clouds. ॥ 1 ॥ If it rains during the four asterisms starting with Svātī, then in the months starting with Śrāvaṇa, the conception should be known as "overflowing," meaning there will be no rain <note>original: "pariplutā", implying the moisture is spent too early</note>. ॥ 2 ॥ If these four days are identical, it is auspicious; if the opposite occurs, they are not bringers of joy; rather, there is fear of thieves. The verses spoken by Vasiṣṭha-ji on this subject are as follows: ॥ 3 ॥ Lightning, water droplets, and wind mixed with dust, and the sun or moon being covered by clouds—this type of cloud conception is the best. ॥ 4 ॥ When excellent lightning shines in auspicious directions, the wise man should know that there will be an increase in grain. ॥ 5 ॥ If children playing together shower water or dust, or if the sounds of birds are very sweet, or if birds frolic in water etc., it is auspicious. ॥ 6 ॥ If the circles <term>halos</term> of the moon and sun are glossy and not very distorted, then at that time...

# Chapter Twenty-Three
## On Rainfall

Once the full moon of the month of Jyeshtha <note>typically falling in May-June</note> has passed, those knowledgeable in the matter should predict the good or bad effects and the quantity of water based on the rain that falls during the lunar mansion of Purvashadha and others. || 1 || The measurement of water is determined by using a round vessel <term>kundaka: a basin or bowl used for measurement</term> one cubit <note>the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</note> wide. One should measure the fallen water with this; fifty *palas* <note>a traditional unit of weight</note> constitute one *adhaka* <note>a standard unit of liquid volume</note>. || 2 || The first measurement of water should be stated based on that rain which leaves an impression on the earth or leaves droplets on the tips of blades of grass. || 3 || Some say the rainfall extends over a circle of ten *yojanas* <note>a yojana is roughly 8-9 miles</note>; however, according to the opinions of the sages Garga, Vashistha, and Parashara, it extends no further than twelve...

---

...this rain increases all types of grain. || 7 || If the clouds are smooth, thick, and move in a clockwise circle, then there is a very heavy rain that provides all grain and wealth. || 8 ||

->Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the teacher Varahamihira, with the vernacular commentary written by Pandit Baladeva Prasada Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the northwestern region.<-

When the full moon of Jyeshtha has thoroughly passed, if it rains in the Purvashadha or other lunar mansions, the wise should state the quantity of water and the auspicious or inauspicious results. || 1 || One should state the measure of water by holding a vessel one cubit long and one cubit wide; if this fills with water, one should weigh that fallen water to state the rainfall measurement. The weight of the said vessel is fifty *palas*. If this is filled with water, the measure of the fallen rain is one *adhaka*. || 2 || The first measurement of water should be stated from that rain which leaves a mark on the ground or where water drops stay on the tips of grass. || 3 || Some say that rain only occurs as far as it can be seen; others say that according to the signs mentioned above, rain occurs in a circle of ten *yojanas*. However, according to the views of Garga, Vashistha, and Parashara, beyond twelve *yojanas* (that is, 48 *kos* <note>a traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 2 miles</note>)...

## Now begins the Twenty-Fourth Chapter.

### The Conjunction of Rohini.

In the beautiful gardens situated on the peaks of Mount Sumeru <note>The sacred five-peaked mountain of Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist cosmology, considered the center of all physical and spiritual universes</note>—filled with the humming of bees attracted to the flowers of trees growing in the crevices of golden rocks, the chirping of various birds, and the soft, deep songs of celestial maidens—the deity Brihaspati <note>The preceptor of the gods and the planet Jupiter</note> narrated the teachings of the Rohini Yoga to the sage Narada. The same was taught by the sages Garga, Parashara, and Kashyapa, as well as the architect-asura Maya, to their numerous disciples. || 1–2 || Having observed those teachings regarding the conjunction of the Moon with Prajapatya <note>original: "Prajapatya" - another name for the Rohini Nakshatra, as Prajapati is its presiding deity</note>, I am now prepared to describe those very meanings in this brief work with accuracy. || 3 ||

By observing the Moon approaching the star of Prajapati <insert>Rohini</insert> during the dark fortnight <note>original: "tamisra-pakshe" - the waning phase of the moon</note> of the month of Ashadha <note>A month in the Hindu calendar, typically June–July</note>, an astrologer <term>Daivajña (one who knows the divine/fate)</term> should predict the good or evil fortune of the world according to the scriptural teachings. || 4 ||

The manner in which the conjunction is to occur should be stated even before it happens; that <term>Dhishnya-yoga (conjunction of a planet with a star)</term> has already been explained by me in the *Karana* <note>original: "Pancha-siddhantika" - Varahamihira's earlier astronomical treatise</note>. The results should be declared based on the Moon’s size, brilliance, color, path, and any natural portents <note>original: "utpata" - unusual natural phenomena or omens</note>. || 5 ||

The practitioner of the science of planetary positions should go to a spot north or east of the city. Having fasted for three days and being devoted to the sacred fire, he should draw the planets along with the host of constellations and worship them with incense, flowers, and offerings. || 6 ||

In the sacrificial area strewn with Kusha grass, he should place jars <note>original: "kalasha" - ceremonial pots</note> in the four directions. These jars should be filled with water containing gems and medicinal herbs, covered with tree shoots and sprouts, and be well-worshipped...

The Brahmin <note>a member of the priestly caste</note> should occupy a consecrated spot of ground that has been adorned and covered with *Kusha* grass <note>Desmostachya bipinnata, a sacred grass used in Vedic rituals</note>. || 7 || Having consecrated all types of seeds with the *Mahavrata* <note>original: "महाव्रत" - a "Great Vow" or specific potent Vedic chant</note> mantra, he should place them in a jar. These should be sprinkled with water containing gold and *Darbha* grass, and an oblation should be offered into the fire using the mantras dedicated to the wind god (*Maruta*), the water god (*Varuna*), and the moon (*Soma*). || 8 ||

One should fix a smooth, dark-colored flag to a pole. The flag should be four cubits long, and the pole should be three times that height (twelve cubits). Once the directions have been determined on the first day, the wind's movement should be observed via that flag when the Moon enters into conjunction with the star Rohini. || 9 ||

In this observation, the three-hour periods of the day (*Praharas*) correspond to half-months (fortnightly cycles) of the rainy season, and smaller divisions of time correspond to specific days. If the wind moves toward the left (north/east), it is always a harbinger of good fortune. The direction in which the wind blows steadily and with strength is considered the "established" wind for that period. || 10 ||

When the conjunction is complete, one must examine the seeds kept in the jar. Whichever seeds have sprouted, those specific crops will thrive and reach abundance in the coming season; those that do not sprout will not. || 11 ||

If, while the Moon is joined with Rohini, the directions are peaceful, birds and wild animals cry out pleasantly, the sky is clear, and the breeze is delightful, it is considered highly auspicious. Now, the specific results regarding the clouds and the winds shall be told: || 12 ||

In the sky, clouds may appear sometimes black and white, sometimes entirely white, and sometimes dark like serpents. Some appear with coiled bellies and visible backs, resembling the shapes of... <note>The text breaks off describing the specific cloud formations used for weather forecasting</note>

# Chapter 24: The Conjunction of the Moon with Rohini
## A Commentary in the Common Tongue

<page-num>107</page-num>

->**The Characteristics of Clouds**<-

If the sky is encompassed by vast, serpent-shaped clouds whose backs and bellies are visible, and whose tongues are the flickering lightning; **(13)** or if the heavens appear as if painted by diverse clouds—some as pure as the heart of a blooming lotus, others with edges glowing like the dawn, or as bright as honey-bees, saffron, and the blossoms of the Flame-of-the-Forest <note>original: "Kimshuka" (Butea monosperma)</note>; **(14)** or if the sky is blocked by dark clouds, yet decorated with moving lightning and the rainbow, resembling a forest filled with elephants and buffaloes and surrounded by a forest fire; **(15)** or if the firmament is covered by clouds resembling heaps of black antimony <note>original: "Anjana," a dark mineral used as eyeliner</note> stones, or by clouds that steal the luster of snow, pearls, conch shells, and the rays of the moon; **(16)**

Or if the sky is filled with "cloud-elephants" <note>The text uses a metaphor comparing clouds to royal elephants</note> that are dark as the Tamala tree or a swarm of bees, possessing lightning for their golden girth-cinches, cranes for their tusks, rain for their ichor <note>term: "Ichor" (Mada) - the fluid that flows from the temples of an elephant in rut, signifying strength</note>, and moving edges for their trunks, adorned with the high banners of the variegated rainbow; **(17)** or if the masses of clouds, dark as blue water-lilies, situated in a sky reddened by twilight, steal the beauty of Lord Vishnu <note>original: "Hari," who wears yellow garments and has dark skin</note> wrapped in his yellow robes; **(18)**

And if the deep, sharp rumble of the clouds is mingled with the cries of peacocks, Cuckoo-shrikes <note>original: "Chataka," a bird legendary for drinking only raindrops</note>, and frogs, and these clouds, hanging at the edges of the horizon and spreading across the sky, pour forth floods of water upon the earth; **(19)** if the sky remains obstructed by clouds of these described forms for one, two, or three days, then there will be abundance <note>term: "Subhiksha" - a time of good food and plenty, the opposite of famine</note>, the people will be joyful, and the earth will be rich with water. **(20)**

# The Varahi Samhita
->( Page 108 )<-

If the clouds are dry, small, and scattered by the wind, resembling camels, crows, ghosts, or monkeys <note>original: "shakhamriga" - literally 'branch-animals'</note>, or if they take other despised forms and remain silent without the sound of thunder, it brings neither prosperity nor rain. || 21 ||

Alternatively, if the sky is free of clouds but the sun shines with soft, gentle rays, it will surely rain. If the night sky is clear, filled with bright stars, and looks like a lake blooming with white water-lilies, it indicates a season of excellent rainfall. || 22 ||

The results of clouds appearing in different directions are as follows:
*   **East:** The crops will reach full maturity.
*   **South-East:** There will be danger or outbreaks of fire.
*   **South:** The crops will suffer decay or destruction.
*   **South-West:** Prices will rise, causing a dearness of grain.
*   **West:** There will be beautiful and pleasant rainfall. || 23 ||

*   **North-West:** There will be wind accompanied by scattered rain.
*   **North:** There will be abundant and nourishing rainfall.
*   **North-East:** The crops will be of the highest quality.
The winds blowing from these directions carry the same results as the clouds. || 24 ||

The falling of meteors, lightning strikes, thunderbolts, "burning" of the horizons <note>a reddish atmospheric glow</note>, earthquakes, and the cries of wild animals and birds should all be observed during this time; their omens are interpreted in the same way as the clouds. || 25 ||

One should perform a ritual with four water-pots <term>Kumbha: ceremonial clay pots</term> marked with the names of the months starting from Shravana <note>July-August</note>, placed in the cardinal directions starting from the North in a clockwise order. If a pot remains full, its corresponding month will provide plenty of water. If it leaks, there will be a drought; if the water level decreases, the rainfall will be scanty. || 26 ||

In the same manner, other pots may be marked with the names of kings and various countries <margin>to predict the fortune of specific rulers and regions</margin>...

And the same applies to others. Based on whether the pots are broken, leaking, depleted of water, or full, the fortunes should be declared accordingly. <note>This refers to a ritual test mentioned in previous verses where water pots represent different regions.</note> ॥ 27 ॥ Whether the Moon is situated far away or near, if it joins with the star <term>Rohini</term> <note>The fourth lunar mansion, associated with fertility and growth</note> while positioned on the southern path, one should predict nothing but hardship for the entire world. ॥ 28 ॥ When the Moon touches the northern part of the constellation as it passes, there will be good rain but also many calamities. If it moves to the north without touching the junction, it brings abundant rain and auspiciousness. ॥ 29 ॥ If the Moon resides in the middle of the <term>Cart of Rohini</term> <note>original: "Rohini-shakat"; a specific V-shaped formation of five stars in Taurus</note>, people will be left without shelter; they will wander everywhere with children, begging for food and drinking water from pots heated by the sun. ॥ 30 ॥ If the Moon rises first and Rohini follows behind it, then it is auspicious; however, women will be distressed by desire and remain under the influence of lustful men. ॥ 31 ॥ If the Moon follows behind Rohini like a lover following a beloved woman, then men, tormented by the arrows of <term>Makardhwaj</term> <note>The god of love, similar to Cupid</note>, will fall under the sway of women. ॥ 32 ॥ If the Moon is situated in the South-East direction, there will be great calamities; if it is in the South-West, the crops will be afflicted by pests and perish. If the Moon is in the West or North-West, there will be a moderate harvest; if it is in the North-East, there will be many virtues—

---

Place the pots in a clockwise direction according to the names of the countries, then observe them the next day. Whichever is broken, leaking, has less water, or remains full, its fortune should be judged accordingly. ॥ 27 ॥ Whether the Moon is far or near, if it is joined with Rohini in the southern path, it is distressing for the world in every way. ॥ 28 ॥ When the Moon touches the northern stars of Rohini, there is good rain along with many disturbances; and if it goes to the northern stars without touching the junction, there is still much rain and well-being. ॥ 29 ॥ If the Moon is seated in the "Cart" of Rohini (there are five stars in the shape of a cart in the sky), then men spend their time without shelter, hungry, with children, drinking water from handis <note>earthen pots</note> heated by the sun. ॥ 30 ॥ If the Moon rises first and after that Rohini rises, then it is auspicious; women troubled by the god of love fall under the control of lustful men. ॥ 31 ॥ Like a lustful man following a dear wife, if the Moon follows behind Rohini, then men, tormented by the five arrows of love, fall under the control of women. ॥ 32 ॥ If the Moon is seated in the South-East corner, great disturbances occur; if in the South-West corner, all grains are seized by pests and destroyed; if the Moon is in the West or North-West corner, there is a medium collection of crops; if in the North-East corner, there are many benefits.

# Now begins the Twenty-Fifth Chapter.
## The Conjunction with Swati.

Whatever results were predicted for the conjunction with Rohini, the same should be considered for the Moon's conjunction with the stars Swati and Ashadha. All of this should be observed during the bright fortnight of the month of Ashadha <note>June–July</note>. I shall now speak of the specific differences regarding this. || 1 || If it rains during the first part of the night while the Moon is in Swati, all crops will reach prosperity. If it rains in the second part, then sesame, mung beans, and black gram will flourish. If in the third part—

---

<margin>Hindi Commentary</margin>
...and the price of grain also increases, and so forth. || 33 || If the Moon strikes the junction-star or hides it with its body, then accordingly there is terrible fear and the killing of the King by a woman. || 34 || At evening time, when the cows return from grazing in the forest (and at that time it is the moment of the Moon's entry), if a bull or a black animal comes before them, then there is much rain. By a white animal coming in front, there is moderate rain. If a multi-colored animal is in front, then even rain-clouds do not shower rain. || 35 || If the Moon joined with Rohini is not seen in the sky covered by clouds, then a very great fear of illness comes, and on earth there is much water and grain. || 36 ||

In the second and third parts of the day, the summer grains flourish, but the autumn harvest will not occur. <note>The text refers to the division of the day into parts to predict agricultural success.</note> || 2 || If it rains in the first part of the day, there will be good rainfall for the season; if in the second part, there will be an infestation of snakes and insects. The star to the north of *Chitra* <note>Spica</note> is called <term>Apamvatsa</term> <note>Literally "Child of the Waters," identified as the star Theta Virginis</note>. When the Moon is near this star and joins with *Swati* <note>Arcturus</note>, it is considered auspicious. || 4 ||

If, on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of *Magha* <note>January/February</note>, during the conjunction of *Swati*, snow falls, or if there are fierce winds, or if water-laden clouds thunder incessantly, or if the sky is filled with streaks of lightning such that the light of the moon, sun, and stars is obscured—then it should be known that the coming rainy season will bring joy to the countryside and will be rich with all types of grain. || 5 ||

Similarly, one should observe the conjunction of *Swati* in the months of *Phalguna*, *Chaitra*, or the dark fortnight of *Vaishakha*; however, the conjunction in the month of *Ashadha* <note>June/July</note> is especially significant to understand. || 6 ||

# Now begins the Twenty-Sixth Chapter

## The Conjunction of the Full Moon in Āṣāḍha

> On the day of the full moon in the month of Āṣāḍha <note>June/July</note>, when the moon enters the lunar mansion of Uttarāṣāḍhā, one should weigh equal amounts of various seeds and leave them overnight. On the following day, whichever seed increases in weight will thrive in the coming season; that which decreases will not flourish. The following mantra <note>sacred chant</note> should be recited to consecrate the scales for this weighing. || 1 ||

> Goddess Sarasvatī, the embodiment of Truth, should be praised with this mantra: "O Goddess Sarasvatī! You are devoted to the vow of truth regarding all that is real; therefore, reveal that which is true. || 2 || By that truth through which the Moon, the Sun, the planets, and the hosts of stars rise in the East and set in the West; || 3 || that truth which is in all the Vedas, that truth which is among the knowers of the Absolute <note>original: Brahmavādiṣu</note>, and that truth which exists in the three worlds—let that truth be seen here. || 4 || You are the daughter of Brahma, celebrated as Ādityā; you are of the Kaśyapa lineage <note>original: Kaśyapī</note> by family and are famously known by the name Tulā <note>The Scales</note>." || 5 ||

> The scale's pans should be made of linen cloth, bound by four strings, and measure six fingers in width. The length of these strings should be ten fingers each. The handle-cord <term>kakṣā: the central string or grip used to lift the scales</term> between the two pans should measure six fingers. || 6 || Gold should be placed in the southern <note>right-hand</note> pan, and the remaining substances and water should be placed in the northern <note>left-hand</note> pan. Using well-water...

---

On the day of the Āṣāḍhī full moon, when the Moon moves into the constellation of Uttarāṣāḍhā, one should weigh all types of grain seeds equally and set them aside. On the next day, the grain whose seed has increased in weight will see an increase in yield; the grain that has decreased will not grow well. For this, the mantra for consecrating the scales should be recited. || 1 ||

The Goddess Sarasvatī, the soul of truth, should be praised with this mantra: "O Goddess Sarasvatī! You hold the vow of truth in all matters of reality; therefore, show us that which is true. || 2 || In this world, by the power of that truth through which the Moon, Sun, planets, and stars rise in the East and set in the West; that truth which is in all the Vedas and that truth which is in the three worlds—show that truth here. For you are the daughter of Brahma, famous by the name Ādityā; you are of the Kaśyapa lineage and are known by the name Tulā." || 3 || 4 || 5 ||

The scale-pan is made of six fingers' width, tied with four strings made of hemp. The measurement of those four strings should be ten fingers each. In this manner, a handle-cord of six fingers' measurement should be kept between the two pans (the string held to lift the scale is called the *kakṣā*). || 6 || Gold should be placed in the right-hand pan, and the other materials and water in the upper <note>northern</note> pan...

# Chapter 26: With Vernacular Commentary

<page-num>113</page-num>

->**The Secret of the Balance**<-

If the water flows from wells, lakes, or rivers, the rainfall will be poor, middling, or excellent respectively. <note>The text describes a ritual weighing of water samples taken on successive days to predict the coming monsoon.</note> Specifically, if the water from a well becomes heavier on the second day compared to the first, there will be no rain. If rainwater itself is heavier, there will be middling rain. If river or pond water is heavier, there will be proper rainfall. If all water weights increase, there is a risk of floods; if all decrease, there will be a drought. || 7 ||

The loss or gain of various groups is known through specific materials: ivory for elephants, hair for horses and cattle, gold for kings, and a <term>Sikthaka</term><note>A measure of wax roughly the size of a mouthful.</note> (wax) for the twice-born classes <note>The "twice-born" or Dvijas refers to the upper social strata: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas.</note>. Similarly, the fate of the central regions, the year, the month, the directions, and remaining commodities (like grain) should be judged by weighing the actual objects themselves. || 8 ||

A balance-scale made of gold is best; one of silver is middling. If these are unavailable, the beam should be made of Khair wood <note>Acacia catechu</note>, or shaped like an arrow that can pierce a man, measuring one <term>Vitasti</term><note>A traditional unit of length, approximately the span of a hand from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger (about 9 inches).</note> in length. || 9 ||

In the weighing process, a decrease in weight indicates destruction, while an increase indicates growth. When the weights are equal, the results are balanced. This is called the "Secret of the Balance" (<term>Tula-kosha-rahasya</term>). A person should also perform this during the <term>Rohini-yoga</term> <note>The conjunction of the Moon with the star Aldebaran.</note>. || 10 ||

The presence of malefic planets during the conjunctions of the Moon with the Nakshatras <note>Lunar mansions</note> Swati, Ashadha, or Rohini is not considered auspicious. However, in a year where there is an <term>Adhimasa</term> <note>An intercalary or "leap" month added to the lunar calendar to keep it in sync with the solar seasons.</note>, both previously mentioned conjunctions should be observed. || 11 ||

If the results of all three conjunctions (Rohini, Swati, and Ashadha) are identical, then the auspicious or inauspicious results can be predicted without a doubt. If they differ, the results derived from the Rohini conjunction are considered the most significant.

# Chapter Twenty-Seven
## The Wind-Circle

When the Eastern wind descends from the sky, having swirled by striking the crests of the waves of the Eastern Ocean, and is touched by the mane-like rays of the Moon and Sun; when it encounters masses of dark clouds that are not stationary, and nourishes the branches of the lush spring crops...

<insert>The vernacular commentary explains:</insert> Declare the result as it is; if there is a change, the fruit produced by the Rohini conjunction is considered more significant. || 12 || If the wind blows from the East, the grain is well-settled. If the wind blows from the Southeast, there is the wrath of fire. Similarly, following the clockwise direction from the South, there is light rain, medium rain, best rain, storm rain, strong rain, and auspicious rain. || 13 || After the Ashadha Full Moon, on the fourth day of the dark fortnight and in the Purva Ashadha constellation, if the clouds rain, the monsoon is praised; otherwise, it is not. || 14 || On the Ashadha Full Moon, if the wind blows from the Northeast at sunset, then the grain on earth will be excellent. || 15 ||

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the Brihat Samhita composed by the great teacher Sri Varahamihira, with the vernacular commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the Northwest region. || 26 ||

When the southern wind, sounding like a noble man, blows during this conjunction, making the monkeys dance among the canopies of palm leaves and vines; then the clouds, rising with all their effort like elephants struck by palm-hooks <note>An *ankusha* or elephant goad</note>, release only meager drops of water like a miserly person. || 3 ||

When a gale, fickle with the tossing of its great mane caused by rising dust, blows in the west at the time of the falling of the sun's rays; then the earth, though filled with crops, becomes a battlefield for great kings, covered in every place with incessant fat, flesh, and blood. || 5 ||

...with groups and, having attained growth through the fruits and grains of the autumn season, the earth becomes beautiful with all the springtime crops. || 1 ||

When in this conjunction the harsh southern wind, making a sound, keeps the monkeys dancing along with the clusters of palm trees and vines, then the clouds—exerting every kind of effort like an elephant struck by a palm-branch or a goad—release only a little rain, like a stingy man. || 3 ||

At the time of the sun's setting, when the South-Western wind swirls small cardamom and clove trees on the seashore, then it shows the earth to be like the fierce and fickle bride of a maddened ghost, covered with the weight of clusters of straw and the bone-fragments of humans who died of hunger and thirst. || 4 ||

At the time of twilight, when the wind blows in the west, fickle due to the tossing of its mane <note>A metaphor comparing the wind to a lion</note> and restless due to pride because of the raining of dust, then the earth—though possessed of grain—becomes the battlefield of primary kings and remains constantly covered in fat, flesh, and blood in various places. || 5 ||

# Now begins the Twenty-Eighth Chapter.
### Signs of Immediate Rain.

In the matter of a query regarding rain, if the Moon occupies a "watery sign" <note>Sanskrit: Salila-rashis; these include Cancer, Aquarius, Pisces, Virgo, and the latter half of Capricorn</note> and is situated in the Ascendant <note>The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon</note> or in a Quadrant <note>The 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses of a horoscope</note> during the bright fortnight—if it is aspected by benefic planets, it creates abundant water; if aspected by malefic planets, it creates little water during the rainy season.

When a question about rain is asked, if at that time the Moon takes refuge in a watery sign—namely Cancer, Aquarius, Pisces, Virgo, and the latter half of Capricorn—and is in the Ascendant or a Quadrant...

# Chapter 28: With Vernacular Commentary

Just as the Moon, so too does Venus <note>original: "Bhargava," a name for the planet Venus</note> act before long. || 1 ||

If the person asking the question touches a moist object, or water, or something named after water; or if they are standing near water, or are about to engage in an activity related to water; or if, at the time of the inquiry, the word "water" or its equivalent is heard, then the inquirer should be told without a doubt: there will be rain very soon. || 2 ||

During the rainy season, if the Sun, situated on the eastern mountain <note>the horizon at sunrise</note>, is difficult to look at due to its intense brilliance, resembling molten gold or possessing the smooth luster of a cat's-eye gem <term>Vaidurya: a chrysoberyl or cat's-eye gemstone highly valued in Vedic astrology</term>, it will bring rain that very day. Likewise, if the Sun shines with extreme intensity while high in the sky, it indicates rain. || 3 ||

The following are causes for the arrival of water: water becoming tasteless, the sky taking on the color of a cow's eye, the directions appearing perfectly clear, salt becoming moist <note>original: "lavana-vikritih," referring to the chemical change or sweating of salt due to humidity</note>, the sky appearing the color of a crow's egg, the cessation of wind, fish leaping frequently out of the water onto the bank, and the repeated croaking of frogs. || 4 ||

Cats scratching the ground intensely with their claws, an accumulation of rust on iron giving off a raw, fleshy smell, and groups of children building bridges <insert>out of sand or dust</insert> in the streets—all these announce that water will arrive shortly. || 5 ||

If the mountains resemble heaps of collyrium <note>black eye-pigment; implying deep, dark blue-black clouds resting on peaks</note>, or if their caves are choked with vapor, or if the halos around the moon resemble the eyes of a rooster, they are givers of rain. || 6 ||

...and if it is aspected by a benefic planet, then it rains heavily; if it is aspected by a malefic planet, then there is little rain and it does not rain for a long time. Venus also gives results similar to the Moon. || 1 ||

If at the time of making an inquiry, the questioner touches a wet object or water, or any object named after water, or is engaged in some work near water or related to water, or if at the time of the question the word "water" or a synonym is heard, then it can be said to the inquirer without a doubt that it will rain very soon. || 2 ||

In the rainy season, on the day when the Lord Sun, stationed on the rising mountain, causes distress to the eyes with his splendor; or possesses a smooth luster like molten gold or the Vaidurya gem, it will rain on that day. And if, having reached the high point of the sky, he burns with sharp rays, then at that time it will rain. || 3 ||

The spoiling of the taste of water, the color of the sky becoming like a cow's eye, the directions becoming clear, the sweating of Sambhar salt, the rising of clouds colored like a crow's egg, the stopping of the blowing wind, fish jumping repeatedly out of the water, and frogs making noise again and again—these are signs of the arrival of water. || 4 ||

# The Varāhī Compendium
<note>original: "वाराहीसंहिता" (Varāhīsaṃhitā). This is a celebrated 6th-century Sanskrit encyclopedic work by Varāhamihira covering astrology, planetary movements, and natural omens.</note>

If ants move their eggs from one place to another without any apparent disturbance, if snakes mate, if serpents climb trees, or if cows are seen jumping and frolicking, these are all signs that bring rain. (7)

If chameleons climb to the tops of trees and fix their gaze toward the sky, or if cows likewise lift their eyes upward to look at the sun, then water will surely fall before long. (8)

When domestic animals show no desire to leave the house, but instead keep shaking their ears and hooves, and if dogs behave in this same manner as the livestock, one should declare that water is about to fall. (9)

When dogs sit upon the roofs of houses or look steadily upward toward the heavens, and if lightning flashes in the northeast <note>original: "Pinaki-dik," the direction of Shiva/the Northeast</note> during the day, then the earth will become submerged in a great flood of water. (10)

At such a time when the moon appears with a reddish hue like the eyes of a parrot or a pigeon, or if it takes on the color of honey, and when a "mock moon" <note>original: "pratishashi," a parselene or optical phenomenon where a second moon appears</note> shines in the sky, then water will fall from the heavens without delay. (11)

If there is the sound of thunder at night, and during the day lightning streaks appear as red as blood or straight like a staff, and if a cool breeze blows from the front, then the arrival of water is imminent. (12)

If the new shoots of climbing vines point upward toward the sky, if birds "bathe" in water or dust, and if serpents or other crawling insects sit perched upon the tips of blades of grass, then the falling of rain is near at hand. (13)

# Chapter 28: Signs of Immediate Rain
## With Hindi Commentary

> When the evening clouds possess the colors of a peacock, a parrot, a blue jay, or a cuckoo <note>original: "chātaka"</note>, or if they steal the luster of the hibiscus flower and the lotus; and if they take the shapes of water waves, mountains, crocodiles, tortoises, boars, or fish, then they will yield water without delay. || 14 ||

> Those clouds which are white like nectar or the moon at their edges, but dark as eye-salve <note>original: "añjana"</note> or a swarm of bees in the center; which are glossy, multi-layered, dripping with water droplets, and arranged like a flight of stairs; and which, rising in the East, move toward the West—these clouds will soon pour forth abundant water upon the earth. || 15 ||

> If at the time of the sun's rising or setting, there appears a rainbow, a cross-bar of clouds <term>parigha: a horizontal line of clouds crossing the sun</term>, a mock sun <note>original: "pratisūrya"</note>, a red bow, or a halo like lightning, it indicates that much rain will fall very soon. || 16 ||

> If at the time of sunrise or sunset the sky takes on the color of a partridge's wing <note>speckled or mottled</note> and flocks of birds chirp joyfully, the clouds will release water day and night without delay. || 17 ||

> If at the setting of the thousand-rayed Sun, his "unfailing rays" <term>amogha-kiraṇa: clear, distinct shafts of light</term> appear high like the peaks of the sunset mountain, and if the clouds rumble close to the earth, these are to be known as great signs of rain. || 18 ||

> During the rainy season, if the Moon is aspected by a benefic planet and is situated in the seventh house from Venus, or in the ninth, fifth, or seventh house from Saturn, it is a cause for the arrival of water. || 19 ||

> Generally, at the time of the rising or setting of the planets, during their conjunctions, their entry into a new celestial circle <note>original: "maṇḍala-saṃkrama"</note>, at the end of a fortnight, or at the change of the sun's course <note>solstices</note>...

<margin>Hindi Translation and Commentary</margin>

When in the evening sky the clouds are the same color as a peacock, parrot, blue jay, or cuckoo, or if they take the luster of the hibiscus or lotus; and if they are shaped like water waves, mountains, crocodiles, tortoises, boars, or fish, then it will rain soon. || 14 ||

Clouds that are straight and white like the moon at the four edges, but in the middle have the brilliance of eye-salve or a black bee; which drip glistening drops of water and are stacked one above the other like steps; and which come from the East and go toward the West—those clouds soon rain much water on the earth. || 15 ||

At the time of sunrise or sunset, if a rainbow, a horizontal cloud-bar, a second sun, a staff-shaped rainbow, or a halo like lightning is visible, then it rains heavily very soon. || 16 ||

At the time of sunrise or sunset, if the color of the sky becomes like the wings of a partridge and flocks of birds chirp with joy, then the clouds soon rain day and night. || 17 ||

If at the setting of the thousand-rayed Sun, the "unfailing rays" are present, high like the rays of the sunset mountain, and if the clouds make a sound near the earth, then these things can be called great signs of rain occurring. || 18 ||

If during the rainy season the Moon is seen by auspicious planets and is in the seventh sign from Venus, or in the ninth, fifth, or seventh sign from Saturn, this is a cause for the arrival of water. || 19 ||

At the end of a lunar fortnight, or at the conclusion of the Sun's solstice, rain occurs; likewise, rain falls as a rule when the Sun enters the lunar mansion of Ardra <note>The 'Moist One,' a star cluster associated with the god Rudra and the onset of the monsoon</note>. || 20 ||

Water falls during the conjunction of Mercury and Venus, Mercury and Jupiter, or Jupiter and Venus. However, a conjunction of Saturn and Mars—if not witnessed by or joined with beneficial planets—brings fear of wind and fire. || 21 ||

When the planets that follow the Sun's path are positioned either in front of or behind it, they then make the earth appear as if it were a single vast ocean <note>implying heavy, widespread flooding</note>. || 22 ||

# Chapter 29
## Signs from Flowers and Creepers

By observing the abundant growth of fruits and flowers on trees and plants, one can determine the easy availability of commodities and the successful ripening of crops. || 1 ||

The growth of the *Shala* tree <note>Shorea robusta</note> indicates the success of *Kalama* rice; the Red *Ashoka* indicates red rice; the *Kshirika* <note>a milky tree, likely Sapota</note> indicates pale rice; and the Blue *Ashoka* indicates *Sukaraka* rice. || 2 ||

The *Nyagrodha* <note>Banyan tree</note> indicates the growth of barley; the *Tinduka* <note>Persimmon family</note> indicates the sixty-day ripening rice; and the *Ashvattha* <note>Sacred Fig</note> indicates the success of all types of crops. || 3 ||

The *Jambu* <note>Java Plum</note> indicates the success of sesame and black gram; the growth of the *Shirisha* indicates the success of foxtail millet. And wheat is indicated by...

...at the end, and when the Sun enters Ardra, rain usually occurs according to the rules. || 20 ||

Rain falls from the meeting of Mercury and Venus, the meeting of Mercury and Jupiter, and the union of Jupiter and Venus. If Saturn and Mars join without being seen by or meeting a good planet, there is a fear of fire. || 21 || When the planets that depend on the Sun stay either to the East or the West of the Sun, they make the earth like the ocean. || 22 ||

From the growth of the Banyan, barley; and from the growth of *Tinduka*, *Vrishtika* grains occur; and from the growth of the *Pipal*, all grains increase. || 2 || 3 || From the growth of the Rose Apple (*Jamun*), sesame and black gram (*Urad*); from the growth of the *Shirisha*, foxtail millet (*Kangni*)...

An increase in Wheat is known by the *Madhuka* <note>original: "मधूक"; Butter tree</note> and Barley by the *Saptaparna* <note>original: "सप्तपर्ण"; Seven-leaf tree</note>. || 4 ||

# Chapter 30
->Signs of the Twilight<-

The period of twilight <note>Sanskrit: Sandhyā</note> lasts from the time the sun is half-set until the stars become clearly visible in the sky; similarly, in the morning, it lasts from the first appearance of stars until the sun is half-risen. During this time, the following signs indicate future results: || 1 || Wild beasts, birds, wind, halos <note>pariveṣa</note>, atmospheric circles <note>paridhi</note>, horizontal clouds <note>parigha</note>, clouds, trees, rainbows, "cities of the Gandharvas" <note>mirages or Fata Morgana</note>, sunbeams, rod-like light formations, dust, moisture, and colors. || 2 ||

A wild beast <note>mṛga - often referring to deer or forest animals</note> crying out loudly and terrifyingly repeatedly foretells the destruction of a village. If the beast is positioned to the south of an army and makes a great noise while facing the sun, it brings about the destruction of that army. || 3 || If the beast is on the right <note>south</note> in a calm state, it indicates battle; if on the left, it indicates the meeting of armies. If the wind blows from mixed directions during twilight while deer or ruddy geese <note>cakravāka</note> are active, there will be rain. || 4 || The morning twilight, if filled with the cries of beasts and birds facing the sun in the east, announces the ruin of the country. If these creatures face the sun from the southern direction while crying out, it indicates the capture of the city by enemies. || 5 ||

---

<note>The following is the Hindi commentary/translation by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra of Moradabad</note>

In a land where such signs appear, there will be auspicious rain, and in a land where the leaves of trees are dry and full of holes, it rains only a little. || 14 ||

->Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the vernacular commentary<-
->written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad<-
->in the North-Western province, for the Bṛhat Saṃhitā<-
->composed by the great teacher Varahamihira. || 29 ||<-

Every day, from the time the sun is half-set until the stars are clearly visible in the sky, it is twilight; likewise, before the sun is half-risen, from the time stars are visible, it is twilight. || 1 || The results of the twilight are told through these signs: wild beasts, birds, wind, halos, circles, horizontal clouds, clouds, trees, rainbows, celestial cities, sunbeams, rods of light, dust, oiliness/moisture, and color. || 2 || A beast making a loud, fearful sound repeatedly gives information of the destruction of a village. If a beast situated on the right side of an army makes a great sound while facing the sun, the army is destroyed. || 3 || If it is calm in the south, there is battle; if it is on the left, there is a gathering of the army. During twilight, if the wind moves in mixed directions along with the deer and geese, there will be rain. || 4 || At the time of morning twilight in the east, a twilight joined with the sounds of beasts and birds facing toward the sun reveals the destruction of the country. Beasts and birds facing the sun in the south indicate the city will be seized by enemies...

# Chapter 30 with Language Commentary
<page-num>123</page-num>
->**Header: Chapter 30 with Language Commentary**<-

If a strong wind blows, destroying houses, trees, and <term>monumental gateways</term><note>Sanskrit: Torana; ceremonial arched gateways</note>, scattering dust and clods of earth with a terrifying, harsh sound that brings down birds, such a **twilight** is considered **inauspicious**. || 6 ||

Conversely, a **twilight** is **venerated** when the wind is gentle, lightly rustling the leaves of the <term>Palash trees</term><note>Butea monosperma, often called 'Flame of the Forest'</note>, or when the air is still and the birds and deer cry out with sweet, peaceful notes in the quiet directions. || 7 ||

During the time of twilight, if the following are glossy and clear—the <term>Staff</term><note>Danda; a vertical atmospheric glow</note>, lightning, the <term>Fish</term><note>Matsya; a specific cloud formation resembling a fish</note>, the <term>Halo</term><note>Paridhi/Parivesha</note>, the <term>Bow of Indra</term><note>Surapatichapa; the rainbow</note>, and the <term>Airavata</term><note>A specific type of straight, multi-colored solar ray</note>—they bring immediate rain. || 8 ||

If the rays of the sun at twilight are broken, uneven, destroyed, hideous, crooked, turned toward the left, thin, short, agitated, or dirty, they portend **war** and a **lack of rain**. || 9 ||

In a cloudless and darkness-free sky, if the rays of the **Sun** are radiant, clear, straight, long, and revolve toward the right <note>clockwise/circumambulatory</note>, it brings auspiciousness and well-being to the world. || 10 ||

If the rays of the sun at the beginning, middle, and end of the day are white, glossy, continuous, and straight, they bring rain; these rays are specifically named **Amogha** <note>meaning 'unfailing' or 'fruitful'</note>. || 11 ||

If the rays appear variegated, brownish, reddish-brown, or have the tints of madder-red or green, and stretch across the heavens, they cause rain but also bring a small amount of fear for seven days. || 12 ||

If the rays are copper-colored, it signifies the **death of the commander-in-chief**; if they are a mixture of yellow and red, the commander-in-chief suffers distress. If they are green, there is destruction of cattle and grain. If they are smoke-colored, cows perish. If they have the luster of madder-red, there is fear of weapons and fire...

# The Varahi Samhita

### Chapter on Portents

...that leads to misery. If the clouds are the color of pigeon-peas <note>original: "haritah"</note>, there is destruction of cattle and crops; if they are the color of saffron, it signifies the loss of cows. || 13 ||

If they appear the color of madder <note>a reddish-purple dye</note>, there is alarm from weapons and fire; if tawny, there is wind and rain. If they resemble ashes, there is a lack of rain; and if they are variegated or spotted, it indicates a thinning or scarcity of rainfall. || 14 ||

When the evening dust, resembling the color of the Bandhuka flower <note>a bright red flower</note> or powdered collyrium <note>black eye-salve</note>, approaches the sun, the world is then afflicted by hundreds of diseases. However, white dust leads to the prosperity and peace of the people. || 15 ||

A phenomenon formed by the combination of sunbeams, clouds, and wind, standing straight like a staff, is called a **Danda** <term>Danda: literally 'Staff'; a vertical atmospheric phenomenon like a sun pillar</term>. If it appears in the intermediate directions <note>North-east, South-east, etc.</note>, it is inauspicious for kings; if in the cardinal directions, it is inauspicious for the twice-born classes <note>the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas</note>. || 16 ||

If seen at dawn, midday, or twilight, it causes fear of weapons and disease. If it is white or other specific colors, it harms the Brahmins and others respectively, and it destroys whichever direction it faces. || 17 ||

A blue cloud that covers the sun, has edges resembling curd <note>thick and white</note>, and stands in the middle of the sky is called an **Abhrataru** <term>Abhrataru: 'Cloud-Tree'; likely a cumulonimbus or a tree-shaped cloud formation</term>. These, along with clouds tinged with yellow and having a thick base, bring abundant rain. || 18 ||

If an 'Abhrataru' rises behind a king who is marching against an enemy and suddenly vanishes, it portends the death of the Crown Prince and the Minister. || 19 ||

An evening sky that possesses the luster of blue lilies, lapis lazuli, or the filaments of a lotus, is free from heavy winds, and is illuminated by the rays of the sun, brings immediate rain. || 20 ||

Clouds of inauspicious shape, or those associated with 'Gandharva-cities' <note>mirages</note>, mist, dust, or smoke... in the rainy season...

...increase the strength of kings. || 28 || Clouds that hang low, resembling trees, or those reflecting the sharp, reddish light of the sun during the two twilights <note>dawn and dusk</note> bring well-being. If the clouds resemble the shapes of cities at these times, they bring good fortune. || 29 || If the twilight is filled with the cries of birds, jackals <note>original: "shiva," referring to the female jackal, often an omen-bearer</note>, or deer facing the sun, or if it is accompanied by "staffs" <note>vertical light streaks</note>, dust storms, or "bolts" <note>horizontal clouds</note>, or if the sun appears distorted daily, it leads to the destruction of the country, the king, and the abundance of food. || 30 || The morning twilight gives its results immediately; the night or evening twilight gives results within three days. If the halo, dust, and "cloud-bolts" do not yield results on the same day, they do so within a week. Similarly, sunbeams, rainbows, lightning, mock suns <note>parhelia</note>, clouds, and winds ripen their effects by the eighth day, while the omens of birds and deer take a week. || 31 || Twilight illuminates one <term>yojana</term> <note>a traditional measure of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> with its light; lightning illuminates six yojanas. The sound of thunder travels five yojanas, but there is no fixed limit to the distance a falling meteor may be seen. || 32 || The glow of the mock sun <note>original: "pratyarka"</note> extends three yojanas, the "cloud-bolt" <note>parigha</note> five yojanas, and the circle of the halo is visible for five or six yojanas. The bow of the Lord of Immortals <note>the rainbow of Indra</note> shines across ten yojanas. || 33 ||

# Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, named "Characteristics of Twilight," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 30 ||

---

Clouds that take a form increase the power of kings. || 28 || If at twilight the clouds appear like trees reflecting the sharp sun, or if they hang down, it is auspicious. At this same time, if the clouds look like a city, it is favorable. || 29 || If birds, jackals, and deer cry out while facing the sun, and if the twilight is joined with "staffs," dust, and "bolts," or if it causes a daily distortion of the sun, it is the cause of the destruction of the country, the king, and the harvest. || 30 || The eastern <note>morning</note> twilight gives results instantly; the night or evening twilight in three days. If the halo, dust, and "bolts" do not give results that day, they give them in one week. Likewise, sun-rays, rainbows, lightning, mock suns, clouds, and wind ripen their results in eight days, and birds and deer in a week. Twilight illuminates one yojana with its glow, and lightning illuminates six yojanas with its brilliance. The thundering of clouds reaches five yojanas, and there is no measure to the yojanas of a falling meteor. || 31 || 32 || The glow of the halo named the "mock sun" is three yojanas, the glow of the "bolt" is five yojanas, the glow of the halo-circle is seen up to five or six yojanas, and the rainbow illuminates ten yojanas. || 33 ||

->Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the vernacular commentary composed by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, inhabitant of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the Brihat Samhita authored by the venerable teacher Varahamihira. || 30 ||<-

# Now begins the Thirty-First Chapter
## Characteristics of the Burning of the Quarters

A yellow glow in the directions <note>original: "digdaha"; an atmospheric phenomenon where the horizon appears to be on fire, likely referring to unusual auroras, dust storms, or twilight glows</note> brings fear to the king; a fire-colored glow causes the destruction of the country; and if it appears reddish-brown accompanied by a wind blowing from the right <note>original: "apasavya-vayu"; an unfavorable wind direction in Vedic meteorology</note>, it destroys the standing crops. || 1 ||

That glow which shines with extreme intensity, casting shadows as if from the sun itself, brings great peril to the king. If the glow resembles the color of blood, it foretells the outbreak of war and the fury of weapons. || 2 ||

If the glow appears in the East, it causes suffering to the warrior class <note>Kshatriyas</note> and their rulers. In the South-East, it brings distress to artisans and princes. In the South, it affects fierce men, the merchant class <note>Vaishyas</note>, messengers, and women who have remarried. || 3 ||

In the West, the laboring class <note>Shudras</note> and farmers suffer. In the North-West, it brings trouble to thieves along with their horses. In the North, the priestly class <note>Brahmins</note> are afflicted, and in the North-East, it brings suffering to heretics and traders. || 4 ||

If the sky is clear, the stars are bright, the wind blows in a favorable clockwise direction, and the glow in the quarters is the color of pure gold, then it serves the welfare of the people and the king alike. || 5 ||

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "Characteristics of the Burning of the Quarters," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira.

---

A yellow-colored <term>Digdaha</term> <note>The "burning of the directions"</note> is a cause for fear of the king; a fire-colored glow causes the destruction of the nation; and a red glow with a southern wind destroys the grain. || 1 ||
A glow that possesses extreme brilliance and reveals shadows like the sun—that blood-like burning brings great fear to kings and manifests the rage of weapons. || 2 ||
If the glow occurs in the Eastern direction, then kings and warriors are pained; in the South-East corner, it gives pain to groups of princes and practitioners of crafts; in the South, it is painful to fierce men, merchants, messengers, and women married a second time. || 3 ||
In the West, the laborers and farmers; in the North-West corner, thieves along with their horses; in the North, the Brahmins; and in the North-East corner, heretics and shopkeepers suffer pain. || 4 ||
When the sky is pleasant, the lunar mansions are stainless, and the wind moves in a circling motion, then a gold-colored glow is the cause of benefit for the people and the king. || 5 ||

# Chapter Thirty-Two
## Signs of Earthquakes

Some authorities assert that earthquakes are caused by massive creatures living deep within the subterranean waters. Others maintain that they occur when the "Elephants of the Directions" <note>The Diggajas: mythical elephants who support the world at the cardinal points</note>, exhausted by the burden of the earth, shift their positions to rest. (1)

One school of thought suggests that when one wind strikes another and falls to the earth, it creates a roar and causes the ground to tremble. Other masters, however, claim that earthquakes are produced by unseen forces <note>Adṛṣṭa: often referring to karmic or supernatural destiny</note>. (2)

In ancient times, the earth was shaken by mountains that possessed wings, as they constantly plummeted down or soared upward. Distressed, the Earth spoke to the Grandfather <note>Lord Brahma, the Creator</note> in the assembly of the gods, filled with shame: (3)

"O Lord! The name 'Achala' <note>The Immovable One</note> which you bestowed upon me is no longer true. I am being made to move by these shifting mountains, and I can no longer endure this suffering." (4)

Seeing her face—her voice trembling with emotion, her lips quivering slightly, her head bowed, and her eyes filled with tears—the Grandfather spoke: (5)

"Indra, remove the sorrow of the Earth! Cast your thunderbolt <note>The Kulisha or Vajra</note> to break the wings of the mountains." Indra replied, "It shall be done," and told the Earth, "Fear no more. (6)

However, the gods of Wind, Fire, Indra, and Varuna <note>The god of the waters</note> shall hereafter cause you to tremble during the first, second, third, and fourth parts of the day and night, respectively, in order to signal the coming of good or evil results." (7)

The four constellations beginning with Aryaman <note>Uttara Phalguni</note>—namely Uttara Phalguni, Hasta, Chitra, and Swati...

# Chapter Thirty-Three

## Characteristics of Meteors

Meteors are the forms of those who, having exhausted the fruits of their good deeds in heaven, are now falling back to earth. They are divided into five types: *Dhishnya* <note>a spark-like meteor</note>, *Ulka* <note>a standard meteor</note>, *Ashani* <note>a thunderbolt or meteorite</note>, *Vidyut* <note>lightning</note>, and *Tara* <note>a shooting star</note>. || 1 ||

A meteor yields its effects within a fortnight <note>fifteen days</note>; similarly, the *Dhishnya* and the thunderbolt yield results within three fortnights <note>forty-five days</note>. Lightning and shooting stars bring their effects to fruition in six days. || 2 ||

The shooting star is said to give one-quarter of the predicted result, while the *Dhishnya* gives half. The other three—lightning, the meteor, and the thunderbolt—give their results in full. || 3 ||

The thunderbolt (*Ashani*) falls with a great roar, tearing the surface of the earth in a circular shape; it falls upon men, elephants, horses, deer, stones, houses, trees, and cattle. || 4 ||

Lightning (*Vidyut*) suddenly creates terror in living beings with a crackling sound; it falls in a crooked and wide shape, blazing upon living creatures and piles of fuel. || 5 ||

The *Dhishnya* is thin with a small tail, appearing like a glowing coal; it is seen over a distance of more than ten bows <note>a unit of length, roughly 60 feet</note> and measures two cubits in size. || 6 ||

A shooting star (*Tara*) is one cubit long and may be white, copper-colored, or like the fiber of a lotus; it moves horizontally, downwards, or upwards...

---

If an earthquake occurs again on the fourth or seventh day, or within a month, a fortnight, or three fortnights, then the primary king is destroyed. || 32 ||

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by Sri Varahamihira, with the vernacular commentary by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region. || 32 ||

The form taken by persons who have enjoyed the fruits of their merits in heaven at the time of their fall is called a meteor. There are five divisions of meteors: *Dhishnya*, *Ulka*, *Ashani*, lightning, and stars. || 1 || The effect of a meteor occurs in 15 days; likewise, the *Dhishnya* and thunderbolt in three fortnights (meaning 45 days); and the result of a star or lightning occurs in six days. || 2 || The star is the bringer of one-fourth of the fruit, the *Dhishnya* gives half the fruit, and lightning, meteors, and thunderbolts—these three give the full fruit. || 3 || The shape of the thunderbolt is like a wheel; it tears the earth with a loud sound and falls upon humans, elephants, horses, deer, stones, houses, trees, and animals. || 4 || Making a *tad-tad* sound, lightning suddenly causes fear to creatures; being curved and large, it falls blazing upon living beings and heaps of wood. || 5 || The thin, small-tailed *Dhishnya* appears like a burning ember for a distance of a little more than ten bows; its measure is two cubits. || 6 || A star is copper-colored, lotus-like, thread-like, or white;

# Chapter 33: With Vernacular Commentary
### Page 135

If a meteor should strike a temple of Brahma, it destroys the Brahmins <note>The priestly and scholarly class</note>; if it falls in a cowshed, it destroys the owners of cattle. **(22)** When the fall of a meteor is accompanied by sounds of *kshveda* <note>original: "क्ष्वेड" - the lion-like roar of a warrior in battle</note>, the clapping of hands, instrumental music, singing, or loud cries of distress, it portends danger to the nation and its king. **(23)**

A meteor that remains in the sky for a long time in the shape of a staff <note>danda</note> brings fear to monarchs. Likewise, one that appears to be suspended in the sky as if held by a thread, or one that resembles the banner of Great Indra, is a bringer of fear to the King. **(24)**

A meteor that moves in a reverse direction <note>returning to its point of origin</note> destroys the chief merchants <note>term: Shreshthin - wealthy guild leaders or bankers</note>. One that moves horizontally destroys the royal women. If it moves downward, it destroys kings, and if it moves upward, it destroys the Brahmins. **(25)**

One shaped like a peacock's tail brings about the destruction of the people. One that glides like a serpent is inauspicious for women. **(26)** A circular meteor destroys the city; one shaped like a parasol <note>chhatra</note> destroys the royal priest. A meteor appearing like a clump of bamboo causes defects and disorders in the nation. **(27)**

Meteors resembling a serpent or a boar, those garlanded with sparks, or those that break into fragments or travel with a great noise, are givers of sin and suffering. **(28)** If a meteor resembles the bow of the Lord of the Gods <note>original: "Surapatichapa" - the rainbow</note>, it destroys the kingdom. If it dissolves into the atmosphere, it destroys the clouds <note>preventing rain</note>. One that travels crookedly against the wind or turns back upon itself is never auspicious. **(29)**

From whichever direction a meteor falls upon a city or an army, from that very direction shall danger come to the monarch. However, if a king marches toward the direction where the meteor’s light was cast, he shall swiftly conquer his enemies. || 30 ||

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "Characteristics of Meteors," in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the illustrious Varahamihira. || 33 ||

# Chapter 34
## Characteristics of Halos

The rays of the sun or moon, when reflected by the wind and formed into a circular shape within a sky containing thin clouds, appear in various colors and forms; these are called <term>Parivesha</term> <note>Halos or atmospheric rings around celestial bodies</note>. || 1 ||

These halos may be red, blue, pale white, pigeon-colored, cloud-colored, variegated <note>multi-colored or dappled</note>, greenish, or bright white. They are created, respectively, by Indra, Yama, Varuna, Nirriti, Vayu, Mahadeva <note>Shiva</note>, Brahma, and Agni. || 2 ||

Kubera, the Giver of Wealth, creates a dark-colored halo. Those halos that arise from a combination of qualities and dissolve repeatedly are caused by the wind and yield little result. || 3 ||

A halo that possesses the luster of a blue jay’s wing, a peacock, silver, oil, water, or milk; which appears in its proper season; which is a complete, unbroken circle; and which is glossy <note>smooth or oily in appearance</note>, brings about prosperity and an abundance of food. || 4 ||

A halo that traverses the entire sky, possesses many tints, resembles blood, or appears rough and dry...

---

<margin>Note: This section contains the Hindi commentary by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra of Moradabad.</margin>

...is. || 29 || From whichever side a meteor comes and falls upon a city or an army, from that very direction the King faces fear. If the King travels toward the direction illuminated by the fall, he becomes capable of quickly conquering his enemies. || 30 ||

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the vernacular commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the Great Teacher Varahamihira. || 18 || <note>The numbering 18 likely refers to the specific section of the commentary.</note>

The rays of the sun or moon, reflected above <insert>the clouds</insert> and made circular by the wind, appear in many colors and shapes in a sky with few clouds; these are called halos. || 1 || Red, blue, slightly white, pigeon-colored, cloud-colored, variegated (endowed with many types of colors), green, and white halos are produced, in order, by Indra, Yama, Varuna, Nirriti, Vayu, Mahadeva, Brahma, and Agni. || 2 || Kubera, the Giver of Wealth, is said to produce a black-colored halo. That which dissolves repeatedly due to the influence of various qualities is the halo of Vayu (the Wind), which gives meager results. || 3 || A halo that has an aura like a blue jay, a peacock, silver, oil, milk, or water; which is produced in its proper season; whose circle is not broken; and which is glossy, is the bringer of good harvests and auspiciousness. || 4 || A halo that travels across the whole sky, has many glows, is like blood, or is dry...

If the halo appears rough in texture and resembles a broken cart, a bow, or a <term>Shringataka</term> <note>a triangular aquatic fruit or a crossroad shape</note>, it is considered sinful and inauspicious. || 5 ||

If the halo is the color of a peacock's neck, there will be excessive rain. If it is multicolored, it foretells the death of a king. A smoke-colored halo brings fear. If it resembles a rainbow or the brilliance of an Ashoka flower, it indicates impending war. || 6 ||

When a halo appears very glossy with a single uniform color in its proper season, and is surrounded by small clouds shaped like razors, or if the sun's rays appear yellow, it brings immediate rain. || 7 ||

A massive halo appearing during the three periods of twilight <note>dawn, noon, and dusk</note>, accompanied by the cries of birds and wild animals facing the sun, is terrifying. However, if this halo is pierced by lightning or meteors, the king will meet his death by a weapon. || 8 ||

If the halos of the sun and moon appear blood-red day and night, it signifies the slaughter of the ruler. The same result occurs if halos frequently appear at sunrise, sunset, or high noon. || 9 ||

A double halo <note>two concentric rings</note> brings fear to the <term>Senapati</term> <note>Commander-in-Chief</note>, but does not cause extreme military conflict. # Now begins the Thirty-Fifth Chapter.

## Characteristics of Indra’s Weapon <note>The Rainbow</note>.

The multi-colored rays of the sun, when dispersed by the wind in a cloudy sky and appearing in the shape of a bow, are called Indra’s Bow <note>Indradhanush — the rainbow</note>. || 1 || Some teachers <note>original: ācāryāḥ</note> say it is produced by the breath of the infinite lineage of serpents <note>Ananta-kula-nāga</note>. If kings march facing this rainbow, it brings them defeat in battle. || 2 || If it is unbroken, touching the earth, radiant, glossy, thick, multi-colored, and—

---

<note>The following is the Hindi vernacular commentary on the preceding Sanskrit verses</note>

If a halo occurs on the twelfth day, the city is besieged, and on the thirteenth, there is agitation from weapons. || 20 || A halo on the fourteenth causes pain to the Queen; on the fifteenth, it causes pain to the King. || 21 || If a line is visible inside the halo, then the city-dwellers suffer; if the line is outside the halo, then the kings who are attacking suffer; if it is in the middle of the halo, one should judge the good or bad fortune of the *Akrandasara*. || 22 || By dividing the country according to planetary devotion or the *Kūrma* division, the region where the halo's color is red, dark, or rough will be defeated. Those in whose portion a glossy, white, or brilliant halo falls will be victorious. || 23 ||

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the vernacular commentary composed by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the *Brihat Samhita* authored by the illustrious teacher Varahamihira. || 34 ||
