A rainbow that is smooth, thick, multi-colored, appearing twice <note>original: "dviruditam" - referring to a double rainbow</note>, and following the natural order <note>curving in the expected direction</note> is considered excellent and bestows abundant water. || 3 ||

If it arises in the intermediate directions <note>the corners: Northeast, Southeast, Southwest, or Northwest</note>, it destroys the ruler of that quarter. If it appears in a cloudless sky, it causes death. If it displays the colors of the trumpet-flower <note>pale red</note>, yellow, or dark blue, it brings about defects caused by weapons, fire, and famine. || 4 ||

A rainbow appearing in the middle of water causes a drought; appearing on the earth, it destroys the crops; appearing on a tree, it brings disease; appearing on an anthill <term>Valmika: a mound of earth made by termites or ants, often seen as a sensitive earth-point in Sanskrit literature</term>, it brings fear of weapons; and appearing at night, it leads to the assassination of a royal minister. || 5 ||

During a drought, a rainbow in the east brings rain; during a rainy period, a rainbow in the east stops the rain. However, a rainbow appearing in the west always indicates that rain is established. || 6 ||

If Indra's bow <note>the rainbow</note> appears at night in the eastern direction, it causes suffering to kings. If it arises in the south, west, or north, it destroys the general of the army, the leader, and the minister respectively. || 7 ||

A rainbow at night that is white or other specific colors causes pain to the social classes starting with the Brahmins <note>white for priests, red for warriors, yellow for merchants, and black for laborers</note>. Furthermore, in whichever direction it is visible, it will shortly destroy the chief ruler of that region. || 8 ||

If it rises twice and is in the natural direction, it is excellent and rains much water. || 3 ||

If a rainbow rises in the four corners—Northeast, Southeast, Southwest, and Northwest—the king of that establishment is destroyed. If the rainbow is in the water, there is a lack of rain; if on the earth, there is loss of grain; if on a tree, there is disease; if on an anthill, there is fear of weapons; and if it occurs at night, it is the cause of a minister's death. || 5 ||

If at a time of no rain the rainbow is in the eastern direction, it rains; if it is in the east during a time of rain, it stops the rain. If the rainbow is in the west, there is always rain. || 6 ||

# Now begins the Thirty-Sixth Chapter.
## The City of the Gandharvas <note>original: "Gandharvanagara." This refers to a Fata Morgana or superior mirage—an atmospheric optical phenomenon where complex structures like towers or cities appear in the sky.</note>.

A celestial city appearing in the North and other directions brings harm respectively to the Royal Priest, the King, the Commander-in-Chief, and the Crown Prince. If it appears white, red, yellow, or black, it causes the destruction of the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras <note>The four traditional social classes of ancient India</note> respectively. || 1 ||

If situated in the North, it brings victory to the city and its kings. If situated in the intermediate directions <note>Northeast, Southeast, and Northwest</note>, it leads to the destruction of the lower classes. If a "City of the Gandharvas" is seen in a peaceful quarter <note>a direction not afflicted by harsh winds or solar glare</note> adorned with triumphal arches, it signifies victory for the King. || 2 ||

If it appears constantly in all directions, it brings fear to the King and the kingdom. If it resembles smoke, fire, or a rainbow, it destroys thieves and forest-dwellers. || 3 ||

A slightly pale-white celestial city brings lightning strikes and stormy winds. If it appears in a "blazing" direction <note>the direction where the sun is currently positioned</note>, the King will die. If it appears to the left, there is fear of the enemy; if to the right, there is victory. || 4 ||

When a city appears in the sky with many colors and shapes, equipped with banners, flags, and arches, then the earth drinks a great deal of blood from elephants, men, and horses in battle. || 5 ||

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Characteristics of the City of the Gandharvas," in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the illustrious Varahamihira.

---

If the City of the Gandharvas is in the North, East, South, or West, then in that order, there is an obstacle for the Priest, King, General, and Prince. If it is white, red, yellow, or black in color, it is the cause of destruction for the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras. || 1 ||

If it is in the North, it gives victory to the city and kings. If it is located in the Northeast, Southeast, or Northwest corners, the lower castes are destroyed. If a City of the Gandharvas with a triumphal arch is seen in a peaceful direction, the King is victorious. || 2 ||

If the City of the Gandharvas is always in all directions, it is fearful for both the King and the state; and if it is like smoke, fire, and a rainbow, it kills thieves and forest-dwellers. || 3 ||

If the City of the Gandharvas is somewhat pale in color, then lightning falls and a storm wind blows. If the City of the Gandharvas is in a "blazing" direction, the King dies. If it is in the left direction, there is fear of enemies, and if located in the right part, there is victory. || 4 ||

When a Gandharva city with many colored banners, flags, and arches is manifest in the sky, then the earth drinks much blood of elephants, men, and horses in battle. || 5 ||

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the vernacular commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region, on the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the Great Teacher Varahamihira. || 36 ||

# Chapter 37
## Characteristics of the Mock Sun

A mock sun <note>original: "Pratisurya"; also known as a parhelion or "sun dog," an atmospheric optical phenomenon</note> is considered auspicious when it possesses the same brilliance and color as the sun itself, appearing glossy, clear like a cat's-eye gem <note>original: "Vaidurya"</note>, and white; such a sight brings safety and abundance. || 1 || If it appears yellow, it generates disease; if it takes the color of an Ashoka flower <note>a bright orange-red</note>, it leads to conflict with weapons. A "garland" of mock suns—meaning many appearing at once—indicates fear of bandits, widespread anxiety, and the downfall of the king. || 2 || A mock sun situated to the north of the sun brings rain; to the south, it brings wind. If situated on both sides, there is a danger from water. If it appears above the sun, it destroys the king, and if below, it brings destruction to the people. || 3 ||

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Circle of the Mock Sun," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira.

# Chapter 38
## Characteristics of Dust

Sages say that the death of a king is foretold by dust <note>original: "Rajas"</note> that resembles a mass of thick darkness, covering all directions so completely that mountains, cities, and trees cannot be distinguished. || 1 || In whichever direction the heavy accumulation of dust first appears or vanishes...

---

In whatever season the sun possesses a certain color, if the mock sun likewise possesses that same glossy color—clear like a cat's-eye gem and white—it is a bringer of safety and good harvests. || 1 || If the color is yellow, it produces illness; if it bears a color like the Ashoka flower, it is a cause for the fury of weapons; and if there is a "garland" of mock suns—that is, many mock suns rising together—then fear of thieves, terror, and the destruction of the king occurs. || 2 || If the mock sun is in the north, it rains water; if in the south, it makes the wind blow; if in both directions, there is fear of water; if situated above, it destroys the king; and if below, it destroys men. || 3 ||

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the Brihat Samhita composed by the teacher Sri Varahamihira, with the vernacular commentary <note>original: "Bhasha-tika"</note> composed by Pandit Baladeva Prasada Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province.

When dust, like a mass of deep darkness, covers all directions so that mountains, towns, or trees etc. are not visible at all, then know for certain that the destruction of the king will occur. || 1 || In whichever direction the mass of dust is first seen, or in whichever direction...

<note>This chapter was not explained or mentioned by Bhattotpala <insert>a famous 10th-century commentator</insert>, but it is included here because it was seen in the original manuscript copies.</note>

...or in whichever direction it [the dust] settles. Within seven days, fear will undoubtedly arrive in that place. || 2 || If the mass of dust clouds is white in color, there will be suffering for the ministers and the common people <note>original: "janapada," referring to the inhabitants of the countryside or districts</note>. Soon, the fury of weapons <note>warfare</note> arrives, and the accomplishment of tasks occurs only with great difficulty. || 3 || If, at the time of sunrise, the dust spreads for one or two days as if covering the vault of the sky, it announces a subject of intense fear. || 4 || If the dust continues to accumulate for one full night, it brings death to the primary king, but brings auspicious results and well-being to the remaining wise kings. || 5 || In whichever nation a thick mass of dust spreads for two consecutive nights, it should be well understood that the arrival of an enemy army <note>original: "parachakra," literally 'the circle of the enemy'</note> is imminent in that land. || 6 || If the dust falls for three or four nights, it leads to the destruction of grain and liquids <note>original: "anna-rasa," referring to food crops and essential fluids like water or sap</note>. If the dust falls for five nights, there will be a great upheaval in the armies of the kings. || 7 || When dust appears without the rising of comets <note>original: "ketu"</note> and such, it gives rise to intense fear. The ancient teachers say that these effects are fully realized in seasons other than the cool season <note>original: "shishira," the late winter season in the Indian calendar</note>. || 8 ||

### Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, named "Signs of Dust," in the Brihat Samhita composed by the illustrious Varahamihira. || 38 ||

---

If that mass of dust settles first, then without a doubt, fear will come there in seven days. || 2 || If the cloud-like mass of dust is white, then the ministers and the districts suffer. Soon the wrath of weapons arrives, and the success of work happens with extreme difficulty. || 3 || At the time of sunrise, if the dust remains visible for one or two days, covering the sky, it is called a matter of fierce fear. || 4 || If dust continues to gather for one night, the main king dies, and it produces auspicious results for the rest of the intelligent kings. || 5 || In whichever country thick dust spreads for two consecutive nights, it should be thoroughly understood that there will be the rule of another king <note>foreign invasion</note> in that country. || 6 || If dust keeps falling for three or four nights, then grain and juices are destroyed; if dust falls for five nights, then a commotion arises in the armies of the kings. || 7 || If dust falls after the rising of comets etc., there is intense fear. The teachers say that its results are more significant in seasons other than the cool season. || 8 ||

# Chapter Thirty-Nine
## On the Characteristics of Thunderclaps

When wind, struck by wind, falls from the sky to the earth, it is then called a *Nirghata* <note>original: "निर्घात" (Nirghata); a sudden atmospheric explosion, thunderclap, or meteor-like sound occurring in a clear sky</note>. It is an omen of evil when accompanied by the harsh cries of birds facing the sun. **1**

If the *Nirghata* occurs at sunrise, it destroys judges <note>original: "अधिकरणिक" (Adhikaranika); officials of the court</note>, kings, the wealthy, warriors, women, merchants, and courtesans. If it occurs during the first part of the morning, it strikes down those who tend goats and sheep, the laboring class <note>original: "शूद्र" (Shudra)</note>, and city-dwellers. **2**

If it occurs until midday, it brings suffering to royal servants and priests <note>original: "ब्राह्मण" (Brahmins)</note>. In the third watch of the day, it harms the merchant class <note>original: "वैश्य" (Vaishya)</note> and the rain-giving clouds. In the fourth watch, it afflicts thieves. **3**

When the sun has set, it destroys the lowly; in the first watch of the night, it destroys the crops. In the second watch of the night, it afflicts the hosts of malevolent spirits <note>original: "पिशाच" (Pishacha); carnivorous ghosts or demons</note>. **4**

In the third watch of the night, it destroys horses and elephants; in the fourth watch, it strikes down infantry. In whichever direction the terrifying, shattering sound of the *Nirghata* travels, that region is brought to ruin. **5**

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Thunderclaps," in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by Sri Varahamihira.

---

When wind is struck by wind and falls to the earth, it is known as a *Nirghata*. If, at the time of this explosion, birds cry out while facing the sun, it is a bringer of sin and misfortune. **1** If the *Nirghata* occurs at the time of sunrise, then judges (meaning legal thinkers), kings, the wealthy, warriors, women, merchants, and courtesans are destroyed. If it occurs during the first watch, the keepers of goats, the laboring class, and the residents of cities are destroyed. If it occurs in the middle of the day, men in royal service and priests are pained. If the *Nirghata* occurs in the third watch of the day, it afflicts the merchant class and the clouds that provide water; in the fourth watch, it afflicts thieves. **2-3** After sunset, it destroys the base-born, and if occurring in the first watch of the night, it destroys the grain. If it occurs in the second watch of the night, it afflicts the spirits. **4** In the third watch of the night, it destroys elephants and horses, and if the *Nirghata* occurs in the fourth watch, it kills those on foot. Furthermore, the direction from which the terrifying and cracked sound of the *Nirghata* calamity arises is the direction that shall be destroyed. **5**

->Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter in the Hindi commentary<-
->written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad<-
->in the North-Western province, for the Brihat Samhita<-
->composed by the teacher Sri Varahamihira.<-

# Now begins the Fortieth Chapter.

## The Nativity of Crops.

The auspicious and inauspicious combinations for the summer and autumn crops, as declared by the sage Badarayana <note>A celebrated ancient sage often identified with Vyasa, credited here as an authority on astrological botany</note> regarding the Sun’s entry into Scorpio and Taurus, are as follows: || 1 || When the Sun enters Scorpio, if the cardinal houses <term>Kendra: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses</term> from it are occupied by benefic planets, or if they are aspected by powerful benefics, there will be an abundance of the summer harvest. || 2 || When the Sun is in the eighth sign (Scorpio), if Jupiter is in Aquarius and the Moon is in Leo, or if Jupiter is in Leo and the Moon is in Aquarius, the summer crops will reach full maturity. || 3 || If Venus or Mercury are in the second house from the Sun, or if both are there together, or even if they are in the twelfth house, the result is the same; and if there is an aspect from Jupiter, the grain will be of the highest quality. || 4 || If the Sun in Scorpio is hemmed in by benefics, and Jupiter and the Moon are in the seventh house from it, there will be supreme prosperity. If the Sun is at the very beginning of Scorpio and Jupiter is in the second house, only half the crop will reach maturity. || 5 || If Venus, the Moon, and Mercury are in the eleventh, fourth, or second houses from the Sun in Scorpio, there is great wealth of grain; and if Jupiter is in the tenth house, there is excellent prosperity for the cows. || 6 || At the time when the Sun is in the mouth of Scorpio, Jupiter is in Aquarius, the Moon is in Taurus, and Mars and Saturn are in Capricorn...

The auspicious and inauspicious omens determined by the sage Badarayana regarding the grain produced in the summer and autumn seasons at the time of the Sun's entry into Scorpio or Taurus are these: At the time of the Sun's transit into the sign of Scorpio, if all its cardinal centers—namely Scorpio, Aquarius, Taurus, and Leo—are joined by benefic planets or are seen by powerful benefic planets, then the summer grain increases. || 1 || 2 || When the Sun transits the eighth sign (Scorpio), if at that time Jupiter is in Aquarius and the Moon is in Leo, or Jupiter is in Leo and the Moon is in Aquarius, then the grain produced in summer flourishes. || 3 || If Venus or Mercury goes to the second sign from the Sun, or if they both go together to the twelfth sign from the Sun, even then such grain will be produced; and if there is an aspect of Jupiter upon them, then that grain will be of an excellent kind. || 4 || If both sides of the Sun, which has gone into the sign of Scorpio, are occupied by two benefic planets, and the Moon and Jupiter are in the seventh from it, then there is very excellent farming. The Sun being at the start of Scorpio and the presence of Jupiter in its second place indicates half a crop. || 5 || If the planets Venus, Moon, and Mercury are in the second, fourth, or eleventh signs from the Sun which has gone into Scorpio, then the finest wealth of grain is obtained; and if Jupiter is in the tenth (Action) house, then the finest wealth is obtained for the cows. || 6 || At the time when the Sun is in Scorpio...

## Determination of Commodities.

Whichever signs have been designated by the Sages as the lords of specific commodities, I shall now declare them according to the ancient scriptures <note>original: "Agama"</note> for the purpose of determining good and evil fortune. || 1 ||

Aries <note>original: "Mesha"</note> is said to be the ruler of clothing, blankets made of sheep's wool, blankets made of goat's hair, lentils, wheat, resin <note>original: "Raal" - tree resin or incense</note>, barley, medicinal herbs grown on land, and gold. || 2 ||

Clothing, safflower <note>original: "Kusuma"</note>, wheat, rice <note>original: "Shali"</note>, barley, buffaloes, and cows belong to Taurus <note>original: "Vrishabha"</note>. Grains, autumn-born products, creepers, lotus roots <note>original: "Shaluka"</note>, and cotton are under the influence of Gemini <note>original: "Mithuna"</note>. || 3 ||

In the sign of Virgo <note>original: "Kanya"</note> are linseed, peas, horse-gram, wheat, moong beans, and kidney beans <note>original: "Nishpava"</note>. In the sign of Libra <note>original: "Tula"</note> are black gram <note>original: "Urad"</note>, wheat, mustard, and barley. || 5 ||

Sugarcane, products derived from water-sprinkled cane <note>original: "Saikya"</note>, iron, sheep, and goats are ruled by Scorpio <note>original: "Vrishchika"</note>. Horses, salt, clothing, weapons, and sesame... <note>The text continues into the next page</note>

# Now begins the Forty-Third Chapter
## The Glory of Indra’s Banner

The immortals <note>the gods or Devas</note> spoke to Brahma: "O Lord, we are not capable of fighting the demons in battle. Therefore, we have come to you for refuge, for you are the protector of those seeking shelter." || 1 ||

The Lord <note>Brahma</note> said to the gods: "Lord Keshav <note>Vishnu</note>, who resides in the Ocean of Milk, will give you a banner. Upon seeing that banner, the demons will no longer be able to stand against you in combat." || 2 ||

Having received this boon, the gods, led by Indra, went to the Ocean of Milk and offered hymns of praise to Vishnu—the Lord of Fortune, whose chest is illuminated by the rays of the Kaustubha gem and marked by the Shrivatsa <note>a sacred curl of hair on Vishnu's chest</note>. || 3 ||

They praised the Lord of Lakshmi, who is inconceivable, peerless, subtle, dwelling within all embodied beings, the Supreme Soul, without beginning, and whose limits are unknown. || 4 ||

Being thus praised, Lord Narayana was pleased and gave them a banner. This banner acted like the sun to the lotus-forest of the faces of the gods' wives <note>making them bloom with joy</note>, but like a harsh frost to the lotus-faces of the demons' wives <note>causing them to wither in grief</note>. || 5 ||

That banner, born of Vishnu’s own splendor, was placed upon a brilliant chariot with eight wheels, adorned with various jewels, and shining like the sun in the autumn sky...

---

...In this way, by knowing the state of each planet, one should predict the good and bad results. || 13 || 14 ||

Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the great teacher Varahamihira, with the commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region. || 42 ||

---

The gods had said to Brahma, "O Lord! We do not have the strength to fight with the demons; therefore, O Giver of Refuge! We take shelter in you to wage war against them." || 1 || Lord Brahma said to the gods, "Lord Keshav is present in the Ocean of Milk; He will give you a (flag) banner. Seeing that banner, the demons will not be able to stand before you in battle." || 2 || Having received this boon, all the gods along with Indra went to the Ocean of Milk and praised Vishnu, the Lord of Fortune, whose chest is shining with the rays of the Kaustubha gem and marked with the Shrivatsa sign; who is inconceivable (beyond thought), impartial, dwelling within all creatures, subtle, whose boundaries cannot be measured, the beginningless Supreme Soul. || 3 || 4 || When the gods praised Narayana in this manner, He satisfied them by giving a banner that was like the sun to the lotus-forest of the faces of the gods' wives and like the moon <note>original: "moon" in the Hindi commentary, though the Sanskrit implies "frost" or "harsh sun" for the demons</note> to the lotus-forest of the faces of the demons' wives. || 5 || King Indra [received the banner] which was shining like the autumnal sun, born from the splendor of Vishnu, having eight wheels, radiant, and decorated with jewels...

# Varahi Samhita

Upon obtaining that banner, Indra rejoiced. || 6 || Adorned with a network of small tinkling bells, and equipped with garlands, umbrellas, bells, and *pitakas* <note>original: "pittaka" — a specific type of box-shaped ornament or basket-like decoration attached to the banner</note>, Indra used this towering celestial banner to bring destruction to the enemy armies in battle. || 7 ||

The Lord of the Immortals <note>Indra</note> gave this staff made of bamboo to Vasu, the King of Chedi, known as Uparichara. That king worshipped the staff according to the prescribed rites. || 8 || Pleased by this festival, Indra declared: "Those kings who perform this ceremony as Vasu did shall become wealthy like Vasu and their commands shall be fulfilled on this earth." || 9 || 

"Their subjects shall be joyful, free from fear and disease, and possessed of abundant food. Furthermore, through various omens, this very banner shall indicate the good or evil fortune of the world." || 10 || 

I shall now describe, according to the sacred traditions, the worship of this banner as it was performed by kings of old seeking the growth of their armies and victory, in accordance with Indra's command. || 11 || 

The ritual for this should begin on a day with an auspicious *Karana* <note>a technical division of the Hindu calendar</note>, lunar mansion, and a favorable moment for departure. The astrologer <term>Daivajna (one who knows the divine will through stars)</term> and the master carpenter <term>Sutradhara (literally 'the holder of the string')</term> should proceed together into the forest. || 12 ||

Trees that grow in gardens, temples, cemeteries, anthills, on the roadside, or near funeral pyres are to be avoided. Also excluded are trees that are stunted, withered while standing, thorny, covered in creepers, or those with parasitic plants <note>original: "vandaka"</note> growing on them. || 13 || 

Trees that house many bird nests, those with hollows, or those damaged by wind or fire are also unsuitable. Furthermore, trees with feminine names <note>The Hindi gloss provides the example of the Khirni tree</note> are not considered auspicious for the purpose of the Indra-ketu <note>Indra's Banner</note>.

# Chapter 43: With Commentary in Common Language

Those trees with feminine names are not auspicious for the purpose of the <term>Shakraketu</term><note>The Banner of Indra, a monumental wooden pole raised during a royal festival to ensure the kingdom's prosperity.</note>. ## 14 ##

The following five trees are considered the best: the **Arjuna**, the **Ashvakarna**, the **Priyaka**, the **Dhava**, and the **Udumbara** <note>original: "gular" or wild fig</note>. If none of these are available, another commendable tree may be selected. ## 15 ##

After performing the prescribed worship of a tree growing on either pale or dark soil, a Brahmin should go to the secluded forest at night, touch the tree, and recite this <term>mantra</term><note>A sacred ritual chant.</note>: ## 16 ##

"May it be well with those spirits who dwell in this tree; I bow to you. Having accepted this offering, please change your residence elsewhere. ## 17 ## O Best of Trees! The King chooses you for the banner of the King of the Gods <note>Indra</note>. May prosperity be yours; please accept this worship." ## 18 ##

Afterward, at dawn, one should cut the tree while facing either North or East. If the sound of the axe is jarring or harsh, it is inauspicious; a smooth, deep, and resonant sound is beneficial. ## 19 ##

If the tree falls without breaking, without bending, without getting caught on another tree, and falls toward the East or North, it grants victory to kings. A fall contrary to these conditions should be abandoned as it yields opposite results. ## 20 ##

Having cut four inches from the top and eight inches from the base, one should cast the timber into water. After taking it out, it should be brought to the city gate by cart or by men. ## 21 ##

If the spokes of the wheel break during transport, it signifies a split in the army; the breaking of the rim indicates the destruction of the army. If the <term>aksha</term><note>The axle of the cart.</note> breaks, it signifies the loss of wealth; similarly, if the linchpin breaks <unclear>the text cuts off</unclear>

...and if the wood is damaged, it brings ruin to the carpenter. **(22)** On the eighth day of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapada <note>August-September</note>, the King, surrounded by the citizens and accompanied by the **astrologer**, the **ministers**, the **chamberlains**, and the **priests**—all dressed in their finest attire—should proceed. **(23)** The pole of Indra, wrapped in new, unblemished cloth and adorned with garlands, perfumes, and incense, should be brought into the city by the townspeople to the sounding of conchs and trumpets. **(24)**

The city squares should be filled with actors, dancers, and musicians. **(26)**

In this procession, white banners signify victory, while yellow ones bring disease. Multi-colored banners grant success, but red banners portend the fury of weapons <note>war</note>. **(27)** If an elephant or any other animal should knock down the pole while it is being brought in, it is an omen of fear. If children clap their hands or if animals fight at that moment, it indicates an approaching battle. **(28)**

The carpenter should then refine the pole according to the prescribed rites and mount it upon the <term>lathe</term> <note>original: "khairāt", a turning machine</note>. The King should observe a vigil on the eleventh day of the lunar fortnight. **(29)** Wearing white garments and a white turban, the **priest** should offer oblations into the fire using hymns dedicated to Indra and Vishnu. Meanwhile, the **astrologer** should observe and interpret the omens for the coming year. **(30)** If the fire takes the shape of desired objects, is fragrant, and bright...

A fire that is dense, radiant, and full of flames brings good fortune; any other kind is not considered desirable for a journey. This has been explained in detail in the <term>Yogayatra</term> <note>A specific treatise by Varahamihira concerning omens for military expeditions</note>. || 31 ||

At the conclusion of the "Svaha" <note>The ritual exclamation made when offering oblations to the fire</note>, if the fire spontaneously produces bright flames, appears glossy, and the smoke or flames circle toward the right, then the King shall bring under his subjection the Earth—she who wears the beautiful waters of the Ganges and the Yamuna <note>original: "Divakarasuta," daughter of the Sun</note> as a necklace and the ocean as her waistband. || 32 ||

If the fire possesses the hue of gold, the Ashoka flower, the Kurantaka flower, the lotus, <term>Vaidurya</term> <note>Chrysoberyl or cat's-eye gem</note>, or the blue water-lily, then darkness finds no place within the King's palace, being dispelled by the brilliance of jewels. || 33 ||

If the sound of the fire resembles the roar of a fleet of chariots, the ocean, a thundercloud, an elephant, or a kettle-drum, then when that King marches to war, the horizons will appear dark as night, crowded by his masses of elephants blinded by rut. || 34 ||

If the fire takes the shape of a banner, a water-pot, a horse, or an elephant, then the Earth—bounded by the mountains of sunrise and sunset, and whose breasts are the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains—comes under the King's control. || 35 ||

If the fire emits a fragrance like that of an elephant's temporal juice <note>Mada</note>, fresh earth, lotuses, parched grain, ghee, or honey, then the King's court will be suffused with the luster of the jewels set in the crowns of subordinate kings as they bow before him. || 36 ||

The auspicious and inauspicious signs described via the forms of the seven-rayed fire during the raising of the <term>Indradhvaja</term> <note>The Banner of Indra; a major royal festival and ritual</note> apply also to births, sacrifices, and planetary rituals...

**Vernacular Commentary:**
Fire that is well-formed, fragrant, glossy, dense, and flaming is auspicious. Aside from this, fire does not grant the desired fruits. This is described extensively in the <term>Yogayatra</term>. || 31 ||

At the time of offering ghee into the fire for the deities, if at the end of the mantra recitation the sacrificial fire spontaneously develops bright flames, is glossy, and encircles from the right side, then the Earth—who wears the beautiful necklace of the waters of the Ganges and Yamuna and wears the ocean as a girdle—will come under the King's control. || 32 ||

If the fire is the color of gold, Ashoka, Kurantaka, lotus, <term>Vaidurya</term>, or the blue lotus, then the darkness will not find a place in the King's house, being distressed by the light of jewels; that is, the darkness will not remain. || 33 ||

If there is a sound in the fire like the ocean, a cloud, an elephant, or a drum, then at the time the King sets out for war, all directions will appear black like darkness, filled with groups of elephants in rut. || 34 ||

If the fire is shaped like a banner, a pot, a horse, or an elephant, then the Earth—which holds the mountains of sunrise and sunset and possesses the Himalayas and Vindhya mountains as breasts—falls under the King's power. || 35 ||

If the fire has a fragrance like elephant-rut, earth, lotus, parched grains, ghee, or honey, then the royal assembly becomes pervaded by the brilliance of the gems studded in the crowns of kings who are bowing down. || 36 ||

One should also consider these factors during birth ceremonies, sacrifices, planetary pacification rituals <note>Shanti: rituals to avert evil or bad luck</note>, journeys, and weddings. || 37 ||

After honoring the Brahmins with offerings of jaggery, cakes, milk porridge, and other foods, along with monetary gifts <note>Dakshina</note>, the banner should be raised on the twelfth lunar day <note>Dvadashi</note> under the Shravana asterism <note>Shravana Nakshatra</note>, or at another time when Shravana is prevalent. || 38 ||

The sage Manu has stated that those skilled in the craft should create five or seven "Indra’s Daughters" <note>Shakra-kumaris: smaller decorative poles or figurines attached to the main banner</note>. Two others, named *Jaya* and *Vijaya*, should be slightly taller than one-sixteenth of the height. Two more are called *Vasundharas*. In the middle of these, the "Mother of Indra" <note>Shakra-janitri</note> should be placed, exceeding the others by an eighth part. || 40 ||

One should sequentially offer the various colorful "baskets" <note>Pitakas: box-like ornaments or containers</note> which were anciently fashioned as ornaments for the celestial banner by the delighted gods. || 41 ||

The first ornament, square and resembling the red Ashoka flower, was given by Vishvakarma <note>the divine architect</note>. The second, a girdle of many colors, was given by Brahma <note>the Creator</note> and Shiva. || 42 ||

The third ornament, eight-sided and colored blue and red, was given by Indra. The fourth, a shining lentil-shaped ornament <note>Masuraka</note> of dark hue, was given by Yama <note>the god of death</note>. || 43 ||

Varuna <note>the god of the waters</note> gave the fifth, which is the color of madder <note>a reddish dye</note>, six-sided, and resembling the waves of water. Vayu <note>the god of wind</note> gave the sixth, an armlet <note>Keyura</note> colored like a peacock and blue like a rain cloud. || 44 ||

Skanda <note>the god of war</note> gave his own armlet, the seventh, which is highly variegated, to the banner. The eighth, resembling a flame of fire... <note>The text breaks off here mid-description</note>

# Chapter 43: With Language Commentary

The eighth ornament was given by Agni <note>original: "Havyabhug" - the eater of oblations</note>, shining like a flame. ## 45 ## The Moon gave the ninth ornament, a necklace <term>Graiveyaka: an ornament worn around the neck</term> resembling a cat's-eye gem <term>Vaidurya: chrysoberyl or cat's-eye</term>. The Vishvedevas <note>A group of various Vedic deities</note> gave the eleventh ornament, which resembles a lotus. The Sages gave the twelfth, called the *Nivamsha*, which has the luster of a blue water-lily. ## 47 ##

Jupiter and Venus placed the thirteenth ornament upon the head of the Banner; it is wide at the top, slightly curved from bottom to top, and possesses the deep red color of lac-dye <note>original: "Laksha-rasa"</note>. ## 48 ##

Wise men should understand that whichever deity fashioned an ornament for the sake of the Banner, that specific ornament belongs to that deity. ## 49 ##

The circumference of the first basket-ornament <term>Pitaka: the decorative structures or "baskets" attached to the pole</term> should be one-third the total height of the Banner. Each subsequent ornament's circumference should be reduced by one-eighth from the one preceding it. ## 50 ##

On the fourth day, one who is learned in the scriptures should complete the Indra-dhvaja. Being self-controlled, he should recite these mantras <note>sacred chants</note> as sung in the traditions <insert>Agamas</insert> by Manu: ## 51 ##

"By Shiva, the Sun, Yama, Indra, the Moon, Kubera, Agni, and Varuna; by the hosts of Great Sages, the Directions, the Apsaras <note>celestial nymphs</note>, Venus, Angiras, Kartikeya, the Wind-gods, and the Ganas— ## 52 ##

Just as you, O God, have been honored by these many-formed, energy-giving, and noble ornaments, please now accept these auspicious decorations with a joyful heart. ## 53 ##

You are the unborn, the undecaying, the eternal, the uniform; you are Vishnu, the Boar, the Ancient Spirit..."

# The Varahi Samhita
## Chapter on the Festival of Indra's Banner

-> You are the Destroyer, the all-consuming Fire, the thousand-headed one, the worshipful Indra of a hundred sacrifices. I invoke you, the wise poet, the seven-tongued <note>referring to Agni/Fire</note>, the protector, the lord of gods, the slayer of the demon Vritra, and the leader of the fine army. May our warriors be victorious! (Verses 54–55) <-

At the time of filling the sockets, raising the banner, entering the city, bathing the icon, adorning it with garlands, and finally bidding it farewell, the King should remain fasted and recite these auspicious mantras dedicated to the banner of Indra <note>original: "Puruhuta," an epithet of Indra meaning 'much-invoked'</note>. (Verse 56)

The banner should be decorated on all sides with:
*   Umbrellas, flags, and mirrors
*   Half-moon shapes and colorful garlands
*   Plantain trees and stalks of sugarcane
*   Figures of serpents and lions
*   Baskets and latticed windows
*   Images of the Guardians of the Directions <term>Lokapalas: deities who preside over the eight compass points</term>. (Verse 57)

The King should raise this symbol of the Thousand-Eyed Lord <note>Indra</note>, which must be made of strong heartwood and held by unbroken ropes. It should be fitted with well-joined mechanical parts, bolts, a base, and a pedestal, and adorned with "little maidens" <note>small decorative figurines or dolls attached to the banner</note>. (Verse 58)

The banner <note>original: "Ketu"</note> should be raised amidst a continuous roar of the people, with auspicious blessings, prostrations, and the rhythmic sounds of drums, clay drums, conchs, and trumpets. It should be accompanied by the loud chanting of Brahmins reciting the sacred words of the Vedas. (Verse 59)

While the citizens hold fruits, curd, clarified butter, parched grain, honey, and flowers in their hands, bowing their heads and singing praises, the Lord of the People <note>the King</note> should cause the tip of Indra's banner to lean toward the city of his enemies to ensure their destruction. (Verse 60)

The banner should be raised neither too quickly nor too slowly, without shaking, and without its garlands or baskets falling—

# Chapter 43: Including the Vernacular Commentary

->**The Ornament of the Heavens**<-

If the banner is raised successfully without falling, it is considered auspicious. Any other manner of raising it is inauspicious; in such cases, the royal priest should pacify the ill effects through <term>Shanti</term> <note>rituals for peace and averting evil</note> to bring calm to the king. || 61 ||

If meat-eating birds, owls, pigeons, crows, or vultures perch upon the <term>Indra-dhvaja</term> <note>The ceremonial banner pole dedicated to the god Indra</note>, it foretells great unrest and fear for the king. If a blue jay perches upon it, they say it brings fear to the Crown Prince <note>original: "Yuvaraja"</note>. A hawk falling upon the banner causes diseases or injuries to the eyes. || 62 ||

If the ceremonial umbrella is shattered and the banner falls, it signifies the death of kings. If bees should build a hive and deposit honey upon the banner, it brings death to thieves. If a meteor strikes the banner, it destroys the royal priest; if a lightning bolt strikes it, it destroys the King's consort. || 63 ||

The falling of the flag-cloth causes the destruction of the Queen, while the falling of the <term>Pitaka</term> <note>a basket-like ornament on the pole</note> causes a drought. If the middle, the top, or the base of the banner breaks, it destroys the ministers, the King, and the citizens respectively. || 64 ||

If the banner is shrouded in smoke, there is fear of fire; if shrouded in darkness, there is mental confusion. If the banner breaks and falls in the middle, there will be a lack of ministers. If it breaks and falls toward the North or other cardinal directions, it causes distress to the <term>Brahmins</term> <note>priests</note>, <term>Kshatriyas</term> <note>warriors</note>, <term>Vaishyas</term> <note>merchants</note>, and <term>Shudras</term> <note>laborers</note> in succession. If the <term>Kumaris</term> <note>smaller side-poles or "maiden" poles</note> are torn or broken, it is said that unchaste women will perish. || 65 ||

If the ropes become entangled or snap during the raising, it brings suffering to children. If the <term>Matrika</term> <note>supporting wooden side-posts</note> are damaged, it brings suffering to the King's mother. Whatever actions are performed by children or messengers <note>original: "Charana"</note> near the banner, whether good or bad, will manifest as corresponding results in the future. || 66 ||

After the banner has been raised and honored for four days...

On the fifth day, the King, accompanied by his subjects, should bid farewell to the emblem of Indra <note>The King of the Gods</note> in order to increase the strength of his own forces. || 67 || This rite was first inaugurated by King Uparichara Vasu and has been continuously observed by subsequent monarchs. # Chapter Forty-Four
->The Lustration Ritual<-
<note>The term 'Nirajanam' refers to a ceremonial purification of the army, involving the waving of lights and spiritual cleansing of weapons and animals.</note>

When the Lord whose navel is a lotus <note>Lord Vishnu</note>—whose eyelashes are the clouds and whose eyes are the Moon and the Sun—opens his eyes <note>referring to the end of the four-month divine sleep, Chaturmasya</note>, the King should perform the Lustration ritual for his horses, elephants, and men. || 1 || This pacification rite, known as *Nirajana*, should be performed on the twelfth, eighth, or fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kartika <note>October–November</note>, or alternatively in the month of Ashvin <note>September–October</note>. || 2 || In the north-eastern direction of the city, upon auspicious ground, an ornamental archway <term>Torana: a ceremonial gateway</term> should be constructed of fine wood, measuring sixteen cubits in height and ten cubits in width. || 3 || A "House of Pacification" should be built using branches of the Sarja, Udumbara, and Kakubha trees, and it should be strewn with plenty of Kusha grass. Its entrance should be decorated with fish, banners, and wheels fashioned from bamboo. || 4 || For the protection and nourishment of the horses, one should use amulets containing marking-nut, rice, costus, and white mustard...

---

<note>The following is the Hindi commentary/translation of the preceding Sanskrit verses</note>

After performing the worship thoroughly for four days, the King should dismiss the Banner of Indra on the fifth day along with his subjects; by doing so, the strength of the King's army increases. || 67 || This method was started by King Uparichara Vasu and has been practiced ever since by kings. Those rulers who worship the Banner of Indra in this manner will not suffer fear from their enemies. || 68 ||

Thus ends the forty-third chapter in the vernacular commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the great teacher Sri Varahamihira. || 43 ||

When the Lord whose navel is a lotus—whose eyelids are the clouds and whose two eyes are the Moon and the Sun—opens his eyes (that is, wakes up), then the Lustration of horses, elephants, and men should be performed. || 1 || One should perform the pacification known as *Nirajana* on the full moon, the twelfth, or the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Kartika, or in the month of Ashvin. || 2 || On excellent ground in the north-east direction of the city, one should build an archway of good wood, sixteen cubits high and ten cubits wide. || 3 || One should build a "House of Peace" from the wood of the Vijayasara, Gular, and Arjun trees, in which many stalks of Kusha grass are placed. On its door, fish, banners, and wheels made of bamboo should be attached. || 4 || For the peace and nourishment of all...

# Chapter 44: With Commentary

One should bind <term>Bhilawa</term> <note>Semecarpus anacardium, the marking nut</note>, <term>Shashti</term> rice <note>a variety of rice that ripens in sixty days</note>, <term>Kushtha</term> <note>Saussurea lappa, an aromatic medicinal root</note>, and mustard seeds around the necks of the horses for their nourishment and for the peace of the stables. ॥ 5 ॥

One should perform the pacification ritual for the horses in the <term>Shanti-griha</term> <note>a dedicated "house of peace" or ritual chamber</note> for one week, using the sacred hymns dedicated to the Sun, Varuna, the Vishvedevas, Prajapati, Indra, and Vishnu. ॥ 6 ॥

The horses should be honored and rendered free from fear by the sounds of "auspicious day" greetings, the blowing of conch shells, the beating of kettledrums, and the singing of songs; they must not be spoken to harshly nor should they be struck or threatened in any way. ॥ 7 ॥

When the eighth day arrives, one should establish the ritual fire of the hermitage—covered with <term>Kusha</term> grass and bark cloth—upon the altar, positioned to the south of the ceremonial archway and facing north. ॥ 8 ॥

Sandalwood, <term>Kushtha</term>, madder, orpiment, red arsenic, foxtail millet, sweet flag, <term>Danti</term>, <term>Amrita</term> <note>Guduchi</note>, collyrium, turmeric, <term>Suvarnapushpa</term> <note>golden flowers</note>, and <term>Agnimantha</term>... ॥ 9 ॥

...white <term>Phatkari</term> <note>alum</note>, <term>Purnakosha</term>, <term>Kutki</term>, <term>Trayamana</term>, <term>Sahadevi</term> herb, white <term>Purnakosha</term>, <term>Nagakesar</term>, cowhage, <term>Shatavari</term>, and <term>Somavalli</term> <note>the Moon-plant</note>. ॥ 10 ॥

Placing all these ingredients in equal measure into water-pots, one should properly offer the sacrificial tribute along with various kinds of foods, including plenty of honey, rice-milk pudding, and barley-gruel. ॥ 11 ॥

The ritual fuel-sticks should be made from the wood of <term>Khadira</term> <note>Acacia</note>, <term>Palasha</term> <note>Flame of the Forest</note>, <term>Udumbara</term> <note>Cluster Fig</note>, <term>Gambhari</term>, and <term>Pippala</term> <note>Sacred Fig</note>. One who desires prosperity should have the sacrificial ladle made of gold or silver. ॥ 12 ॥

Seated upon a tiger skin and facing the east, the illustrious King should stay near the fire, accompanied by the horse-physicians and the <term>Daivajña</term> <note>astrologer or seer</note>. ॥ 13 ॥

Whatever has been prescribed regarding the altar, the priest, and the characteristics of the fire in the rites of planetary sacrifice, during journeys, and in the festival of Indra’s Banner <note>Mahendra Ketu</note>, all those should be understood to apply to this ceremony as well.

# The Varahi Samhita

### On the Characteristics of the Altar, Priest, and Fire

The characteristics of the altar, the priest, and the fire should be understood as previously described in this context. || 14 ||

One should select a horse and a noble elephant possessing auspicious marks <note>Sanskrit: lakshana; physical traits indicating good fortune</note>, initiate them, and bathe them. They should be adorned with new white garments, perfumes, flower garlands, and incense, and duly worshipped. || 15 ||

One should lead the animal to the base of the hermitage gateway <note>Sanskrit: ashrama-torana</note>, soothing it with gentle words. This should be done while the sounds of musical instruments, conch shells, and auspicious chants fill the quarters of the sky. || 16 ||

If the horse, upon being brought there, stands still while lifting its right forefoot, the king will then conquer his enemies quickly and without effort. || 17 ||

The remaining behaviors of elephants and horses, which are desired by the king, have been explained in the chapter on marches <note>referring to the Yatra-adhyaya, a section on military expeditions</note>; those should be considered here according to one's ability. || 18 ||

The priest should consecrate a ball of food <term>Pinda: a ritual offering of food</term> with mantras and offer it to the horse. If the horse smells it or eats it, it brings victory. Anything contrary to this is said to be inauspicious. || 19 ||

The priest should dip a branch of the Udumbara tree <note>Ficus racemosa, a sacred fig tree</note> into the water of the consecrated jars and sprinkle the horses, as well as the entire army including the king and the elephants, using hymns for peace and prosperity <term>Shantika-paustika: rituals for averting evil and increasing well-being</term>. || 20 ||

After performing the peace rites for the growth of the kingdom, the priest <insert>the Brahmin</insert> should repeatedly use malevolent incantations <term>Abhichara: magic used for aggressive or defensive purposes against enemies</term> to pierce the chest of an enemy effigy made of clay with a spear. || 21 ||

The priest should then consecrate the bridle and give it to the horse. After that, the king, having performed the lustration ceremony <term>Nirajita: a ritual purification involving lamps and water</term>, should mount the horse and set out with his army toward the northeast. || 22 ||

With elephants delighted by the sounds of drums and conch shells, and with ichor <note>Mada: the fluid secreted by rutting elephants, seen as a sign of strength</note> flowing...

# Chapter Forty-Five
## The Sight of the Wagtail

I shall now proclaim the results, as declared by the ancient sages, regarding the first sighting of the bird known as the wagtail <note>Sanskrit: Khanjana; a small bird whose movements were closely watched for divination</note> in its season. || 1 ||

The wagtail that is thick-set, with an elevated neck and a black throat, is called **Bhadra** <note>meaning "The Auspicious One"</note>; it brings good fortune. One that is black from its beak all the way down to its throat is called **Sampurna** <note>meaning "The Full or Complete One"</note>; it fulfills all desires. || 2 ||

One with a black spot on its throat and white edges on its cheeks is called **Rikta** <note>meaning "The Empty One"</note>; it brings emptiness or loss. A yellow-colored wagtail is called **Gopita**; its sight is known to cause distress. || 3 ||

Now, if the wagtail is seen upon trees bearing sweet and fragrant fruits or flowers, near sacred reservoirs of water, or upon the heads of elephants, horses, or snakes; upon palaces, in gardens, or on the balconies of mansions; || 4 ||

Near cow-pens, gatherings of virtuous people, sacrifices, festivals, kings, or twice-born men <note>term for the upper three castes, particularly Brahmins</note>; near elephant or horse stables, or upon umbrellas, banners, and fly-whisks <note>symbols of royalty and divinity</note>; || 5 ||

Upon gold, white garments, lotuses, water-lilies, or in places that have been worshipped or smeared with cow-dung; or upon vessels of curd and heaps of grain—in all these places, the wagtail brings prosperity. || 6 ||

If seen in the mud, it signifies the obtaining of delicious food; if on cow-dung, an abundance of dairy products; if on green grass, the acquisition of new clothes; but if situated on a cart, it signifies the ruin of the country. || 7 ||

If seen on the roof of a house, it signifies the loss of wealth; if on a leather thong, it signifies imprisonment; if on an impure place, it signifies disease. If on the back of <unclear>...</unclear>

# Now begins the Forty-Sixth Chapter:

### The Characteristics of Portents

I shall now describe those portents which Garga <note>An ancient legendary sage and astronomer</note> related to Atri. In brief, a portent is any deviation from the natural order of things. || 1 || Due to the misconduct of men, a collection of sins arises, leading to calamities. These are signaled by portents occurring in the heavens, the sky, and on the earth. || 2 || When gods are displeased by the wrongdoings of humans, they create these omens. To counteract them, a king should perform rites of pacification <term>Shanti: rituals intended to avert evil or calm divine wrath</term> in his kingdom. || 3 || Abnormalities of the planets and stars, meteors, thunderbolts, fierce winds, and halos are considered "heavenly" portents. "Atmospheric" portents include such things as cities of the Gandharvas <note>Fata Morgana or mirages in the clouds</note> and Indra’s bow <note>The rainbow</note>. || 4 ||

---

<note>The following section is a Hindi commentary/translation of the preceding Sanskrit verses</note>

Those who do not eat meat do not receive inauspicious results. || 15 || The fruit of the first sighting of the wagtail occurs within one year; but if the wagtail is seen again during this interval, its fruit is obtained by sunset of that same day. However, learned men, regarding the sighting of the wagtail, should decide the total results—good or bad—after knowing the location, appearance, rising sign, constellation, and the peaceful or blazing state of the directions. || 16 ||

->Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the vernacular commentary<-
->written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the Northwest region,<-
->on the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the great teacher Sri Varahamihira.<-

The portents that the great sage Garga described to Atri are now being described here. To be contrary to nature is indeed a "portent" <term>Utpata: an unnatural phenomenon or omen</term>. This is its brief meaning. || 1 || From the accumulation of sins caused by the improper conduct of men, disturbances arise. Heavenly, atmospheric, and all earthly portents provide information about them in a proper manner. || 2 || Because of the misbehavior of men, the gods become displeased and produce these portents. To remove those portents, it is proper for a king to have pacification rites performed in his kingdom. || 3 || Here, abnormalities of the constellations, meteors, thunderbolts, wind, and circles <note>halos</note> are heavenly portents; the city of the Gandharvas and...

# Chapter 46 | With Commentary

-> Rainbows and similar phenomena are called atmospheric portents. <-

Portents arising from moving or stationary objects are known as **terrestrial** <note>original: "Bhauma"</note>. These portents are pacified when met with the appropriate propitiatory rites. Some authorities say that **atmospheric** <note>original: "Nabhas/Antariksha"</note> portents become mild through such rites, but **divine** <note>original: "Divya"</note> portents are never truly pacified.

However, even divine portents can be pacified through the donation of abundant gold, grain, cows, and land; by milking cows upon the grounds of a temple of Shiva <note>original: "Rudrayatane"</note>; and by performing the *Koti Homa* <note>a massive fire ritual involving ten million offerings</note>.

The destiny <note>original: "Daiva"</note> ordained for a king ripens in eight ways, affecting: his own body, his sons, his treasury, his vehicles, his cities, his wives, his priests, and his subjects.

If the phallic symbols of Shiva <note>Shivalinga</note>, idols of deities, or sacred temples should break without cause, move, sweat, shed tears, or appear to speak, it foretells the destruction of the King and the nation.

During a festival procession of the deities, if the cart, the axle, the wheels, the yoke, or the banner should break, fall, overturn, sink, get stuck, or collide, it does not bode well for the welfare of the country or the King.

Abnormalities <note>original: "Vaikrita"</note> arising from images of Sages, the God of Dharma, or Brahma affect the twice-born <note>term: Dvijati (the upper three social classes: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas)</note>. Those arising from Rudra or the World-Guardians <note>term: Lokapala (deities presiding over the cardinal directions)</note> are harmful to livestock.

Portents arising from Jupiter, Venus, or Saturn affect the royal priests. Those arising from Vishnu affect all the people. Those arising from Skanda or Vishakha <note>deities associated with war and youth</note> bring misfortune to provincial rulers and kings.

Portents arising from images of Veda Vyasa <note>the legendary compiler of the Vedas</note> affect the ministers. Those from Vinayaka <note>Ganesha</note> affect the commanders of the army. Those from Dhata or Vishwakarma <note>the divine architect</note> affect the subjects...

If palaces, mansions, arched gateways, or banners are consumed by fire or struck by lightning, the arrival of an enemy army is certain within six months. || 20 ||

# Chapter 46: On Portents (Page 169)

->**The Commentary in Common Language**<-

A rain of dust and sudden darkness are givers of great fear. The disappearance of stars in a cloudless night sky, or the visibility of stars during the day, is a source of misfortune. <note>original: "पांशुजं" (dust-born/dust storm) and "उडुनाश" (destruction/disappearance of stars)</note> || 21 ||

If fire behaves in a terrifying manner, it is said to bring danger to the city, to four-legged animals, to birds <note>original: "अण्डज" (egg-born)</note>, and to humans. If smoke or sparks of fire are found upon one's bed, clothing, or hair, it portends certain death. || 22 ||

The spontaneous burning of weapons, their emitting of sounds, their sliding out of scabbards, or their trembling—if these or other abnormalities are seen in weaponry—one should predict a fierce and tumultuous battle in the kingdom very soon. || 23 ||

To pacify these fire-related portents, one should perform a <term>Homa</term> (sacred fire ritual) using the <term>Vahni-mantra</term> (fire-invoking chants), utilizing fuel-wood from <term>Kshira-vrikshas</term> (milky-sap trees), mustard seeds, and <term>Ghee</term> (clarified butter). In this rite, gold should be gifted to the <term>Brahmins</term> (priests). This is how the disturbance of fire is pacified. || 24 ||

**Thus ends the section on Portents of Fire.**

If the branches of trees break suddenly without cause, it indicates preparations for war. If trees appear to "laugh," it signifies the destruction of the country; if they appear to "weep," it signifies an increase in disease. || 25 ||

If trees flower out of their proper season, it leads to divisions in the state. If very young saplings flower excessively, it portends the death of children. If milk-like sap flows from trees, it results in the loss of all wealth and goods. || 26 ||

If wine flows from a tree, it means the destruction of vehicles/mounts; if blood flows, there will be war; if honey flows, there will be disease; if oil flows, there is fear of <term>famine</term>; and if water flows, it signifies a great terror. || 27 ||

If sprouts wither, there is a complete loss of potency and food grains. If healthy trees wither without cause, the army and food supplies will also perish. If fallen trees stand up on their own, it indicates fear born of divine or providential wrath. || 28 ||

# Varāhī Saṃhitā

If flowers and fruits appear on trees out of season, it is specified as a sign of the king's death. If smoke or flames appear on a tree, that too signifies the death of the king. || 29 ||

If trees appear to weep <note>original: "srapsu" - to drip or exude fluid like tears</note> or if they seem to speak, a great destruction of people is foretold. The ripening of the results <note>the manifestation of the omen's effect</note> of such tree abnormalities occurs within ten months. || 30 ||

One should worship the tree with garlands, scents, incense, and cloths, and place an umbrella over the tree. Having performed a propitiatory rite for Shiva, the <term>Rudra-japa</term> <note>the repetitive chanting of Vedic hymns dedicated to Rudra/Shiva</note> should be performed here, along with a six-limbed <term>Homa</term> <note>fire sacrifice</note> using the mantra "To the Rudras" <note>original: "Rudrebhyah"</note>. || 31 ||

The king should feed Brahmins with <term>Payasa</term> <note>sweet rice pudding</note> mixed with honey and clarified butter. The great sages have declared that in the event of such tree abnormalities, the donation of land is the prescribed gift <note>dakshina</note>. || 32 ||

**Thus ends the section on Tree Abnormalities.**

If two or three stalks emerge from a single lotus or barley plant, or if twin flowers or fruits are born, it foretells the death of the owner of that plant. || 33 ||

If there is an excessive growth of crops, or if many different kinds of fruits and flowers appear on a single tree, then by law, the arrival of an enemy army is certain. || 34 ||

When sesame seeds yield only half the usual oil, or if they yield no oil at all, and if grain loses its flavor, then one should know that a very great danger is imminent. || 35 ||

Abnormal flowers or fruits should be taken outside the village or the city. For the sake of peace <note>Shanti</note>, a <term>Saumya Charu</term> <note>an offering of boiled rice dedicated to the Moon or Soma</note> should be prepared, or an animal sacrifice should be performed for pacification. || 36 ||

If an abnormality is seen in the crops, that entire field should be given to the Brahmins...

If it rains continuously for a week out of season, the principal king will die. If it rains blood, there will be mobilization of weapons <note>warfare</note>; if it rains flesh, bones, fat, and the like, a plague <note>original: 'maraka'</note> will occur. **(40)**

From the raining of milk, clarified butter <note>ghee</note>, honey, curds, or hot water, the destruction of the country is to be known. From a rain of blood, there is war between kings. **(43)**

If no shadow is seen even when the sun is clear, or if a reversed shadow is seen, then it should be declared that a great fear has come upon the land. **(44)**

When a rainbow is seen in a cloudless sky during the day or at night, in either the east or the west, then a very great fear of hunger <note>famine</note> will occur. **(45)**

# The Varahi Samhita

### On Anomalies of Rain
When the Sun, Moon, and Wind align during a time of unnatural rainfall <note>original: "vrishti-vikara"; refers to rain falling out of season or in strange forms</note>, a sacrificial rite should be performed. At that time, gifts of grain, food, cows, and gold must be given as dakshina <note>a ritual fee or gift given to priests</note>; through this, the evil omen is pacified. || 46 ||
**Thus ends the section on Rain Anomalies.**

### On Anomalies of Water
If rivers that flow near a city suddenly shift their course away from it, or if perennial pools and lakes that never dry up should suddenly go dry, that city will soon become desolated. || 47 ||

If rivers appear to carry oil, blood, or flesh, or if the water becomes turbid and begins to flow backward <note>upstream</note>, it foretells the arrival of an enemy army within six months. || 48 ||

If flames or smoke are seen in wells, or if the water appears to boil, or if sounds of weeping, shouting, singing, or senseless chattering are heard coming from them, these are declared to be signs of a coming plague <note>original: "maraka"; a deadly epidemic</note>. || 49 ||

The sudden appearance of water where no hole has been dug, or a change in the natural smell and taste of water, or any unnatural transformation of a reservoir is a cause of great fear. The remedy for this is as follows: || 50 ||

In the event of water anomalies, one should perform a worship of Varuna <note>the Vedic deity of the waters</note> using the Varuna mantras. With those same mantras, one should perform chanting and fire-offerings <note>japa and homa</note>. In this way, the evil omen reaches tranquility. || 51 ||
**Thus ends the section on Water Anomalies.**

### On Anomalies of Birth
Regarding anomalies of birth: if women give birth to two, three, four, or more children at once, or if birth occurs significantly before or after the natural term, it signifies the destruction of the country and the family lineage. || 52 ||

If twins are born to mares, camels, buffaloes, cows, or female elephants, it foretells the death of those specific animals. The results of such births manifest within six months. Regarding the pacification of this, there are two verses spoken by the sage Garga: || 53 ||

If women [give birth] in a foreign territory...

# The Varahi Samhita

### On Changes in Moving and Fixed Objects
If there is an echo, or if a trumpet sounds <note>original: "vishwaraturye"</note> or if there is an unnatural occurrence in the signs of the zodiac such as Cancer, then disease or death follows. If the sound of the trumpet is toneless, it signifies the defeat of the enemy. || 62 ||

He should satisfy the Brahmins with sweetened rice-milk <note>original: "paramanna"</note> and monetary gifts. Sacrificial offerings <note>original: "homa"</note> with abundant food and gifts must be performed with great effort. || 65 || Thus ends the section on Wind Disturbances.

## Chapter Forty-Seven
->The Variegated Colors of the Peacock<-

I have previously described in detail the auspicious and inauspicious effects relating to the celestial and intermediate regions, mostly concerning the movements of the planets, their conjunctions, planetary wars, and their paths. <note>Verse 1</note> It is not proper for Varāhamihira to repeat these things frequently, for his only fault is that he is a "summarizer" <note>one who prefers brevity</note>. However, those who know this subject should not say... <margin>The commentator Baldev Prasad Mishra notes that this chapter on the "Peacock's Variegated Colors" is essential for practitioners despite the author's usual brevity.</margin>

<column-break/>

...they occur. <note>Verse 96</note> The songs and stories of the insane, the words of children, and whatever a woman says—these are never bypassed <note>they always come to pass</note>. <note>Verse 97</note> This Goddess Sarasvatī, the embodiment of truth and speech, unbidden by others, first moved among all the gods and then reached the mortals. <note>Verse 98</note> Even an astrologer who does not know the science of mathematics, if he understands portents well, will become famous and beloved by the King. This secret of the sages' words has been told so that by knowing it, a man can see into the three divisions of time. <note>Verse 99</note>

# Chapter 47 (179)

The result is sung in the same manner as the famous and beautiful limb of poetry known as the "Varangam" or "Vichitrakam." <note>original: "Vichitrakam" — a specific poetic meter or arrangement</note> ॥ 2 ॥ Its very nature is the repetition of what has already been proclaimed. Even if I do not speak of this, I would still be subject to criticism here <note>The author suggests that even if the information seems repetitive, it is necessary to include to avoid the charge of incompleteness</note> ॥ 3 ॥

When all the planets are situated in the **Northern Path** <term>Uttara Vithi - the northern celestial roadway</term> and are radiant, they bring safety, abundance of food, and auspiciousness. If they move in the **Southern Path** <term>Dakshina Marga - the southern celestial roadway</term> and are devoid of luster, they cause hunger, fear of thieves, and death ॥ 4 ॥

When the son of Bhrigu <note>Venus</note> is in the "Storehouse" <note>The constellation Magha</note> and the Lord of Speech <note>Jupiter</note> resides in the constellation Pushya, kings become free from enmity and enjoy happiness; the people are joyful and free from disease ॥ 5 ॥

If the other planets—excluding the Sun—afflict the constellations of Krittika, Magha, Rohini, Shravana, or Jyeshtha <note>original: "Aindram"</note>, then the western direction is afflicted by injustice and lawlessness ॥ 6 ॥

If at the end of the day <note>twilight</note> the planets stand in the East in the shape of a banner, there will be war among the kings of the East. If they are in the middle of the sky, there is affliction for the Middle Country <term>Madhya-desha - the central heartland of ancient India</term>. This occurs if they appear harsh/dim, but not if they are beautiful and possessed of bright rays ॥ 7 ॥

If they take refuge in the Southern quarter, there is a destruction of the clouds and the people of the Southern Path <note>the Deccan region</note>. If the planets are diminished and harsh in appearance, there is war; but if they are possessed of large bodies and bright rays, it is auspicious ॥ 8 ॥

In the Northern Path, if they have clear rays, they bring peace to the kings of that region. If they have small bodies and the color of ash, they bring harm to the countries and their kings ॥ 9 ॥

<column-break/>

...learned scholars will not criticize them at all ॥ 2 ॥ (Previously regarding the clouds) that is the nature of the "Mayurachitrakam" <note>The "Variegated Peacock" omen system</note>; for that reason, it should not be described again. However, even if not described, the criticism will not be avoided ॥ 3 ॥

If the planets travel in the **Northern Path** and are luminous, then there is well-being, plenty of food, and welfare. If they go to the **Southern Path** and are lusterless, they are the cause of famine, fear of thieves, and death ॥ 4 ॥

If the planet Venus is in the "Storehouse"—that is, in the Magha constellation—and Jupiter is seated in the Pushya constellation, then kings are without enemies. The subjects remain happy, delighted, and free from disease ॥ 5 ॥

If the group of planets, excluding the Sun, afflict the Krittika, Magha, Rohini, Shravana, and Jyeshtha constellations, then the Western direction suffers through injustice ॥ 6 ॥

If at the time of evening the group of planets are situated in the Eastern direction like a banner, then a war occurs among the kings living in the East. If this happens in the middle part of the sky, the Middle Country is afflicted. However, if these are harsh, or beautiful, or possess rays <note>The Hindi commentary clarifies the Sanskrit: if they are harsh, they cause pain; if radiant, they do not</note>, the Middle Country is not afflicted ॥ 7 ॥

If the planets are in the Southern direction, there is a loss of the Southern Path and the clouds. If at this time the planets have diminished bodies and harsh appearances, there is conflict; but if they have large bodies and possess rays, it is auspicious ॥ 8 ॥

If they shine with clear rays in the Northern Path, they bring peace among the kings there. If they have small bodies and a color like ash, they [bring harm] to the country and the kings...

# Varahi Samhita
<page-num>180</page-num>

If the stars of the <term>Nakshatras</term><note>Lunar mansions or star clusters used in Vedic astrology</note> and the planets appear to be joined with flames of smoke and sparks, or if they lose their light without any apparent cause, then the entire world, along with its kings, will meet with destruction. || 10 ||

When two moons appear shining in the sky, it brings great prosperity to the <term>Brahmins</term><note>The priestly and scholarly class</note>. If two suns are seen, it leads to war among the <term>Kshatriyas</term><note>The warrior and ruling class</note> and others. If three, four, or many such suns or moons appear, it signifies the dissolution of the world. || 11 ||

If <term>Shikhi</term><note>original: "शिखी" - a name for the shadow planet Ketu, often associated with comets</note>, that is, <term>Ketu</term><note>The descending lunar node, often depicted as a comet or a headless celestial body</note>, touches the <term>Saptarshi-mandala</term><note>The Big Dipper or Great Bear constellation</note>, <term>Abhijit</term><note>The 28th intercalary Nakshatra, Vega</note>, the Pole Star (<term>Dhruva</term>), or the <term>Jyeshtha Nakshatra</term>, it causes the destruction of clouds, hinders auspicious works, and brings sorrow. If it touches the <term>Ashlesha Nakshatra</term>, there will certainly be a failure of rain, and the inhabited lands, filled with sand and turmoil, will quickly face ruin. || 12 ||

When <term>Shani</term><note>Saturn, the son of the Sun</note> wanders through the "Eastern Gates"—that is, the seven Nakshatras beginning with <term>Kruttika</term>—and becomes retrograde, it causes famine, intense fear, and conflict between friends, and it prevents the rains from falling. || 13 ||

If Saturn, Mars, or Ketu pierces the <term>Rohini-shakata</term><note>The "Cart of Rohini," a specific T-shaped configuration of stars in the Aldebaran cluster</note>, the misfortune that befalls the entire world is so great that it cannot be described; the world sinks into an ocean of evil. || 14 ||

When Ketu is constantly rising or wanders through the entire circle of the Nakshatras, the world—both moving and unmoving—experiences the bitter fruits of its past misdeeds. || 15 ||

If the Moon appears in the shape of a bow, looks dry or rough, and has the color of blood, it produces hunger and fear. However, it also indicates the mobilization of armies and victory for the side from which it rises. If its "horn" is turned downward...

<margin>These omens are considered highly inauspicious.</margin>

...they become harbingers of evil. || 9 || If the stars of the planets and Nakshatras are possessed of smoky flames and sparks, or if their light fails without cause, then all people perish along with the king. || 10 || When two moons are radiant in the sky, it is extremely auspicious for the Brahmins. By the appearance of two suns, there is war among the Kshatriyas and others, and from the emergence of three, four, or many such moons and suns, the world meets its end. || 11 ||

If <term>Shikhi</term>, meaning <term>Ketu</term>, touches the <term>Saptarshi-mandala</term>, <term>Abhijit</term>, the Pole Star, or the <term>Jyeshtha Nakshatra</term>, it results in the destruction of clouds, loss in good deeds, and brings grief. If it touches the <term>Ashlesha Nakshatra</term>, the destruction of rain is certain, and the countryside, becoming distressed and filled with dust, soon goes to ruin. || 12 ||

Saturn, by moving through the Eastern Gates (the seven Nakshatras starting with Kruttika) and becoming retrograde, causes famine, fierce dread, and opposition among friends, and does not allow for rain. || 13 || If Saturn, Mars, or Ketu should pierce the <term>Rohini-shakata</term>, such misfortune comes to the whole world that it cannot be told. || 14 || When Ketu rises continually or travels through the cycle of many Nakshatras, the world constantly experiences all the inauspicious results of its own past actions. || 15 || If it is shaped like a bow, rough, and colored like blood, it creates hunger and fear...

# Chapter 47: With Vernacular Commentary
### Page 181

If the moon appears to destroy cows, it also causes the destruction of crops. If it appears to be burning or smoldering with smoke, it surely signifies the death of kings. ॥ 16 ॥ 

When the moon is glossy, thick, possesses symmetrical horns, and is large and high, moving through the <term>Naga-vithi</term><note>The "Serpent's Path," a specific northern division of the ecliptic</note> in the north—provided it is viewed by auspicious planets and separated from inauspicious ones—it brings immense joy to the world. ॥ 17 ॥ 

When the Moon <note>original: "Shashanka," meaning the hare-marked one</note> reaches the constellations of <term>Magha</term><note>Ancestral</note>, <term>Anuradha</term><note>Friendly</note>, <term>Jyeshtha</term><note>Indra's</note>, <term>Vishakha</term>, or <term>Chitra</term><note>Tvashtar's</note>, and moves to the south, it is not auspicious. # The Varahi Samhita
### Page 182

If a rainbow or lightning appears in the northeast, or when the <term>Cloud-Tree</term><note>Sanskrit: Meghataru; likely referring to a specific cloud formation resembling a tree</note> is embraced by the rays of the sun and appears glossy, or if a massive cloud covers the sun at the time of sunset, then rain will occur. || 23 ||

If at the time of sunrise or sunset, an image of a <term>City of Gandharvas</term><note>Sanskrit: Gandharvapur; a superior mirage or complex cloud formation resembling a celestial city</note> equipped with banners obstructs the solar disc, one should declare that the King will soon face a terrifying battle. || 26 ||

Whatever has been described in great detail by the ancient Sages, I have stated all of that in this work, excluding only the repetitions. Even after hearing the song of the cuckoo, the crow caws; that is merely its nature, for the crow's cawing can never truly conquer the melody of the cuckoo. <note>This is a metaphorical humble-statement by Varahamihira, comparing his work to the ancient sages.</note> || 28 ||

**Hindi Commentary by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra**

If a rainbow or lightning is present in the northeast direction, or when the <term>Cloud-Tree</term> becomes glossy due to the falling rays of the sun, or if a great cloud covers the sun at the time of its setting, then rain occurs. || 23 || In the country where the sun is fragmented, bent, black, small, pierced by marks of crows etc., and is rough, there is often an absence of the King. || 24 || The kings who desire to wage war and find their army joined from behind by meat-eating birds face a very great fear for their army; but if the birds move ahead, there is victory. || 25 || At the time of sunrise or sunset, if an image of a <term>City of Gandharvas</term> possessing banners obstructs the sun, it reveals that the King will obtain a fear-filled battle. || 26 || A twilight with glossy and sweet winds, and the sounding of birds and deer in the eastern direction is good; but if the twilight is destroyed by dust or is rough like blood, then the destruction of the populace occurs. || 27 || That which the Sages have told in detail, I have told all of that in this scripture, leaving out those repetitions. Hearing the cooing of the cuckoo, it is the very nature of the crow to make a sound; in reality, the crow's sound is not for the sake of defeating the cuckoo. || 28 ||
