# Now begins the Forty-Eighth Chapter.
## The Ritual Bath of Pushya.

The King is the very root of the tree of his subjects; because the harm or refinement <note>Sanskrit: *upaghata-samskara*</note> of that root results in misfortune or prosperity for the entire world, one must always be concerned with the welfare of the monarch. || 1 || Listen now to that rite of pacification <note>Sanskrit: *shanti*; a ritual to avert evil</note> which was originally explained by the Self-Born Creator <note>Brahma</note> to the Preceptor of the Gods <note>Brihaspati</note> for the sake of Great Indra; having received this knowledge, the elder sage Garga related it to Bhaguri. || 2 || The King should perform the *Pushya* Bath <note>A royal consecration or purificatory bath performed when the moon is in the lunar mansion of Pushya</note> guided by the royal astrologer and the family priest. There is no other ritual more purifying than this, nor any that better destroys all portents of evil. || 3 ||

The rite should be performed in a forest region free from trees such as the *Shleshmantaka* <note>Glue-berry or Lasora</note>, *Aksha* <note>Beleric myrobalan</note>, thorny trees <note>such as Khair</note>, or those that are pungent, bitter, or odorless. It should be a place avoided by inauspicious birds like owls and vultures. || 4 || The area should be covered with young trees, shrubs, creepers, and spreading vines, filled with delightful, sweet-smelling trees with undamaged leaves and sprouts. || 5 || It should resonate with the sounds of the wild cock, the *Jivajivaka* <note>a type of pheasant or Greek partridge</note>, parrots, peacocks, woodpeckers, blue jays, and green pigeons; as well as the *Krakara* <note>a species of partridge or crab-like bird</note>, the *Kapinjala* <note>Francolin partridge</note>, the *Vanjula* <note>a water bird</note>, and pigeons. || 6 || One should perform this in a clean temple or a field near the forest, where the air is filled with the humming of bees intoxicated by the nectar of flowers and the song of the male cuckoo. || 7 || Or perhaps on the lovely banks of rivers, which are marked by the claws of water-birds...

---

The King is the root for the tree-like subjects; therefore, for the refinement of the subjects, there are auspicious and inauspicious results; thus, one should always worry about the auspicious matters of the King. || 1 || Listen to what the elder Garga, having obtained it, said to Bhaguri—that rite of pacification which Brahma himself told to Brihaspati for Indra. || 2 || It is proper for the King to perform the *Pushya* bath through the astrologers and priests. Other than this, there is nothing else so holy and capable of destroying all types of calamities. || 3 || It is proper to perform the *Pushya* bath in a forest full of many sweet and beautiful trees with intact leaves and buds, thick with young trees, vines, shrubs, and creepers, and devoid of *Shleshmantaka* (Lasora), *Aksha* (Baheda), thorny trees (Khair), or pungent, bitter, and scentless trees, and abandoned by inauspicious birds like owls and vultures. In a place where there is the beautiful sound of the wild cock (chameleon/lizard) <note>The Hindi commentary glosses *Krikavaku* as a lizard/chameleon, though in Sanskrit it usually refers to a cock</note>, the *Jivajivaka* (Chakor), parrot, peacock, *Shatapatra* (Woodpecker), *Chasha* (Blue Jay), *Harita* (Pigeon), *Krakara* (Crab/Partridge), *Kapinjala* (Chataka), *Vanjula* (a specific bird), and pigeons, and where there are swarms of bees intoxicated by drinking the nectar of flowers and birds like the cuckoo; in such a holy field-house near the forest, this pacification should be done. || 4 || || 5 || 6 || 7 || Or else, on the banks of rivers which please the eyes and mind, marked by the [claws of] water-birds...

# Varahi Samhita

<page-num>184</page-num>
->The Compendium of Varahamihira<-

One should perform this pacification ritual <note>Shanti: a propitiatory rite to avert evil</note> on the beautiful, thigh-like sandy banks of rivers, which inspire love and delight. || 8 ||

One should perform the ritual on the banks of a sacred lake that bears the splendor of the thousand-eyed Indra <note>original: "Sahasraksha"</note>; where the soaring swans serve as its royal umbrella, where the songs of the Karandava, Kurara, and Sarasa birds provide the music, and where the blooming blue lotuses serve as its eyes. || 9 ||

Or in a place where the lotus-plants appear like playful women, whose faces are full-blown lotuses, whose speech is the melodious warbling of the Kalahansa swans, and whose high, firm breasts are the lotus buds. || 10 ||

One should perform the Pushya-bath <note>Pushya-snana: a royal ritual bath performed when the moon is in the lunar mansion of Pushya</note> in a cow-pen <term>Gostha (a place for cattle)</term> that is covered with bits of foam from the cows chewing their cud, marked by the striking of hooves, and filled with the festive sounds of the lowing and gamboling of newborn calves. || 11 ||

Or on the seashore, crowded with ships that have safely arrived laden with jewels, and where the shoreline is multicolored by the presence of water-birds and white cranes nestled among the dense Nichula <note>original: "water-cane" or Barringtonia acutangula</note> trees. || 12 ||

Or in those hermitages where even a lion is overcome by a doe—just as anger is conquered by patience—and where the young of birds and deer roam without fear. || 13 ||

Or in the magnificent home of deer-eyed women, whose gait is slowed by the weight of their heavy hips and the adornment of their tinkling waist-bands and anklets, and whose speech is as sweet as the call of the cuckoo. || 14 ||

One may also perform it in holy temples, at sacred pilgrimage sites <term>Tirthas (crossings or holy water sites)</term>, in the lovely areas of gardens, on the leveled grounds previously described, or where water flows in a clockwise direction <note>original: "Pradakshina"</note>. || 15 ||

# Chapter 48: With Language Commentary
## Page 185

The water should flow, specifically towards the East or the North; in such a descending terrain, the <term>Pushya-snana</term><note>A ritual bath taken when the moon is in the lunar mansion of Pushya, intended for royal sanctification and victory.</note> should be performed. || 15 ||

Land that is free from charcoal, bones, barren soil, husks, hair, pits, crab holes, the burrows of porcupines or mice, and anthills <note>original: "valmika"</note>—and where the earth is firm, fragrant, smooth, sweet-smelling, and level—is the cause of victory. Even in the case of a military camp, the site should be selected according to these qualities. || 16 || 17 ||

The astrologer <note>original: "daivajna"</note>, the minister, and the priests should depart from the city and go to such a place in the East, the North, or the North-East <note>original: "ishanakona"</note> direction. Thereafter, the priest, having bowed with great effort, should offer a sacrifice <note>original: "balidan"</note> consisting of parched grain, unbroken rice, curd, and flowers. The invitation mantra for this, as declared by the ancient sages, is as follows: || 18 || 19 ||

"May all the gods who desire worship here approach; may the guardians of the directions, the serpent-deities <note>original: "nagas"</note>, the twice-born <note>original: "dvija" or Brahmins</note>, and whoever else is entitled to a share, please come." || 20 ||

After thus invoking them all, the priest should say: "Having received worship tomorrow, you may depart after granting peace to the King." || 21 ||

Having worshipped the invited deities, they should spend that night <note>original: "sharvari"</note> there. The good or bad omens of the dreams seen during that night should be interpreted; the rules regarding dreams have been explained in the Chapter on Journeys <note>original: "Yatradhyaya"</note>. || 22 ||

On the following day at dawn, one should bring the materials of the specified qualities and go to that plot of land. Regarding what is to be done there, these are the verses sung by the sages: "The learned priest, having drawn a circle <note>original: "mandala"</note> there, should represent the Earth as a mine of various jewels and imagine various locations within it. In their respective places, he should establish the serpent-deities, the nature-spirits <note>original: "yakshas"</note>, the ancestors <note>original: "pitris"</note>, the celestial musicians <note>original: "gandharvas"</note>, the celestial nymphs <note>original: "apsaras"</note>, the sages, and the perfected beings <note>original: "siddhas"</note>..." || 23 ||

# The Varahi Samhita

### The Creation of the Earthly Map
Having drawn the design, one should fashion the Earth <note>original: "medini"</note> there, depicted as possessing various jewel mines and diverse locations. ## 24 ## The priest <note>term: "purohita" - a family priest or royal chaplain</note> should then place the Nagas <note>serpent deities</note>, Yakshas <note>nature spirits</note>, Gods, Ancestors <note>original: "pitrin"</note>, Gandharvas <note>celestial musicians</note>, Apsaras <note>celestial nymphs</note>, Sages, and Siddhas <note>perfected beings</note> in their respective proper positions. ## 25 ##

One should also depict the Planets along with the Lunar Mansions <note>term: "nakshatras" - the 27 divisions of the sky</note>, the Rudras <note>forms of Shiva</note> along with the Divine Mothers, Skanda, Vishnu, Vishakha, the Guardians of the World <note>term: "lokapalas" - deities presiding over the cardinal directions</note>, and the wives of the gods. ## 26 ## Having created these using various beautiful colors and endowed with fragrant qualities, the wise practitioner should worship them according to tradition with perfumes, garlands, and ointments. ## 27 ##

### Offerings and Libations
The worship should include various types of edible foods, rice, fruits, roots, and meat, as well as various pleasant drinks such as wine, milk, and distilled spirits <note>original: "asava"</note>. ## 28 ## I shall hereafter describe the specific worship for those depicted herein. For the Planets, the procedure prescribed in the "Sacrifice to the Planets" <note>original: "graha-yajna"</note> must be performed. ## 29 ##

### Specific Rites for Spirits and Deities
The Pisachas <note>flesh-eating spirits</note>, the sons of Diti <note>Titans/Demons</note>, and the Danavas <note>giants/demons</note> are to be worshipped with meat, cooked rice, and wine. The Ancestors should be worshipped with ointments, collyrium <note>eye-salve</note>, sesame seeds, meat, and cooked rice. ## 30 ##

The Sages are worshipped with the chanting of the Sama, Yajur, and Rig Vedas, along with fragrant incense and garlands. The Nagas <note>serpent deities</note> should be worshipped with various colors and the "Three Sweets" <note>note: typically a mixture of sugar, honey, and clarified butter</note>. ## 31 ##

The Gods <note>original: "vibudhan"</note> are worshipped with incense, offerings of clarified butter in the fire, garlands, gems, hymns of praise, and prostrations. The Gandharvas and Apsaras are worshipped with perfumes and highly fragrant garlands. ## 32 ## For all the remaining beings, one should present worship with "universal" offerings <note>offerings of all colors/types</note>. One should also provide cords, garments, banners, ornaments, and the sacred thread <note>term: "yajnopavita" - the triple-strand thread worn by the initiated</note> for all of them. ## 33 ##

The King, being of noble mind, should sit upon that throne covered with gold, surrounded by his ministers, trusted confidants, the royal priest, the court astrologer, and citizens with auspicious names. **[48]**

One should release those in bondage <note>original: "bandhanamokṣaṃ"; referring to the pardoning of prisoners</note>, except for those who have committed internal crimes against the state. || 81 || When performed during every Pushya lunar mansion <note>Pushya is considered the most auspicious star for royal rituals</note>, this rite increases happiness, fame, and wealth. If the Pushya star does not fall on the full moon of the month of Pausha, the "Pausha Peace Rite" previously described yields only half its fruit. || 82 || In the event of portents or calamities in the kingdom, or upon the appearance of Rahu or Ketu <note>the lunar nodes associated with eclipses and comets</note>, or during the affliction of the planets, one should perform the Pushya Bath. || 83 || There is no portent in this world that is not pacified by this rite, and there is no other auspicious ceremony that surpasses this one. || 84 || This procedure is highly recommended for a King desiring supreme sovereignty, for one longing for the birth of a son, and as a preliminary to a royal consecration. || 85 || The great and famous Brihaspati <note>the preceptor of the gods</note> spoke of this to Lord Indra. This bath is the ultimate means of increasing lifespan, progeny, and good fortune. || 86 || Whosoever bathes their elephants and horses according to this same ritual will be liberated from fear and attain the highest success. || 87 ||

One should release the bonds of all except those who have committed internal offenses. || 81 || This peace-giving rite, which increases happiness, fame, and wealth, should be performed in every Pushya lunar mansion. The peace-giving rite to be performed therein has been described previously. || 82 || When there are portents or other types of disturbances in the kingdom, or upon seeing Rahu and Ketu, or when the planets are tormenting the state, the Pushya Bath should be performed. || 83 || There is no portent on this earth that cannot be removed by this peace-rite, and there is no inauspiciousness capable of overcoming this ritual. || 84 || For this reason, this method of consecration is the very best for a King desiring to sit upon the throne or desiring the birth of a son. || 85 || The highly renowned Brihaspati said this for Indra. This excellent Pushya Bath method increases lifespan, progeny, and is a great enhancer of good fortune. || 86 || The King who bathes his elephants and horses by this method is freed from sin and attains superior perfection. || 87 ||

# Chapter Forty-Nine

## Characteristics of the Royal Diadem

The characteristics of royal diadems <note>original: "patta" - a decorative gold band or crown worn on the forehead</note> have been described in great detail by the ancient teachers. I shall now provide a concise summary of those teachings, containing all the essential meanings. || 1 ||

A diadem that is eight fingers wide in the center brings good fortune to Kings. One that is seven fingers wide is prescribed for the Chief Queen, and one of six fingers is specified for the Crown Prince. || 2 ||

A diadem of four fingers in width at the center is for the Commander-in-Chief. One of two fingers width is known as the "Diadem of Favor" <note>original: "prasada-patta" - a simplified crown gifted by a king as a mark of honor</note>. These are the five types of diadems described. || 3 ||

All these diadems should be twice as long as they are wide, and their width at the sides should be half of their central width. They should all be crafted from pure gold <note>original: "kanchana"</note> to ensure the increase of prosperity. || 4 ||

The King’s diadem should have five peaks <note>original: "shikha" - crests or pointed extensions</note>; those of the Crown Prince and the Queen should have three peaks; the Commander-in-Chief’s should have one peak; and the Diadem of Favor is made without any peaks at all. || 5 ||

If, while being fashioned, the gold leaf of the diadem expands with ease, it signifies the growth and victory of the King, as well as the happiness and wealth of the subjects. || 6 ||

If a blemish or wound appears in the center of the diadem during its making, it causes the destruction of life and the kingdom. If it cracks in the center, it must be discarded. If it cracks at the sides, it brings obstacles. || 7 ||

In the event of such inauspicious omens...

## Chapter Fifty
### Characteristics of the Sword

A sword measuring fifty fingers <note>term: "angula" - a traditional unit of measurement approximately equal to the width of a finger</note> in length is considered excellent; one measuring twenty-five fingers is inferior. One should judge the flaws <note>original: "vrana" - literally 'wounds' or 'scars,' referring here to spots or blemishes in the metal</note> based on finger-measurements; a flaw located at an odd-numbered finger-mark is inauspicious. || 1 ||

Blemishes that resemble the Shrivatsa <note>a sacred curl or mark</note>, the Vardhamana <note>a specific auspicious diagram</note>, a parasol, a Shiva-linga, an earring, a lotus, a banner, a weapon, or a swastika are considered auspicious. || 2 ||

Marks shaped like a lizard, a crow, a vulture, a beast of prey, a headless torso, or a scorpion, or those that follow the grain of the metal in great numbers, do not bring good fortune. || 3 ||

A sword that is cracked, too short, blunt, notched along the spine, unpleasing to the eye or mind, or which lacks a clear ring <note>original: "asvara"</note> is considered undesirable. Those possessing the opposite qualities are said to grant desired results. || 4 ||

If a sword rings spontaneously, it foretells death; if it rattles in its scabbard, it indicates defeat. If it unsheathes itself, it signifies an impending war, and if the sword appears to glow, it brings victory. || 5 || A king should not [unsheathe] without cause—

<note>The following section is a Hindi commentary/translation by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra included in the original manuscript.</note>

The experts should command peace; the crown which has no inauspicious marks, by wearing it, the king's empire increases. || 8 ||

A sword of fifty fingers in measure is excellent, and a sword of twenty-five fingers in measure is low. One should know the flaws by the measure of fingers; if the flaw is at an odd finger-measure, i.e., 3, 5, 7, 9, etc., it is inauspicious. || 1 ||

Marks similar to the Shrivatsa, Vardhamana, parasol, Shiva-linga, earring, lotus, banner, weapon, and swastika are auspicious. || 2 ||

A sword with marks shaped like a lizard, crow, vulture, carnivore, headless torso, or scorpion, or with many marks like bamboo grain, is not auspicious. || 3 ||

A sword that is broken, small, blunt, cut at the spine, unpleasant to the sight and mind, and soundless is harmful. If it is the opposite of this, it gives the desired fruit. || 4 ||

If a sound suddenly comes from the sword, it is a cause of death; rattling upon leaving the scabbard means defeat; if it falls out of the scabbard on its own, there will be war; and if it is radiant, there is victory. || 5 || The king should not [draw] the sword from the scabbard in vain—

# Chapter 50: With Language Commentary

->**The Ritual Handling of the Sword**<-

One should not unsheathe the sword without cause, nor should one rattle or shake it. One must not look at their own reflection in the blade, nor discuss its price. The place of its origin should not be revealed, and a king must never touch the sword-blade while in a state of ritual impurity. <note>original: "aprayato" - referring to a state of being ritually unwashed or spiritually distracted.</note> || 6 ||

->**Auspicious Shapes**<-

Swords that are shaped like a cow's tongue, or resemble the petal of a blue lotus, a bamboo leaf, or the leaf of an oleander <term>Karavira: the Nerium oleander plant, known for its long, tapering leaves</term> are considered excellent. Likewise, those with points shaped like a spear-head or those with rounded tips are praised. || 7 ||

Once a sword is finished according to the prescribed proportions, it should not be cut or filed down. If the tip of the sword breaks, the owner's mother will die; if it breaks at the hilt <note>original: "mule" - literally the root or base</note>, the owner himself will perish. || 8 ||

->**The Science of Hidden Flaws**<-

Just as one can predict the presence of a mole on a woman's private parts by observing a mole on her face, so too can the flaws <term>Vrana: literally 'wounds' or 'scars', referring here to internal spots or structural defects in the steel</term> within a sword be predicted by observing the hilt. || 9 ||

Alternatively, if a person carrying a sword asks a question, the diviner <term>Daivajña: an astrologer or seer</term> should observe which part of the body the questioner touches. By following this science of weaponry, the diviner can declare exactly where a flaw exists on the blade while it is still hidden within its scabbard. || 10 ||

If the questioner touches their head, the flaw is in the first inch <term>Angula: a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to a finger's width</term> of the blade. If they touch the forehead, it is in the second inch. If they touch between the eyebrows, it is in the third inch, and if they touch the eyes, the flaw is in the fourth inch. || 11 ||

If the questioner touches the nose, lips, cheeks, chin, ears, neck, or shoulders, the flaws are located respectively in the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh inches. Touching the chest indicates a flaw at twelve inches, and touching the armpits indicates a flaw at the thirteenth inch. || 12 || If they touch the breasts, heart, stomach, flanks, or navel, then in that order...

### Page 196

From fourteen <term>angulas</term> <note>An 'angula' is a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to a finger's breadth, approximately 0.75 inches.</note> onwards, the locations of the <term>vranas</term> <note>Literally 'wounds' or 'scars'; in this context, it refers to spots, pits, or physical flaws on the sword blade.</note> should be known. By touching the base of the navel, the waist, or the private parts, the flaws are located at nineteen, twenty, and twenty-one <term>angulas</term> respectively. || 13 ||

By touching both thighs, a flaw is indicated at the 22nd <term>angula</term>; by touching the middle of both thighs, at the 23rd <term>angula</term>. By touching the knee, it is at the 24th, and by touching the shank, it is at the 25th <term>angula</term>. || 14 ||

If at that time the inquirer touches the middle of the shanks, the ankle, the heel, the foot, or the toes, one should determine the location of the flaw from the twenty-sixth to the thirtieth <term>angula</term> respectively. This is the opinion of the sage Garga. || 15 ||

The results of flaws located from one to five <term>angulas</term> should be declared in order as follows: death of a son, gain of wealth, loss of wealth, prosperity, and imprisonment. || 16 ||

Gain of a son, quarrel, acquisition of an elephant, death of a son, and gain of wealth; then, from the sixth <term>angula</term> onwards, the results are destruction, obtaining a woman, and mental sorrow. || 17 ||

Gain, loss, obtaining a woman, slaughter, increase, death, and contentment—these results should be known for flaws located from the fourteenth to the twentieth <term>angula</term> respectively. If a flaw occurs at the 21st <term>angula</term>, there will be a loss of wealth. || 18 ||

Acquisition of wealth, <insert>extinction or liberation</insert>, arrival of money, death, prosperity, poverty, sovereignty, death, and kingship—these are the results for flaws from the twenty-second up to the thirtieth <term>angula</term> respectively. || 19 ||

Beyond this, no specific result is mentioned. However, flaws located at odd-numbered <term>angulas</term> give inauspicious results, while those at even-numbered ones give auspicious results. Some authorities state that after thirty <term>angulas</term>, there is no effect...

# Chapter 50: The Characteristics of Swords
### From the Brihat Samhita by Varahamihira

...beyond three hundred <note>referring to the measurement of "fingers" or units discussed on the previous page</note>, it is of this sort. || 20 ||

A sword that possesses the fragrance of **Oleander**, **Blue Lotus**, **Elephant-must** <term>Mada: a scent-secreting liquid from rutting elephants</term>, **Ghee**, **Saffron**, **Jasmine**, or **Champaka** is a bringer of good fortune. Conversely, a sword is considered inauspicious if it smells like **cow urine**, **mud**, or **fat**. || 21 ||

If the scent resembles that of a **tortoise**, **marrow**, **blood**, or **alkali**, it brings fear and sorrow. However, a sword that possesses the brilliance of **Beryl**, **Gold**, or **Lightning** increases victory, health, and prosperity. || 22 ||

The following is the "Drinking of the Blade" <term>Shastrapana: a ritual tempering or coating of the edge</term> according to the teachings of **Ushanas** <note>original: "Aushanasam"; referring to Shukracharya, the preceptor of the Daityas and an ancient authority on polity and weaponry</note>:
*   One desiring **wealth and sovereignty** should treat the blade with **blood**.
*   One desiring a **virtuous son** should treat the blade with **ghee**.
*   One desiring **imperishable wealth** should treat the blade with **water**. || 23 ||

If one seeks the **attainment of wealth through sinful or ruthless means**, the blade should be treated with the milk of a **mare**, a **female camel**, or a **female elephant**. If treated with a mixture of **fish-gall**, and the milk of **deer**, **horses**, and **goats** combined with **toddy-palm juice**, the sword becomes capable of severing an **elephant's trunk**. || 24 ||

<margin>The tempering process</margin>
First, rub the weapon with oil. Then, apply a paste made of **Milk-hedge** <term>Arka: Calotropis gigantea</term> sap, the **ash of a ram's horn**, and the **dung of pigeons and mice**. After this application, if the weapon is sharpened, it will not break even when struck against **stone**. || 25 ||

When a steel blade is treated with a solution of **Plantain-tree ash** <note>original: "Kadali-kshara"</note> mixed with **buttermilk** and allowed to stand for a full day, and is then properly sharpened, it will not break against stone, nor will it be blunted by other metals. || 26 ||

**Thus ends the Fiftieth Chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Swords," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Shri Varahamihira.**

A sword with the luster of Beryl, gold, or lightning increases victory and health. || 22 || According to the scriptures of **Shukracharya**, those desiring Lakshmi (wealth) should give their weapons a "drink" of blood; those desiring a worthy son should use ghee; and those desiring eternal wealth should use water. || 23 || If one desires wealth through evil deeds, use the milk of a mare, camel, or elephant. With fish-gall, deer, horse, and goat milk mixed with palm-juice, even an elephant's trunk can be cut. || 24 || First rub the weapon with oil, then apply a paste of Arka-tree sap, ram-horn ash, and pigeon/mouse dung. Then, even if struck on stone, the edge will not break. || 25 || Mixing the alkali of the Plantain tree with buttermilk for one day...

# Chapter Fifty-One
## The Science of Bodily Omens <note>Sanskrit: Angavidya; the study of physical movements, gestures, and body parts to predict the future.</note>

An astrologer should predict good or bad fortune by observing the direction, the objects brought to the scene, and the location. By mentally analyzing the movements of the questioner’s body, their own body, and the bodies of others, they can determine the outcome. Indeed, the All-Knowing Lord <note>referring to the Divine as the soul of all moving and unmoving things</note>, being omnipresent and all-seeing, reveals the fruits of good and evil to seekers through their own gestures and speech. || 1 ||

A location is considered auspicious for asking questions if it is level and shaded by trees that seem to "smile" with beautiful flowers, are laden with abundant fruit, possess glossy bark, and are free from birds of ill omen. Such a place should be the dwelling of gods, sages, twice-born <term>Dvija; members of the three upper castes in traditional Indian society</term>, and perfected beings <term>Siddhas; enlightened or spiritually accomplished ones</term>. It should be strewn with fine flowers and grain, and possess the joy born from the purity of sweet water...

---

...leave it to soak, then let a sword made of iron "drink" it <note>a metaphor for quenching the metal in the solution</note>. If one then sharpens that sword and strikes it against a stone, it will not break; even if struck against other iron, the blade will not be blunted. || 26 ||

->Thus ends the fiftieth chapter of the Brihat Samhita,<-
->composed by the Great Teacher Varahamihira,<-
->with the vernacular commentary written by Pandit Baladev Prasad Mishra,<-
->resident of Moradabad in the North-Western provinces. || 50 ||<-

Astrologers who observe the knowledge of directions as stated in the scriptures and the objects brought before them can declare good or bad results by using their intellect to observe the occurrences related to the questioner's limbs, their own limbs, and the limbs of others. Because they possess thorough knowledge of all moving and unmoving things, the astrologer is all-knowing, all-seeing, and powerful like Lord Narayana <note>a name for Vishnu, the sustainer of the universe</note>. This is because, through these gestures and conversations, they show the good and bad fruits to those seeking answers. || 1 ||

A place that is endowed with the beautiful "smile" of flowers, filled with many fruits, possessing smooth bark, devoid of bad birds, and filled with trees of excellent names is level; it is the home of gods, sages, the twice-born, and the perfected. Where noble men and grains abound, and which is green with the attachment of beautiful new grass, filled with the joy created by the purity of delicious water—such a place is auspicious for making an inquiry...

---

Since the Teacher previously mentioned 'The Science of Architecture and Bodily Omens,' we shall explain it." Similarly, at the start of the Characteristics of Baskets, he says: "Beyond this, some also read the Characteristics of Baskets. We shall explain that as well." For this reason, he did not include them in the chapter numbering.</margin>

# Chapter 51: With Commentary

->...and lush green grass is auspicious.<-

### On Inauspicious Landscapes
A place where the trees are broken, shattered, eaten by insects, thorny, burnt, withered, or crooked is not auspicious. Similarly, locations surrounded by cruel birds <note>such as vultures or crows</note>, or places with trees bearing derogatory names, or those where the trees are dry, decayed, and rustling with too many fallen leaves, are considered unfavorable.

### On Forbidden Grounds
A site that resembles a cremation ground, a deserted house, or a crossroads is not pleasing. Land that is uneven, perpetually salty <term>ūṣara (barren/saline soil)</term>, or uninhabited is ill-omened. Furthermore, ground covered in sweepings, charcoal, human skulls, ashes, husks, or dry grass does not bring good fortune.

### On Inauspicious Company and Trade
A place occupied by wandering mendicants, naked ascetics, barbers, enemies, prisoners, butchers, or outcasts is not auspicious. Likewise, locations frequented by rogues, those in pain, or sites where weapons and liquor are sold are considered harmful for seeking omens.

### On Directions and Timing
The East, North, and Northeast directions are excellent for the querent <note>the person asking the question</note>. However, the Northwest, West, South, and Southwest directions are not good. Asking questions is auspicious during the forenoon, but not at night, during the two twilights <note>dawn and dusk</note>, or in the afternoon.

### On Signs and Portents
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious omens have been described for the rites of travel <term>yātrā-vidhāna</term> should also be applied here. One should judge the outcome by observing what is brought before the querent, or by looking at the marks on their palms or clothing.

### On Masculine and Feminine Body Parts
The thighs, lips, breasts, scrotum, feet, teeth, arms, hands, cheeks, hair, throat, nails, thumb, temples, armpits, shoulders, ears, and the joints of the anus are considered "masculine" terms in this system of divination. The eyebrows, nose, buttocks, waist, and fingers with beautiful lines are "feminine" names. Also the tongue, neck, calves, heels, shanks, navel, earlobes, and the nape of the neck...

# Varahi Samhita

### Page 200

The mouth, back, collarbone, knees, ribs, heart, palate, eyes, penis, chest, the *trika* <note>the lower spine or sacrum</note>, the head, and the forehead—these are designated as "neuter" body parts. If the mouth or other such parts are touched, success will only be achieved after a long delay. Success is never achieved if the aforementioned parts are dry, wounded, broken, or emaciated, nor is it achieved through the touching of these neuter parts. ॥ 9-10 ॥

If the big toe is touched or moved, the querent will suffer from eye disease. If the fingers are struck, there will be grief concerning a daughter. If the head is struck, there is fear of the king <note>or government authorities</note>. ॥ 11 ॥

If the querent touches their chest, there will be separation from a loved one. If a piece of cloth falls or is removed from their body, it signifies a great calamity. However, if they take hold of a cloth and move backward while asking the question, they will attain their beloved. ॥ 12 ॥

If the querent scratches the earth with their big toe, they are thinking about a field <note>landed property</note>. If they scratch their feet with their hands, they are thinking of a female servant. ॥ 13 ॥

The sight of a palm leaf or birch bark indicates thoughts of clothing. Seeing hair, chaff, bones, or ashes also relates to concerns about garments. Seeing a rope net indicates disease, and seeing tree bark <note>valkala</note> indicates imprisonment or bondage. ॥ 14 ॥

If, at the time of the inquiry, the following are mentioned or seen: long pepper, black pepper, dry ginger, nutgrass, *lodhra* bark, *kustha* <note>costus</note>, clothing, *netra-bala* <note>a fragrant herb</note>, cumin, spikenard, fennel, or the *tagara* flower—then, in that order, it signifies: the destruction of a woman's faults, the destruction of a man's faults, the end of suffering, total ruin, the loss of a path, the loss of a son, the loss of wealth, the loss of grain, and the loss of a child... ॥ 15 ॥

## On Thought-Reading (Chinta) || 23 ||

If the client says, "Speak my thought after careful consideration," or "Direct me," it indicates a concern regarding victory or a journey. If they say to the astrologer sitting among a crowd, "Look into this quickly," the concern relates to a kinsman or a thief. || 24 ||

All these aforementioned signs, if accompanied by the sight of chaff, bones, or poison, or by the sounds of weeping or sneezing, bring death to those who are already suffering from pain. If an internal limb is touched firmly...

# Now begins the Fifty-Second Chapter.
## The Characteristics of Boils.

White, red, yellow, and black boils <term>Pitaka; small inflammatory swellings or pustules</term> appearing on Brahmins and the other castes respectively, yield their results for the classes starting with the twice-born <note>The four social classes: Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra</note>. If they are glossy and of clear beauty on the head, they bring wealth; if on the forehead, they bring good fortune. **(1)**

---

The teeth, throat, right shoulder, left shoulder, both hands, chin, navel, stomach, breasts, the center of the heart and both sides, the belly, the waist, the buttocks, the anus, the joints, the pair of thighs, both knees, both shanks, and both feet—in these, all the lunar mansions reside in order starting from Krittika. **(42-43)** Having reflected well upon all the scriptures, this "Sign of Touching the Limbs" has been well-stated for the satisfaction of scholars. The astrologer <term>Daivagna; one who knows the divine will through stars</term> who is extremely intelligent and of generous nature, if he understands this thoroughly, he will always be worshiped by the King and the subjects. **(44)**

->Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the vernacular commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the Brihat Samhita composed by the teacher Shri Varahamihira. 51.<-

White, red, yellow, and black colored boils, if they are smooth and beautiful, reveal their results in relation to the castes such as the twice-born in order; otherwise, they are fruitless. That is, white boils are fruitful for Brahmins, and red boils are fruitful for Kshatriyas. **(1)** If there is a boil on the head, wealth comes near. If it is on the forehead, it indicates good fortune...

---

<margin>1. Here, the term "twice-born" does not refer to those who are Brahmins by birth alone. It should be understood to refer to those whose four castes (Brahmin, etc.) are determined according to their birth rashi <note>Zodiac sign at birth</note>.</margin>

# The Varahi Samhita

->Page 206<-

...[the presence of marks on the forehead] brings wealth; on the eyebrows, it causes misfortune <note>original: "daurbhagyam"</note> but also the meeting of beloved friends. If they arise between the eyebrows or on the eyelids, they cause grief. If located on the eyes themselves, they grant the sight of desired things. Marks on the temples lead to a life of renunciation <term>Pravrajya: the act of going forth as a wandering ascetic</term>, while those on the areas where tears fall indicate extreme anxiety. || 2 ||

On the nose and cheeks, they bestow clothing and children. On the lips, they bring the gain of food. Below the chin, they similarly grant sustenance. On the forehead, they bring abundant wealth. On the jaws, they likewise bring ornaments, food, and drink. If they appear on the ears, they grant ear-ornaments and even self-knowledge <note>original: "jnanam atmasvarupam"; the realization of one's true nature</note>. || 3 ||

If pustules <term>Pitaka: small boils, spots, or inflammatory marks used in physiognomy for divination</term> appear on the joints of the head, the neck, the heart, the breasts, the flanks, or the chest, they result respectively in: injury by a weapon, a general blow, the birth of a son, grief, and the attainment of a beloved. On the shoulder, they cause frequent wandering for the sake of begging and destruction; however, if they arise in the armpit, they grant much happiness through wealth. || 4 ||

Those born on the back or on both arms bring about the destruction of suffering and of the multitude of one's enemies. Those on the wrist bring self-restraint, and those on the upper arms lead to the acquisition of ornaments and finery. || 5 ||

If a pimple appears on the hand, the fingers, or the belly, it results respectively in the acquisition of wealth, good fortune, and grief. On the navel, it brings excellent food and drink, but below the navel, it indicates the theft of wealth by thieves. In the bladder area, it brings wealth and grain; on the penis, it brings a young woman and a handsome son...

# Chapter 52: Signs of Boils and Marks

<page-num>207</page-num>
<header>With Commentary - Chapter 52</header>

Boils or marks appearing on the anus or the scrotum bestow good sons, wealth, and general good fortune. || 6 || If they appear on both thighs, one gains vehicles <note>original: "yana" - referring to carriages or mounts</note> and a wife. If on both knees, one suffers loss caused by enemies. On the shins, they indicate injury by a weapon, and on the ankles, they bring the distress of travel and confinement. || 7 ||

However, if they appear on the buttocks, the heels, or the feet, they signify the loss of wealth, sexual union with an improper woman <note>original: "agamya-gamana" - forbidden or socially unacceptable relationships</note>, and constant wandering. If they appear on the cluster of toes, they indicate imprisonment, but on the big toe, they signify honor received from one's kinsmen. || 8 ||

A boil appearing on the right side of a man is called an "Utpata-ganda" <note>a sign of sudden occurrence or portent</note>, while one on the left is called an "Abhighata" <note>signifying a blow or injury</note>. For men, marks on the right side are auspicious and bring wealth, whereas for women, the opposite is true <note>meaning the left side is auspicious for women</note>. || 9 ||

Thus, the classification of boils from the head down to the feet has been declared. The effects of scars <note>original: "vrana"</note> and moles <note>original: "tilaka" - small dark spots</note> should be understood in exactly the same way. Furthermore, the presence of "Mashaka" <note>elevated warts or larger moles</note> and "Avarta" <note>hair-whirls or circular skin patterns</note> on the bodies of living beings also produce the results previously described. || 10 ||

->Thus ends the Fifty-Second Chapter, titled "Signs of Boils,"<-
->in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira.<-

---

<note>The following is the Hindi vernacular commentary by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra</note>

If a mark is on the private parts or the scrotum, it ordains wealth and good fortune. || 6 || If on both thighs, one obtains a vehicle and a woman; if on both knees, one must suffer loss from enemies; if on both shins, a wound from a weapon; and if on the ankle, the distress of the road and bondage. || 7 || But if on the buttocks, the heel, or the feet, it results in the destruction of wealth, intercourse with an unfit woman, and the toil of travel. If on the toes, it means bondage, and if on the big toe, one receives honor from people of one's own caste. || 8 ||

A boil on the right side of a man is called "Utpata-ganda," and on the left side, it is called "Abhighata." Such marks on the right side of a man bring prosperity, but for women, the results are reversed. That is, for women, a boil on the right is an "Abhighata" and on the left is an "Utpata-ganda"; thus, the left side is auspicious for women, otherwise, they yield inauspicious results. || 9 ||

This division of boils across all limbs starting from the head has been stated. The results of a scar or a mole (a black-colored spot) should be known in this same manner. And the two types of marks called "Mashaka" <term>Mashaka: a raised wart-like growth</term> or "Avarta" <term>Avarta: a circular pattern or cowlick</term>, if they exist on the bodies of creatures, also give the same results. || 10 ||

Thus ends the Fifty-Second Chapter in the vernacular commentary composed by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the Brihat Samhita composed by the great teacher Sri Varahamihira.

# Now begins the Fifty-Third Chapter
## Architectural Science <note>original: "Vāstu-vidyā"</note>

I now compose this knowledge of architecture, which has descended from the Lotus-Born Creator <note>Lord Brahmā</note> through a lineage of sages, for the pleasure of learned astrologers. ॥ 1 ॥

It is said that once there was a certain being <note>a "bhūta" or spirit</note> who obstructed both heaven and earth with his massive body. The host of gods suddenly seized him and cast him down, pinning him face-first against the ground. ॥ 2 ॥

Whichever deity held down a specific part of his body remained there as the presiding ruler of that spot. Consequently, the Creator ordained that this god-filled being be known as the "Vāstu Puruṣa" <note>the Spirit of the Site or the Architectural Man</note>. ॥ 3 ॥

The finest palace for a King should be one hundred and eight cubits <note>term: "hastam" - a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the length of a forearm</note> in width. There are five types of royal residences, each decreasing in width by eight cubits, while the length is always one and a quarter times the width. ॥ 4 ॥ <note>The five types of royal houses are: 108x135, 100x125, 92x115, 84x105, and 76x95 cubits.</note>

The finest residence for a General <note>original: "Senāpati"</note> is sixty-four cubits in width. There are five types of these as well, each decreasing by six cubits in width. The length is calculated by adding one-sixth of the width to the width itself. For example: the first is 64 cubits wide and 74 cubits 16 fingers long; the second is 58 wide and 67 cubits 16 fingers long; the third is 52 wide and 60 cubits 16 fingers long; the fourth is 46 wide and 53 cubits 16 fingers long; and the fifth is 40 wide and 46 cubits long.

->One cubit consists of 24 fingers <note>original: "angula"</note>, and one finger consists of 8 barley-corns <note>original: "vyangula"</note>.<-

# Chapter 53: Commentary on Architecture (Page 209)

...the length is increased by one-sixth of the width.

### Dimensions for Ministers and Queens
The residences of the Ministers <term>Sachiva; a high-ranking government official or counselor</term> are of five types. The primary house is 60 cubits wide. The subsequent four types are decreased by 4 cubits each—namely 56, 52, 48, and 44 cubits wide. To determine the length, one must add one-eighth of the width to the width itself. 

The specific dimensions are as follows:
*   **First:** 60 cubits wide; 67 cubits and 12 finger-widths long.
*   **Second:** 56 cubits wide; 63 cubits long.
*   **Third:** 52 cubits wide; 58 cubits and 12 finger-widths long.
*   **Fourth:** 48 cubits wide; 54 cubits long.
*   **Fifth:** 44 cubits wide; 49 cubits and 12 finger-widths long.

The residences for the Queens <term>Rajamahishi; the consecrated royal consorts</term> should be half the size of the Ministers' houses in both length and width. 
**Lengths:** 33:18, 31:12, 29:6, 27:0, and 24:18 cubits. 
**Widths:** 30, 28, 26, 24, and 22 cubits respectively.

### Dimensions for the Crown Prince and Royal Siblings
The residences of the Crown Prince <term>Yuvaraja; the heir apparent</term> are also of five types. The best among them is 80 cubits wide. The width of the subsequent houses decreases by 6 cubits each. The length is determined by adding one-third of the width to the width.

*   **First:** 80 cubits wide; 106 cubits and 16 finger-widths long.
*   **Second:** 74 cubits wide; 98 cubits and 16 finger-widths long.
*   **Third:** 68 cubits wide; 90 cubits and 16 finger-widths long.
*   **Fourth:** 62 cubits wide; 82 cubits and 16 finger-widths long.
*   **Fifth:** 56 cubits wide; 74 cubits and 16 finger-widths long.

The houses for the Crown Prince's younger brothers should be half the size of these. 
**Widths:** 40, 37, 34, 31, and 28 cubits. 
**Lengths:** 53:8, 49:8, 45:8, 41:8, and 37:8 cubits.

### Dimensions for Feudatories and Court Officials
The difference between the dimensions of the King's house and the Minister's house defines the scale for the residences of Feudatory Chiefs <term>Samanta; a neighboring or vassal noble</term> and high-ranking royal officers. 
**Widths (in descending order):** 48, 44, 40, 36, and 32 cubits. 
**Lengths:** 67:12, 62:0, 56:12, 51:0, and 45:12 cubits/finger-widths.

The difference between the King's and the Crown Prince's house dimensions determines the scale for the houses of the Chamberlains <term>Kanchuki; an attendant of the inner apartments, often an elderly man or eunuch</term>, courtesans, and performers (dancers and singers). 
**Lengths (in descending order):** 28:8, 26:8, 24:8, 22:8, and 20:8 cubits/finger-widths.

## On the Knowledge of Arts for Courtesans

...for those skilled in the arts of courtesans. || 8 || For all superintendents and authorized officials, the dimensions of their houses should be equal to those of the treasury and the pleasure-house. However, in houses consisting of only a single hall, the length should be double the width. || 11 || The width for the four classes begins at thirty-two and decreases by four.

# The Varahi Samhita
## On the Dimensions of Royal Officers' Dwellings

...from the opening for royal officers. || 14 || Now, for the *Parasava* <note>A person born of a Brahmin father and a Shudra mother</note> and the *Ambastha* <note>A person born of a Brahmin father and a Vaishya mother</note> and other mixed castes, the house should be built according to the average of the measurements prescribed for their parent castes. That is, one should add the length and breadth of the houses of the two source castes and divide by two to determine the dimensions for their five-room complex. For all classes, a building site that is smaller or larger than their prescribed measure is considered inauspicious. || 15 ||

For animal sheds, the dwellings of ascetics, granaries, armories, fire-houses <note>kitchens or ritual fire rooms</note>, and pleasure houses (sitting rooms), the dimensions may be made according to one's desire. However, the authors of the Shastras <note>sacred technical treatises</note> do not desire any building to exceed a height of one hundred cubits <term>Hasta: a unit of measurement roughly equal to 18 inches or the length of a forearm</term>. || 16 ||

For the houses of the Commander-in-Chief and the King, add seventy to the sum of their two breadths and divide the result by two. Place this figure in two locations: dividing by fourteen at the first location gives the measure of the *Shala* <note>the inner room or hall</note>. Dividing the figure at the second location by fifteen gives the measure of the *Alinda* <note>the veranda or latticed gallery outside the room walls</note>. This applies to the King. To find the measures for other classes, one should take the sum of the breadths of the King's and Commander's houses, subtract the breadth specific to the subject's own rank, add seventy, and then divide by fourteen and fifteen respectively to find the *Shala* and *Alinda*. || 17 ||

In the previous four verses, where the breadth of the houses for the four castes (starting with Brahmins) was stated to be thirty-two cubits, the *Shala* should be constructed according to the following decreasing scale:
*   4 cubits and 17 digits <term>Angula: a finger's breadth, 24 of which make a Hasta</term>
*   4 cubits and 3 digits
*   3 cubits and 15 digits
*   3 cubits and 13 digits
*   3 cubits and 4 digits

The *Alinda* (veranda) measurements for these houses, in the same descending order, are:
*   3 cubits and 19 digits
*   3 cubits and 8 digits
*   2 cubits and 20 digits...

...ten and three. || 19 || A gallery <term>vithika: an external porch or walkway</term> should be constructed outside the main building, equal to one-third of the hall's <term>shala: the main room or wing</term> measurement. If this gallery is situated at the front <note>the eastern side</note>, the building is named **Soshnisha** <note>literally "wearing a turban"</note>. || 20 || If it is at the back <note>the western side</note>, it is called **Sayashraya** <note>meaning "with shelter"</note>. If it is situated on the sides <note>north or south</note>, it is called **Savashtambha** <note>meaning "with support"</note>. If the gallery surrounds the building on all sides, it is called **Susthita** <note>meaning "well-established"</note>. All of these are praised by those learned in the scriptures <note>the Shastras</note> as being highly auspicious. || 21 ||

The height of the house should be determined by taking one-sixteenth of its width and adding four cubits <term>hasta: a traditional unit of length, roughly 18 inches</term>. For each subsequent floor or house type, the height is reduced by one-twelfth of the total. || 22 || The thickness of the wall for all houses built of baked bricks should be one-sixteenth of the width. However, for houses made of timber, the thickness may vary according to choice. || 23 || For the palaces of kings and commanders, the width of the main entrance is calculated by adding seventy to the house width and dividing by eleven. The height of the door in cubits should be equal to the number of finger-breadths <term>angula: a unit of measure, about 3/4 inch</term> found in the width. The width of the door-post <term>vishkambha</term> is half of the door's width. || 24 || For the homes of Brahmins and other classes, the door measurement is found by taking one-fiftieth of the house width and adding eighteen finger-breadths. One-eighth of the door's height shall be the width of the door-post...

---

...will be of the measure of two cubits and eighteen finger-breadths, or two cubits and three finger-breadths. || 18 || 19 ||

The space outside the building, measuring one-third of the previously mentioned hall-measure, is called a **Vithika** <gloss>gallery</gloss>. If this gallery is in the eastern part of the building, the name of said building is "**Soshnisha**." If the gallery is on the western side of the building, it is called a "**Sayashraya**" building. If the gallery is in the north or south direction, it is called a "**Savashtambha**" building. And if such a gallery exists on all four sides of the building, it is called "**Susthita**." The authors of the scriptures always worship <note>highly recommend</note> all these types of buildings; that is, such architecture is extremely auspicious. || 20 || 21 ||

Whatever the width of that house may be, adding four cubits to its sixteenth part will give the height of that house in cubits. The height of the other four types of houses will be progressively less by one-twelfth part. || 22 || One-sixteenth of the width of all houses is the measure of the wall. This measurement applies to houses made of **baked bricks** <gloss>pakkishtaka</gloss>, but for houses made of wood, the wall thickness should be made according to one's preference. || 23 || For the width of the houses of a **King** <gloss>nripaveshma</gloss> and a General, add seventy and divide by 11; the result is the width of the main door in cubits. However many finger-breadths the width is, the height will be that many cubits. Half of the door's width is considered the **door-post width** <gloss>vishkambha</gloss>. || 24 || For men of other castes such as Brahmins, adding eighteen finger-breadths to one-fiftieth of the house width will be the measure of that house's door. One-eighth of the door measure is the door-post width...

# The Vārāhī Saṃhitā
->Page 214<-

The height of a door should be double its width <note>original: *viṣkambha*</note>. || 25 || The thickness of the doorframe should be as many finger-breadths <note>term: *angula* (a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the width of a finger)</note> as the height of the door is in cubits <note>term: *hasta* (a cubit, approximately 18 inches)</note>. This thickness applies to the two side-posts; however, the two horizontal sills <note>original: *udumbara*</note> should be one and a half times that thickness. || 26 ||

The width of these pillars at the base is determined by multiplying the height by seven and dividing by eighty. For the top of the pillar, multiply the height by nine, divide by eighty, and then subtract one-tenth of that value from the result. || 27 ||

A square pillar is called **Rucaka**.
An eight-sided pillar is called **Vajra**.
A sixteen-sided pillar is called **Dvivajra** <note>literally "Double-Vajra"</note>.
A thirty-two-sided pillar is called **Pralīnaka**.
A circular pillar is called **Vṛtta**.
These five types of pillars are considered auspicious. || 28 ||

Divide the pillar into nine parts to define its ornaments: one part for the base <note>original: *vahana*</note>, another part for the pot-capital <note>original: *ghaṭa*</note>, followed by the lotus-motif <note>original: *padma*</note>, and the upper lip or coping <note>original: *uttaroṣṭha*</note>, each occupying one part. || 29 ||

The thickness of the main load-bearing beams <note>original: *bhāratula*</note> placed above should be equal to the thickness of the pillar. The secondary beams <note>original: *tulā*</note> and minor beams <note>original: *upatulā*</note> should each be reduced in size by one-quarter successively. || 30 ||

A building that has an unobstructed gallery <note>original: *alinda*</note> on all sides is known as **Sarvatobhadra** <note>literally "auspicious on all sides"</note>. Such a structure, featuring four doors, should be constructed for kings or for assemblies of the learned. || 31 ||

A building where the galleries follow the sequence of the hall walls in a circumambulatory fashion <note>clockwise</note> is called **Nandyāvarta**...

The layout known as **Nandyavarta** <note>literally "joyful turning," a complex symmetrical pattern</note> is described as follows: there should be no door in the West, while the remaining directions may have doors. || 32 ||

In a layout where the galleries (*alindas*) <note>term: alinda - a veranda or gallery space surrounding the central courtyard</note> extend to the end in a circumambulatory <note>clockwise</note> direction, it is considered auspicious. This layout is named **Vardhamana** <note>meaning "prospering"</note>. In this design, a Southern door should not be constructed. || 33 ||

When there is one gallery in the West and two in the East extending to the ends, with the other two sides raised and the remaining boundaries open, it is called the **Svastika** layout. In this design, an Eastern door is inauspicious. || 34 ||

When the two galleries of the East and West terminate, and the remaining two extend to meet those boundaries, it is called the **Ruchaka** house. In this design, a Northern door is not auspicious, while all other doors are beneficial. || 35 ||

The **Nandyavarta** and **Vardhamana** layouts are the best and most auspicious for everyone. The **Svastika** and **Ruchaka** are of middling quality. The remaining layouts are auspicious specifically for kings and royalty. || 36 ||

A house lacking a hall (*shala*) <note>term: shala - a room or wing of a house</note> on the North side is called **Hiranyanabha** <note>Golden-naved</note>. A three-winged house is called **Dhanya** <note>Fortunate</note>. If it lacks a hall in the East, it is called **Sukhetra** <note>Good Field</note>; this layout brings growth and prosperity. || 37 ||

A three-winged house lacking a Southern hall is called **Chulli**; this brings about the loss of wealth. A layout lacking a Western hall is called **Pakshaghna** <note>Side-destroying</note>; this leads to the loss of sons and creates enmity. || 38 ||

A layout with halls only in the West and South is called **Siddhartha**. With halls in the West and North, it is called **Yamasurya**. If the halls are in the North and East, it is called **Danda** <note>The Staff</note>, and if in the East and South, it is called... <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing to "Vatarukhya" on the next page</note> || 39 ||

Regarding the eight deities on the **Eastern** side, from Agni to Antariksha, the results of placing a door are, in order: fear of fire, the birth of only daughters, great wealth, the favor of the king <note>original: "Narendra-vallabhyam"</note>, a tendency toward anger, speaking falsehoods, cruelty, and theft. || 72 ||

Regarding the eight deities on the **Southern** side, from Pavana to Mriga, the results of a door are, in order: few sons, servitude, meanness, an abundance of food, drink, and sons, fierceness, ingratitude, poverty, and the destruction of the strength of one's sons. || 73 ||

Regarding the eight deities on the **Western** side, from Pitri to Papa, the results of placing a door are, in order: suffering for sons, increase of enemies, lack of wealth and sons, attainment of sons, wealth, and strength, prosperity of wealth, fear of the king, loss of wealth, and disease. || 74 ||

Regarding the eight deities on the **Northern** side, from Yakshma to Diti, the results of placing a door are: death, imprisonment, increase of enemies, gain of sons and wealth, possession of all good qualities, and the gain of sons and wealth...

Dig a pit in the center of the house site, one cubit wide and one cubit deep. Then, fill the pit again with the same earth that was removed. If the earth is insufficient to fill the hole, it is inauspicious. If it fills it exactly, it is neutral. If the earth overflows after the pit is full, the site is auspicious in every way. || 92 ||

Alternatively, fill the pit with water. Walk one hundred paces away and return; if the water level has not decreased in that time, the land is excellent. Another test involves the weight of the soil: fill an <term>Adhaka</term><note>A traditional measure of volume, roughly equivalent to 3 kilograms or 4 seers</note> with the local dust and weigh it. Place a four-wicked lamp in an unbaked clay pot and set it inside the pit. Assign the four wicks to the four classes—Brahmin and the others—starting from the North. Light the lamp; the direction in which the wick burns most brightly indicates that the land is most favorable for that specific class. || 94 ||

If the ground is elevated in the East or North, it leads to the loss of wealth and sons. 1. **East:** Loss of sons.
2. **South-East:** Fear of fire.
3. **South:** Fear of enemies.
4. **South-West:** Quarrels among women.
5. **West:** Immorality in women.
6. **North-West:** Poverty.
7. **North:** Increase in wealth.
8. **North-East:** Increase in sons. **(119)**

For the purpose of building a house, one should avoid cutting down trees that: house bird nests, are broken, withered, or burnt; trees located in temples or cremation grounds; or trees that exude milky sap. # Now Begins the Fifty-Fourth Chapter

## Water Divination
<note>original: "Dakargalam" — a technical term for the science of locating underground water sources.</note>

I shall now describe the science of water divination, which brings both spiritual merit and fame, and by which the presence of water is discovered. Just as there are veins <term>shiras: channels or veins within the body or the earth</term> in the bodies of men, so too are there veins situated within the earth, some higher and some lower. **(1)**

The water falling from the sky originally possesses only one color and one taste, but it acquires various tastes and colors due to the specific qualities of the soil. Therefore, one should examine the water as being identical in quality to the earth in which it resides. **(2)**

Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirriti, Varuna, Vayu, Soma, and Ishana are to be known, in that order, as the lords of the eight directions starting from the East. **(3)**

The veins are known by the names of these directional lords <note>e.g., the Aindri vein in the East, the Agneyi in the Southeast, etc.</note>. There is a ninth vein in the center known as the "Great Vein" <insert>Mahashira</insert>. From these, hundreds of other veins have branched out, famous by their own names. **(4)**

The vein that rises upward from the netherworld <note>Patala</note> is auspicious, as are those situated in the four cardinal directions (East, South, West, and North). Those originating in the intermediate corners <note>Southeast, Southwest, Northwest, and Northeast</note> are not auspicious. I shall now describe the signs for identifying these veins. **(5)**

If a Cane tree <note>original: "Vetasa"; often identified as Calamus rotang or a type of willow</note> is found in a waterless region, then at a distance of three cubits <term>hasta: a measurement from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, roughly 18 inches</term> to the west of it, water will be found at a depth of one and a half "man-lengths." There, a western vein flows. **(6)**
<margin>A "man-length" <term>purusha</term> is defined as the height of a man with his arms raised; it is equal to 120 digits <term>angula</term>.</margin>

There, this sign—

# The Varahisamhita

### Chapter on the Exploration of Water Veins

At the depth of one *purusha* <note>A 'purusha' is a unit of measurement equivalent to the height of a man with his arms upraised, roughly 6 to 7 feet.</note>, a pale frog appears, followed by yellow earth. Then, a layer of split rock is found, beneath which lies the water. || 7 ||

If a Rose Apple tree <note>original: "Jambu"</note> is found in a waterless region, there is a water vein to the north of it at a distance of three *hastas* <note>A 'hasta' or cubit is approximately 18 inches.</note>, at a depth of two *purushas*. The soil there smells like iron and is pale in color; at a depth of one *purusha*, a frog will be encountered. || 8 ||

If an anthill <note>original: "Valmika"</note> is situated to the east of a Rose Apple tree, sweet water exists three cubits to the south of that tree at a depth of two *purushas*. || 9 ||

At a depth of half a *purusha*, a fish is found, along with a stone colored like a pigeon. The soil here is blue, and the water is abundant and lasts for a long time. <note>The commentator notes that where a specific distance in cubits is not mentioned, the previously mentioned distance of three cubits should be assumed.</note> || 10 ||

If a Cluster Fig tree <note>original: "Udumbara"</note> is seen in a waterless tract, a water vein exists three cubits to the west at a depth of two and a half *purushas*. At one *purusha* deep, a white snake is found, followed by a stone as black as eye-salve <note>original: "Anjana"</note>; beneath this lies a vein of excellent water. || 11 ||

If an anthill is visible to the north of an Arjuna tree, water will be found three cubits to the west of that tree at a depth of three and a half *purushas*. || 12 ||

At a depth of half a *purusha*, a white lizard <note>original: "Godha"; likely a monitor lizard</note> appears. At one *purusha*, the soil is grey, then black, then yellow, and finally white soil mixed with sand is found, beneath which an inexhaustible supply of water should be predicted. || 13 ||

# Chapter 54: With Language Commentary

In a region where signs of marshy land are visible: where **Viraṇa** <note>Fragrant grass; Vetiver</note> and **Durva** <note>Cynodon dactylon; a sacred medicinal grass</note> are found to be very soft, there is water at a depth of one **Purusha** <note>A "man's height," a traditional unit of measure approximately 6 feet</note>. ॥ 47 ॥

Where the **Viraṇa** (Gandar) and **Durva** are extremely tender, water is found one man's height below. ॥ 47 ॥

Where the **Bhargi**, **Vivruta** <note>Nisoth</note>, **Danti** <note>Dantyuni</note>, **Shukarpadi**, **Lakshmana**, and **Navamalika** <note>Maltis</note> herbs are found, water is located two cubits to the south at a depth of three men's heights. ॥ 48 ॥

Where these herbs—**Bharangi**, **Nisoth**, **Danti**, **Sukarpadi**, **Lakshmana**, and **Malati**—exist, water is found two cubits to the south of them, three men's heights deep. ॥ 48 ॥

Trees that are glossy, possess long hanging branches, or are stunted shrubs indicate that water is nearby. Conversely, trees that are hollow, have withered leaves, or appear parched are devoid of water. ॥ 49 ॥

Where there are small, spreading trees with glossy, long branches, water is close by. Where there are trees with holes, withered leaves, and a dry appearance, there is no water. ॥ 49 ॥

Where the **Tilaka**, **Amrataka** <note>Hog plum</note>, **Varunaka**, **Bhallataka** <note>Marking nut</note>, **Bilva** <note>Bael fruit</note>, **Tinduka** <note>Persimmon</note>, **Ashoka**, **Pindara**, **Shirisha**, **Anjana**, **Parushaka**, **Vanjula**, and **Atibala** trees are found... ॥ 50 ॥

Where **Tilak**, **Ambada**, **Varun**, **Bhilawa**, **Bel**, **Tendu**, **Ankol**, **Pindar**, **Siras**, **Anjan**, **Phalsa**, **Ashok**, and **Atibala**... ॥ 50 ॥

...If these trees are very glossy and surrounded by **ant-hills** <note>original: "valmika"</note>, then water is found three cubits to the north at a depth of four and a half men's heights. ॥ 51 ॥

If these trees are extremely glossy and surrounded by ant-hills, then water is found three cubits to the north of these trees at a depth of four and a half men's heights. ॥ 51 ॥

Where the ground is generally grassless but a specific spot is covered in grass, or where the ground is grassy but a specific spot is bare, a **water-vein** <note>original: "shira"</note> is indicated there; or it should be said that wealth is buried there. ॥ 52 ॥

In land where there is no grass anywhere but one spot appears grassy, or if the whole land has grass but one spot is grassless, then in that spot, four and a half men's heights down, there is a water-vein or buried treasure; this should be stated. ॥ 52 ॥

Where there is an anomaly between thorny and thornless trees <note>e.g., a single thornless tree among thorny ones, or vice versa</note>, water is found three cubits to the west. After digging three and one-third men's heights, water or wealth will be found. ॥ 53 ॥

Where among thorny trees there is one tree without thorns, or among thornless trees there is one tree with thorns, then three cubits west of that tree, by digging three and a third men's heights, water or wealth emerges. ॥ 53 ॥

Where the earth gives off a deep sound when struck by the foot, there is water at a depth of three and a half men's heights, and a **northern water-vein** <note>original: "kauberi shira"</note> exists there. ॥ 54 ॥

Where a deep sound is produced in the earth by the striking of a foot, water is found three and a half men's heights below, and a northern vein emerges there. ॥ 54 ॥

# The Varāhī Saṃhitā
## Chapter on the Exploration of Water

One should know that water exists at a depth of three <term>puruṣas</term><note>A 'puruṣa' or 'man-length' is a traditional unit of measurement, roughly equivalent to the height of a man with his arms raised, approximately 6 to 7 feet.</note> beneath the branches of such a tree. || 55 ||

If a tree shows abnormalities in its fruits or flowers <note>original: "phala-kusuma-vikāro"</note>, a water-vein <note>original: "śirā"</note> exists three cubits to its east at a depth of four men. Below this, there is rock and the earth is yellow. || 56 ||

If a <term>kaṇṭakārikā</term> <note>Yellow-berried nightshade (Solanum xanthocarpum)</note> is seen without thorns and bearing white flowers, water should be declared to be beneath it at a depth of three and a half men. || 57 ||

Where a date-palm <note>original: "kharjūrī"</note> with two heads is found in a waterless region, one should point out water to its west at a depth of three men. || 58 ||

If there is a <term>karṇikāra</term> tree <note>Pterospermum acerifolium</note> or a <term>palāśa</term> tree <note>Butea monosperma, often called 'Flame of the Forest'</note> with white flowers, water exists two cubits to its left <note>the south</note> at a depth of three men. || 59 ||

In whatever ground heat or steam <note>original: "ūṣmā"</note> or smoke rises, there is water at a depth of two men. One should point out a vein there with a great flow of water. || 60 ||

In a field where the crops are destroyed after sprouting, or appear excessively glossy, or very pale, there is a great water-vein at a depth of two men. || 61 ||

I shall hereafter describe how water-veins occur in the <term>Maru</term> <note>The desert region, specifically referring to Marwar in Rajasthan</note> desert. The veins there run deep within the earth like the necks of camels. || 62 ||

If there is an anthill <note>original: "valmīka"</note> to the northeast of a <term>pīlu</term> tree <note>Salvadora persica, or the Toothbrush tree</note>, water is found to the west. A vein flowing toward the north should be known to exist at a depth of five men. || 63 ||

The first sign found there while digging is a frog; thereafter the earth becomes reddish-brown, and then green. At the depth of one man—

# Chapter 54 | Page 237
## Commentary on Water Divination

If a stone is found, water should be indicated beneath it. || 64 ||

If an ant-hill <term>Valmika: a mound of earth created by ants or termites, often used as a bio-indicator</term> is found to the east of a **Pilu** tree <note>Salvadora persica, commonly known as the Toothbrush tree</note>, then water is located four and a half cubits <term>Hasta: a traditional unit of length, approximately 18 inches or the length of a forearm</term> to the south of that tree, at a depth of seven men <term>Purusha: a unit of depth based on the height of a man with up toraised arms, roughly 6-7 feet</term>. || 65 ||

At the depth of the first man, a black-and-white snake, one cubit in length, will be found. Below this, a southern vein <term>Shira: an underground stream or "vein" of water</term> flows, providing abundant but brackish water. || 66 ||

If an ant-hill is situated to the north of a **Karira** tree <note>Capparis decidua, a leafless shrub found in arid regions</note>, water is found ten men deep, four and a half cubits to the south of the tree. This water is sweet. At the depth of one man, a yellow frog will be encountered. || 67 ||

If an ant-hill is found to the west of a **Rohitaka** tree <note>Tecomella undulata, often called the Desert Teak or Ruhida</note>, one should dig twelve men deep at a distance of three cubits to the south. A western vein of brackish water will be found there. || 68 ||

If an ant-hill is visible to the east of an **Arjuna** tree <note>Terminalia arjuna; the text uses 'Indrataru' or 'Arjuna'</note>, the water vein is one cubit to the west at a depth of fourteen men. At the depth of the first man, a brownish-red monitor lizard <insert>Goh</insert> appears. || 69 ||

If an ant-hill is located to the left of a **Suvarnanama** tree <note>literally "the tree with the golden name," likely referring to the Dhatura or the Amaltas</note>, water is found fifteen men deep at a distance of two cubits to the south. || 70 ||

The water here is brackish. At a depth of half a man, a mongoose and a copper-colored stone are found, along with red earth. A southern vein flows there. || 71 ||

If a **Badari** <note>Jujube</note> and a **Rohitaka** tree are found growing together, even without an ant-hill, water is found sixteen men deep at a distance of three cubits to the west. || 72 ||

Initially, the water is very pleasant to the taste. A southern vein flows here, followed by another vein from the north.

->**The Three Types of Land**<-

A land with abundant water is called <term>Anupa</term><note>marshy or riparian land</note>. A land lacking water is called <term>Marusthala</term><note>desert</note>. If these same signs are found in <term>Jangala</term> <gloss>temperate</gloss> land, water is at five man-lengths. In the <term>Maru</term> <gloss>desert</gloss> region, one should declare the depth to be seven man-lengths. || 89 ||

# The Varāhī Saṃhitā
-> <note>original: "वाराहीसंहिता" - also known as the Bṛhat Saṃhitā by Varāhamihira, an encyclopedic work on divination and natural science.</note> <-

Where the earth is of a uniform color and devoid of grass, trees, anthills, or shrubs, but shows a specific abnormality <note>a "vikāra" or change in texture/appearance</note> in the soil, water is found there at a depth of five <term>Purusha</term> <note>A "Purusha" is a unit of measure based on the height of a man with arms raised, roughly 120 digits or 6-7 feet.</note>. **[90]**

Where the ground is moist, low-lying, sandy, or produces a resonant sound when stepped upon, water is found at a depth of four and a half or five <term>Purusha</term>. **[91]**

South of a cluster of glossy, lush trees, there is abundant water at a depth of four <term>Purusha</term>. Even in a dense forest, if one tree appears "deformed" <note>showing unusual fruit, flowers, or growth patterns compared to its neighbors</note>, one should predict water south of that tree at the same depth. **[92]**

In either a <term>Jāngala</term> <note>arid or desert-like region</note> or an <term>Anūpa</term> <note>marshy or humid region</note> land, if the earth sinks underfoot, water is at a depth of one and a half <term>Purusha</term>. Likewise, where many insects are seen without a visible nest or hole, water is also found there. **[93]**

Where the ground is generally hot but cold in one spot, or generally cold but hot in one spot, water exists at three and a half <term>Purusha</term>. If a rainbow-like shimmer, a fish-shaped mark, or an anthill is seen in such lands, water is just four cubits <note>approx. 6 feet</note> away. **[94]**

In a row of anthills, if one is significantly taller than the others, a water-vein <note>original: "शिरा" (shira) - an underground stream</note> lies beneath it. Also, where crops wither after sprouting or fail to grow at all, water is found at a depth of four cubits. **[95]**

Where the Banyan, Pipal, and Gular <note>original: "न्यग्रोधपलाशोदुम्बरै" - Ficus benghalensis, Ficus religiosa, and Ficus racemosa</note> trees grow together...

...if these signs are seen, then instead of three <term>Purusha</term>, one should say the water is five <term>Purusha</term> deep. If these same signs are observed in a desert region, one should state the water is seven <term>Purusha</term> deep. **[89]**

In land of a single color where there is no grass, trees, anthills, or shrubs, if that land appears "transformed" (meaning it looks different from the surrounding area), water is five <term>Purusha</term> deep. <gloss>A "Gulma" refers to a cluster of many branches arising from a single root in the ground.</gloss> **[90]**

Where the ground is moist, low-lying, sandy, or where a sound is produced by placing one's foot, water is four and a half or five <term>Purusha</term> deep. **[91]**

Where there are many glossy trees, one should say there is much water four <term>Purusha</term> to the south of those trees. If among many trees, one tree is "deformed"—meaning its fruits and flowers are of a different kind—then water is found four <term>Purusha</term> to the south of that tree. **[92]**

In a <term>Jāngala</term> or <term>Anūpa</term> country where the ground sinks when stepped upon, water is one and a half <term>Purusha</term> deep. Where many insects are seen and there is no visible hole for them to live in, water is also one and a half <term>Purusha</term> deep. **[93]**

Where the whole ground is hot but one spot is cold, or where the whole ground is cold but one spot is hot, water stays at three and a half <term>Purusha</term>. Where a rainbow, a fish-shape, or an anthill is seen in <term>Jāngala</term> or <term>Anūpa</term> lands, water is four cubits deep. **[94]**

Where there is a row of many anthills in <term>Jāngala</term> or <term>Anūpa</term> lands and one anthill is the tallest, a water-vein emerges by digging four cubits beneath that tall anthill. Also, where a crop withers after growing or does not grow at all, water is four cubits deep. **[95]**
