# Chapter 54: The Science of Underground Water (Page 241)

In the northwest, the same should be said, and the water-vein <note>original: "shira" - a subterranean stream or channel</note> flows toward the north. || 96 || If a well is situated in the southeast corner of a village or a city, it constantly causes fear and frequently brings about fires that consume even human beings. || 97 || If a well is in the southwest corner, it leads to the loss of children; if in the northwest, it causes danger to women. Leaving aside these three directions, wells in the remaining five directions are auspicious. || 98 || Having observed the "Science of Water Divining" <term>Dakargala: the ancient Indian science of detecting underground water through environmental signs</term> composed by the Sage Sarasvata, I have composed this in *Arya* meters. Now, I shall also describe the system of Manu in various other meters. || 99 ||

Where trees, shrubs, and creepers are glossy and have leaves without holes, a water-vein exists there. Also, where there are land-lilies, puncture-vine, fragrant grass, *kula*, *gundra* (reeds), *kasha* or *kusha* grass, or the *nalika* and *nala* reeds. || 100 ||

Where there are date palms, rose-apple, *Arjuna*, or cane trees; or where trees, shrubs, and creepers are full of milky sap; or where there are *Chatra*, *Hastikarni*, *Nagakesar*, lotus, *Kadamba*, *Naktamala*, and *Sindhuvara* trees. || 101 ||

# Varahi Samhita
->Page 246<-

One should first sow sesame seeds in the ground; when they have flowered, they should be crushed into the soil. This is the primary task to be performed on the earth. <note>This refers to green manuring, a practice where crops are grown and plowed back into the soil to increase fertility.</note> **|| 2 ||**

The Soapberry <note>original: "Arishta" or Neem</note>, Ashoka, Punnaaga, Shirisha, and Priyangu are considered auspicious. These should be planted first in gardens or around houses. **|| 3 ||**

Jackfruit, Ashoka, Banana, Rose-apple, Lakucha <note>a species of breadfruit</note>, Pomegranate, Grape, Palivata, Citron, and Atimuktaka <note>a flowering creeper</note>— **|| 4 ||**

These trees are to be propagated by cuttings <term>Kandaroppya: plants grown from stem cuttings rather than seeds</term>. They should be carefully smeared with cow dung and then planted, either by cutting at the root or by grafting onto a branch. **|| 5 ||**

Trees that have not yet developed branches should be transplanted during the cool season <note>Shishira: approx. Jan-March</note>. Those with branches should be moved in the winter <note>Hemanta: approx. Nov-Jan</note>, and those with well-developed trunks should be transplanted during the rainy season, ensuring they maintain their original orientation toward the cardinal directions. **|| 6 ||**

By using a mixture of ghee <note>clarified butter</note>, Vetiver, sesame, honey, Vidanga <note>a medicinal fruit used here as a pesticide</note>, milk, and cow dung, one should smear the tree from the root to the branches before transplanting. **|| 7 ||**

After becoming pure and performing a ritual worship of the tree with baths and ointments, one should plant it. When planted thus, the tree thrives with its original leaves <note>meaning it does not suffer from transplant shock or lose its foliage</note>. **|| 8 ||**

Planted trees should be watered both morning and evening at the end of the hot season; during the cold season, they should be watered every other day; and during the rainy season, they should be watered only when the ground is dry. **|| 9 ||**

Rose-apple, Cane, Vanira, Kadamba, Udumbara <note>Cluster Fig</note>, Arjuna, Citron, Grape, Lakucha, Pomegranate, **|| 10 ||**

The best spacing between trees is sixteen cubits <note>original: "shodashantaram"; a cubit or 'hasta' is approximately 18 inches</note>; a distance of twelve cubits is considered middling, and a distance of ten cubits is the minimum required. || 12 ||

Trees that are planted too close together, touching one another, or whose roots become entangled, become "oppressed." Because of this crowding, they do not yield fruit properly. || 13 ||

Diseases in trees are caused by excessive cold, wind, or heat. The symptoms include yellowing of the leaves <note>original: "pandupatrata"</note>, failure of new shoots to grow, the drying up of branches, and the oozing of sap. || 14 ||

**The Treatment of Trees**
To treat these, first clean the affected parts with a blade <note>the text suggests pruning away rot or dead wood</note>. Then apply a paste made of *Vidanga* <term>Vidanga: Embelia ribes, a medicinal plant used as an antimicrobial</term>, clarified butter <note>ghee</note>, and silt. After this, water the tree with a mixture of milk and water. || 15 ||

If the fruit fails to grow, one should boil horse-gram, black gram, mung beans, sesame, and barley in milk. Once the decoction has cooled, water the tree with it to increase the growth of flowers and fruits. || 16 ||

Take two *adhakas* <note>an ancient measure of volume, roughly 3 kg</note> of powdered sheep and goat dung, one *adhaka* of sesame seeds, one *prastha* <note>approx. 750g</note> of meal, one *drona* <note>approx. 12kg</note> of water, and one *tula* <note>approx. 4kg</note> of beef. || 17 ||

Mix these together and let them sit for seven nights. This liquid should then be used to water trees, creepers, shrubs, and climbing plants to ensure they always produce flowers and fruit. || 18 ||

**Seed Preparation**
For ten days, soak the seeds in milk, handling them only with hands smeared with clarified butter. Then, rub the seeds repeatedly with cow dung and fumigate them with the smoke of hog and deer meat. || 19 ||

Then, mix the seeds with the fat of fish and hogs and plant them in prepared soil. Water them with a mixture of milk and water...

## Chapter on Agriculture and Botany

->( Page 248 )<-

If one plants a seed treated with fat in soil that has been purified by first sowing sesame, and waters it with a mixture of milk and water, the tree that grows from it will emerge already laden with flowers. <note>This refers to a botanical marvel where the plant skips the juvenile phase, a common theme in ancient Sanskrit "wonder-working" texts.</note> **|| 20 ||**

Even the tamarind <term>Tintiḍī; Tamarindus indica</term>, which has an extremely hard seed, can be made to produce a creeper. One should treat the seed with a powder made of rice, black gram, and sesame, along with flour and putrid meat. If it is constantly fumigated with turmeric smoke, new sprouts will emerge from that seed without a doubt. **|| 21 ||**

To transform the Wood Apple <term>Kapittha; Limonia acidissima</term> into a climbing creeper, one should take the roots of these eight plants: *Āsphoṭā* <note>Jasmine or Butterfly Pea</note>, *Dhātrī* <note>Indian Gooseberry</note>, *Dhava* <note>Axlewood</note>, *Vāsikā* <note>Malabar Nut</note>, *Palāśī* <note>Flame of the Forest</note>, *Vetasa* <note>Cane-reed</note>, *Sūryavallī* <note>Sun-plant</note>, and *Śyāmā* <note>Indian Sarsaparilla</note>, along with *Atimuktaka*. **|| 22 ||**

Boil these roots in milk and let it cool. Soak the Wood Apple seeds in this milk for a duration of "one hundred claps." <note>original: "nālaśataṃ"; a traditional measure of time</note> Remove them and dry them in the sun. Repeat this process daily for one entire month before planting. **|| 23 ||**

Dig a pit one cubit <note>approx. 18 inches</note> long and wide, and two cubits deep. Fill it with the milk-water mixture mentioned previously. Once the liquid has dried, scorch the pit with fire and then plaster the inside with a mixture of honey, clarified butter <term>Ghee</term>, and ashes. **|| 24 ||**

Fill the pit with soil mixed with the powders of black gram, sesame, and barley. Pour in water mixed with fish flesh and pound the earth until it becomes dense and firm. **|| 25 ||**

Plant the treated seed four fingers deep and water it with fish-water and meat-broth. A creeper with beautiful sprouts will quickly grow, covering the trellis and amazing all who see it. **|| 26 ||**

# Chapter Fifty-Six

## Characteristics of Temples

Having first ensured an abundance of water and having laid out beautiful gardens, one should then construct a temple for the gods to increase one's fame and religious merit. <note>Verse 1</note>

Those who desire to attain the heavenly worlds reached through "Ishta" <note>sacrificial rites and rituals</note> and "Purta" <note>charitable acts like building wells or tanks</note> should build a home for the gods; for in such an act, both types of merit are seen to be fulfilled. <note>Verse 2</note>

Whether in places crafted by human hands or in those formed naturally, the gods draw near to and reside in locations blessed with water and groves. <note>Verse 3</note>

The gods always delight in those lakes where the sun's rays are warded off by the umbrellas of lotus leaves, and where the clear waters are stirred into ripples by white lilies brushed by the shoulders of swimming swans. <note>Verse 4</note>

They dwell where the calls of swans, ducks, cranes, and ruddy geese resound, and where aquatic creatures rest in the cool shadows of the *Nichula* <note>the Indian Willow or Barringtonia acutangula</note> trees along the banks. <note>Verse 5</note>

The gods reside near rivers where the cranes form a tinkling waistband, the soft song of the swans is the music, the water is the silken garment, and the glistening fish are the jeweled belt. <note>Verse 6</note>

Where the flowering trees on the banks are the hair-ornaments, the confluence of waters is the broad hips, the sandy banks are the high breasts, and the laughter is the cry of the geese—near such downward-flowing rivers, the gods remain. <note>Verse 7</note>

In the lands near forests, rivers, mountains, and waterfalls...

<summary>This passage describes the spiritual merit gained from temple building and emphasizes that deities prefer to reside in beautiful, natural settings near water and lush vegetation. It uses highly poetic imagery to compare the features of a river to the adornments of a woman.</summary>

# Chapter 56: With Commentary

->...in the lands near the water. The gods always take delight in these places, as well as in cities equipped with beautiful groves.<- || 8 ||

The types of soil that were previously described in the section on <term>Vastu Vidya</term><note>The traditional Indian science of architecture and placement</note> as being suitable for the four castes—starting with the Brahmins—are the very same soils recommended for those castes when constructing temples for the gods. || 9 ||

A temple for a deity should always be constructed using a grid of sixty-four squares <note>original: "chatus-shashti-pada"</note>. It is highly recommended that the main entrance be placed exactly in the middle of the side, aligned perfectly with the cardinal direction. || 10 ||

Whatever the width of the temple may be, its height should be exactly double that measure. The "waist" <note>original: "kati"; the portion of the temple structure rising above the foundation platform</note> of the temple is said to be equal to one-third of the total height. || 11 ||

The inner sanctum <note>original: "garbha" or womb-chamber</note> should be half the size of the total width; the remaining width is used for the thickness of the walls surrounding it. The width of the door should be one-fourth of the width of the sanctum, and the height of the door should be twice its own width. || 12 ||

The width of the doorposts <note>original: "shakha"</note> and the threshold/lintel <note>original: "udumbara"</note> should be one-fourth of the door's height. The thickness of these doorposts is prescribed to be one-fourth of their own width. || 13 ||

The entrance is considered most auspicious if it is composed of three, five, seven, or nine parallel decorative doorpost sections. At the bottom fourth of the doorposts, one should place the figures of two door-keepers <note>original: "pratiharas"</note>. || 14 ||

The remaining three-fourths of the doorposts should be decorated with auspicious birds <note>such as swans</note>, the <term>Shrivriksha</term><note>a lucky symbol resembling a tree or flower</note>, <term>Swastikas</term><note>an ancient solar symbol of well-being</note>, sacred water-pots, <term>Mithunas</term><note>sculptures of amorous couples representing fertility and joy</note>, foliage, creepers, and playful attendants <note>original: "pramathas"</note>. || 15 ||

Take the total height of the door and subtract one-eighth of that measure; the remainder is the correct height for the divine image including its pedestal <note>original: "pindika"</note>. Divide this total height of the image-plus-pedestal into three parts: two parts shall be the height of the deity's image itself, and one...

Among these, the **Meru** temple is hexagonal, has twelve stories <note>original: "bhauma"</note>, and is adorned with various wonderful windows <note>original: "kuhara/gavaksha"</note>. It is equipped with four doors and has a width of thirty-two cubits <note>A "hand" or cubit is approximately 18 inches</note>. <insert>Its height is sixty-four cubits.</insert> ॥ 20 ॥

The **Mandara** temple is hexagonal, thirty cubits wide, has ten stories, and is topped with spires <note>original: "shikhara"</note>. The **Kailasa** temple also has spires, is twenty-eight cubits wide, has eight stories, and is hexagonal. ॥ 21 ॥

The temple called **Vimanachhanda** is equipped with latticed windows, is twenty-one cubits wide, <insert>has eight stories</insert>, and is hexagonal. The **Nandana** temple is hexagonal, has six stories, is thirty-two cubits wide, and is adorned with sixteen domes <note>original: "anda"</note>. ॥ 22 ॥

The temple named **Samudra** is circular; the **Padma** is shaped like a lotus. Both these temples are eight cubits wide. They each have a single spire and consist of only one story. ॥ 23 ॥

The **Garuda** temple is shaped like the mythical bird Garuda <note>The divine eagle and vehicle of Vishnu</note>, but without wings and a tail. The **Nandi** <insert>Nandivardhana</insert> is twenty-four cubits wide and should be built with seven stories...

# Chapter Fifty-Seven
## Characteristics of "Vajralepa" (Adamantine Glue)

Unripe fruits of the *Tinduka* <note>Persimmon; Diospyros embryopteris</note> and unripe *Kapitthaka* <note>Wood-apple</note>, flowers of the *Shalmali* <note>Silk-cotton tree</note>, seeds of the *Shallaki* <note>Boswellia serrata</note>, bark of the *Dhanvana* tree, and *Vacha* <note>Orris root/Sweet flag</note> || 1 || These should be boiled in one *drona* <note>A traditional unit of volume, approx. 12.27 liters</note> of water until only an eighth part remains. This decoction should then be removed from the heat and mixed with the following substances to form a paste: || 2 || Resin of the *Shrivasa* <note>Pine resin</note>, *Guggulu* <note>Indian Bdellium</note>, *Bhallataka* <note>Marking nut</note>, *Kunduruka* <note>Frankincense</note>, *Sarjarasa* <note>Sal tree resin</note>, linseed, and the pulp of the *Bilva* <note>Bael fruit</note>. This resulting paste is known as *Vajralepa* <note>Literally "Diamond Paste" or "Adamantine Glue"</note>. || 3 || When heated and applied to temples, mansions, vaulted roofs, Shiva-lingas, idols, walls, and wells, it lasts for ten thousand years. || 4 || Lac, *Kunduru*, *Guggulu*, soot from the house, the pulp of *Kapittha* and *Bilva*...

<margin>If the measurement of the *Kapotapalika* <note>The pigeon-holding cornice</note> is added, it becomes equal to the measurement stated by Maya.</margin>

I have described these temple characteristics in brief. However, everything composed by the Sage Garga regarding temple characteristics is included here. To preserve the memory of the vast treatises on temple characteristics composed by ancient masters like Manu, Vashistha, Maya, and Nagnajit, I have authored this section. || 31 ||

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter in the Hindi commentary of the Bṛhat Saṃhitā, composed by Varahamihira and translated by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province.

# Now begins the Fifty-Eighth Chapter.
## The Characteristics of Idols.

The smallest particle of dust that becomes visible in a beam of sun-light passing through a lattice window should be known as a "Particle" <note>original: "Paramānu"; literally 'atom'</note>; it is the first of all measurements. || 1 || Eight Particles make one Speck of Dust; then follow a hair's tip, a nit, a louse, a barley-corn, and a digit <note>original: "Angula"; roughly the width of a finger</note>. Eight-fold—

---

The pulp of Wood-apple, *Nagabala* (Gangeran) fruit, *Mahua* fruit, and *Manjistha*. || 5 || By mixing the paste of Resin, *Bol* <note>Myrrh</note>, and *Amla* into a *Drona* <note>a traditional unit of volume</note> of water prepared as before, the second Adamantine Glue is perfected. It has the same properties mentioned for the first glue and is used in the coating of temples and other structures just like the first. || 6 || From the horns of these three—cow, buffalo, and goat; the hides of these three—donkey, buffalo, and cow; and from Neem fruit, Wood-apple fruit, and Indigo—the third paste is prepared as before. Its name is *Vajratara*. It also possesses the previously mentioned qualities and is used for the same tasks. || 7 || Melt together eight parts lead, two parts bell-metal, and one part brass. This is the combination told by Maya, and its name is *Vajrasanghāta*. || 8 ||

The measurements increase eightfold at each step: eight particles of dust make one hair-tip; eight hair-tips make one nit; eight nits make one louse; eight lice make one barley-corn; and eight barley-corns make one <term>Angula</term> <note>a traditional unit of measurement, roughly equivalent to a finger-breadth</note>. This is the scale used for calculations. || 2 ||

Take the height of the temple door and subtract one-eighth of it. One-third of the remaining value is the measurement for the <term>Pindika</term> <note>the pedestal or base of the idol</note>. The <term>Pratima</term> <note>the idol or image itself</note> should be double the measurement of the pedestal. || 3 ||

The face should be twelve <term>Angulas</term> in width and length according to standard measures. However, the teacher <insert>named</insert> Nagnajit states that in the Dravidian style, the face is traditionally fourteen <term>Angulas</term> in length. || 4 ||

The nose, forehead, chin, neck, and ears should each be four <term>Angulas</term> long. The jaws should be two <term>Angulas</term> long, and the chin should be two <term>Angulas</term> wide. || 5 ||

The forehead is eight <term>Angulas</term> wide. Beyond the forehead on either side are the <term>Shankha</term> <note>the temples of the head</note>, which are two <term>Angulas</term> wide. The length of the temples should be four <term>Angulas</term>, and the ears should be two <term>Angulas</term> thick. || 6 ||

The outer edge of the ear should be made four and a half <term>Angulas</term> long, aligned with the eyebrows. The ear-hole and the <term>Sukumaraka</term> <note>the fleshy prominence near the ear canal, likely the tragus</note> should be level with the corner of the eye. || 7 ||

The sage Vashistha states that the distance between the corner of the eye and the ear should be four <term>Angulas</term>. The lower lip should be one <term>Angula</term> in measurement, and the upper lip should be half of that. || 8 ||

The <term>Goccha</term> <note>the philtrum or the area between the nose and lip</note> should be half an <term>Angula</term> wide. The mouth should be four <term>Angulas</term> long and one and a half <term>Angulas</term> wide when closed...

# Chapter 58: Descriptions of Divine Images

### The Attendants and the Creator
...five. The two wives of these <note>referring to Samba and Pradyumna from the previous verse</note> should be depicted holding a shield and a sword. **(40)**
**Brahma** <note>the creator god</note> should be shown holding a water-pot in his hand, possessing four faces, and seated upon a lotus throne. **Skanda** <note>also known as Kartikeya, the god of war</note> should have the appearance of a young boy, holding a spear, and featuring a peacock as his emblem. **(41)**

### The King of Gods and the Great Lord
The white elephant of **Mahendra** <note>Indra, the King of the Gods</note> should have four tusks. Indra himself should hold a thunderbolt in his hand; a third eye placed horizontally on his forehead is his distinguishing mark. **(42)**
On the head of **Shambhu** <note>Shiva</note> is the crescent moon; he has a bull as his banner and a third eye placed vertically on his forehead. He holds a trident and the bow named *Pinaka*. Alternatively, the left half of the image may consist of the left half of the Daughter of the Mountain <note>Parvati, forming the androgynous Ardhanarishvara</note>. **(43)**

### The Buddha and the Jina
The **Buddha** should have the palms of his hands and the soles of his feet marked with lotus signs. He should have a serene expression and very short, curly hair. Seated upon a lotus throne, he should appear like the father of the entire world. **(44)**
The god of the **Arhats** <note>a Tirthankara or Jain deity</note> should be depicted with arms reaching down to his knees. He is marked with the *Shrivatsa* <note>a sacred curl of hair on the chest</note>, possesses a peaceful form, is sky-clad <note>naked, representing the Digambara tradition</note>, youthful, and handsome. **(45)**

### The Sun God
The nose, forehead, shanks, thighs, cheeks, and chest of the **Sun** should be prominent. He should be dressed in the "Northern Style" <note>referring to Central Asian or Scythian influence, including boots and a long tunic</note>, with his body covered from the feet up to the chest. **(46)**
Holding two lotuses by their stalks in his hands, he should wear a crown. His face should be adorned with earrings, and he should wear a long dangling necklace...

# The Varāhīsaṃhitā (The Great Compilation)

...surrounded by birds. ॥ 47 ॥ The face should have the luster of the interior of a lotus; the body should be covered by a garment <note>original: "kañcuka" - a protective tunic or bodice</note>; and the face should appear pleasant with a gentle smile. An icon one cubit <note>original: "hasta" - the length from elbow to fingertip</note> high is auspicious; one two cubits high grants wealth; and those measuring three or four cubits bring safety and abundance. ॥ 49 ॥ An icon with excessive limbs causes fear of the king; one with missing limbs makes the maker sickly. These auspicious and inauspicious results described for the Sun icon should be applied similarly to all other divine images. ॥ 52 ॥

### The Proportions of the Linga

Measuring the circumference of the Linga <note>the symbolic representation of Shiva</note> with a cord, one should divide its total length into three equal parts. The bottom section should be square; the middle section should be octagonal; and the top section should be circular. ॥ 53 ॥ The square portion is to be buried in the earth; the middle octagonal portion is to be set within the cavity of the pedestal <note>original: "piṇḍikā" - the base or yoni-pitha</note>. The visible circular portion at the top should be equal in height to the width of the pedestal extending from the cavity. ॥ 54 ॥

A thin and long Lingam <note>The aniconic representation of Shiva</note> brings destruction to the country; one lacking sides <note>asymmetrical or narrow</note> brings destruction to the city. A Lingam that has a wound or crack on its head brings about the destruction of its owner. || 55 ||

The group of Mothers <note>The Matrikas, a group of mother goddesses</note> should be made with emblems corresponding to the gods of their respective names <note>e.g., Brahmani should look like Brahma, Indrani like Indra</note>. <insert>However, their feminine features like breasts should also be depicted to show their female form.</insert> The image of Revanta <note>a son of the Sun god</note> should be shown mounted on a horse, surrounded by a retinue engaged in the sport of hunting. || 56 ||

# Now begins the Fifty-Ninth Chapter.
## Entering the Forest.

On a day favorable to the maker, at an auspicious moment purified by the astrologer, and observing the favorable omens and signs prescribed for journeys, one should enter the forest <note>to seek wood for the idol</note>. || 1 ||

<margin>Trees found on</margin> the path to a cemetery, near a temple, on an anthill, in a garden, or at a hermitage...

---

<column-break/>

A thin and long Lingam destroys the country; one deficient on both sides destroys the city; a Lingam with a wound on its head destroys the master. || 55 ||

The group of Mothers should be made with signs similar to the gods of their own names. For example, the form of Brahmani is like Brahma, Indrani like Indra, and so on. But their breasts and other limbs should also be fashioned so that the beauty of the female form is apparent. The image of Revanta (a son of the Sun) should be made mounted on a horse and his attendants should be shown playing at hunting (the chase). || 56 ||

The image of Yama should be made holding a staff in his hand and mounted on a buffalo. The image of Varuna should be made mounted on a swan and holding a noose. The image of Kubera should be made riding on a man, wearing a crown on the left side, and having a large stomach. || 57 ||

The image of Ganapati should have an elephant's face and a long belly; he should hold an axe in his hand; the image should have one tooth (tusk) and be shown holding a radish bulb and dark blue leaves. || 58 ||

# Varahi Samhita

<page-num>264</page-num>

->**The Selection of Trees**<-

Trees located in monasteries <note>original: "matha"</note>, hermitages of ascetics, near sacred shrines <note>original: "chaitya"</note>, at the confluence of rivers, or those nourished by pitcher-water should be avoided. Similarly, one must reject trees that are stunted, those grown too close to another for support, those strangled by creepers, struck by lightning, broken by the wind, damaged by elephants, withered, scorched by fire, or those housing beehives. // 2–3 //

Such trees must be avoided as they bring misfortune if used for making images. Conversely, trees with glossy leaves, flowers, and fruits are auspicious. Upon finding a desired tree in the forest, one should approach it and perform a worship ceremony with offerings <note>original: "bali"</note> and flowers. // 4 //

### Trees Suited to the Four Castes

The Deodar (Himalayan Cedar), Sandalwood, Shami, and Mahua trees are auspicious for **Brahmins** <note>the priestly class</note>. The Neem, Peepal, Khair, and Bael trees bring prosperity to **Kshatriyas** <note>the warrior and ruling class</note>. // 5 //

The Jivaka, Khair, Sindhu, and Syandana trees yield auspicious results for **Vaishyas** <note>the merchant and farmer class</note>. The Tendu, Nagkesar, Sarja, Arjun, Mango, and Saal trees are beneficial for **Shudras** <note>the laboring class</note>. // 6 //

### Preparation for Carving

A Lingam <note>an abstract representation of Shiva</note> or a divine image <note>original: "pratima"</note> must be installed according to the original orientation of the tree. For this reason, before felling the tree, one must mark the directions—noting which part is the top and which is the bottom—so the feet of the image are carved from the lower portion. // 7 //

One should worship the tree with offerings of rice-pudding <note>original: "kheer"</note>, sweetmeats <note>original: "laddu"</note>, cooked rice, curd, and *ullopika* <note>a specific type of traditional food preparation</note>, along with wine, flowers, incense, and perfumes. // 8 //

One must then address the spirits—the Gods, Ancestors, Pishachas <note>flesh-eating spirits</note>, Rakshasas <note>demons</note>, Nagas <note>serpent deities</note>, Asuras <note>titans</note>, and the followers of Vinayaka <note>Ganesha</note>—during the night...

After performing the worship of Ganesha <note>original: "Vinayaka," the remover of obstacles</note> and others at night, one should touch the tree and recite the following mantra: || 9 ||

> "O Tree! You have been chosen for the worship of such-and-named deity; salutations to you. May you accept this worship performed according to the sacred rites." || 10 ||
> "Whatever spirits <note>original: "bhutani," referring to nature spirits or elementals residing in the tree</note> dwell here, may they accept this duly offered sacrifice and establish their residence elsewhere. May they grant us forgiveness today; salutations to them." || 11 ||
> Having sprinkled the tree with water at dawn, one should smear the axe with honey and clarified butter <note>term: "ghrita" or ghee, used here to sanctify the tool and minimize the "injury" to the tree</note>. One should first strike the tree on its northeastern side and then cut the remainder by moving in a clockwise direction. || 12 ||
> If the tree falls toward the East, Northeast, or North, it brings prosperity. If it falls toward the Southeast or other directions in sequence, the results are fire, minor ailments, diseases, and the loss of horses. || 13 ||
> Whatever has not been explicitly stated here regarding the entry into the forest—such as the omens of the tree's fall, the characteristics of the wood's interior, or the cutting process—I have already explained in the chapters on Indra's Banner and Architecture <note>term: "Vastu Vidya," the science of sacred geometry and construction</note>. Those same rules should be applied here as well. || 14 ||

### Thus ends the Fifty-Ninth Chapter, titled "Entry into the Forest," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 59 ||

---

At night, after worshipping Ganesha and others, touch the tree and read this mantra: || 9 ||

O Tree! You are intended for the worship of such-and-such a deity <note>The practitioner should substitute "amukasya" with the specific name of the god in the genitive case</note>; salutations to you. Accept this worship according to the prescribed rituals. The creatures that reside upon this tree, having accepted the ritual worship, should imagine their dwelling elsewhere. May they forgive [this act] today; I bow to them. || 10 || 11 || At the time of dawn, drench the tree with water, smear the axe with honey and ghee, and then first cut the tree in the Northeast direction <note>term: "Ishan-kon," the direction of the Lord Shiva, considered highly auspicious</note>. Afterward, cut the rest of the tree following a clockwise sequence. || 12 || If the cut tree falls in the East, Northeast, or North direction, it is a bringer of growth. If it falls in the five directions starting from the Southeast, the results are respectively: fire-burns, hunger/ailments, and the destruction of horses. || 13 || In this chapter on entering the forest, that which I have not mentioned—namely the auspicious and inauspicious fruits of the tree's fall, its sections, and the "womb" or interior of the tree—I have already described in the Chapter on Indra's Banner and the Chapter on the Science of Architecture. One should understand them here in the same way; that is, the same good and bad results should be known here. || 14 ||

### Thus ends the Fifty-Ninth Chapter in the Hindi commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the Northwestern province, on the Brihat Samhita composed by the great teacher Sri Varahamihira. || 59 ||

# Chapter Sixty
## The Installation of Sacred Images

<margin>(In the south)</margin>
A wise practitioner should construct a pavilion for the preliminary consecration <note>original: "adhivāsana-maṇḍapa"; a temporary structure for the ritual purification of an image before installation</note> in either the north or the east. It should be equipped with four ceremonial arches <note>original: "toraṇa"</note> and covered with the auspicious young leaves of trees. || 1 || In the eastern part of the pavilion, multicolored garlands and banners are prescribed; in the southeast, they should be red; and in the south and southwest, they should be black. || 2 || In the western direction, they should be white; in the northwest, pale yellow; in the northern side, multicolored; and in the northeast, yellow banners and garlands should be placed. || 3 || A sacred image made of wood or clay bestows long life, prosperity, strength, and victory. An image made of gemstones brings welfare to the people, while one made of gold grants physical nourishment and health. || 4 || An image made of silver brings fame, and one made of copper increases one's progeny. An image or a Lingam <note>the aniconic representation of Shiva</note> made of stone <note>original: "śailī"</note> grants a great acquisition of land. || 5 || An image marred by a "pin-like" defect <note>original: "śanku"; a protrusion or splinter</note> destroys the patron and his lineage. One marred by a hollow or pit causes incurable diseases and constant calamities. || 6 || In the center of the pavilion, having smeared a sacrificial altar <note>original: "sthaṇḍila"</note> with cow dung, one should spread sand and then sacred Kusha grass.

---

The learned person performing the installation should build a pavilion for the ritual preparation of the image in the eastern direction. It should have four arches in the four directions and be covered with the tender leaves of trees. || 1 || In the eastern direction of that pavilion, one should hang flower garlands and banners of various colors; in the southeast, red; in the south and southwest, black. || 2 || In the west, white; in the northwest, pale yellow; in the north, multicolored; and in the northeast corner of the pavilion, it is proper to hang yellow garlands and banners for beauty. || 3 || A divine image made of wood or clay gives long life, wealth, strength, and victory. A divine image made of gems benefits the people, and a golden image gives bodily nourishment. || 4 || Silver brings fame, and copper increases offspring. An image made of stone or a Shiva-lingam brings the gain of much land. || 5 || An image in which a nail-like piece remains standing in any limb destroys the primary patron and the lineage; and an image that has a hole or depression causes incurable diseases and many types of disturbances. || 6 || In the middle of the consecration pavilion, having prepared a sacrificial mound, one should plaster it with cow dung, etc. Over that, spread sand, and over the sand, spread Kusha grass and lay the image down upon it. The head of the image should be on a throne <note>original: "bhadrāsana"; a ceremonial seat or posture</note>...

One should place the image <term>Pratima; a consecrated icon or statue</term> upon a throne <term>Bhadrasana; a specific ritual seating posture or auspicious throne</term> with its feet resting upon a pillow. ## 7 ## Using astringent waters prepared from the bark of the White Fig, Sacred Fig, Cluster Fig, Siris, and Banyan trees; along with auspicious herbs known as the "Mangala" group <note>These typically include plants like Jaya, Punarnava, and Vishnukanta</note>, and sacred Kusha grass. ## 8 ## With earth <term>Mrittika; sacred soil</term> taken from the tusks of an elephant, the horns of a bull, a mountain peak, an anthill, the confluence of rivers, and from lotus-filled lakes; along with the five products of the cow <term>Panchagavya; a purifying mixture of milk, curd, ghee, urine, and dung</term> and water from holy pilgrimage sites. ## 9 ## The image, facing eastward, should be bathed with water containing gold and gems and infused with fragrances, amidst the sounding of various trumpets and musical instruments, and the chanting of "Auspicious Day" <term>Punyahavachan; a rite to declare the day favorable</term> and Vedic hymns by the priests. ## 10 ## In the eastern direction, the chief Brahmins should mutter mantras addressed to Indra, and in the southeast, mantras addressed to Agni <note>the Fire God</note>; the patron must worship these priests with sacrificial fees <term>Dakshina</term>. ## 11 ## The Brahmin should perform a fire sacrifice <term>Havan</term> using the specific mantras of the deity being installed. I have already described the omens related to the sacrificial fire in the chapter on the Raising of Indra’s Banner. ## 12 ## If the fire is choked with smoke, if the flames flicker toward the left, or if it repeatedly emits sparks, it is not auspicious. It is also declared inauspicious if the priest suffers a lapse in memory <note>forgetting the mantras</note> or if he slips from his seated position during the rite. ## 13 ## Having bathed the image, dressed it in unwashed <insert>new</insert> garments, adorned it with ornaments, and worshipped it with flowers and perfumes, the installer should place the image upon a well-prepared bed. ## 14 ## While the image "sleeps," one should keep a vigil with dance and song; having thus performed the preliminary consecration <term>Adhivasa; the rite of 'dwelling' where the deity is invited to inhabit the form</term>, at the time appointed by the astrologer...

One should perform the installation at the appointed time. || 15 || Having worshipped the image with flowers, garments, and ointments, and amidst the sounds of conch shells and trumpets, one should carefully lead the procession clockwise around the temple. || 16 || Having offered an abundant sacrifice and honored the Brahmins and the assembled guests, one should place a piece of gold into the cavity of the pedestal <term>Pindika; the base or socket that holds the idol</term> and then set the image upon it. || 17 || By specifically honoring the installer, the astrologer, the Brahmins, the assembly, and the architects, the patron becomes a sharer of auspiciousness in this world and attains heaven in the next. || 18 ||

The devotees of Vishnu <note>Bhagavatas</note> should install the image of Vishnu; the Magas <note>Maga: Sun-worshipping priests originally from Sakadvipa</note> should install the image of the Sun; the ash-smearing Brahmins should install Shambhu (Shiva); those familiar with the sequence of the Circle <note>Mandala-krama: specific tantric or ritual arrangements</note> should install the Mothers; and the learned Brahmins should install Brahma. The Shakyas <note>Buddhist monks</note>, who are of peaceful mind, should install the image of the All-Beneficent (Buddha), and the naked ones <note>Jinas/Digambara monks</note> should install the Jinas. The ritual of any deity should be performed by those who are devoted to that specific deity according to their own prescribed rules. || 19 ||

The installation of the gods should be done during the northern transit of the sun <term>Uttarāyan; the period between the winter and summer solstices</term>, in the bright fortnight of the month, when the Moon is in the divisions of Jupiter, in a fixed zodiac sign and a fixed subdivision <note>Navamsha</note>, while the gentle planets are in the fifth, ninth, first, fourth, seventh, or tenth houses. || 20 || While the malefic planets are in the third, sixth, tenth, or eleventh houses, and under the fixed, soft, or friendly lunar mansions—specifically the two Uttaras, Rohini, Mrigashira, Revati, Chitra, Anuradha, Shravana, Pushya, and Swati—on a favorable day...

<margin>Perform the preliminary consecration <term>Adhivāsan</term> and then install the image at the auspicious moment indicated by the astrologer.</margin>

Having worshipped that image with flowers, clothes, and sandalwood paste, lift it from the consecration pavilion, circle the temple clockwise, and with great effort, bring it into the inner sanctum. At that time, conch shells, trumpets, and other musical instruments should be played. || 16 || Going there, offer a great sacrifice and worship the Brahmins and the "Sabhyas"—meaning the people present in that assembly—with clothes and monetary gifts. Place a piece of gold in the hole of the pedestal <note>Pindika</note> and install the image upon it. || 17 || Specially worship the installer <note>Pratishthāpaka</note>, the astrologer, the Brahmins, and the craftsmen <note>Sabhya/Sthapati</note>. A man who performs the installation of a deity in this manner shares in blessings in this world and finds a residence in heaven in the afterlife. || 18 ||

The installation of Vishnu should be done by Bhagavatas (Vaishnavas). The installation of the Sun should be done by Magas (Brahmins residing in Sakadvipa). The installation of Shiva should be done by Brahmins who wear sacred ash. The installation of the Mothers, such as Brahmi, should be done by Brahmins who know the "Mandala Krama," or the rules for their worship. The installation of Brahma should be done by Vedic Brahmins. The installation of the All-Beneficent, namely Buddha, should be done by the peaceful-minded Shakyas (those in red robes). The installation of the Jinas should be done by the naked ones (Digambara monks). Whichever deity a person is a great devotee of, they should perform the installation and all other rituals of that deity according to the procedures mentioned in their own scriptures. || 19 ||

It should be the northern transit of the sun, the bright fortnight, the Moon should be situated in the six-fold divisions of Jupiter, there should be a fixed ascendant and a fixed subdivision, and the benefic planets should be in the fifth, ninth, first, fourth, seventh, and tenth houses. || 20 || Malefic planets should be in the third, sixth, tenth, and eleventh houses; [the lunar mansions should be] both Uttaras, Rohini, Mrigashira, Revati, Chitra, Anuradha, Shravana, Pushya, and...

# Chapter Sixty-One
## Characteristics of Cows

The sage Parashara explained the characteristics of cows to his pupil Brihadrath; from that work, I have created this summary. Although all cows are inherently auspicious, I shall describe their specific good and bad traits according to the traditional scriptures <note>original: "Agama"</note>. || 1 || Cows whose eyes are filled with tears, are muddy, or appear dry are not givers of prosperity. Those with eyes like a mouse are also not auspicious. Furthermore, cows with shaking or flat horns, those of a variegated black-and-red color <note>original: "Karata"</note>, or those whose color resembles that of a donkey are considered unlucky. || 2 || Those possessing ten, seven, or only four teeth; those with long, drooping, or hornless faces; those with sunken backs; and those with short, thick necks, midsections shaped like a grain of barley <note>original: "Yavamadhya"</note>, or split hooves are likewise unfavorable. || 3 || Those with dark-colored or excessively long tongues, or with ankles that are either too thin or excessively large, [are also considered inauspicious].

The sage Parashara told the characteristics of cows to his disciple Brihadrath; taking from that book, we summarize here. Those with eyes like a mouse are also not auspicious. Those whose horns move and are flat are not auspicious. Those whose color is a mix of black and red, and those whose color is like a donkey, are also not auspicious. || 2 || Those who have ten, seven, or four teeth in their mouth; whose face is long and "Munda" (meaning without horns); whose back is bent; whose neck is short...

# The Varahi Samhita
## Chapter on the Characteristics of Cattle

Those with an excessively high hump or a perpetually emaciated body are not desired, nor are those with missing or extra limbs. **(4)** A bull is likewise unfavorable if it possesses the following traits: thick and excessively long testicles, a chest covered in prominent veins, or cheeks covered in thick veins. Furthermore, a bull that "urinates from three places"—meaning tears drip from both eyes while urine flows from the penis—is considered inauspicious. **(5)**

One with eyes like a cat, or one that is tawny or of a dull reddish-blue color, does not bring good fortune even to a <term>Brahmin</term> <note>The priestly or scholarly class; the text implies if it is bad for them, it is bad for everyone</note>. A bull with black lips, palate, and tongue, or one that is "a breather" <note>meaning fearful or constantly panting</note>, brings destruction to the entire herd. **(6)** Even if born in one's own house, a bull should be abandoned if it has thick dung, a thick <insert>tip of the penis</insert> <note>original: "mani"</note>, and thick horns; or if it has a white belly and a body color that is a mixture of black and white. Such a bull brings about the ruin of the herd. **(7)**

A bull whose body is covered in dark, flower-like spots, or is the color of ash or reddish-brown, and has cat-like eyes, will not bring prosperity even to Brahmins if accepted by them. **(8)** Those bulls that lift their feet with great effort as if pulling them out of deep mud when yoked, or those with thin necks, glassy eyes, or stunted hindquarters, are not capable of carrying heavy loads. **(9)** Those with soft, well-joined, copper-colored lips, small <term>buttocks</term> <note>original: "sphik"; the fleshy part of the hips</note>, and a copper-colored palate and tongue...

# Now begins the Sixty-Third Chapter
## Characteristics of Roosters

A rooster that has a straight body and straight toes, with a face, claws, and crest as red as copper, and is white in color, is auspicious. If he crows with a pleasant voice at the end of the night <note>dawn</note>, he brings prosperity to the King, the nation, and the horses. || 1 ||

A bird whose neck is shaped like a grain of barley, or resembles a ripe jujube fruit <note>referring to a deep reddish-orange color</note>, who has a large head and is beautiful with many varied colors—he is praised for battle. One who is the color of honey or the color of a black bee also brings victory. Any rooster other than these is not auspicious; those with thin bodies, weak voices, or who are lame in the feet are not favorable. || 2 ||

And a hen who makes soft and beautiful sounds, possesses a glossy body, and has a lovely face and eyes—she grants for a long time to the rulers of the earth the wealth of fortune, fame, victory, and valor. || 3 ||

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "Characteristics of Roosters," in the *Brihat Samhita* by the venerable Varahamihira. || 63 ||

# Now begins the Sixty-Fourth Chapter.
## Characteristics of Tortoises.

A tortoise that possesses the color of crystal or silver, is decorated with blue streaks, has a body shaped like a water-pot <note>original: "kalasha"</note>, and a beautiful spine—or one that has a body as red as the dawn and is speckled with marks the size of mustard seeds—brings great importance and status to all kings when kept within the palace. || 1 ||

One whose body is as dark as eye-salve <note>collyrium</note> or a black bee, is variegated with spots, has a complete and symmetrical body, a head like a serpent's, and a thick neck, also serves to increase the kingdom and prosperity of kings. || 2 ||

A tortoise with the luster of a cat's-eye gem <note>original: "vaidurya"</note>, a thick neck, a triangular shape, concealed orifices, and a beautiful spine is considered auspicious. Such a tortoise should be kept by rulers for the sake of good fortune in a pleasure-pool or in a vessel filled with water. || 3 ||

# Now begins the Sixty-Fifth Chapter.

## Characteristics of Goats.

I shall now describe the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of goats. Those possessing nine, ten, or eight teeth are considered fortunate and should be kept in the home. However, those with only seven teeth should be discarded, as they bring misfortune. || 1 ||

If a white goat has a black circular mark on its right flank, it brings good fortune. For goats that are dark blue like a deer <note>original: "rishya-mruga," referring to a specific type of forest antelope</note>, black, or reddish-brown, a white circular mark on the right flank is likewise auspicious. || 2 ||

The fleshy protuberance that hangs from the throat of a goat like a teat is known as a <term>Mani</term> <note>literally "jewel" or "pendant"</note>. A goat with one such pendant brings good results, but those with two or three pendants are considered the most fortunate of all. || 3 ||

All hornless goats are auspicious. Those whose bodies are entirely white or entirely black are also favorable. Goats that are half-black and half-white are lucky, as are those that are half-tawny and half-black. || 4 ||

A goat that walks at the head of the herd and is the first to enter the water is auspicious. Also favorable is a goat with a white head, or one that has a mark on its head resembling the <term>Krittika</term> constellation <note>The Pleiades; specifically a mark consisting of six dots</note>; such a goat is called a <term>Kuttaka</term>. || 5 ||

A goat is praised if it has spots of a different color on its throat and head, or if its color resembles <term>Tilapishta</term> <note>ground sesame paste; a mixture of white and yellowish-grey</note>, and if it has copper-colored eyes. A goat that is white with four black feet, or—

Now the auspicious and inauspicious signs of the goat are explained: Those goats who have nine, ten, or eight teeth are auspicious and should be kept in the house. One should not keep those with seven teeth because they are inauspicious. || 1 || If there is a black circle on the right side of a white-colored goat, it is auspicious. For a goat whose color is blue like a deer, black, or red, a white circle on the right side is also auspicious. || 2 || That which hangs like a breast from the throat of goats is called a <term>Mani</term>. A goat that has one pendant produces auspicious results, and those goats which have two or three pendants are very auspicious indeed. || 3 || All goats without horns are auspicious; those whose entire body is white or whose entire body is black are auspicious goats; those goats who are half black and half white are auspicious. Those goats who are half tawny and half black are also auspicious. || 4 || The goat that walks ahead of its flock and enters the water first is auspicious, or one whose head is white, or one who has a mark on the head like the Krittika constellation—meaning it has six dots—is auspicious; the name of such a goat is <term>Kuttaka</term>. || 5 || One who has dots of another color on the throat and head, whose color is like ground sesame—that is, a mixture of white and yellow—and who has red eyes like the color of copper, is auspicious. One whose body color is white and all four feet are black, or—

A goat whose body is black and all four feet are white is also auspicious; such a goat is called *Kutila*. || 6 || A goat whose body color is white, has black testicles, and a black band in the middle is inauspicious <note>original: "अशुभ" (ashubha)</note>. # Now Begins the Sixty-Sixth Chapter

## Characteristics of Horses

> A horse that possesses a long neck and <term>Akshikuta</term><note>The sockets or orbits of the eyes</note>, a broad <term>Trika</term><note>The upper part of the waist or sacrum</note> and chest; whose palate, lips, and tongue are red like copper; whose skin, mane, and tail-hair are fine; whose <term>Shapha</term><note>Hooves</note>, gait, and face are beautiful; and whose ears, lips, and tail-bone are short; whose shanks, knees, and thighs are well-rounded; who has even, white teeth and a handsome form—such a horse, if free from all bodily defects, constantly brings about the destruction of a king's enemies. || 1 || Whorls of hair located where tears fall, on the jaw, the <term>Ganda</term><note>Cheeks</note>, the heart, the throat, the <term>Protha</term><note>The tip of the nose or snout</note>, the <term>Shankha</term><note>The temples near the ears</note>, the waist, the <term>Basti</term><note>The lower abdomen/bladder area</note>, the knees, the scrotum, the navel, the <term>Kakuda</term><note>The hump or the area near the nape of the neck</note>, the anus, the right flank, and the legs are considered inauspicious. || 2 || Those hair-whorls located at the <term>Prapana</term><note>The edge of the upper lip</note>, the throat, the ears, the middle of the back, above the eyes near the eyebrows, the lips, the <term>Sakthi</term><note>The thighs or hindquarters</note>, the <term>Bhuja</term><note>The forelegs</note>, the left flank, the sides, and the forehead are highly auspicious. || 3 || In the bodies of horses, there are ten essential whorls known as <term>Dhruvavarta</term><note>Fixed or constant whorls</note>. Among them, one whorl is located at the <term>Prapana</term> (the underside of the upper lip) and one on the forehead below the hair. A horse whose neck and <term>Akshikuta</term> (eye sockets) are long, whose <term>Trika</term> (waist area) and heart/chest are expansive, whose palate, lips, and tongue are red like copper, whose body skin, head hair, and tail hair are fine/thin, whose <term>Shapha</term> (hooves), gait, and face are beautiful, and whose ears, lips, and tail—here the word "tail" refers specifically to the bone within the tail—are small; whose shanks, knees, and thighs are round, who has even and white teeth, and whose shape and form are beautiful—such a horse, if it is "pure in all limbs" (meaning it has no inauspicious hair-whorls on any part of its body), will always destroy the enemies of the king who owns it. || 1 ||

It is inauspicious to have hair-whorls in the following places: the <note>original: "Ashrupata"</note> path of tears, the jaw, the face, the <term>Ganda</term> (cheeks), the heart, the throat, the <term>Protha</term> (lower part of the nose), the <term>Shankha</term> (temples near the ears), the <term>Kati</term> (waist), the <term>Basti</term> (the area between the navel and the genitals), the knees, the scrotum, the navel, the <term>Kakuda</term> (near the nape of the neck/upper back), the anus, the right flank, and the feet. || 2 ||

Those hair-whorls that are situated on the <term>Prapana</term> (the surface of the upper lip), the throat, the ears, the middle of the back, above the eyes, near the eyebrows, the lips, the <term>Sakthi</term> (hindquarters), the <term>Bhuja</term> (forelegs), the left flank, the sides, and the forehead are auspicious. || 3 ||

There are ten hair-whorls that must exist on a horse's body; these are called <term>Dhruvavarta</term> (fixed whorls). Among them, one whorl is in the <term>Prapana</term> (the underside of the upper lip) and one whorl is on the forehead below the hair. In the tradition, there are two of each. <note>Referring to the pairs of permanent teeth mentioned in the previous verse.</note> || 4 || A foal has six teeth of a bright white color; when these turn a brownish-red <note>original: "kashaya"</note>, the horse is two years old. By the falling and regrowing of the central, middle, and end teeth, a horse reaches five years of age. Following the sequence of these teeth, and counting in groups of three years based on colors—black, yellow, white, glass-colored, honey-colored, and conch-white—as well as the appearance of hollows, loosening, and finally the falling out of teeth, one may know the age. || 5 ||

### Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "Characteristics of Horses,"
### in the Brhat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 66 ||

These are the ten fixed whorls <note>original: "dhruvaavarta," referring to hair patterns discussed in the preceding section</note>. || 4 || In the dental row of horses, if the six teeth between the two molars are white, it is a one-year-old colt. If those same six teeth are of a "kashaya" color (a mixture of black and red), it is a two-year-old horse. In both rows of teeth, the two identical teeth in the very center are called the "Sandamsha" <term>Sandamsha: central incisors</term>. The tooth on either side of the central ones is called the "Madhya" <term>Madhya: middle incisors</term>, and the teeth on the outer edges of those are called the "Antya" <term>Antya: corner incisors</term>. If the central incisors have fallen out and regrown, the horse is four years old; if the corner incisors have fallen and regrown, it is a five-year-old horse.

Following the sequence of these teeth, the age increases by three years for each color, starting with "Kalika" <note>black spots</note>. The meaning is this: if there are black spots on the central incisors, the horse is six years old; if on the middle incisors, seven years; and if on the corner incisors, the horse's age is eight years. Similarly, if there are yellow spots on the central incisors, it is nine years; on the middle, ten; and on the corner incisors, eleven years. By the appearance of white spots on the central, middle, and corner teeth, know the age to be twelve, thirteen, and fourteen years respectively. If the spots are the color of glass <note>original: "kacha"</note>, the ages are fifteen, sixteen, and seventeen. If the spots are the color of "Makshika" (honey), the ages are eighteen, nineteen, and twenty. If the spots are the color of a conch shell, the ages are twenty-one, twenty-two, and twenty-three. If hollows or pits <note>original: "avata"</note> appear in the teeth, the ages are twenty-four, twenty-five, and twenty-six. When the teeth begin to loosen, the ages are twenty-seven, twenty-eight, and twenty-nine. Finally, when the teeth actually fall out—the central at thirty, the middle at thirty-one, and the corner at thirty-two—the horse has reached the end of its life. The maximum lifespan of a horse is thirty-two years, which is why the signs for determining age are written up to thirty-two years. || 5 ||

### Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter in the Brhat Samhita composed by the Great Teacher Sri Varahamihira, with the Hindi commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province. || 66 ||

# Chapter Sixty-Seven
## Characteristics of Elephants

Those elephants whose tusks are the color of honey, whose limbs are well-proportioned and distinct, who are neither overweight nor emaciated, who are capable of endurance, whose bodies are symmetrical, whose <term>backbone</term> <note>original: prishthavamsha</note> is curved like a bow, and whose <term>hindquarters</term> <note>original: jaghana</note> resemble those of a boar, are known as the **Bhadra** (Noble) type. || 1 ||

The **Manda** (Slow/Stately) type of elephant is characterized by a loose chest and folds around the middle, a long belly, thick skin and neck, and a thick abdomen and <term>root of the tail</term> <note>original: pechaka</note>. Their gaze is steady and fierce like that of a lion. || 2 ||

The **Mriga** (Deer-like) type of elephants have a short lower lip, short tail-hair, and a small <term>penis</term> <note>original: medhra</note>. Their feet, neck, tusks, trunk, and ears are also small, while their eyes are large. These are the signs of the Mriga type. Those elephants that possess a mixture of the characteristics described for these three types should be known as the **Sankirna** (Mixed) type. || 3 ||

The height of a Mriga elephant is five cubits, its length from the root of the tail to the <term>frontal globes of the head</term> <note>original: kumbha</note> is seven cubits, and its <term>circumference</term> <note>original: parinaha</note> at the middle is eight cubits. By increasing these measurements by one cubit, one finds the proportions of the Manda type, and by two cubits, the proportions of the Bhadra type. Specifically, the Manda elephant has a circumference of nine cubits, while the Bhadra elephant stands seven cubits high, is nine cubits long, and has a circumference of ten cubits. The Mixed type has no fixed proportions; they are of irregular size. || 4 ||

The <term>ichor</term> <note>original: mada; the rutting secretion of an elephant</note> of the Bhadra type is green in color; that of the Manda type is yellow like turmeric; and—

---

There are four types of elephants: **Bhadra**, **Manda**, **Mriga**, and **Sankirna**. Their characteristics are now described in order: Those elephants whose tusks are the color of honey, whose limbs are all well-divided, whose bodies are neither too fat nor too weak, who are fit for work, possessed of symmetrical limbs, whose <term>backbone</term> is shaped like a bow, and whose <term>hindquarters</term> are like those of a boar, belong to the Bhadra caste. || 1 || The Manda caste elephant has a loose chest and middle folds, a long stomach, thick skin and throat; the flanks and the <term>root of the tail</term> are also thick, and the sight is like a lion's; this is the sign of the Manda. || 2 || For the Mriga caste elephants, the lower lip, tail hair, and <term>penis</term> are small. The feet, throat, tusks, trunk, and ears are also small, and the eyes are large. These are the signs of the Mriga; elephants in whom the signs of all three castes are found should be known as the Sankirna (Mixed) caste. || 3 || The height of the Mriga elephant is five cubits, the length from the tail-root to the <term>frontal globe</term> is seven cubits, and the thickness of the middle part is eight cubits. Adding one cubit gives the measure of the Manda, and adding two cubits gives the measure of the Bhadra; thus, the <term>circumference</term> of the Manda elephant is nine cubits, and the Bhadra elephant is seven cubits in height, nine cubits in length, and ten cubits in <term>circumference</term>. There is no rule for the height etc. of the Mixed caste elephants; they are of indefinite proportions. || 4 || The <term>ichor</term> of the Bhadra elephant is green, the ichor of the Manda elephant is yellow like turmeric, and—

<summary>This page classifies elephants into four distinct types—Bhadra, Manda, Mriga, and Sankirna—based on their physical proportions, temperament, and the color of their rutting secretions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the physical characteristics of elephants (Gajalaksana) from the Brihat Samhita, focusing on the classification of musth (temporal secretion) and the auspicious versus inauspicious physical traits of royal elephants.</meta>

# The Varahi Samhita

The secretion <note>musth</note> of the *Mriga* <note>Deer-type</note> elephant is said to be black, resembling the color of the *Haridraka* <note>likely the yellow-throated marten or a specific dark bird</note>. The secretion of the *Sankirna* <note>Mixed-breed</note> elephant is of a variegated or mixed color. || 5 ||

Those elephants whose lips, palate, and mouth are copper-red, whose eyes resemble those of a house sparrow, and whose tusks are smooth, elevated at the tips, and well-proportioned are highly prized. They should have a wide and long face, a spine that is curved like a bow, long, well-concealed, and firm <note>original: *prishthavamsha*</note>, and cranial bosses <note>the two bumps on an elephant's forehead</note> that are shaped like the shell of a tortoise and covered with fine, single hairs. || 6 ||

The ears, jaw, navel, forehead, and private parts should be expansive. They should possess eighteen or twenty nails that are raised in the center like a tortoise shell. The trunk should be round and marked with three distinct lines. Those elephants whose temporal secretion and the breath from their trunk are fragrant are considered blessed and bringers of prosperity. || 7 ||

The finger-like tip of the trunk <note>original: *anguli*</note> should be long, and the orifice of the trunk <term>Pushkara|The tip or 'nostril' area of the elephant's trunk</term> should be reddish. Their roar <note>original: *brimhita*</note> should resonate like the thundering of water-laden clouds. Elephants with large, long, and well-rounded necks are auspicious for a sovereign ruler. || 8 ||

The King should banish to foreign lands those elephants that never enter musth, those with missing or extra nails <note>fewer than 18 or more than 20</note>, or those with deformed limbs. Likewise, elephants that are hunchbacked, dwarfed, or have tusks shaped like a ram's horns should be removed. Those with visible testicles, those lacking a proper trunk-tip, or those with palates that are dark gray, blue, multicolored, or black are equally undesirable. || 9 ||

Elephants with very small tusks, those that are naturally tuskless <note>original: *matkuna*</note>, or those that are impotent <note>original: *shanda*</note>, as well as any female elephant that displays masculine traits or is pregnant—all these should be sent away by the King to another country, for they bring extremely unfavorable results. || 10 ||

->Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Characteristics of Elephants," in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 67 ||<-

# Now Begins the Sixty-Eighth Chapter

## The Characteristics of Men
<note>Sanskrit: Purusha Lakshana. This section shifts from animal omens to human physiognomy, the study of physical features to determine character and destiny.</note>

> A skilled expert in the science of body-marks <note>original: "Samudravid" or one who knows Samudrika Shastra</note>, after duly observing a person's height, weight, gait, joints, essence, color, luster, voice, nature, temperament, previous births, the ten bodily regions, and the physical radiance, may then declare their past and future. || 1 ||
>
> The feet of a lord of men <note>a King</note> are free from sweat, possess soft soles, and have the hue of the interior of a lotus. The toes are closely set, the nails are beautiful and copper-colored, and the heels are well-formed. Such feet are warm to the touch, devoid of visible veins, have hidden ankles, and are arched like the back of a tortoise. || 2 ||
>
> Conversely, feet that are shaped like a winnowing basket <note>flat and broad</note>, possess rough or pale nails, are crooked, covered in prominent veins, appear shriveled, or have widely spaced toes, indicate poverty—

---

And any female elephant that possesses the characteristics of a male elephant—meaning she has large tusks, becomes intoxicated with rut, and so forth—or a female elephant that becomes pregnant <note>likely referring to specific inauspicious timing or conditions</note>, the King should banish her from his kingdom. If they remain in the realm, they produce very evil results. An elephant whose chest and hindquarters are narrow, whose back is high, who is deficient in standard proportions, and whose navel is prominent is called a "hunchback" <note>original: Kubja</note>. An elephant that is correct in length and girth but significantly lacking in height is called a "dwarf" <note>original: Vamana</note>. One who possesses all the correct features but lacks tusks is called a "tuskless male" <note>original: Matkuna or Makuna</note>. An elephant whose legs strike each other while walking is called a "eunuch" <note>original: Shandha</note>. || 10 ||

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter of the Brihat Samhita composed by the Great Acharya Varahamihira, with the Hindi commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region. || 67 ||

---

Height measured in fingers <note>term: Angula - a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to a finger's width</note>, weight, gait, the firmness of the joints, essence, color, sound, nature, temperament <note>term: Sattva - a quality of the mind that prevents despair and fear</note>, previous births <note>original: Anuka</note>, the "field" or ten parts of the body starting with the feet which will be described hereafter, and the physical radiance <note>term: Mrija - the aura or luster of the body associated with the five elements</note>; a clever man who understands the science of body-marks <note>Samudrika Shastra</note> must first observe all these things before he can predict the past and future auspicious or inauspicious fortunes of men. || 1 ||

The feet of a King are characterized by a lack of sweat, soft soles, a radiance like the center of a lotus, toes that touch one another, shiny and red-tinted nails, beautiful heels, warmth, an absence of visible veins, and hidden ankles <note>meaning the ankle bones do not protrude sharply</note>. Furthermore, the top of the foot should be curved and high like a tortoise shell. A man whose feet possess these marks becomes a King. || 2 || Feet shaped like a winnowing basket...

# ( 282 ) The Varahi Samhita

...give misery. Feet that are wide at the front, with white-colored nails, crooked, covered in prominent veins, dry, and with widely spaced toes belong to those who are poor and suffer distress. Feet that are raised in the middle like the shape of a frog keep a person constantly wandering on the road. Feet that are the color of astringent <note>original: "kashaya" - a reddish-brown or tawny hue</note> (slightly red) cause the destruction of the lineage; that is, the family line of a man with such feet does not continue. One whose soles have the luster of well-baked earth <note>terracotta or kiln-fired clay</note> commits the sin of killing a Brahmin <note>considered one of the highest sins in classical Indian ethics</note>, and a man with yellow-colored feet is addicted to forbidden women. ॥ 3 ॥

One who has sparse and fine body hair, round thighs resembling the trunk of an elephant, and well-fleshed, symmetrical knees—a man with all these characteristics becomes a king. Those whose shanks <note>the part of the leg between the knee and ankle</note> resemble those of a dog or a jackal are destitute of wealth. ॥ 4 ॥

Those who have only one hair per follicle on their shanks become kings; those with two hairs per follicle are learned scholars and <term>Shrotriyas</term> <note>priests or scholars well-versed in the Vedas</note>; those with three, four, or more hairs per follicle are poor and suffer misery. The auspicious or inauspicious nature of the hair on the head should also be understood by this same rule. ॥ 5 ॥

One whose knees are devoid of flesh dies while traveling abroad. One with small knees is fortunate. Those with formidable or misshapen knees are poor. Those whose knees are sunken are dominated by women. One with well-fleshed knees attains a kingdom, and those with large knees enjoy a long life. ॥ 6 ॥

A man with a small penis is wealthy but childless. One with a thick penis is devoid of wealth. He whose penis leans toward the left is deprived of both wealth and sons. If the penis leans toward the right...

A navel that sits unevenly amidst the abdominal folds <note>original: "vali"</note> indicates a man who may face execution by impalement or suffer extreme poverty. A navel that is elongated horizontally on both sides grants a long life. If it is elongated toward the top, it makes a man wealthy and powerful. Regarding the lines or folds on the abdomen known as <term>Vali</term> <note>natural skin folds or creases on the stomach</note>:
- One fold: Death by a weapon.
- Two folds: One who enjoys many women.
- Three folds: An <term>Acharya</term> <note>a preceptor, teacher, or spiritual guide</note>.
- Four folds: One who has many sons.
- No folds: One who becomes a king. ॥ 24 ॥

Men with uneven folds (some small, some large) are sinful and pursue forbidden women. Those with straight, even folds are blessed with happiness and remain averse to the wives of others. ॥ 25 ॥

Those whose nails resemble husks are impotent; those with flat or cracked nails are abandoned by fortune. Those with discolored or ugly nails are prone to arguing or criticizing others, while those with nails as red as copper are kings. || 41 ||

# Chapter 68: Including the Vernacular Commentary

### Page 291

Those who sneeze with a sound that is concentrated, resonant, and echoing <note>original: *pinditam hladi sanunadam*</note>, or those whose sneeze is prolonged and continuous, should be known as long-lived. ॥ 63 ॥

Those with eyes like lotus petals are wealthy; those whose eye-corners are reddish possess great fortune <note>referring to Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth</note>. Those with honey-colored or tawny eyes possess great means, while those with eyes like a cat's <note>original: *marjara-vilocana*</note> are sinful. ॥ 64 ॥

Those with eyes like a deer, or round eyes, or eyes that are crooked <note>original: *jihma*; implying shifty or unmoving</note> are thieves. Those with squinted eyes are cruel, and those whose eyes resemble an elephant's are kings <note>the commentary suggests "army commanders" or "leaders"</note>. ॥ 65 ॥

Deep-set eyes indicate lordship and power. Eyes with the luster of a blue lotus belong to the learned. Those whose pupils are excessively black suffer the plucking out of their eyes <note>likely a karmic warning or a reference to ancient punishments</note>. ॥ 66 ॥

Those with thick or large eyes become ministers to kings. Those with brownish-grey eyes <note>original: *shyaava*; commentary uses *kapish*</note> possess good fortune. Those with pitiful or weak eyes are poor; those with glossy, large eyes are wealthy and enjoy life's pleasures. ॥ 67 ॥

Those with very high eyebrows have a short lifespan. Those with large, elevated eyebrows are exceedingly happy. Those with uneven eyebrows are destitute. Those whose eyebrows are curved like the young crescent moon are wealthy. ॥ 68 ॥

Those with long eyebrows that do not meet in the middle are wealthy. Those with broken or fragmented eyebrows are devoid of wealth. Those whose eyebrows are depressed or missing in the middle are attached to forbidden women <note>original: *agamya*; women with whom sexual relations are prohibited by law or custom</note>. ॥ 69 ॥

If the temples <term>Shankha: the anatomical region of the temples</term> are high and broad, the person is fortunate and wealthy. If the temples are sunken, they are bereft of sons and wealth. Those with an uneven or crooked forehead are poor. Those whose forehead is shaped like a half-moon are wealthy. ॥ 70 ॥ Those with a forehead broad like a pearl-oyster shell become teachers—

### The Nature of Luster (Chhaya)

The "Chhaya" <note>literally 'shadow,' but here referring to the aura, complexion, or radiant luster of a person</note>, which indicates auspicious and inauspicious results, should be observed by experts in signs <term>Lakshana-gya: those skilled in the science of physiognomy</term> in humans, animals, and birds. Just like the glow of a lamp placed inside a crystal vessel, it reveals the internal qualities of energy <term>Tejas: vital fire or brilliance</term> even on the outside. || 89 || 

When the "Earthly Luster" <note>original: "Mahi-samuttha" - arising from the earth element</note> is present, the teeth, skin, nails, body hair, and hair on the head appear glossy and the body possesses a pleasant fragrance. This earthly luster brings contentment, gain of wealth, prosperity, and a daily inclination toward righteousness <term>Dharma</term>. || 90 || 

The "Watery Luster" <note>original: "Jala-chhaya"</note> is glossy, white, clear, slightly greenish, and pleasing to the eyes. It bestows good fortune <note>the quality of being loved by all</note>, softness, happiness, and progress.

# Chapter Sixty-Nine
## The Characteristics of the Five Great Men

When the non-luminary planets <note>The "star-planets": Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn</note> are powerful, situated in their own zodiac signs or in their signs of exaltation, and occupy the quadrants <note>The 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses of a horoscope</note>, five types of illustrious men are born. I shall now describe them. || 1 || Through Jupiter, the *Hansa* type is born; through Saturn, the *Shasha* type; through Mars, the *Ruchaka* type. The *Bhadra* type comes from a powerful Mercury, and the *Malavya* type from the son of Bhrigu <note>Venus</note>. || 2 || One’s inherent strength and essence are derived from the Sun, while the qualities of the physical body and the mind are derived from the strength of the Moon. A man possesses the characteristics of the specific planetary divisions <note>The various subtle divisions of the zodiac like the Decanate or Ninth-part</note> in which these two luminaries are placed. || 3 ||

---

Those men in whom these characteristics appear at the right opportunity are called blessed (possessing auspicious signs) by those who know the science of human traits. || 116 || Having seen the views of many sages, we have stated these characteristics of men in brief; by reading this, a man becomes respected by the King and dear to all people. || 117 ||

->Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter in the vernacular commentary on the Brihat Samhita of Shri Varahamihira, composed by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province.<-

---

If the five planets—Mars and the others—are endowed with strength of position, direction, motion, and time, and are situated in their own signs or exaltation while sitting in the first, fourth, seventh, or tenth houses, then five excellent types of men are born. We shall describe them. || 1 || If Jupiter is powerful and sits in a quadrant in its own sign or exaltation, that man is a *Hansa*; by the placement of Saturn, he is a *Shasha*; by Mars, a *Ruchaka*; if Mercury is powerful, he is a *Bhadra*; and by the presence of Venus, he is a man named *Malavya*. || 2 || From the strength of the Sun comes the fullness of that man's essence (*Sattva*), and from the strength of the Moon come the qualities of the body and mind. Whichever planet's sign, decanate, ninth-part, twelfth-part, or thirty-degree-part the Sun and Moon occupy, the man will be endowed with the elements, great-elements, nature, luster, color, essence, and form associated with that planet.
