One should not attempt to assign a price to these, nor should they be perforated <note>drilled for jewelry</note>, for they are exceedingly radiant. When worn by kings, they are most holy and bestow children, victory, and health. || 22 ||

At the root of the tusk of a boar <note>Sanskrit: *vārāha*</note>, a pearl is found that shines with the luster of the moon and possesses many virtues. That which is produced from a whale <note>Sanskrit: *timi*; likely referring to large sea creatures</note> resembles the eye of a fish; it is large, very pure, and highly meritorious. || 23 ||

There is a pearl born of the clouds, resembling a hailstone, which falls from the seventh layer of the wind <note>Sanskrit: *vāyuskandha*; ancient Indian cosmology divided the atmosphere into seven layers</note>. It is said that these, flashing like lightning, are snatched away by celestial beings in the sky before they reach the earth. || 24 ||

Among the serpents descended from the lineages of Takshaka and Vasuki <note>legendary serpent kings in Hindu mythology</note> who can travel at will, smooth and blue-tinted pearls are formed at the tip of their hoods. || 25 ||

If, when placed in a silver vessel on a consecrated piece of ground, the heavens suddenly begin to rain, that pearl should be recognized as one born of a serpent. || 26 ||

A serpent-born pearl, when worn by kings, wards off poison and misfortune, destroys enemies, spreads one's fame, and grants victory. Such a pearl should never be priced. || 27 ||

# Now begins the eighty-second chapter.
## The Examination of Rubies.

The origin of the <term>Padmaraga</term> <note>literally "lotus-colored," referring to the Ruby</note> is from three types of stone: Saugandhika, Kuruvinda, and Crystal. Those born from <term>Saugandhika</term> stones possess the luster of bees, collyrium <note>eye-salve</note>, or the juice of the Jambu fruit. ॥ 1 ॥ Those produced from <term>Kuruvinda</term> stones are variegated in color, possess a duller luster, and are often pierced by mineral impurities. Those produced from <term>Crystal</term> are brilliant, of various colors, and highly pure. ॥ 2 ॥

The qualities of excellent gemstones of all types are: being glossy, spreading their radiance around, clear, brilliant, heavy, well-shaped, possessing internal luster, and having deep color. ॥ 3 ॥ The defects of gems are: being turbid (dull), having a faint luster, being filled with lines or scratches, containing mineral impurities, being broken, being poorly pierced, and containing "gravel" <note>sandy or gritty inclusions</note>; such gems are not pleasing. ॥ 4 ॥ Those with the color of a bee or a peacock's neck...

The gem that shines like the flame of a lamp and is found in the heads of serpents is indeed priceless. || 5 ||

The king who wears that priceless gem is never afflicted by the evils of poison or disease. By the power of that gem, the gods grant regular rainfall in his kingdom, and his enemies are destroyed. || 6 ||

The price of a single <term>Padmaraga</term> <note>original: "Padmaraga" - literally "lotus-colored," referring to a high-quality ruby</note> weighing one <term>Pala</term> <note>a traditional unit of weight, approximately 48 grams</note> is twenty-six thousand. For a ruby weighing three <term>Karshas</term> <note>one Karsha is about 12 grams; three Karshas equal 3/4 of a Pala</note>, the price is stated as twenty thousand. || 7 ||

A ruby weighing half a <term>Pala</term> is worth twelve thousand; one weighing a single <term>Karsha</term> is worth six thousand. That which weighs eight <term>Mashakas</term> <note>a smaller unit; 12 Mashakas typically make one Karsha</note> has a value of three thousand. || 8 ||

A weight of four <term>Mashakas</term> costs one thousand, while two <term>Mashakas</term> are valued at five hundred. For gems falling between these weights, the price should be calculated based on whether their qualities are superior or inferior. || 9 ||

A <term>Padmaraga</term> lacking in color is worth half the standard price. One lacking luster is worth one-eighth. A gem with few good qualities and many flaws receives only one-twentieth of the value. || 10 ||

One that is slightly smoky in color, full of fissures <note>original: "Vrana" - literally wounds or scars, referring to internal fractures or inclusions</note>, and possessing few virtues receives a twentieth part of the price. Thus has the valuation of rubies been well-taught by the ancient masters. || 11 ||

# Chapter Eighty-Four
## The Characteristics of Lamps

> A lamp whose flame turns to the left, possesses a dull radiance, emits sparks, is small in size, and—despite being supplied with pure oil and a good wick—extinguishes quickly, foretells an evil result. So too does a lamp that makes a crackling sound, trembles, has scattered rays, or goes out even in the absence of insects or wind. || 1 ||
> A lamp whose flame is compact, tall, steady, and bright; which is silent, beautiful, and turns toward the right; and which possesses the luster of a beryl <note>Sanskrit: *vaidurya*</note> or gold, quickly manifests prosperity. A lamp that burns with a pleasing and rising glow is likewise auspicious. The remaining characteristics should be understood as being similar to the omens of fire <note>referring to the sacrificial fire omens described in earlier chapters</note>, applied as appropriate. || 2 ||

# Chapter Eighty-Five

## Characteristics of Tooth-Sticks
<note>Dantakastha: Twigs used as disposable toothbrushes, selected from specific trees for medicinal and spiritual benefits.</note>

There are thousands of varieties of tooth-sticks derived from creepers, climbing plants, shrubs, and trees. To avoid excessive detail regarding all their possible effects, I shall describe only those that grant desired results. ॥ 1 ॥

One should not use tooth-sticks that are unknown, those still bearing leaves, those with an even number of joints <note>nodes</note>, those that are split, those that have dried up while still on the tree, or those stripped of their bark. ॥ 2 ॥

Using tooth-sticks from the *Vaikankata* <note>Flacourtia sapida</note>, *Shriphala* <note>Bael or Coconut</note>, or *Kashmari* <note>Gmelina arborea</note> trees brings divine luster. The *Kshema* tree brings a good wife; the Banyan (*Vata*) brings growth; the *Arka* <note>Calotropis</note> brings great energy; the *Madhuka* <note>Mahua</note> brings sons; and the *Kakubha* <note>Arjuna</note> tree makes one beloved by others. ॥ 3 ॥

Prosperity is gained from the *Shirisha* and *Karanja* trees. Success in one's desires is achieved through the *Plaksha* <note>Wavy-leaf fig</note>. One gains the respect of people through the Jasmine (*Jati*) and attains preeminence through the *Ashvattha* <note>Sacred Fig</note>. ॥ 4 ॥

Health and long life [are gained from the Jujube and Kantakari]...

->Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter in the Bhasha-tika <note>vernacular commentary</note> written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region, on the Brihat Samhita composed by the venerable teacher Varahamihira. ॥ 84 ॥<-

# The Varahi Samhita (Brihat Samhita)

Wealth increases by using tooth-sticks made from the Jujube or the Brihati plant, as well as from the Khadira <note>Acacia catechu</note> and Bilva <note>Wood apple</note> trees. Desired objects are obtained through the Atimuktaka <note>a mountain climber plant</note>, and the same results are gained from the Kadamba tree. || 5 ||

From the Neem tree comes the acquisition of wealth; from the Karavira <note>Oleander</note> comes the gain of food; and from the Bhandira tree, this same gain of food is produced in abundance. By using the wood of the Shami tree, one destroys enemies, and the Arjuna tree—as well as the Shyama creeper—likewise causes the destruction of those who hate you. || 6 ||

The Shala and Ashvakarna trees are said to bring dignity, as do the Bhadradaru <note>Deodar cedar</note> and the Atarushaka <note>Malabar nut</note>. A person becomes beloved by all people through the use of Priyangu, Apamarga <note>Prickly chaff flower</note>, Jambu <note>Java plum</note>, and Dadimba <note>Pomegranate</note> trees. || 7 ||

Facing either the North or the East, holding the desire of one's heart in mind, and being comfortably seated, one should brush with a blameless tooth-stick. Afterward, having washed it, one should discard it in a pure place. || 8 ||

If the discarded stick falls facing the person or stays in a peaceful direction <note>referring to auspicious compass points in Vastu/astrology</note>, it is auspicious; if it stands upright, it is exceedingly fortunate. Anything otherwise is declared inauspicious. If the stick stands up and then falls, it indicates that one will receive excellent food that day. || 9 || <meta>Checkmark symbol present after Sloka 9</meta>

->Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "Characteristics of Tooth-sticks," in the Shri Varahamihira Brihat Samhita. || 85 ||<-

Wealth increases from the tooth-brushing sticks of the Bilva and Khair trees, and all desired objects are obtained from the Atimuktaka tooth-stick; the fruit of the Kadamba tree is the same. || 5 || From the tooth-wood of the Neem comes the acquisition of money, from the Kaner comes the gain of food, and by using the tooth-stick of the Bhandira tree, much food is also obtained. By practicing tooth-cleansing with the wood of the Shami tree, one kills enemies, and the tooth-stick of the Arjuna tree destroys those who act with malice. || 6 ||

The tooth-sticks of the Shala and Ashvakarna trees give honor; honor is also gained by using the tooth-sticks of the Devdaru and Bamboo. If the tooth-stick is made from the Priyangu, Chirachita <note>Apamarga</note>, Jamun, and Pomegranate trees, then a man attains popularity in every way. || 7 || Facing East or North, keeping the water-oriented <note>purifying</note> desire well in the heart, and sitting comfortably, one should perform tooth-cleansing with a tooth-stick free of defects. Then, having washed it, throw it in a holy place. || 8 ||

If the thrown wood falls in front while situated in a peaceful direction, it is beneficial, and if it stands upright, it is extremely beneficial. Contrary to this (if it neither falls in a peaceful direction nor stands up), it is called inauspicious. Similarly, if the thrown tooth-stick stands up and then falls, it grants sweet food on that day. || 9 ||

# Now begins the Eighty-Sixth Chapter
## Chapter on Miscellaneous Omens

Having observed the opinions of Shukra <note>The planet Venus or the preceptor of the Asuras</note>, Indra, Brihaspati, Kapishthala, and Garuda, which Rishabha related from the views of Bhaguri and Devala; (1) and having seen the views of Bharadwaja and those expressed by the Great King of Kings, Shri Dravyavardhana, the ruler of Avanti <note>Modern-day Ujjain</note>; (2) and the views of the Seven Sages <note>The Saptarishi</note> composed in both Sanskrit and Prakrit <note>The vernacular languages of ancient India</note>, as well as the many teachings spoken by Garga and other authors of travel-manuals; (3) having seen all these, Varahamihira has affectionately composed this "Compendium of All Omens" for the excellent knowledge of his disciples. (4)

The good or bad karma <note>The law of cause and effect</note> performed by men in previous births—omens reveal the ripening <note>The fruition or result</note> of that karma to those who are setting out on a journey. (5)

Creatures that dwell in villages, forests, water, on land, or in the sky, and those that roam by day, by night, or both—their gender as male, female, or hermaphrodite should be understood through their cries, movements, looks, and utterances. (6)

Because of the differences in species and their unstable nature, the specific identity of these creatures is often not clearly perceived. For this reason, the Sages have composed these two verses regarding their general characteristics: (7)

Those creatures that have thick, high, and broad shoulders, a wide neck, a fine chest, a somewhat deep voice, and a steady gait are males. (8) Those with a thin chest, a small head, and a thin neck—

Having seen what Rishabha said to Bhaguri and Devala based on the opinions of Shukra, Indra, Brihaspati, Kapishthala, and Garuda; (1) and observing the opinion of Bharadwaja, and what the Great King of Kings of Ujjain, Shri Dravyavardhana, said, and the opinions of the Seven Sages written in Prakrit and Sanskrit, and what Garga and other travel-experts have said—having seen all that, I, Varahamihira, have created this "Compendium of All Omens" filled with excellent knowledge for the pleasure of my disciples. (2-4) The auspicious or inauspicious deeds that men have done in a previous life, birds and other creatures manifest the ripening of those deeds at the time of departure; this is what is known as "Shakuna" <note>Omens</note>. (5) Creatures living in villages, forest-dwellers, water-dwellers, land-dwellers, sky-dwellers, day-roamers, night-roamers, and those roaming both day and night are known as male, female, or hermaphrodite by their gait, sight, sound, and speech. Those with small mouths, small feet, little prowess, and who always make sweet sounds should be considered female creatures, and those in whom the characteristics of both male and female are found should be considered neuter. || 9 || Which omen belongs to the village and which to the forest will be known through worldly practice. Because I favor brevity, I will only discuss the subject as it pertains to the requirements of a journey. || 10 || On the road, the fruit of the omen falls upon oneself; in the army, upon the King; in the city, upon the Deity (the lord of the city); and in trade, upon the leader. Among equals, it falls upon the one who is eldest in caste, knowledge, or age. || 11 || From sunrise until the first watch of the day has passed, the Northeast is the direction the sun has left, the East is where the sun has arrived, and the Southeast is where the sun is going. In this way, during the eight watches <note>a 'pahar' or watch is roughly 3 hours</note>, the sun moves through the East and other directions one by one. The direction from which the sun has departed is called *Angarini* (Burning). The direction in which the sun is currently situated is called *Dipta* (Blazing). The direction into which the sun is about to enter is named *Dhumita* (Smoking). The remaining five directions are *Shanta* (Peaceful). If a bad omen occurs in the "Released" direction, consider its fruit to have already passed. In the "Attained" direction, the fruit of a bad omen occurs that very day. In the "Approaching" direction, the fruit of the bad omen should be known to occur in the future. || 12 || The auspicious or inauspicious results from the fifth direction relative to the Burning/Blazing directions are equal at all times, and for the remaining two directions, the result should be told according to the nearest direction. || 13 || The fruit of an omen situated nearby or below occurs quickly; the fruit of an omen situated high up or far away occurs with delay. The omen reveals its fruit based on the growth or injury of its location; that is, if the omen is perched on a place that grows daily, such as a tree, the fruit is auspicious. If the omen sits in a place that daily decays, it is a giver of inauspicious results. || 14 || Moment, lunar day, lunar mansion, wind...

The intensity of an omen increases progressively when influenced by the sun. An omen is considered **Action-Intense** <note>Sanskrit: *kriyadipta*</note> based on its movement, position, disposition, voice, and physical gestures. || 15 ||
There are ten such varieties of intensity. Furthermore, those omens <note>birds or animals</note> that consume grass and fruits are considered **Gentle** <note>Sanskrit: *saumya*</note> and peaceful. Those that consume meat or impure substances <note>such as excrement</note> are considered **Fierce** <note>Sanskrit: *raudra*</note>, while those that eat grain are known as **Mixed** <note>neither entirely gentle nor fierce</note>. || 16 ||
Omens are considered most auspicious when they are situated on palaces, temples, auspicious objects, or beautiful places; or when they are perched upon trees yielding honey, sap, milk, fruits, or flowers. || 17 ||
Diurnal creatures are powerful during their time <note>daylight</note> when situated on mountains or high ground. Nocturnal creatures are powerful when near water. Among these beings, the female is more powerful than the neuter, and the male is more powerful than the female. || 18 ||
They possess strength when endowed with speed, noble breed, physical power, proper positioning, joy, vital essence <note>Sanskrit: *sattva*</note>, and a clear voice, or when moving in a favorable direction from their natural habitat. Lacking these qualities, they are considered powerless. || 19 ||

# Chapter 86: With Commentary

<page-num>357</page-num>
->Header: With Language Commentary, Chapter 86<-

During the final watch of the night, the <term>Naptrika</term><note>A specific nocturnal bird, likely a nightjar</note>, the Owl, and the <term>Pingala</term><note>The spotted owlet</note> are all considered auspicious. However, for women, all these omens should be interpreted in the reverse manner. **[49]**

When going to meet a king, or when entering a house, all omens should be observed in the same way as one would for a journey. This also applies when ascending a mountain, entering a forest, or crossing a river. **[50]**

If two birds exhibiting <term>Kriya-dipta</term><note>Agitated or "burning" behavior/calls</note> move to the left and right, they are beneficial. However, if those same two birds move to the front and the back of the traveler, they are known as <term>Paridha</term><note>Literally "a bolt" or "obstruction"</note>, which leads to the destruction of the traveler. **[51]**

But if those same two birds stay in their respective positions—the left one on the left and the right one on the right—and remain calm in their cries and movements, this is called the <term>Shakuna-dwara</term><note>The "Gateway of Omens"</note>, which ensures the success of the objective. **[52]**

Some authorities maintain that the "Gateway of Omens" occurs when birds of the same species, exhibiting peaceful behavior and remaining silent, are positioned on both sides of the traveler. **[53]**

If one bird gives permission for the journey and another forbids it, this is known as a "Contradiction." This is highly inauspicious for the traveler, or one must follow whichever omen is considered more powerful. **[54]**

If an omen first indicates "entry" and then indicates "departure," it foretells success with ease. In the case of entering a home, the reverse of this pattern indicates success. **[55]**

If a bird first permits a journey but then the same bird blocks it, it foretells death at the hands of an enemy, a riot, or a disease for the traveler. **[56]**

---

<margin>If the rules for a journey are met, these are auspicious during the day.</margin> In the forenoon, the Indian Roller, the <term>Vanjula</term><note>A type of wagtail or cane-bird</note>, and the Cock should be observed as they would be for a departure (journey). **[48]**

In the remaining part of the night, the Naptrika, Owl, and Pingala should be counted as auspicious, but for women, all omens should be taken in reverse. **[49]**

When visiting a King or entering a home, all omens should be observed just as they are for a journey; similarly, when climbing a mountain, entering a forest, or crossing a river, omens should be viewed as if one were on a journey. **[50]**

If two birds with "agitated action" go to the left and right directions, they are bringers of welfare. If those same two birds move to the front and back, they are named *Paridha*, which is a cause for the destruction of the traveler. **[51]**

However, if those same two birds are situated in their proper places—meaning the one on the left stays left and the one on the right stays right—and they make sounds and movements with a peaceful disposition, then it is called the "Gateway of Omens" and they fulfill the work of the traveler. **[52]**

Some say that if birds of a single species, with peaceful movements and without sound, are situated on both sides of the traveler, it is auspicious. **[53]**

If one bird gives the order for the journey and another bird stops the journey, that omen is given the name "Contradiction"; this is extremely inauspicious for the one who is traveling. **[54]**

If an omen first enters and then leaves, success is achieved with happiness. However, in an entry (such as entering a house), the opposite of this leads to the success of the work. **[55]**

If a bird first gives the order for the journey and then that same bird later stops it, it tells of the traveler's death by an enemy, or a riot, or even a disease. When moving— <note>The text ends mid-sentence as a catchword for the next page.</note>

<term>Shakuna</term> <note>omens, usually derived from the flight or cries of birds</note> situated to the left in a "blazing" <note>dipta: a technical term for an omen that is ill-omened due to its direction, timing, or harsh nature</note> direction reveal fear. If a <term>shakuna</term> is "blazing" right at the start of an undertaking, it causes fear regarding that work for an entire year. || 57 ||

<term>Shakuna</term> that are "blazing" by virtue of the lunar day, the wind, the sun, the asterism, the location, or their physical movement are, in that order, terrifying for one's wealth, army, strength, body, desires, and actions. || 58 ||

If a <term>shakuna</term> is "blazing" due to the sound of clouds <note>thunder</note>, there is fear from the wind. <term>Shakuna</term> that are "blazing" during both twilights <note>dawn and dusk</note> create fear arising from weapons. || 59 ||

If a <term>shakuna</term> is perched upon a funeral pyre, hair, or a skull, it bestows death, imprisonment, or execution. If perched upon thorny trees, wood, or ashes, it gives strife, exhaustion, and sorrow. || 60 ||

If all the aforementioned "blazing" <term>shakuna</term> are situated upon worthless stones, an unknown fear occurs. However, "peaceful" <note>shanta: favorable or calm</note> omens diminish all the [negative] results previously mentioned. || 61 ||

One should know that those making harsh noises and those engaged in eating are, respectively, givers of failure and givers of success. If a <term>shakuna</term> moves from its place while continuing to cry out, it indicates a journey; if it returns to that same spot, it signifies someone's arrival. || 62 ||

A <term>shakuna</term> "blazing" in its voice indicates strife; one "blazing" in its location indicates war. If a <term>shakuna</term> first makes a high-pitched sound and then a low-pitched sound, it indicates that the traveler will be a victim of theft. || 63 ||

If a <term>shakuna</term> remains "blazing" and crying out in a single location for one week, it brings destruction to the village. If it cries out in one location for two seasons <note>four months</note>, six months, or a full year, it becomes the destroyer of the city, the country, and the kings, respectively. || 64 ||

...fear. If all these birds cry out with a uniform tone, they foretell death. || 72 ||

If the omen-bird is perched on the top, the middle, or the root <note>the base</note> of a tree, it signifies the arrival of men mounted on elephants, horses, and chariots respectively. If the bird is perched on a long object, on a lotus, or on the front of a frame <note>likely a door frame or pedestal</note>, it signifies the arrival of men on boats or palanquins. || 73 ||

If the bird sits on a high part of a cart or in its shadow, in the East or the intermediate directions, a person accompanied by a royal umbrella <note>a sign of high status or royalty</note> will arrive within one, three, five, or seven days. || 74 ||

Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirriti, Varuna, Pavana, Chandra, and Shankara <note>Shiva</note> are the eight lords of the directions starting from the East. Among these, all cardinal directions are considered masculine, and the intermediate directions <note>the corners</note> are feminine. || 75 ||

By dividing the eight directions into thirty-two sections, one should arrange the following signs: trees, palms, split bamboo, clothes, aquatic products, reeds, leather, and silk strips; also physical exercise, fire, chirping, strife, water, fetters, mantras, and the sound of cows; the colors red, yellow, black, and white (with mixed colors in the corners); and the signs of a flag, a burnt object, a cremation ground, a cave, water, a mountain, a sacrifice, and a roar. Through these, one should understand the fears arising from specific combinations or other localized dangers. || 76 || 77 || 78 ||

In the classification of women <note>corresponding to the intermediate directions</note>, there are the large woman, the maiden, the deformed woman, the foul-smelling woman, the woman in blue garments, the wicked woman, the very tall woman, and the widow. These serve as indicators for interpreting specific combinations of omens. || 79 ||

...a widow in the Northwest corner; a meeting occurs with a woman from whichever direction the omen appears, or that woman causes anxiety. || 79 || Furthermore, following the order of the directions, there are correspondences for: a handsome person, gold, the sick, or women; or sheep, goats, vehicles, sacrifices, or herds of cows. # Now begins the eighty-eighth chapter.

## On Omens—The Cries of Creatures.

The Shyama <note>Indian Robin</note>, the Hawk, the Eagle <note>literally "hare-killer"</note>, the Vanjula, the Peacock, the Shrikarna <note>a species of bird</note>, the Chakravaka <note>Ruddy Shelduck</note>, the Blue Jay, the Andiraka, the Wagtail, the Parrot, the Crow, the three types of Pigeons, the Bharadwaja <note>Skylark</note>, the Kulala, the Rooster, the Donkey, the Green Pigeon, the Vulture, the Monkey, the Phenta bird, the Kukkuta, the Purnakuta, and the Sparrow—all these are declared to be day-wanderers. ॥ 1 ॥ The Fox, the Pingala <note>Spotted Owlet</note>, the Chippika, the Bat, the Owl, and the Hare—all these wander at night. If any of these wander outside of their natural time, it signifies the destruction of the country or the King...

---

<margin>Artisans face fear.</margin> In the south, there is the destruction of righteousness, and if an omen occurs in the section following that, death occurs via fire, sudden assault, or a cunning person. ॥ 43 ॥ If an omen occurs on the spoke of the western direction, artisans face fear; in the northwest corner, there is the killing of donkeys and camels, and in this same place, humans face fear from cholera and poison. ॥ 44 ॥ If a "blazing" omen occurs in the north, there is loss of wealth and distress to Brahmins, and in the northeast corner, there is agony of the mind. If a "blazing" omen occurs at the center <note>navel</note>, there is distress for villagers and cowherds, and the death of the one who is traveling. ॥ 45 ॥

# The Varahi Samhita
## Chapter on Omens

...otherwise, it leads to the destruction of crops or the downfall of kings. **(2)**

The horse, man, snake, camel, leopard, lion, bear, monitor lizard, wolf, mongoose, deer, dog, goat, cow, tiger, swan, spotted deer, forest deer, jackal, porcupine, cuckoo, cat, crane, and hog—these creatures wander both by day and by night; that is, they are <term>amphibious in time</term><note>Original: "ubhayachara," meaning they are active during both day and night cycles.</note>. **(3)**

The *Bhasha*, *Kubapuri*, *Karabaka*, and *Karayika* are known by the collective name *Purnakuta*. The owl and its female counterpart are called *Pingalika*, *Pechika*, and *Hakka*. **(4)**

The *Kapotaki* <note>a type of dove</note> is known as *Shyama*, and the *Vanjula* bird is called *Khadirachanchu* <note>literally "catechu-beaked"</note>. The muskrat is called *Nripasuta* <note>"king's daughter"</note>, and the donkey is referred to as *Baleya*. **(5)**

The bird that breaks the banks of ponds is called *Ekaputraka*, and the *Kalahakarika* is called *Rala*. The *Rala* has a body only two fingers long and makes a sound like a cricket on the ground at night. **(6)**

According to the people of the Eastern lands, the *Durvalika* is named *Bhandika*; its appearance on the right side is considered auspicious. The *Chikkara* belongs to the deer family, and the *Krikavaku* is said to be the rooster. **(7)**

The *Gartta-Kukkuta* <note>"ditch-cock"</note> is famously known as the *Kulala-Kukkuta* <note>"potter's cock"</note>. The term *Grihagodhika* <note>"house-lizard"</note> should be understood to mean the *Kudachamatsya* <note>the common wall lizard</note>. **(8)**

The terms *Kroda*, *Divya*, and *Dhanvana* are names for the hog. The word *Usra* refers to the cow. The dog is called *Sarameya*, and the *Chataka* species is called *Shukarika*. **(9)**

In this manner, one should learn the names given to these creatures in various regions from the learned men there. To understand the knowledge of omens and their cries, one must carefully reflect and apply these names according to the scientific treatises. **(10)**

# Chapter 88: The Signs of the Spotted Owlet

If the bird remains silent for a long time after a single cry, or if it only echoes after a long delay, it is not considered auspicious. <note>original: "स्यादेकरुते प्रतिरौति चिरेण"</note> ॥ 37 ॥ The *Pingala* <note>The Spotted Owlet (Athene brama), considered a bird of omen in Sanskrit tradition</note> brings good fortune when it makes the sounds **"Chirill-Virill"**; however, all other sounds it produces are categorized as "Blazing" <term>Pradipta: sounds that indicate danger or negative energy</term>. ॥ 38 ॥

The cry **"Ishi"** forbids one from starting a journey, while the sound **"Kushu-Kushu"** foretells a quarrel. I shall now describe the ritual method by which the bird reveals the success of a desired task. ॥ 39 ॥

### The Ritual of Inquiry

At the time of twilight at the end of the day, one should approach the tree where the bird resides. After purifying oneself, one should worship the gods—starting with the Great Ancestor Brahma—and the tree itself using new cloths and fragrant substances <note>such as incense or sandalwood paste</note>. ॥ 40 ॥

At midnight, standing alone in the South-East direction <note>original: "Agni-dik," the direction governed by the fire-god Agni</note> from the tree, one should bind the bird with oaths—both divine and earthly—and ask about the intended matter using the following *Mantra* <note>sacred chant</note>, spoken loudly enough for the bird to hear: ॥ 41 ॥

> "O Auspicious One! Know that I have prompted you for this specific purpose. O Blessed Lady, you are celebrated as the knower of all speech." ॥ 42 ॥
>
> "I take my leave now and shall depart, but I must know the truth. Returning in the morning, I shall ask you again while standing in the South-Eastern direction." ॥ 43 ॥
>
> "Whatever I have urged you to reveal, you ought to explain to me through your own movements and cries, O Blessed One, so that I may understand it clearly and without confusion." ॥ 44 ॥

When these words have been spoken to the bird perched high in the tree, if it responds with the cry **"Chirill-Virill,"** it signifies the successful accomplishment of one's goal. However, if there is great agitation in that direction...

# Chapter 89
## Omens: The Circle of Dogs

When a dog, after urinating, moves forward stretching its body toward a man, a horse, an elephant, a water-pot, a saddle, a milky tree <note>trees that exude sap, like the Banyan or Peepal</note>, a heap of bricks, an umbrella, a bed, a seat, a mortar, a banner, a fly-whisk, a grassy plot, or a place in flower, then the traveler’s task will be successful. If it urinates on moist cow-dung, there will be an arrival of sweet food. If it urinates on something dry, the food received will be dry. If it urinates on jaggery or sweetmeats—

---

If it makes the sound *Kara*, the task is successful. If it utters the sounds *Kucha-kucha* or *Dishikara*, there will be great distress || 45 || If it does not give voice—that is, if it makes no sound at all—the desired goal is achieved. Then, one should determine the fruit from the previously mentioned directional circle. The result of the *Pingala* bird sitting on a high, middle, or low branch can be said to be high, middle, or low accordingly || 46 || The omens of the lizard occur in the inner and outer parts of the directional circle. The *Chichid* sound of the musk-shrew is called "blazing" and the *Tittid* sound is called "full" || 47 ||

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter in the vernacular commentary composed by Pandit Baladev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the *Brihat Samhita* authored by the great teacher Sri Varahamihira. || 88 ||

# Chapter 89: Including the Vernacular Commentary
### Page 375

If a dog eats jaggery <note>unrefined cane sugar</note> or sweetmeats while walking, it indicates the traveler will obtain the same. However, if a dog urinates upon a poisonous tree <note>original: "vishataru," likely the Strychnine tree</note>, thorny bushes, wood, stones, a withered tree, bones, or at a cremation ground, and then runs ahead of the traveler, it foretells misfortune for the person on the journey.

If a dog urinates on a new or unbroken bed, or on a potter’s vessels, it signifies a moral blemish or "defect" involving a maiden in the household. If these items (the bed or vessels) are already in use, the misfortune falls upon the mistress of the house. The same results apply to omens involving sandals <note>original: "upānah"</note>. If a dog urinates upon a cow and then moves ahead of the traveler, it predicts the birth of "mixed castes" <note>original: "varna-sankara"; a traditional term for the blurring of social boundaries</note>.

When a dog approaches a traveler while firmly holding a shoe in its mouth, it signifies the successful completion of the task. If it approaches with meat in its mouth, it predicts the acquisition of wealth. If it carries a moist bone, it is considered auspicious. However, if it approaches carrying a flaming piece of wood or a dry bone, it foretells the death of the traveler.

If a dog approaches a man while carrying a human head, hand, foot, or a "peaceful" (extinguished) coal in its mouth, it signifies the acquisition of land. If it carries torn cloth or rags, it indicates death; however, <insert>some authorities say</insert> that a dog arriving with cloth is actually an auspicious sign.

If a dog enters a house carrying a dry bone in its mouth, the master of that house will die. If it enters the house carrying a chain, a piece of wet vine, an elephant’s tethering rope, or any binding material, it foretells imprisonment or bondage <note>original: "bandhana"</note>. During the time of departure, if a dog licks the traveler's feet, flaps its ears, or jumps upon them, it indicates that the traveler will face obstacles and opposition.

# Varahi Samhita
### Page 376

If a dog scratches its own body, it opposes a journey; if it sleeps with its legs pointing upward, it is always a harbinger of misfortune. || 1 ||

If a single dog or many gathered together howl in the middle of a village at sunrise while facing the sun, they announce that the land will soon have a different ruler <note>original: "deshadhipamanyamashu" - literally a change in the lord of the land or landlord</note>. || 2 ||

If a dog stands in the southeast <term>southeast (Agni-kon): the direction associated with the fire god Agni</term> facing the sun and howls, it brings fear of thieves and fire in a short time. At midday, howling while facing the sun indicates the fear of fire and death. In the afternoon, such howling portends a quarrel involving the shedding of blood. || 3 ||

At sunset, if it howls facing the sun, it quickly indicates danger for farmers. During the first watch of the night <note>Pradosha: the period just after sunset</note>, if it faces the northwest <term>northwest (Vayu-kon): the direction associated with the wind god Vayu</term> and howls, it creates fear arising from storms and thieves. || 4 ||

At midnight, if it faces north and makes a sound, it foretells distress for Brahmins <note>the priestly or scholarly class</note> and the stealing of cattle. At the end of the night, if it faces the northeast <term>northeast (Ishan-kon): the direction associated with Shiva/the Supreme Spirit</term> and howls, it reveals the defilement of maidens, fire, and miscarriages. || 5 ||

If dogs stand upon heaps of straw or atop palaces and grand houses and howl with high-pitched voices, they predict intense rain during the monsoon; at other times, they signify death, fire, and disease. || 6 ||

If a dog makes a sound in front of a person performing a task, it stops the journey. || 14 || A sound with the 'U' vowel or an 'O' vowel sound on the left side indicates the attainment of wealth/success. An 'Au' sound expresses delay, and all types of sounds made from behind express a prohibition. || 15 || All those dogs who, as if beaten by a staff, repeatedly make a high-pitched sound like a conch and run in a circle, manifest emptiness, death, and fear. || 16 || If a dog shows its teeth and licks the edges of its lips, those who know the fruit of this expect a sweet meal. If it licks the mouth but not the edges of the lips, then even if one has started eating, the food becomes obstructed. || 17 || If dogs gather in a village or city and bark repeatedly, they manifest distress for the lord of that city or village. Wild dogs, being like deer, are not to be considered in this specific way. || 18 || Barking of a dog near a tree results in rain; barking near an Indra-pillar causes pain to the minister; barking in the Vayu (Northwest) corner of the house causes fear for the harvest; and barking at the city gate causes pain to the city dwellers. || 19 || If a dog barks on top of a bed, there is fear for its masters. Making a sound while situated in a vehicle brings fear; if it makes a sound while on the left side of a human settlement, it expresses fear of enemies. || 20 ||

<header>Chapter 90 with Commentary</header>

# Now Begins the Ninetieth Chapter
## On Omens: The Cries of Jackals

In terms of the results they portend, jackals are similar to dogs; the primary distinction is that jackals reach their rutting season during the <term>Shishira</term> <note>the dewy or late winter season, typically January to March</note> season. A cry that begins with "Hoo-hoo" and ends with "Ta-ta" is considered a "full" or auspicious sound; all other vocalizations are classified as "blazing" <note>original: "pradipta" — a technical term in augury for harsh, alarming, or inauspicious sounds</note>. || 1 ||

The "Kakka" sound of the female fox <note>original: "Lomashika"</note> is her "full" sound, being her natural cry. Any other sounds she makes that deviate from her nature are all declared by the sages to be "blazing" or ill-omened. || 2 ||

A female jackal <note>original: "Shiva"</note> positioned in the East or the North is auspicious. One that is "calm" <note>original: "shanta" — meaning facing a direction not associated with the sun or harsh winds</note> is honored as a good omen everywhere. || 3 ||

<margin>Regarding omens, see page 355, verse 34</margin>

If she faces a "smoky" direction <note>a direction associated with ill fortune in that specific hour</note> and gives a "blazing" cry, it portends the destruction of the regents of those directions. || 3<sup>a</sup> ||

A "blazing" cry is inauspicious in all directions, and it is especially unlucky during the day. A female jackal facing the sun, positioned to the left of an army or within a city, brings great distress. || 4 ||

If she cries "Yahi" <note>Go!</note>, she foretells danger from fire. A "Ta-ta" sound is a herald of death. A "Dhig-dhig" <note>Fie! or Shame!</note> sound announces a great sin or crime, and a jackal whose mouth appears to emit flames <note>sajvala</note> destroys the country. || 5 ||

However, some scholars claim that the "flaming" appearance of a jackal is not necessarily dreadful. They argue that her mouth naturally glows like the sun or fire due to the properties of her saliva. || 6 ||

If a female jackal in the South responds to the cry of another jackal, it foretells death by hanging. If she responds from the West, she predicts death by drowning. || 7 ||

Remaining unagitated while hearing these sounds is desired; it leads to the acquisition of wealth...

---

<note>The following is the vernacular commentary (Bhashatika) translating the Sanskrit verses above.</note>

In terms of results, the jackal is equal to the dog. The specialty is that in the <term>Shishira</term> season, they experience their rut. Following the "Hoo-hoo" sound, the "Ta-ta" sound is their "full" (complete/auspicious) sound, and all other tones are called "blazing" (alarming). || 1 ||

The "Kakka" sound of the female fox is full and is her natural sound. Those sounds which are contrary to her nature are all called "blazing." Female jackals located in the East and North directions are bringers of welfare. A "calm" one is also honored everywhere. If a female jackal faces a "smoky" direction and makes a blazing sound, the lords of the directions are destroyed. || 2 || 3 ||

In all directions, a blazing sound is a bringer of inauspiciousness, especially during the day. A female jackal with her face toward the sun, located to the left of an army or in the South of a city, is a giver of pain. || 4 ||

If the pack of jackals makes the sound "Yahi," it warns of fear of fire; by making the "Ta-ta" sound, she indicates a dead person. The "Dhik-adhik" sound is sinful, and the jackal from whose mouth flames of fire emerge destroys the country. || 5 ||

Some pundits say that the dreadfulness of a "flaming" jackal is not seen, because due to the mixture of saliva, her mouth remains naturally radiant like the sun or fire. || 6 ||

If a jackal in the South direction is "echoed" (meaning another jackal cried first) and then makes a sound, it indicates death will occur by hanging.

<summary>This page details the omens associated with the cries and positions of jackals and foxes, distinguishing between natural "full" sounds and alarming "blazing" sounds. It provides specific predictions for different vocalizations and directions, such as fire, death, or national destruction.</summary>

# Chapter Ninety-One
## Omens: The Movements of Wild Animals

When wild deer come to the borders of a settlement and cry out, or stay there, or wander about, or rush in, they indicate dangers—past, present, or future. If they wander about making "blazing" <note>Sanskrit: 'dipta' - a technical term in omens referring to harsh, distressed, or ill-omened sounds or directions</note> noises, they cause the place to become desolate. || 1 ||

If these wild deer are answered by the cries of domestic animals, it causes fear. If they are answered by other wild animals, it indicates a siege. If they are answered by both domestic and wild animals, it signifies that the people will be taken captive. || 2 ||

If a wild animal stands at the gate of a city, a siege is predicted; if it enters the city, destruction follows. If it gives birth inside a house, it foretells death; if it stays there, it brings fear; and if it simply enters a house, the imprisonment of the owner is predicted. || 3 ||

(Thus ends the sixth chapter on the movements of deer in the General Omens)
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter in the Brihat Samhita of Shri Varahamihira.

---

# Chapter Ninety-Two
## Omens: The Gestures of Cows

Cows that appear miserable or dejected bring misfortune to the ruler. If they scratch or strike the ground with their hooves, they portend disease. If their large eyes are filled with tears, they bring death. If they are frightened and low/bellow, it indicates a threat from thieves. || 1 ||

---

<margin>Hindi Commentary</margin>
If wild deer come to the boundary of a village and make noise, or stay there while wandering, or run about in a particular manner, they reveal fears of the past, future, and present. If they wander around making "blazing" sounds, they make that place empty. || 1 || If village animals cry out after those deer, it is a cause for fear. If wild animals cry out after village animals, the city is surrounded by enemies. If both wild and domestic animals cry out after one another, the enemies will take the people of that city captive. || 2 || If a wild animal comes and stands at the door, enemies will surround the city. If a wild animal enters well into the house, the city will be destroyed. If a wild animal gives birth in the house, there will be death. If it stays in the house, there is fear, and by its coming into the house, the master of the house faces imprisonment. || 3 ||

# Now begins the Ninety-Third Chapter.
## On Omens: The Movements of Horses.

In the discharge of waste, it is not auspicious if a glow <note>original: "jvalanam" - refers to a supernatural fire, smoke, or glowing light appearing on the animal</note> appears on the seat or the left side; in other places, it is praised. # Now Begins the Ninety-Fourth Chapter.
## On Omens: The Movements and Signs of Elephants.

To determine the proper place for carving, one should measure the circumference of the tusk at its root, double that length starting from the root, and discard that portion. The remaining part may be used. For elephants from marshy lands <note>original: "anūpacarāṇām"</note>, one should leave a little more; for mountain-dwelling elephants, a little less. || 1 ||

If, upon cutting the ivory, marks appear resembling the *Shrivatsa* <note>an auspicious curl or knot symbol</note>, the *Vardhamana* <note>a ritual water-vessel or platter</note>, an umbrella, a banner, or a fly-whisk, it portends health, victory, increase in wealth, and happiness. || 2 ||

If the marks resemble weapons, victory is assured. If they look like a *Nandyavarta* <note>a complex labyrinthine palace or temple pattern</note>, one recovers a lost kingdom. If the mark resembles a clod of earth, it signifies the re-acquisition of a territory previously held. || 3 ||

A mark in the shape of a woman portends one's own destruction. If a mark like a *Bhringara* <note>a ceremonial water pitcher</note> appears, it signifies the birth of a son. A mark like a pot indicates the discovery of treasure, while a mark like a staff <note>original: "dandena"</note> signifies obstacles to a journey. || 4 ||

If the marks resemble a lizard, a monkey, or a snake, it foretells famine, disease, and subjugation by enemies. If the shapes resemble a vulture, an owl, a crow, or a hawk, it indicates a plague among the people. || 5 ||

If the cut reveals the shape of a noose or a headless torso <note>original: "kabandha"</note>, it portends the death of the king. If blood flows from the cut, the people will face calamity. If the ivory is black, dark-grey <note>original: "shyava" - a mix of yellow and black</note>, rough, or foul-smelling, it is inauspicious. || 6 ||

If the cut is smooth, white, fragrant, and glossy, it brings good fortune. The falling or withering of the tusks is similar in effect to...

# The Varahi Samhita

### On the Characteristics of Elephants

If the tusk becomes discolored or soiled, the result should be understood as being the same as if the tusk had broken. ॥ 7 ॥

The gods, the demons, and humans reside respectively in the root, the middle, and the tip of the elephant's tusk. I shall now describe the great, middling, and slight effects, as well as the results that manifest quickly, in a moderate timeframe, or after a long duration. ॥ 8 ॥

Now, the results of a broken tusk are described: If the right tusk breaks in the section belonging to the gods, demons, or humans, it brings about the destruction of the king, the country, and the army. If the left tusk breaks, it kills the king's sons, the royal priest, and the elephant keepers <note>original: "hastipala" or mahout</note>, along with the forest-dwellers and the commanders of the vanguard. ॥ 9 ॥

If both tusks are seen to be broken, it indicates the total destruction of the king’s lineage. However, if the <term>Ascendant</term> <note>Lagna</note>, the lunar day <note>Tithi</note>, and the lunar mansion <note>Nakshatra</note> are auspicious, the good effects increase; otherwise, the inauspicious effects prevail. ॥ 10 ॥

If the middle part of the left tusk is broken or chipped by striking it against a "milk-tree" <note>trees with milky sap, often considered sacred or medicinal</note>, a fruiting tree, a flowering tree, or against a riverbank, it brings about the destruction of enemies. If it happens under other circumstances, the result is the opposite. ॥ 11 ॥

If an elephant’s gait suddenly falters, if its ears stop flapping out of fear, if it appears very dejected and rests its trunk <note>original: "hasta" - literally 'hand', referring to the trunk</note> on the ground, if it breathes softly and deeply, if its eyes are quickly half-closed, if it is prone to sleep, moves erratically, eats unwholesome food, or repeatedly voids blood or excrement—such an elephant brings fear to its master. ॥ 12 ॥

On the other hand, if the elephant, by its own will, joyfully crushes anthills, stumps, shrubs, bushes, or trees; if it moves quickly with a cheerful gaze in a direction favorable to a journey, raising and lowering its head; and if, at the time of putting on its girth-ropes <note>harnessing for travel or battle</note>, it repeatedly sprays a fine mist or trumpets loudly, or if it is in a state of <term>Mada</term> <note>rut; a state of high energy and temporal secretion in elephants</note>, it brings victory...

### Now begins the Ninety-Fifth Chapter.

->Omenology: The Behavior of Crows. <gloss>(A detailed explanation of the crow's actions)</gloss><-

For those living in the eastern regions, a crow appearing on the right is auspicious, while the *Karayika* <note>a specific species of bird, likely a crane or a smaller crow-relative</note> is auspicious on the left. If the nest is at the top of the tree in the south or north, there will be excellent rainfall. ॥ 3 ॥ If the nest is in the southeast, there will be scattered rains; if in the southwest, the autumn crops will reach completion; in the remaining directions, there will be a good harvest and plenty...

# Chapter 95: The Omen of the Crow
### With the Vernacular Commentary

If a crow places leaves upon a bed, it portends the death of the husband. However, if it brings jewels, flowers, and similar items, it announces the birth of a son or a daughter. <note>Verse 12</note>

If a crow arrives with its beak full of sand, grain, wet earth, flowers, or fruit, it indicates a gain of wealth. But if the crow carries away vessels or utensils from a human dwelling, it is a sign of impending fear. <note>Verse 13</note>

If a crow strikes a vehicle, a weapon, shoes, an umbrella, a person's shadow, or their limbs, it portends death. If it "honors" these things <note>likely meaning circling or landing gently without aggression</note>, it leads to honor for the person. If it drops excrement upon these items, it signifies the acquisition of food. <note>Verse 14</note>

Whatever object a crow brings from somewhere, the person will gain that very type of wealth; if the crow carries an object away, that wealth will be lost. Bringing a yellow object signifies gold, while a white cloth made of cotton signifies silver. <note>Verse 15</note>

Crows perched upon milky trees <note>trees that exude sap, like the Banyan or Peepal</note>, the Arjuna tree, the Vanjula tree, or on both banks and sandbanks of a river, signify rain if they caw. If they bathe in dust or water out of season, it indicates a period of foul weather or misfortune. <note>Verse 16</note>

A crow sitting in the hollow of a tree making a harsh, terrifying sound brings great fear. If it caws while looking at water or mimics the sound of a thundercloud, it is a bringer of rain. <note>Verse 17</note>

If a crow, agitated and flapping its wings, sits on a branch and strikes its own limbs, or brings a red object, burnt grass, or wood into the house, it portends a fear of fire. <note>Verse 18</note>

If a crow faces the sun while looking toward the East or other cardinal directions and caws from the house of a householder, the master of the house will face fear from the government <term>Rajabhaya: literally 'fear of the King' or legal authorities</term>, fear of thieves, imprisonment, quarrels, or fear related to livestock. <note>Verse 19</note>

# The Varāhīsaṃhitā
## On the Cries of Crows

-> For those desiring to travel <-

<page-num>394</page-num>

The cry *'Kā'* from a crow situated in its own nest is said to be fruitless <note>original: "niṣphala"; meaning it carries no prophetic weight</note>. However, the cry *'Kava'* is for one's own pleasure, and the cry *'Ka'* indicates the acquisition of oily substances <note>likely ghee or oil, signs of prosperity</note> and the meeting of friends. || 50 ||

The sound *'Kara'* indicates a quarrel; *'Kuru-kuru'* indicates joy; *'Kata-kata'* means one will receive curd-rice to eat. The cries *'Keke'* or *'Kuku'* announce the gain of wealth to the traveler. || 51 ||

If a crow in its nest makes the sound *'Khare-khare'*, it foretells the arrival of a traveler. The sound *'Kakhākhā'* portends the death of the traveler, while the sound *'Khal-khal'* indicates immediate rain on that very day. The sound *'Ā'* indicates an obstacle to the journey. || 52 ||

The cry *'Kākā'* foretells destruction for the traveler; *'Kākaṭi'* indicates the spoiling of food. The sound *'Kavakava'* indicates a place of affection or friendship, while *'Kagāku'* indicates imprisonment or bondage. || 53 ||

The sound *'Karakau'* predicts rain; *'Guḍa'* indicates fear or distress; *'Vaṭṭi'* indicates the acquisition of new clothes. If the crow cries *'Kalaya'*, it reveals a meeting between a Shudra <note>the laboring class</note> and Brahmins <note>the priestly class</note>. || 54 ||

The sound *'Phaṭ'* indicates the obtaining of fruit or the sight of fruit-bearers. *'Taṭ'* indicates that blows or an assault may occur. A cry sounding like *'Stri'* <note>Woman</note> indicates the gain of a woman. The sound *'Gaḍiti'* refers to cattle, and *'Puḍiti'* indicates the gain of flowers. || 55 ||

If a crow makes the sound *'Ṭāku-ṭāku'*, it is a cause for war or battle. *'Guhu'* indicates fear of fire. *'Kaṭakaṭa'* indicates a quarrel. The sounds *'Ṭākuli'*, *'Cinṭici'*, *'Kekeke'*, and *'Pura'* are all indicative of misfortune or defects. || 56 ||

These same results, which have been described through the cries and movements of a single crow, apply equally to a pair of crows...

# Chapter 95: On Omens (General Signs)

The behaviors described for crows apply equally to other birds. Similarly, the omens described for dogs apply to all other wild or domestic carnivorous animals with tusks or prominent teeth.
<note>The text draws a parallel between the specific omens of crows/dogs and broader categories of fauna.</note>
|| 57 ||

During the rainy season, if land-dwelling creatures move into the water and aquatic creatures come onto the land, it indicates abundant rainfall. However, if this reversal occurs during any other season, it foretells danger. If honeybees build a hive within a house, that house will soon become empty or deserted. If a blue-colored fly settles upon a person's head, it portends death.
|| 58 ||

If ants are seen casting their eggs into water, it is said that the rains will be withheld. Conversely, when they are seen carrying their eggs from low-lying ground up to a tree or higher ground, they foretell imminent rain.
|| 59 ||

The omen encountered at the very start of an undertaking <note>the "root" omen</note> determines the ultimate success or failure of that task. Any omens appearing during the course of the work will bear fruit only on that specific day. This is how all omens should be analyzed. At the commencement of any work, during a sacrificial rite, or when entering a house, a sneeze is never considered auspicious by the sages.
|| 60 ||

For a king who honors the science of omens, the experts declare that favorable signs indicate a prosperous period, the accomplishment of goals without obstacles, the protection of his capital, the gaining of allies, the fulfillment of desires, and freedom from disease.
|| 61 ||

Some sages, such as Kashyapa and others, say that the cries of birds heard after traveling a distance of one *Kosh* <note>approximately 2 miles or 3.2 km</note> are fruitless. If the first omen encountered is inauspicious, the king should perform five or six *Pranayamas* <note>breath control exercises</note> to neutralize the evil. If the second omen is also bad, he should perform sixteen such breaths. If the third omen is also unfavorable, he must return to his palace immediately.
|| 62 ||

->(Thus ends the tenth sub-section of General Omens, titled "The Cries of the Crow")<-

### Thus ends the Ninety-Fifth Chapter of the Brihat Samhita, composed by Shri Varahamihira.

---

**Commentary:**
The results for crows are the same for other birds. Similarly, the results for dogs apply to all wild or village animals with prominent teeth (carnivores) || 57 ||. In the rainy season, if land animals enter water and water animals come to land, there is much rain; at other times, it brings fear. If bees make a hive in a home, it becomes empty. A blue fly on the head means death || 58 ||. Ants putting eggs in water stops rain; moving them from low ground to trees brings rain || 59 ||. The first omen seen at the start of a journey lasts until the end; intermediate omens last only for that day. Sneezing at the start of work or entering a home is not auspicious || 60 ||. Scholars of omen-lore <term>Shakuna-shastra: the science of interpreting signs and omens</term> say that for a king who respects this science, good omens bring success, protection, and health || 61 ||. Some sages say omens after one *Kosh* are useless. If the first is bad, do breath exercises; if the third is bad, go home.

# Chapter 96
## On Omens: The Concluding Chapter

The expert who understands the cries of creatures should announce the results after considering the strength and weakness of the direction, the region, the physical gestures, the sound, the day, the lunar mansion <term>Nakshatra: one of the 27 sectors of the sky</term>, the auspicious time <term>Muhurta: a unit of time roughly 48 minutes</term>, the hour <term>Hora: an astrological hour</term>, the ritual division <term>Karana</term>, the rising sign, and whether the influence is long-lasting, fixed, or mixed. || 1 ||

Sages describe two types of outcomes for those established in their positions: the "upcoming" and the "fixed." Matters concerning kings, messengers, spies, and those born in foreign lands, as well as the lack of obstacles and one's own kin, are known as "Arrivals" <note>original: "Agama"</note>. || 2 ||

Captivity, gathering, eating, thieves, fire, rain, festivals, the birth of a son, slaughter, strife, and fear—these constitute the "Fixed" category. If the Moon is in a fixed sign at the time of rising, fixed matters are confirmed; if in a movable sign, the results are as described for "Movable" matters. || 3 ||

In fixed locations, such as stone buildings, temples, or near earth and water, fixed things...

---

The sound of an omen-bearer becomes fruitless <insert>if ignored</insert>. If the very first omen among them is inauspicious, one should perform five or six breath-control exercises <term>Pranayama: yogic breathing</term>. If the second omen is also inauspicious, perform sixteen breath-control exercises. If the third omen is also inauspicious, one should not proceed with the journey and should return home. || 62 ||

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter in the vernacular commentary composed by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region, on the Brihat Samhita <note>original: "Varahi Samhita"</note> written by the Great Teacher Varahamihira. || 95 ||

---

Scholars who understand sounds should illuminate all results after knowing the relative strength and weakness of the direction, gesture, region, voice, day, lunar mansion, auspicious time, astrological hour, ritual division, rising sign, long-duration, fixed, and dual-natured signs. || 1 || All omens illuminate the results of actions categorized as present, future, and fixed. Among these, kings, messengers, spies, and those arising from other countries are all "Present." These are famous under the names of "Kinship" and "Arrival." || 2 || Attachment, collection, food, thieves, fire, rain, festivals, offspring, killing, distress, and fear—all these belong to the "Fixed" class. If the Moon is with a fixed zodiac sign or if a fixed sign is rising, then fixed tasks are accomplished; those called "Movable" are determined in movable houses. || 3 || Motionless places, stones, palaces, temples, the earth...

<note>
1. Breath-control <gloss>Pranayama</gloss> is defined as the regulation of inhalation <gloss>Puraka</gloss>, retention <gloss>Kumbhaka</gloss>, and exhalation <gloss>Rechaka</gloss> according to the rule of the Gayatri mantra along with the sacred utterances <note>original: "Vyahriti"</note> and the mantra: "The waters are light, the essence is nectar, Brahman is the earth, atmosphere, and heaven, Om." The sequence is: retention is four times the duration of inhalation, and exhalation is half the duration of retention; this is the natural and reverse order.
</note>

# Chapter 96: With Commentary

->**The Interpretation of Omens**<-

For tasks involving movement or travel to distant lands, one should observe omens in mobile locations. ॥ 4 ॥ Omens that are "blazing" <note>original: "pradipta" - referring to a bird facing the sun or crying harshly</note> in watery signs, constellations, moments, or directions, or near water at the end of a fortnight, all bring rain. Even the peaceful cry of a water-dwelling creature indicates rain. ॥ 5 ॥

If a bird, "blazing" by the sun, cries in the south-eastern direction, at a specific ascendant or moment associated with fire, it foretells fear of fire. If it cries during the *Vishti* <note>an inauspicious astrological timing</note> period, or during the rising of Saturn’s signs <note>Capricorn or Aquarius</note>, or while perched on leafless vines or thorny trees, it indicates a threat from thieves. ॥ 6 ॥

A village bird that is "blazing" through its harsh voice and gestures, perched on a thorny tree, indicates strife—especially if it occurs during the ascendant of a planet like Mars <note>Aries or Scorpio</note> in the southwest direction or facing the observer. ॥ 7 ॥

If the ascendant is Cancer, or if the bird is in the sub-division <term>Navamsha</term> <note>a 1/9th division of a zodiac sign used for precision</note> of Taurus or Libra, and the bird cries facing downward in an intermediate direction while "blazing," it predicts a union with a woman associated with that specific direction. ॥ 8 ॥

When the ascendant is a masculine sign, the date is an odd-numbered day <note>such as the 1st, 3rd, or 5th of the lunar fortnight</note>, and a "blazing" male bird cries in a specific direction, it foretells a meeting between men. If the signs are mixed, a meeting with a eunuch <note>original: "shandaka/napunsaka"</note> is predicted. ॥ 9 ॥

In this manner, if the Sun’s own sign <note>Leo</note>, its sub-division, or the Sun itself is in the ascendant, a "blazing" omen indicates the arrival or departure of an important or high-ranking man. ॥ 10 ॥ Regarding all commenced...

# The Varahi Samhita
->Page 398<-

In all undertakings, one should calculate the *Vilaya* <note>a specific point of dissolution or outcome</note> from the Ascendant <term>Lagna: the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the time of inquiry</term> associated with the Sun. One should declare "Prosperity" or "Adversity" according to the sequence of the calculation. || 11 ||

If the Sun is in the twelfth house from the Ascendant at the time of the omen, the person will be blind in the right eye; if the Moon is in the twelfth, they will be blind in the left eye. If the Sun is in the Ascendant and is aspected by a malefic planet <term>Papagraha: "evil-seizing" planets like Mars or Saturn that portend difficulty</term>, the person is blind. If the Sun is in its own sign <note>Leo</note> and aspected by a malefic, the person will be a hunchback, deaf, or mentally disabled. || 12 ||

If a malefic planet, aspected by another malefic, is in the sixth house from the Ascendant, there will be a wound or scar on the limb corresponding to that zodiac sign. In this manner, all the signs and physical characteristics that I have previously described regarding the time of birth should be considered here as well. || 13 ||

If the Ascendant and its *Navamsha* <term>a one-ninth division of a zodiac sign used for precision</term> are in Moveable signs, the person's name has two syllables. In Fixed signs, the name has four syllables. In Dual signs, there are either two names, or a name of three or five syllables. || 14 ||

The five groups of five letters starting with *Ka* <note>the Sanskrit consonants categorized by their point of articulation</note> are assigned respectively to Mars, Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn. The eight letters starting with *Ya* belong to the Moon, and the vowels starting with *A* belong to the Sun. || 15 ||

The names of Agni (Fire), Varuna (Water), Kumara (Kartikeya), Vishnu, Indra, Indrani (the wife of Indra), and Brahma are assigned to the planets starting from the Sun. To determine the name of a desired object or person, one should use their intellect to combine these deities' names with the previously mentioned syllable counts (two, three, etc.). || 16 ||

# Now begins the Ninety-Seventh Chapter.
## On the Ripening of Effects.

The fruit of the Sun ripens in a fortnight; that of the Moon in a month; that of Mars according to its retrograde motion; that of Mercury until its disappearance from view; and that of Jupiter within a year. || 1 || The fruit of Venus ripens in six months; that of Saturn in a year; that of the Enemy of the Gods <note>original: "Suradvisha" - a title for Rahu, the demon who causes eclipses</note> (lunar eclipse) in half a year; that of a solar eclipse in one year; and the effects of the planet Tvashtar and the dark "Kila" <note>term: "Kila" - dark spots or wedge-shaped shadows observed on the solar disc</note> comets manifest immediately. || 2 || The fruit of a comet appears in three months; that of a white comet after seven nights; and the effects of halos, rainbows, twilight glows, and "cloud-needles" <note>term: "Abhrasuchi" - a specific vertical cloud formation or ray of light</note> manifest within seven days (a week). || 3 || Reversals of cold and heat (such as heat in winter), out-of-season fruits and flowers, the "burning of the quarters" <note>term: "Digdaha" - an atmospheric phenomenon where the horizon appears to be on fire</note>, the unnatural behavior of stable and moving objects, and abnormalities in birth manifest their results within six months. || 4 || The performance of actions that should not be done (unprecedented events), earthquakes, the absence of festivals, and improper sacrifices...

The Moon, Mars, Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, the Sun, and Saturn, according to their states, represent the human stages in omens: the milk-drinking infant, the child, the student (youth), the young man, the middle-aged man, the old man, and the very aged man respectively. || 17 ||
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter in the vernacular commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the Great Teacher Sri Varahamihira. || 96 ||

The numbers are: fire <note>3</note>, Rudra <note>11</note>, the Ashvins <note>2</note>, the Vasus <note>8</note>, and Agni <note>3</note>. || 1 || The elements <note>5</note>, a hundred <note>100</note>, the wings <note>2</note>, the Vasus <note>8</note>, and thirty-two; such is the measurement of the stars. The destruction of a fever or other disease should be predicted within as many days as there are stars. || 3 ||

The Ashvins, Yama, Agni, Brahma, the Moon, Rudra, Aditi, Jupiter, the Serpents, the Ancestors, the Yoni <note>Bhaga</note>, Aryaman, the Sun, Tvashtar, the Wind, Indra-Agni, and Mitra. || 4 || Indra, Nirriti, Water, the Universal Gods, Viranchi <note>Brahma</note>, Hari <note>Vishnu</note>, the Vasus, Varuna, Ajapada, Ahirbudhnya, and Pushan; these are the lords of the hymns <note>the presiding deities of the 28 Nakshatras</note>. || 5 ||

Mula, Ardra, Jyeshtha, and Ashlesha are the **Sharp** <term>Tikshna: intense or piercing</term> constellations. In these, success is found in assaults, mantra-incantations, summoning spirits <note>Vetala</note>, imprisonment, killing, and acts of division or discord. || 7 ||

The three Purvas, Bharani, and Magha—these five are the **Fierce** <term>Ugra: terrible or powerful</term> constellations. They are to be employed for uprooting, destruction, deceit, binding, poisoning, burning, and strikes with weapons for the sake of success. || 8 ||

Hasta, Ashvini, and Pushya are the three **Light** <term>Laghu: swift or small</term> constellations. They bring success in trade, sensual enjoyment, the pursuit of knowledge, ornamentation, the arts, craftsmanship, medicine, and travel...

...are established. ## 9 ## The **Soft** <term>Mridu: A category of Nakshatras known for their gentle and creative qualities</term> group consists of **Anuradha, Chitra, Revati,** and **Mrigashira**. These are beneficial for the rites of love, choosing garments, ornaments, auspicious ceremonies, music, and matters concerning friends. ## 10 ## **Vishakha** and **Krittika** are considered **Soft-Sharp** <term>Mridu-Tikshna: A mixed category</term>; their results are of a mixed nature. In the five Nakshatras of **Shravana, Dhanishta, Shatabhisha, Punarvasu,** and **Swati**, "movable" or "transitory" actions <note>activities requiring movement or change</note> are beneficial. ## 11 ##

**Hasta, Chitra, Swati, Mrigashira, Shravana, Dhanishta, Shatabhisha, Revati, Ashwini, Jyeshtha, Pushya,** and **Punarvasu**—when these Nakshatras are aligned with a person's auspicious star and a favorable Moon, the act of **shaving** <term>Kshaur-karma: Ritual or routine cutting of hair and nails</term> is beneficial at their rising or in an auspicious moment. ## 12 ##

One should not undergo shaving immediately after bathing, when eager to depart on a journey, when already adorned, after an oil massage, or after eating. It is also forbidden during battle, without a proper seat, during twilight or at night. Shaving is not beneficial on Tuesdays, Saturdays, or Sundays; nor on "Empty" <term>Rikta: The 4th, 9th, and 14th lunar days, considered hollow or unlucky for new beginnings</term> dates, the ninth day of the lunar fortnight, or during the **Vishti** <term>Vishti: An inauspicious astrological timing or Karana</term> period. ## 13 ##

However, by the order of kings, by the consent of Brahmins, at the time of a wedding, at the end of the impurity period following a birth or death, upon the release of a prisoner, or during the initiation into a sacrifice—in all these cases, the act of shaving is considered auspicious regardless of the Nakshatra. ## 14 ##

(**Hasta, Mula, Shravana, Punarvasu, Mrigashira,** and **Pushya**—these Nakshatras are designated as "masculine." It is auspicious to perform works associated with masculine endeavors during these times.) ## 15 ##

In the Nakshatras of **Hasta, Revati, Swati, Anuradha, Pushya, Chitra,** and **Mrigashira**, and on Monday, Wednesday, <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing with further auspicious days for sacraments</note> for the purposes of sacraments, initiations, vows, and the tying of the sacred thread...

# Chapter 99: The Qualities of Lunar Days and Half-Days (405)

...should be performed. The <term>Tithis</term><note>Lunar days in the Hindu calendar</note> are of three types: Nanda, Bhadra, Vijaya, Rikta, and Purna. ॥ 2 ॥ Whatever work is prescribed for a particular <term>Nakshatra</term><note>Star constellation or lunar mansion</note>, that same work should be performed on the Tithis presided over by the same deity. <margin>The qualities of the Karana are primary</margin> Even in the <term>Karanas</term><note>A Karana is half of a Tithi or lunar day</note> and <term>Muhurtas</term><note>A unit of time lasting approximately 48 minutes</note>, success is achieved if the activity aligns with the nature of the presiding deity. ॥ 3 ॥

The lords of the Karanas known as Bava, Balava, Kaulava, Taitila, Gara, Vanija, and Vishti are, in order: Indra, Brahma, Mitra, Aryaman, Bhumi (the Earth), Shri (Lakshmi), and Yama. ॥ 4 ॥ Starting from the second half of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the four "fixed" Karanas occur: Shakuni, Chatushpada, Naga, and Kinstughna. Their respective lords are Kali, Vrishabha (the Bull), the Serpent, and Pavana (the Wind). ॥ 5 ॥

In the **Bava** Karana, one should perform auspicious, mobile, stable, and nourishing acts. In the **Balava** Karana, religious ceremonies and acts beneficial to <term>Brahmins</term><note>The priestly or scholarly class</note> should be done. In **Kaulava**, acts of friendship, alliance, and choosing a partner are favored. In **Taitila**, one should seek good fortune, protection, and the founding of homes. ॥ 6 ॥

In **Gara**, activities related to agriculture, seeds, and building a house or shelter are appropriate. In **Vanija**, trade-related unions and stable works should be undertaken. The **Vishti** Karana does not grant auspicious results for general work, but it is effective for striking down enemies or administering poisons. ॥ 7 ॥

In **Shakuni**, one should perform nourishing acts, prepare medicines from roots, and practice <term>Mantras</term><note>Sacred chants or invocations</note>. In **Chatushpada**, work related to cattle, Brahmins, ancestors, and the kingdom should be done. In **Naga**, perform permanent or harsh deeds, or acts involving abduction and causing misfortune. Finally, in **Kinstughna**, auspicious acts, the offering of desired flowers, and ceremonies for success and well-being are recommended. ॥ 8 ॥

# Chapter One Hundred
## The Astrological Timing for Marriage (Nakshatra and Lagna)

> When the Moon is in the constellations of Rohiṇī, the three Uttaras <note>Uttara Phālgunī, Uttara Āṣāḍhā, and Uttara Bhādrapadā</note>, Revatī, Mṛgaśiras, Mūla, Anurādhā, Maghā, Hasta, or Svātī, and when the Ascendant <term>Lagna|The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the time of the event</term> is Virgo, Libra, or Gemini, the marriage ceremony <note>original: "pāṇigrahaḥ" or "taking the hand"</note> should be performed. Benefic planets should be placed in positions other than the 7th, 8th, or 12th houses from the Ascendant. The Moon should be in the 11th, 2nd, or 3rd house. Malefic planets should be in the 3rd, 11th, or 6th houses; however, Venus must not be in the 6th house and Mars must not be in the 8th house. || 1 ||

> For the couple, the birth signs should not be in a 2nd-12th, 9th-5th, or 8th-6th relationship <note>These are specific unfavorable relative positions of the bride and groom's moon signs</note>. The Sun must be favorably placed in transit. The Moon should not be conjoined with Saturn, Mars, the Sun, or Venus, nor should it be hemmed between two malefic planets. One should avoid the yoga periods of Vyatipāta and Vaidhṛti, the Viṣṭi <term>Karaṇa|A division of a lunar day</term>, and the "Empty" <note>Riktā</note> lunar days. Marriage is best performed during the Sun's northern course <note>Uttarāyaṇa</note>, excluding the months of Chaitra and Pausha, on the days of benefic planets, and when the Navāṃśa <term>Navāṃśa|A one-ninth division of a zodiac sign used for fine-tuning predictions</term> is a human sign <note>Gemini, Virgo, or Libra</note>. || 2 ||

> Thus ends the hundredth chapter, titled "Determination of the Nakshatra and Lagna for Marriage," in the Vṛhat Saṃhitā of the illustrious Varāhamihira. 100

And for the sake of the ancestors <note>Pitṛs</note>, it is one's duty to perform rituals and govern the kingdom. In the Nāga <term>Karaṇa</term>, one should perform works related to immovable property, fierce deeds, seizing/capturing, and acts resulting from misfortune. However, in the Ascendant <note>Lagna</note>, it is appropriate to perform deeds that are auspicious, desired, nourishing, and which grant success in celebratory works. || 8 ||

Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter in the vernacular commentary by Paṇḍit Baladeva Prasāda Miśra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the Vṛhat Saṃhitā composed by the Great Teacher Varāhamihira. || 99 ||

---

When the constellations Rohiṇī, Uttarā Phālgunī, Uttarā Āṣāḍhā, Uttarā Bhādrapadā, Revatī, Mṛgaśiras, Mūla, Anurādhā, Maghā, Hasta, and Svātī are present, and the Ascendants of Virgo, Libra, or Gemini are rising; and if benefic planets are seated in places other than the 7th, 8th, and 12th from this Ascendant; if the Moon is in the 2nd, 3rd, or 11th place from the marriage Ascendant; if malefic planets are in the 3rd, 11th, 6th, or 8th places of this Ascendant, and Venus is not in the 6th and Mars is not in the 8th, then the marriage can take place. || 1 ||

Regarding the couple—that is, the groom and the bride—their birth signs should not be the 2nd, 9th, or 8th from each other; meaning, in the consideration of their compatibility <note>Melaka</note>, there should not be the 2-12, 9-5, or 6-8 relationship. Both should have a favorable Sun and Venus in transit. The Moon should not be joined with the Sun, Saturn, Mars, or Venus, nor should it be between two malefic planets. In a Yoga other than Vyatipāta and Vaidhṛti, in a Karaṇa other than Viṣṭi, on a lunar day other than the "Empty" <note>Riktā</note> days, on the weekday of a benefic planet, during the northern transit of the Sun, and excluding the months of Chaitra and Pausha, and if the Navāṃśa of a human sign (Gemini, Virgo, Libra) is present in a non-reproachable Ascendant, then the marriage is excellent. || 2 ||

Thus ends the hundredth chapter in the vernacular commentary by Paṇḍit Baladeva Prasāda Miśra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the Vṛhat Saṃhitā composed by the Great Teacher Varāhamihira. || 100 ||
