# Chapter One Hundred and One
## The Birth-Influence of the Lunar Mansions

-><note>This chapter details the personality traits and physical characteristics of individuals born under each of the 27 Nakshatras or lunar mansions of Vedic astrology.</note><-

One born under the **Ashwini** <note>The first Nakshatra, symbolized by a horse's head</note> stars is fond of ornaments, handsome, fortunate, clever, and wise. One born under **Bharani** is determined, truthful, free from disease, skillful, and happy. || 1 ||

Under **Krittika**, a person eats much, is devoted to the wives of others, is energetic, and famous. Under **Rohini**, one is truthful, pure, speaks kindly, is stable-minded, and beautiful. || 2 ||

Under **Mrigashira**, one is restless, clever, timid, expert, enthusiastic, wealthy, and enjoys life's pleasures. Under the **Raudra** star <note>original: "Raudra-rikshe"; another name for the constellation Ardra, associated with the god Rudra</note>, one is deceitful, proud, ungrateful, violent, and sinful. || 3 ||

A person born in **Punarvasu** is self-controlled, happy, well-behaved, of poor intellect <note>original: "durmedha"</note>, prone to illness, thirsty, and satisfied with very little. || 4 ||

Under **Pushya**, one is peaceful, fortunate, learned, wealthy, and devoted to righteousness. Under the **Bhujanga** star <note>original: "Bhaujang"; another name for Ashlesha, associated with the serpent deities</note>, one is deceitful, eats all kinds of food, is sinful, ungrateful, and crafty. || 5 ||

Under **Magha**, one has many servants and great wealth, is a seeker of pleasure, a devotee of the gods and ancestors, and very industrious. Under **Purva Phalguni**, one is sweet-spoken, generous, radiant, a traveler, and a servant of the king. || 6 ||

Under **Uttara Phalguni**, a person is fortunate, earns through knowledge, is a seeker of pleasure, and happy. Under **Hasta**, one is enthusiastic, bold...

# Now Begins the One Hundred and Second Chapter
## The Division of the Zodiacal Signs

Aries is said to consist of the Ashvini, Bharani, and the first quarter of Krittika. Taurus consists of the remaining three quarters of Krittika, Rohini, and the first half of Mrigashira. **|| 1 ||** Gemini consists of the remaining half of Mrigashira, Ardra <note>original: "Raudra," referring to the deity Rudra who rules Ardra</note>, and three quarters of Punarvasu. Cancer consists of the remaining quarter of Punarvasu, Pushya <note>original: "Tishya"</note>, and Ashlesha. **|| 2 ||** Leo consists of Magha, Purva Phalguni, and the first quarter of Uttara Phalguni. Virgo is known to consist of the remaining three quarters of Uttara Phalguni, Hasta, and the first half of Chitra. **|| 3 ||** In Libra are the latter half of Chitra, Svati, and three quarters of Vishakha. In Scorpio are the remaining quarter of Vishakha, followed by Anuradha and Jyeshtha. **|| 4 ||** Sagittarius consists of Mula, Purva Ashadha, and the first quarter of Uttara Ashadha. Capricorn consists of the remaining three quarters of Uttara Ashadha, Shravana, and the first half of Dhanishtha. **|| 5 ||** Aquarius consists of the latter half of Dhanishtha, Shatabhisha, and three quarters of Purva Bhadrapada. Pisces consists of the remaining quarter of Purva Bhadrapada, Uttara Bhadrapada, and Revati. **|| 6 ||** The groups starting with Ashvini, Magha <note>original: "Pitri," the ancestors who rule Magha</note>, and Mula—corresponding to Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius—proceed from these odd-numbered signs with a gradual increase of quarters in order. **|| 7 ||**

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Division of the Zodiacal Signs," in the Brhat Samhita of the illustrious Varahamihira. **|| 102 ||**

# Chapter 103
## On the Nuptial Chart

-><note>The following verses describe the influence of planets when positioned in specific "houses" or signs at the exact moment of a wedding (the Lagna).</note><-

If the Sun or Mars is in the first house <note>the Ascendant</note> at the time of marriage, the woman becomes a widow. If Rahu <note>the North Node of the Moon</note> is there, her children will face calamities; if Saturn, she will be poor. However, if Venus, Mercury, or Jupiter is in the first house, she will be a virtuous and faithful wife. If the Moon is present, her life span is shortened. || 1 ||

If the Sun, Saturn, Rahu, or Mars is in the second house, they surely cause constant and incomparable poverty. If Jupiter, Venus, or Mercury is there, the woman will possess wealth and her husband will live long. If the Moon is in the second house, she will be blessed with many children. || 2 ||

If the Sun or Saturn is in the fifth house, her children will be lost; but the son of the Moon <note>Mercury</note>, Jupiter, or Venus brings many children...

# The Varahi Samhita

<page-num>412</page-num>
->Header: The Varahi Samhita<-

If the Sun is in the eleventh house <note>The house of gains and income</note>, the woman will have many sons; if the Moon, she will be wealthy; if Mars or Saturn, she will be blessed with children and great riches. If Jupiter is in the eleventh, she will be long-lived; if Mercury, she will be prosperous; if Rahu <note>The North Node of the Moon</note>, she will never be a widow; and if Venus, she will possess great wealth. || 11 ||

If Jupiter is in the twelfth house <note>The house of loss or liberation</note> at the end of the chart, she will be wealthy; if the Sun, she will be poor; if the Moon, she will be a spendthrift; and if Rahu, she will be of unchaste character. If Venus is there, she will be a virtuous wife; if Mercury, she will have many sons and grandsons; and if Saturn or Mars are present, her heart will be addicted to drinking. || 12 ||

The dust that is kicked up by the hooves of cows as they are driven home by cowherds with their sticks at the end of the day is called *Godhuli* <note>literally "cow-dust"</note>. A marriage performed for beautiful women during this time brings immense wealth, children, health, and good fortune. At that specific time, one need not consider the lunar mansion, the lunar day, the half-day, the ascendant, or the planetary combinations. It is well known that the rising dust of the cows destroys the sins of men and brings happiness. || 13 ||

Thus ends the 103rd Chapter, titled "The Section on Marriage," in the *Brihat Samhita* of Sri Varahamihira.

# Chapter One Hundred and Four

->The Results of Planetary Transits<-
<note>term: Gocharaphala — the astrological study of how planets affecting an individual as they move through the zodiac relative to their birth moon sign.</note>

Ancient gems with visible holes, even if not yet threaded with a string, are capable of being adorned with new qualities once they are set in fine metal. In the same way, ancient scriptures <note>Shastras</note> whose meanings are clear, even if not systematically arranged by a "sutra" <note>a double meaning: "sutra" refers to both a thread for gems and a concise rule in literature</note>, are capable of being beautified by new virtues. || 1 || Because the results of planetary transits are so widely used in daily life, I shall describe those results using various poetic meters. May the noble scholars forgive my "boldness of speech" <note>original: "mukhachapalatvam" — literally "flickering of the mouth," a humble apology for the author's perceived audacity</note> in attempting this. || 2 || Perhaps those who have heard the words of the Sage Mandavya <note>an ancient authority on astrology</note> will not find my words pleasing; or perhaps that is not so. After all, a virtuous woman is often not as dear to men as one who is "flickering of hip" <note>original: "jaghanachapala" — a play on words referring to both a flirtatious woman and a specific poetic meter</note>. || 3 ||

The Sun is auspicious in the 6th, 3rd, and 10th houses; the Moon in the 3rd, 10th, 6th, 7th, and 1st; Jupiter in the 7th, 9th, 2nd, and 5th; Mars and Saturn in the 6th and 3rd; Mercury in the 6th, 2nd, 4th, 10th, and 8th. <note>These positions are calculated from the "Janma Rashi" or the sign the Moon occupied at the time of birth.</note>

---

Just as ancient gems with visible openings are enhanced when bound with beautiful metals even without a thread, so too are the ancient scriptures—though not bound by a single thread of rules—often capable of being beautified by new qualities. For this reason, since the transit results of the planets are so frequently utilized, I am illuminating all those transit results through various types of "Vritta" (poetic meters). Therefore, let the noble scholars forgive the primary audacity of my "boldness of speech." (I will present many types of meters in this book, though they may not always follow a strict formula). || 1 || 2 || Those who have heard the sayings of the Sage Mandavya may not find my words appealing; however, it is not proper to say even that. For just as a "Jaghanachapala" (a woman with restless hips) is dear to men, a virtuous woman is sometimes not as beloved. <note>The author is using a double entendre: "Jaghanachapala" is both a type of woman and the name of the specific poetic meter he is using here.</note> || 3 || (One should consider the transit from the birth sign, i.e., the sign where the Moon was at birth). If the Sun is in the 6th, 3rd, or 10th house from the birth sign; if the Moon is in the 3rd, 10th, 6th, 1st, or 7th; if Jupiter is in the 7th, 9th, 2nd, or 5th; if Saturn and Mars are in the 3rd or 6th; if Mercury is in the 2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th, or 10th; and indeed, if any planet is in the 11th house, they provide auspicious results and <meta>catchword: Venus</meta>

---

<note>Footnote provided at the bottom of the page</note>
1. In this chapter, any word placed within brackets (' ') should be understood as the name of a poetic meter. That is, the verse has been composed in that specific meter. Only when the arrangement of short and long syllables <note>term: Laghu-Guru-Vinyasa — the rhythmic structure of Sanskrit prosody</note> is present will it be that meter. The rhythm and the arrangement of syllables for all the named meters in this chapter will be described in the appendix of this chapter.

# Chapter 104 | With Commentary

<page-num>421</page-num>
->**The Effects of Saturn and Ritual Propitiation**<-

If Saturn is in the seventh or eighth house, the person is deprived of wife and children and acts in a miserable or lowly manner. Similarly, if in the ninth house <note>the house of Dharma or fortune</note>, it causes enmity, heart disease, and imprisonment; it destroys all religious merit, including the performance of the *Vaishvadeva* <note>original: "वैश्वदेवी" - a specific Vedic ritual involving offerings to all deities</note> and other pious acts. ॥ 44 ॥

If Saturn reaches the tenth house, one finds employment but suffers loss of wealth and a decline in learning and reputation. In the eleventh house, there is great sharpness <note>or intensity</note> and gains from the wealth or wives of others. In the final <note>twelfth</note> house, one encounters a "garland of waves" of sorrow. ॥ 45 ॥

Even a planet capable of doing good provides results only in accordance with the proper time and the worthiness of the recipient. A canopy of clouds does not pour abundant rain during the spring season or into a small *Kuduva* <note>original: "कुडुवे" - a small wooden measuring cup holding about a handful</note> measure. ॥ 46 ॥

One should worship the Sun and Mars with devotion using red flowers, scents, copper, gold, a bull, and *Mulsari* flowers. Worship the Moon with the gift of a cow, white flowers, silver, and sweet substances. Worship Venus with white flowers and intoxicating or nourishing substances. Saturn should be worshipped with black objects; Mercury with gems, silver, and *Tilaka* flowers; and Jupiter with yellow substances. When the planets are pleased by such worship, even if a person falls from a great height or enters a *Bhujanga-vijumbhita* <note>original: "भुजङ्गविजृंभितम्" - literally 'the yawn of a serpent,' meaning a deadly trap or a specific dangerous omen</note>, they will suffer no pain. ॥ 47 ॥

One should pacify a fierce and inauspicious planetary gaze through the worship of gods and priests... <note>The text concludes by suggesting that peace, chanting, charity, self-restraint, virtue, and the company of the righteous can mitigate all ill effects of planetary transits.</note>

# Varahi Samhita
### Page 412

...defects can be destroyed through peaceful prayers, chanting, self-restraint, charity, and the company and conversation of virtuous people. ॥ 48 ॥

The Sun and Mars give their effects in the first half of a zodiac sign, while the Moon and Saturn give theirs in the latter half. This follows the characteristics of the <term>Arya</term> <note>A specific Sanskrit poetic meter</note> meter's variations known as <term>Giti</term> and <term>Upagiti</term>, where the first and second halves of the verse are compared to the timing of planetary results. ॥ 49 ॥

Just as the syllable count in the <term>Upagiti</term> variation of the <term>Arya</term> meter remains balanced and equal in both the first and second halves, Mercury provides its results equally throughout both the first and second halves of its stay in a zodiac sign. ॥ 50 ॥

In the <term>Arya</term> meter, if a <term>middle-heavy foot</term> <note>A metrical unit where the middle syllable is long/stressed</note> falls in an <term>odd-numbered position</term>, it destroys the beauty of the verse. Similarly, if such a foot appears in the sixth position, it forces a <term>total lightness</term> <note>A sequence of four short syllables</note>. In the same way, Jupiter (the "Guru") causes destruction even among "Aryas" (noble people) when positioned in an odd-numbered zodiac sign. Furthermore, if Jupiter occupies or aspects the sixth house from the birth sign, it causes a person to suffer <term>total lightness</term> <note>A loss of dignity or becoming insignificant in the eyes of others</note>. ॥ 51 ॥

Just as the <term>Narkutaka</term> song remains consistent in its rhythm, a planet that is naturally inauspicious but aspected by a strong auspicious planet, or a strong auspicious planet aspected by an inauspicious one, will result in a neutral or balanced effect. Both the good and bad influences reach a state of equality, much like the structure of the <term>Giti</term> and <term>Narkutaka</term> poetic forms. ॥ 52 ॥

If a planet is in its sign of debilitation, in an enemy's sign, or is combust (hidden by the Sun's light), any aspect from an enemy planet is entirely useless. It is like a beautiful woman casting a playful, flirtatious glance at a blind man—the effort is entirely wasted. ॥ 53 ॥

# Chapter 104 with Language Commentary
->Page 423<-

The son of the Sun <note>Saturn</note> follows the results of the Sun, and the son of the Moon <note>Mercury</note> follows the Moon according to their disposition. This is just as in the *Skandhaka* meter follows the *Aryagiti* style, or as the *Magadhi* follows the *Vaitaliya* in a *Gatha* <note>a type of Prakrit verse</note>. **54**

The Saturnian influence, arising from the color of the Sun's rays, becomes transformed and increases greatly. It acts like bile <note>Pitta, one of the three humors in Ayurvedic medicine</note> toward men, affecting those who follow a healthy path, but it does not affect the *Aryas* <note>noble or virtuous people</note> in the same way. **55**

Just as the expression of the *vaktra* <note>face</note> changes according to the state of the mind, the Moon also takes on the nature of whichever planet it is joined with. **56**

In a *Shloka* <note>the standard poetic verse</note>, the fifth syllable of every quarter and the seventh syllable of the second and fourth quarters attain "lightness" <note>Laghu, a short vowel</note>; in the same way, if the planets are in "bad positions" <note>inauspicious astrological houses</note>, a man suffers a loss of dignity. **57**

Even one who is naturally "light" <note>of low status</note>, when placed at the end of a meter, attains "heaviness" <note>Guru, a long or stressed syllable</note>; similarly, when the planets are "well-placed" <note>in auspicious houses</note>, a man attains greatness in the world. **58**

Whatever work is started by the ignorant for their own advancement while the planets are ill-disposed, that very work destroys them, just like a poorly performed *Vaitaliya* <note>a double meaning: a specific poetic meter or a ritual involving a 'Baital' or vampire-ghost</note>. **59**

A King who observes the auspicious positioning of the planets and begins his expedition at that time, even with small manly effort, reaches the far shore of his goals, just as one masters the *Aupachhandasika* meter. **60**

# Chapter One Hundred and Five
## The Vow of the Constellation Man
->(Regarding the Sacrifice for Beauty)<-

The feet are the constellation *Mula*, the shanks are *Rohini* and *Ashwini*. The thighs are the two *Ashadhas* <note>Purva-ashadha and Uttara-ashadha</note>, and the private parts are the pair of *Phalgunis*. || 1 ||
The waist is *Krittika*, and the two sides are the twin *Bhadrapadas*. *Revati* is known to be located in the belly, and *Anuradha* is the chest. || 2 ||
Know *Dhanishtha* to be the back, *Vishakha* the two arms, and *Hasta* is remembered as the hands. The fingers are *Punarvasu*, and the nails are named *Ashlesha*. || 3 ||
The neck is *Jyeshtha*, the two ears are *Shravana*, *Pushya* is the mouth, and the teeth are *Swati*. The laughter is *Shatabhisha*, the nose is *Magha*, and the eyes are *Mrigashira*. || 4 ||
*Chitra* is located on the forehead, *Bharani* is the head, and the hair of the head is *Ardra*. This "Constellation Man" should be fashioned by those desiring beauty. || 5 ||
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Chaitra <note>March-April</note>, when the moon is in *Mula*—

# Chapter 105: The Ritual of the Star-Man

->**Translation with Commentary**<-

When the Moon is in conjunction with the asterism of *Mula* <note>original: "Mula-nakshatra"; the root star</note>, one should observe a fast after worshiping Lord Vishnu and the presiding deity of that constellation. || 6 || Upon the completion of this religious vow <term>Vrata: a dedicated period of fasting and prayer</term>, one should donate a vessel filled with clarified butter <term>Ghee</term> along with gold to a Brahmin who is learned in the science of time <note>an astrologer or astronomer</note>. Depending on one's financial capacity, one should also gift him jewels and clothing. || 7 ||

A man who desires beauty and grace <note>original: "Lavanya"</note> should worship the Brahmins by offering them grains prepared with abundant milk and ghee, along with jaggery. He should likewise gift them silver and garments. Starting from the constellation representing the feet of the Star-Man <note>the Nakshatra-Purusha, where different stars represent different body parts of the deity</note>, he should fast sequentially month by month. Even during the auspicious sightings of the stars, he should perform the worship of Keshava <note>a name for Vishnu meaning "The Long-Haired One"</note> and the specific constellation according to the prescribed rites. || 8 ||

By performing this worship, a man becomes endowed with long arms, a broad and muscular chest, a face like the moon, and beautiful white teeth. With a gait like that of a majestic elephant and eyes as wide as lotus petals, he becomes as handsome as the God of Love <note>original: "Smara" or Kamadeva</note>, capable of stealing the hearts of women. || 9 ||

If a woman performs this vow, she gains a face radiant like the light of the spotless full moon of autumn, with eyes like lotus petals, beautiful teeth, and elegant ears. Her hair becomes as black as the belly of a bumblebee. || 10 || Her voice becomes as sweet as the male cuckoo, her lips take on the reddish hue of copper, and her hands and feet become as soft as lotus leaves. Her waist bends slightly under the weight of her breasts, and she possesses a deep, clockwise-turning navel. || 11 || With thighs like the trunk of a banana tree, beautiful hips, and lovely dimples, she becomes fortunate and possesses well-joined fingers and toes. Such is the woman or man who observes this. || 12 || As long as the garland of stars <note>original: "Nakshatra-mala"</note> wanders through the sky, beautifying this world...

As long as the stars remain, he wanders through the sky with them for the remainder of the Day of Brahma <note>A 'Day of Brahma' or Kalpa is a vast cosmic cycle lasting 4.32 billion years</note>. Furthermore, being born again in this world, he becomes a king or a wealthy Brahmin. || 13 ||

In the months beginning with Mrigashirsha <note>The lunar month occurring around November-December</note>, the names of the Lord are: Keshava, Narayana, Madhava, Govinda, Vishnu, Madhusudana, Trivikrama, Vamana, || 14 || Shridhara, Hrishikesha, Padmanabha, and Damodara. A man who fasts according to the rules on the twelfth day of the lunar fortnight <term>Dvadashi|The 12th day of the waxing or waning moon, sacred to Vishnu</term> and recites these names while worshipping Keshava, attains that supreme state where there is no fear of rebirth. || 16 ||

# Chapter 106: Conclusion and Summary

->**The Epilogue**<-

Having looked into the nectar of the <term>shastras</term> <note>sacred scientific treatises</note>, O virtuous people, you should strive to study this work according to your desire. || 2 || Furthermore, a virtuous person, upon seeing even a small merit within an ocean of faults, makes it widely known; however, the base person acts in the opposite manner. This is the inherent nature of the good and the bad. || 3 || The gold of poetry attains its highest purity only after being heated in the fire of the wicked; therefore, one should take great effort to let this work be heard by malicious people <note>The author suggests that harsh criticism serves to prove the quality of the work, much like fire refines gold</note>. || 4 ||

Whatever part of this circulating book might be lost or corrupted through the errors of transcribers, it should be restored by learning from the mouths of the learned. Or, if I have committed any small error or oversight here, O wise ones, please set aside any resentment and show affection for this work. || 5 || With a mind graced by bowing at the feet of the Sun God, the Sages, and my Teacher, I have compiled this science. Salutations to the ancient authors! || 6 ||

->**Thus ends the Epilogue.**<-

# Appendix to Chapter 104.
## The Science of Prosody.

The proper arrangement of short and long syllables <term>Laghu-Guru-Vinyasa: the system of marking light and heavy beats in poetry</term> is called <term>Chhanda</term> <note>Meter or Prosody</note>. Meters are of two types: <term>Gadya</term> <note>Prose</note> and <term>Padya</term> <note>Verse</note>. That which has four quarters <note>lines</note> is Verse, and anything different from this is Prose. There are two types of Verse called <term>Vritta</term> and <term>Jati</term>. That in which the number of syllables is fixed is *Vritta*, and that which is formed by the count of matras <note>morae or beats</note> is *Jati*. *Vritta* is of three types: even, uneven, and half-even. That which has an equal number of syllables in all four quarters is *Samavritta* <note>even meter</note>; that in which the first and third quarters, and the second and fourth quarters are equal, is *Ardhasamavritta* <note>half-even meter</note>; and that in which all four quarters are different is called *Vishama-vritta* <note>uneven meter</note>.

<summary>This page contains the author's colophon, dating the work to 1895 CE and identifying Baldev Prasad as the commentator under the patronage of Gangavishnu, followed by an introductory definition of Sanskrit and Hindi poetic meters.</summary>
<keywords>Baldev Prasad, Moradabad, Vikrama Samvat 1952, Prosody, Chhanda, Poetic Meter, Gangavishnu, Syllabic Verse</keywords>

--- Page 456 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of Sanskrit prosody (the study of poetic meters) within the Varahi Samhita, specifically defining the building blocks of verse structure.</meta>

<page-num>432</page-num>
-># The Varahi Samhita<-

**Heavy (Guru)**—The vowels A, I, U, Ri, long Lri, E, Ai, O, Au, Am, and Ah are heavy syllables; a syllable containing these vowels, or a syllable preceding a conjunct consonant <note>a cluster of two or more consonants</note>, is considered **heavy**. A syllable at the end of a verse line may also be treated as heavy by choice.

**Light (Laghu)**—Any syllable other than a heavy one is considered **light** or short.

**Pause (Yati)**—The place where the tongue rests—that is, the stopping point—is called the **pause**.

**Measure (Matra)**—A short syllable consists of one measure, a heavy syllable consists of two measures, and a protracted <note>Pluta</note> syllable consists of three measures.

**Metric Feet (Gana)**—In syllable-based meters <term>Vritta: meters defined by the number and order of syllables</term>, a foot consists of three syllables. In measure-based meters <term>Jati: meters defined by the total count of beats or measures</term>, a foot consists of four measures. For example: three heavy syllables form a **Ma-gana** and three light syllables form a **Na-gana**.
**Bha**—initial heavy; **Ya**—initial light; **Ja**—middle heavy; **Ra**—middle light; **Sa**—final heavy; **Ta**—final light; **Ga**—a single heavy; and **La-gana**—a single light. We shall indicate these using the heavy sign (2) and the light sign (1).

For example: **Ma**—222; **Na**—111; **Bha**—211; **Ya**—122; **Ja**—121; **Ra**—212; **Sa**—112; **Ta**—221; **Ga**—2; and **La**—1.

Among these feet, **Ma, Sa, Ja, Bha**—that is, all-heavy, final-heavy, middle-heavy, and initial-heavy—are the four types used. Including the all-light foot, these five feet are used in measure-based meters <note>Jati-vritta</note>. However, whereas previously each foot was made of three syllables, here they will consist of four measures; that is the only difference. Their signs in order are as follows:
(Since these are measure-based) (22) (112) (121) (211) (1111).

The author has written the meters in sequence; their characteristics are now described according to the verse numbers.

**2–3.** In this chapter, while first naming the meter, the author wrote the name of the **Mukhachapala** Arya meter by saying, <note>original: "mukhachapalatvam kshamantavyah"</note> "forgive the talkativeness of the mouth." Therefore, the characteristics of the **Arya** meter are described first.

**Arya**—A meter containing a total of 57 measures, or 14.25 feet, is called **Arya**. In its first half, there are 30 measures (7.5 feet), and in the second half, there are 27 measures (but still 7.5 feet). (In this calculation, the sixth foot of the second half will be a single light syllable).

In the Arya meter, the odd-numbered feet (1, 3, 5, 7) must not be a middle-heavy foot (**Ja**). The even-numbered feet may be chosen as desired; however, in the first half, the sixth foot can be either a middle-heavy (**Ja**) or an all-light (**Na-La**) foot.

There are nine variations of the Arya meter: 1. **Pathya**; 2. **Vipula**; 3. **Chapala**; 4. **Mukhachapala**; 5. **Jaghanachapala**; 6. **Giti**; 7. **Upagiti**; 8. **Udgiti**; 9. **Aryagiti**.

**Pathya**—That meter in which the foot-break or pause <note>Yati</note> occurs after the first three feet in both the first and second halves is called **Pathya**.

<summary>This page defines the fundamental rules of Sanskrit prosody, including syllable weights (Guru/Laghu), measures (Matra), and the structure of metric feet (Gana), specifically introducing the Arya meter and its variations.</summary>
<keywords>prosody, Sanskrit meter, Arya meter, Guru, Laghu, Gana, Matra, Varahamihira, poetic structure</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of Sanskrit prosody (the study of poetic meters), specifically detailing variations of the Arya meter and various classical syllabic meters.</meta>

<page-num>433</page-num>
<header>Appendix.</header>

**Vipula**—That which has feet in the middle three groups <term>gana: a metrical unit of four beats</term> and lacks a caesura <term>yati: a metrical pause</term> is called Vipula.
**Chapala**—That which has a heavy syllable in the middle of the second and fourth groups (the 'Ja' group) in both halves is called Chapala.
**Mukhachapala**—When the first half possesses the characteristics of the Chapala, it is a Mukhachapala Arya.
**Jaghanachapala**—When the second half possesses the characteristics of the Chapala, it is a Jaghanachapala Arya.
**Giti**—When the second half is equal to the first half of an Arya, it is a Giti Arya.
**Upagiti**—When the first half is equal to the second half of an Arya, it is an Upagiti.
**Udgiti**—An Arya where the first half is like the second half and the second half is like the first half—meaning there are 27 beats in the first half and 30 beats in the second half—is an Udgiti.
**Aryagiti**—That in which the eighth group in both the first and second halves consists of four beats—totaling 32 beats per half and 64 beats in full—is an Aryagiti.
4 **Shardulavikridita**;—M, S, J, S, T, T, G <note>These letters represent specific sequences of light and heavy syllables</note>—pauses at 12 and 7. 2 2 2, 1 1 2, 1 2 1, 1 1 2, 2 2 1, 2 2 1, 2.
5 **Sragdhara**;—M, R, Bh, N, Y, Y, Y—pauses at 7, 7, 7.
6 **Suvadana**; Bh, R, Bh, N, Y, Bh, L, G—pauses at 7, 7, 6.
7 **Suvritta** or **Meghavisphurjita**;—Y, M, N, S, R, R, G—pauses at 6, 6, 7.
8 **Shikharini**;—Y, M, N, S, Bh, L, G—pauses at 6, 11.
9 **Mandakranta**;—M, Bh, N, T, T, G, G—pauses at 4, 6, 7.
10 **Vrishabhacharita** or **Harini**;—N, S, M, R, S, L, G—pauses at 6, 4, 7.
11, 12 **Upendravajra**;—J, T, J, G, G.
13 **Prasabha**;—N, N, R, L, G—its other name is **Bhadrika**.
14 **Malati**;—N, J, J, R.
15 **Aparavaktra**;—In the 1st and 3rd lines—N, N, R, L, G; in the 2nd and 4th feet—N, J, J, R.
16 **Vilambitagati**;—J, S, J, S, Y, L, G—pauses at 8, 9. Its other name is **Prithvi**.
17 **Pushpitagra**;—In the 1st foot—N, N, R, J; in the 2nd and 4th feet—N, J, J, R, G.
18 **Indravamsha**;—T, T, J, R.
19 **Svagata**;—R, N, Bh, G, G.
20 **Drutapada**;—N, Bh, Bh, R. Its other name is **Drutavilambita**.

<header>Appendix.</header>

# Appendix.

58 **Vaktra**—A meter in which each quarter-verse <note>Sanskrit: pada</note> consists of eight syllables. From the first syllable onwards, there should be no **Nagana** <note>a metrical foot of three short syllables</note> or **Sagana** <note>two short syllables followed by one long</note>, and after the fourth syllable, there must be a **Yagana** <note>one short followed by two long syllables</note>; (there are no other rules for the remaining syllables). This is known as Vaktra.

59 **Vaitaliya**—This is a quantitative meter <note>matravritta; based on the duration of sounds rather than syllable count</note>. In this, the first and third quarters contain 14 beats <note>matras</note> each, and the second and fourth quarters contain 16 beats. However, the specialty here is that the beats will be a mixture of **short** <note>laghu</note> or **long** <note>guru</note> sounds, and the even-numbered beats must not be "dependent" <note>parasrita</note>; that is, the 3rd, 5th, and 7th beats should not be formed by a syllable that makes the preceding short syllable long. At the end of each quarter, the feet **Ra**, **La**, and **Gagana** must be placed.

60 **Aupachhandasika**—By adding one extra long syllable <note>guru</note> at the end of the Vaitaliya meter, the meter called Aupachhandasika is formed.

61 **Chandavrishtiprayata**—(A variety of Dandaka meter). The general rule for a Dandaka is that it contains 27 syllables; specifically, it has two **Naganas** followed by seven **Raganas** <note>long-short-long</note>. After arranging the feet in this manner, one may add as many Raganas as desired to form the Chandavrishtiprayata Dandaka; there is no fixed rule for how many syllables this may contain. (In this specific verse, each quarter contains 102 syllables. The Dandaka is a type of meter that follows the poet's will.)

62 **Varna-Dandaka**—The pattern is: Na, Na, Bha, Bha, Bha, Bha, Bha, Bha, Bha, Bha, Ga. <note>A sequence of specific metrical feet ending in a long syllable</note>

63 **Samudra-Dandaka**—The pattern is: Na, Na, Ra, Ja, Ra, Ja, Ra, Ja, Ra, Ja, Ra, La, Ga.

Now, the subject of **Chhandovichiti**, or the Permutation of Meters <note>Prastara</note>, will be briefly discussed.

Permutation <note>Prastara</note>, finding a lost form <note>Nashta</note>, identifying a given form <note>Uddishta</note>, the calculation of combinations of short and long syllables <note>Ekadvayadi-lagakriya</note>, the total count <note>Sankhya</note>, and the space occupied by the permutations <note>Adhvayoga</note>—these six are the foundations of prosody.

1. **Prastara (Permutation)**—The process of expanding a meter by arranging short and long syllables in a specific order is called Prastara. This means explaining how many syllables are in each quarter, and through this knowledge, determining how many different variations of a meter can exist based on the placement of short and long syllables.

The rule for this is: first, place as many long syllable marks <note>guru</note> as there are syllables in the quarter, one after another. Following that, place a short mark <note>laghu</note> beneath the first long mark. Keep all the marks (long or short) that follow it exactly as they were in the line above. Then, in the next row down, place a short mark, and the subsequent marks should match the row above. If there is no syllable before the newly placed short mark (where the mark is placed), then all the short marks that were in the upper section must be replaced with long marks. After this...

<summary>This page defines various complex Sanskrit meters like Vaitaliya and Dandaka and begins explaining Prastara, the mathematical method for calculating all possible permutations of a meter.</summary>
<keywords>Sanskrit prosody, Vaktra, Vaitaliya, Dandaka, Prastara, metrical feet, Nagana, Ragana, short and long syllables, Indian mathematics</keywords>

--- Page 460 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of Sanskrit prosody (the study of poetic meters), specifically focusing on the mathematical permutations of syllables.</meta>

<page-num>436</page-num>
<header>The Varahi Samhita</header>

First, place a short mark <note>original: "laghu," representing a short syllable</note> below the first long mark <note>original: "guru," representing a long syllable</note>, and then apply the subsequent marks in the same manner. Continue placing short marks in this fashion until all possible short marks have been positioned. The total number of variations produced will represent the total number of possible metrical forms. For example:

**The Three-Syllable Foot Meter.** Three long marks: 222. Place one short mark below the first long mark and fill the rest of the foot according to the proper method: 122. Then, place a short mark below the first long mark of that set (the second position) and keep the subsequent marks the same as the previous row. Since the first position is now empty, place a long mark there: 212. Continue this process until all marks become short. For example:

->1. M — 222 — Ma-gana <note>A metrical unit of three long syllables</note><-
->2. Y — 122 — Ya-gana<-
->3. R — 212 — Ra-gana<-
->4. S — 112 — Sa-gana<-
->5. T — 221 — Ta-gana<-
->6. J — 121 — Ja-gana<-
->7. Bh — 211 — Bha-gana<-
->8. N — 111 — Na-gana<-

If one tries to determine the variations of a meter by manually carving out these expansions <term>Prastara: the systematic enumeration of all possible permutations of a meter</term>, there is a high probability of error. A simpler method is as follows: write the number 1 above the first syllable of the foot, and then double the number for each subsequent syllable (1, 2, 4...). By doubling the final number, you will find the total number of possible variations. For example: for three syllables, the numbers are 1, 2, 4. The last number is four; doubling it gives eight. Therefore, there are eight variations in a three-syllable meter. However, if one wishes to know exactly how many variations contain a specific number of long or short syllables, one should use the rule from Bhaskaracharya’s *Lilavati* <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematical treatise</note>:

> "Place the numbers starting from one in increasing order, and divide them by the same numbers placed in reverse order." <note>original Latin/Sanskrit context: "Ekadyekottara anka vyasta bhajyah kramasthitaih"</note>

One can find the answer by calculating according to this rule. Due to the fear of excessive length, I have not described the entire process here. This knowledge can also be gained through the *Meru* <note>The "Mount Meru" diagram, known in the West as Pascal's Triangle</note>, *Khandameru*, or *Pataka* diagrams, but as those are also very extensive, they have not been included.

**2. Nashta <note>The "Lost" calculation</note>:** If someone asks what the specific arrangement of long and short syllables is for a particular variation number in a meter of a certain length, the method used to find that answer is called *Nashta*.

The rule is as follows: If the given number is even (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, etc.), first place a short mark. Then, halve that number. If the resulting number is also even, place another short mark. If the halved numbers continue to be even, the marks remain short. If...

<summary>This page explains the mathematical methods for calculating metrical permutations (Prastara) and identifying specific patterns (Nashta) in Sanskrit poetry, referencing Bhaskaracharya's mathematical rules.</summary>
<keywords>prosody, Sanskrit meter, Bhaskaracharya, Lilavati, Prastara, Nashta, syllables, mathematical permutations, Meru diagram</keywords>

--- Page 461 ---
<page-num>( 437 )</page-num>
<header>Appendix</header>

## Appendix

If the numbers are odd, such as 1, 3, 5, 7, etc., then place the <term>Guru</term> <note>a "heavy" or long syllable, usually marked with a horizontal line</note> symbol. Then, add 1 to that odd number and halve it; if that result is also odd, place a Guru, and if it is even, place a <term>Laghu</term> <note>a "light" or short syllable, usually marked with a vertical line</note> symbol. Continue this process until the required number of syllables for the poetic meter's line is complete.

For example: What is the form of the 4th sequence in a three-syllable meter? Here, 4 is an even number, therefore it is a Laghu; half of four is 2, which is also even, so another Laghu is placed. Half of two is 1, which is odd. Thus, the last one is a Guru. In this way, the sequence becomes | | ऽ <note>Laghu, Laghu, Guru</note>. This is the fourth variation of the three-syllable meter. And if someone asks what the seventh variation is? Since 7 is odd, the first is a Guru; adding 1 to it makes 8, half of which is 4 (even), so the next is a Laghu; half of that is 2 (even), so the next is another Laghu. This becomes the seventh variation— ऽ | | <note>Guru, Laghu, Laghu</note>.

**Uddishta** <note>The method for finding the position number of a specific rhythmic pattern</note>—If someone asks what the sequence number is for a specific arrangement of light and heavy syllables in a meter of a certain length, the method by which that number is known is called *Uddishta*. The rule for this is: place doubling numbers (1, 2, 4, 8...) progressively above each syllable in that meter's line. After that, add together all the numbers that sit above the <term>Laghu</term> (light) symbols. Then, add 1 to that total sum. The resulting number indicates the position of that specific pattern in the sequence of variations for that meter.

For example: What is the sequence number for the three-syllable meter pattern | | ऽ <note>Laghu, Laghu, Guru</note>? Starting from the first syllable, place the doubling numbers 1, 2, 4, etc. Then, adding the numbers above the first two Laghus (1 + 2) equals 3. Adding 1 to this sum makes 4. Therefore, it is known that this is the 4th variation of the three-syllable meter; and so on.

If one wishes to understand the wonderful details of prosody <note>the study of poetic meters</note> such as the combinations of light and heavy syllables, calculations, spatial representations, mora-based variations, the "Mora-Meru" <note>a mathematical pyramid similar to Pascal's triangle used for combinations</note>, the Meru, the Khandameru, and the Pataka (banner) diagrams, one would have to translate the entire science of prosody. Such a translation is extremely necessary for those who recite the Vedas, but it is not of great necessity for the general public. Realizing this, and for fear of making this work too long, I have not considered it appropriate to write more on the subject here.
